questions.front: To act as pilot in command under IFR, what instrument experience must you have logged within the preceding 6 calendar months?
questions.back: Six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.
options: Six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses using navigation systems
Six hours of instrument flight time, including at least three instrument approaches
Three instrument approaches and three hours of simulated instrument time with a safety pilot
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 61.57(c) — the '66 HIT' rule: within 6 calendar months, 6 approaches, Holding, Intercepting and Tracking. There is no hourly requirement.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.169, when is filing an alternate airport NOT required (the '1-2-3 rule')?
questions.back: When the destination has an instrument approach and, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, the forecast ceiling is at least 2,000 ft and visibility is at least 3 SM.
questions.explanation: Remember 1-2-3: ±1 hour of ETA, 2,000-foot ceiling, 3 statute miles visibility. Fail any one and you must file an alternate.

questions.front: Besides an FAA examiner, who else is authorized to administer an instrument proficiency check (IPC) under 14 CFR 61.57(d)?
questions.back: An authorized flight instructor (a CFII) who is qualified in the category, and if required, class and type, of aircraft used — a DPE/examiner is not required for a routine IPC.
questions.explanation: 61.57(d) lists several people who may give an IPC, including examiners and military/company check pilots, but in everyday GA practice the CFII option means a pilot never has to schedule a checkride just to regain instrument currency.

questions.front: An instrument-rated pilot needs an IPC to regain currency. In which of the following may the check legally be conducted?
questions.back: An aircraft, full flight simulator, or a flight training device representative of the aircraft category used.
options: Only in the exact make and model of aircraft the pilot intends to fly IFR
An aircraft, full flight simulator, or representative flight training device
Any basic aviation training device (BATD), the same as recent-experience currency
questions.explanation: 61.57(d) does not require the exact make/model — a full flight simulator or a representative FTD qualifies, though a basic ATD alone (which can satisfy some 61.57(c) currency tasks) is not the same as a complete IPC.

questions.front: A pilot has logged no instrument approaches, holding, or course intercepts/tracking for the past 14 calendar months. What must this pilot do before acting as PIC under IFR?
questions.back: Complete an instrument proficiency check (IPC) with an authorized instructor.
options: Fly six instrument approaches, hold, and intercept/track a course with a safety pilot within the next 30 days
Complete an instrument proficiency check (IPC) with an authorized instructor before acting as PIC under IFR again
Nothing extra — instrument currency automatically renews after logging any dual cross-country flight
questions.explanation: Once the lapse exceeds 6 months of currency plus the following 6-month grace period (more than 12 months total since last current), self-logging approaches with a safety pilot is no longer an option — 61.57(d) requires an IPC.

questions.front: Which statement about who may conduct an instrument proficiency check is correct?
questions.back: Any authorized instructor with the appropriate instrument rating may give an IPC; an FAA examiner is not required.
options: Only a Designated Pilot Examiner (DPE) may give an IPC
Any authorized instructor with the appropriate instrument rating may give an IPC; an FAA examiner is not required
An IPC may only be given by an FAA Aviation Safety Inspector during a ramp check
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes confuse the IPC with the original instrument rating checkride, which does require an examiner — the IPC is instructor-administered training/checking under 61.57(d).

questions.front: What determines which specific instrument tasks and areas of operation are included in a given pilot's IPC?
questions.back: The administering instructor selects the specific tasks from the Instrument Rating ACS based on that pilot's experience and weak areas — 61.57(d) does not mandate one fixed checklist for every pilot.
questions.explanation: Because pilots arrive at an IPC with very different gaps, the regulation gives the instructor discretion to tailor which ACS tasks to test rather than requiring every maneuver every time.

questions.front: An instrument-rated pilot's 6-month currency lapsed 4 months ago, and no instrument flying has been logged since. What is the minimum required to legally act as PIC under IFR again?
questions.back: Six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking a course, logged with a safety pilot if required for the conditions flown.
options: An instrument proficiency check with an authorized instructor
Six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and course intercepting/tracking, logged with a safety pilot if required
A new instrument rating practical test with an examiner
questions.explanation: Because the total lapse (4 months past the 6-month currency window) is still inside the additional 6-month grace period, the pilot may self-regain currency by performing the tasks — an IPC only becomes mandatory once the lapse exceeds that grace period.

questions.front: For logbook purposes, what qualifies as 'actual instrument conditions' when logging instrument flight time?
questions.back: Operating the aircraft solely by reference to instruments because outside visual references are unusable — such as flight in clouds — regardless of whether another pilot is aboard.
questions.explanation: Actual instrument time is defined by the real weather encountered, which is exactly why, unlike hood time, it never requires a safety pilot.

questions.front: What must be used to log 'simulated instrument' flight time while flying in visual conditions?
questions.back: A view-limiting device (a hood or foggles) that blocks the flying pilot's outside visual references, combined with a qualified safety pilot aboard as required by 91.109(c).
questions.explanation: Simulated instrument time exists only because a hood artificially removes outside visual cues in otherwise-VMC — that's precisely why a safety pilot must watch for traffic in that situation.

questions.front: A safety pilot occupies the other control seat while another pilot practices instrument flight under the hood in VMC. At minimum, what must the safety pilot hold?
questions.back: A private pilot certificate (or higher) with the category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown.
options: A private pilot certificate (or higher) with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft
An instrument rating in addition to a private pilot certificate
A current flight review only — no specific certificate level is required
questions.explanation: 91.109(c) requires only private-pilot-level certification with the right category/class — an instrument rating is not required, which surprises pilots who assume the safety pilot must be able to 'supervise' instrument technique.

questions.front: Under 91.109, what must be true of the aircraft used when one pilot practices simulated instrument flight under a hood with a safety pilot aboard?
questions.back: The aircraft (except lighter-than-air) must be equipped with fully functioning dual flight controls.
options: The aircraft must have fully functioning dual flight controls
The aircraft must be equipped with a functioning autopilot as a backup
The aircraft must be a complex or technically advanced airplane
questions.explanation: The safety pilot has to be able to physically take the controls if needed, so 91.109(c) requires functioning dual controls — an autopilot cannot substitute for a human safety pilot's see-and-avoid role.

questions.front: What must be recorded in a pilot's logbook, per 61.51(g), for each instrument approach flown toward recency requirements?
questions.back: The location and type of each instrument approach accomplished, and the name of the safety pilot, if one was required for that flight.
questions.explanation: This logbook-entry requirement is a mechanical recordkeeping rule separate from the currency numbers themselves — an examiner or instructor can only verify recency from a logbook if this detail is actually recorded.

questions.front: A single instrument-rated pilot, alone in the aircraft, is flying in solid cloud on an IFR flight plan. Must another pilot act as safety pilot for this flight?
questions.back: No — the safety pilot requirement of 91.109 applies only to simulated instrument flight, not actual instrument conditions.
options: Yes, actual instrument flight always requires a safety pilot, just like simulated instrument flight
No — the safety pilot requirement of 91.109 applies only to simulated instrument flight, not actual instrument conditions
Only if the flight is conducted at night
questions.explanation: A safety pilot exists to compensate for a hood restricting outside vision in otherwise-VMC; when the aircraft is genuinely in IMC, IFR separation procedures — not visual scanning — provide the protection, so no safety pilot is required.

questions.front: A CFII provides dual instrument instruction to a student while the aircraft is actually inside clouds. How may the instructor log that portion of the flight?
questions.back: As instrument flight time, since the instructor is also operating solely by reference to instruments while instructing.
options: As instrument flight time, since the instructor is also operating solely by reference to instruments while instructing
Only as flight instruction given, never as instrument time, because the instructor isn't manipulating the controls
As cross-country time only, regardless of the weather encountered
questions.explanation: 61.51(g) specifically lets an authorized instructor log instrument time when giving instrument instruction in actual instrument conditions, independent of who has hands on the controls — a narrow exception many pilots miss.

questions.front: A pilot departs in VMC under a view-limiting device with a qualified safety pilot aboard, then 20 minutes later enters actual clouds. How should the instrument time from this flight be logged?
questions.back: Log simulated time for the hooded segment and actual time for the segment flown in the clouds.
options: Log the whole flight as simulated instrument time, since it started under the hood
Log simulated time for the hooded segment and actual time for the segment flown in the clouds
Log only the time actually in the clouds; the hooded time doesn't count as instrument time at all
questions.explanation: Actual and simulated instrument time are classified by the real cause of the instruments-only condition at each moment of flight; the 91.109(c) safety-pilot requirement travels only with the hooded portion, since actual IMC never requires one.

questions.front: What additional rating does 14 CFR 61.3(e) require a pilot to hold in order to act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums?
questions.back: An instrument rating appropriate to the aircraft category, in addition to whatever category/class/type rating the pilot already holds.
questions.explanation: 61.3(e) layers the instrument-rating requirement on top of the pilot's existing category/class privileges — it's a separate gate from the pilot certificate itself.

questions.front: A private pilot without an instrument rating plans a local flight in Class G airspace at 700 feet AGL with 1/2 statute mile visibility, remaining clear of clouds, flown entirely as VFR with no IFR clearance. Is this legal under 61.3(e)?
questions.back: No — flying in weather below the applicable VFR minimums requires an instrument rating, regardless of whether an IFR clearance was used.
options: Yes, because the pilot never filed or flew under an IFR clearance
No — flying in weather below the applicable VFR minimums requires an instrument rating, regardless of whether an IFR clearance was used
Yes, because Class G airspace is exempt from the instrument rating requirement
questions.explanation: 61.3(e) is triggered by either of two independent conditions — flying under IFR, or flying in weather below VFR minimums — so a pilot can violate it while technically 'flying VFR' if the actual weather is below the minimums that apply to that airspace and altitude. At 700 feet AGL in Class G, the basic VFR minimum is 1 statute mile visibility (day); 1/2 mile is below that minimum.

questions.front: What must a pilot have in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft to act as PIC, per 61.3(a)?
questions.back: A pilot certificate (or special purpose authorization) and a government-issued photo identification.
questions.explanation: 61.3(a) requires both items together — carrying only the certificate without photo ID (or vice versa) doesn't satisfy the requirement.

questions.front: Which statement correctly describes the medical certificate requirement of 61.3(c) for a pilot acting as PIC?
questions.back: A medical certificate — or, for eligible pilots, compliance with the BasicMed conditions of 61.113(i) — is required, except for operations specifically exempted, such as glider or balloon PIC duties.
options: A medical certificate — or, for eligible pilots, compliance with the BasicMed conditions of 61.113(i) — is required, except for operations specifically exempted, such as glider or balloon PIC duties
A medical certificate is required for every PIC operation without exception
BasicMed eliminates the need for any medical documentation whatsoever
questions.explanation: 61.3(c) requires a medical certificate but carves out BasicMed as an alternate pathway and also exempts glider and balloon PIC operations entirely — treating the rule as absolute in either direction is a common error.

questions.front: Does a pilot acting solely as PIC of a glider or balloon need to hold an FAA medical certificate under 61.3(c)?
questions.back: No — 61.3(c) specifically exempts a person acting as PIC of a glider or a balloon from the medical certificate requirement.
questions.explanation: This exemption predates BasicMed and is entirely separate from it; glider and balloon PIC operations have never required a medical certificate.

questions.front: A pilot exercises BasicMed privileges instead of holding a current FAA medical certificate. Does BasicMed alone satisfy everything needed to fly IFR in IMC?
questions.back: No — BasicMed only substitutes for the medical certificate of 61.3(c); the pilot must still separately hold an instrument rating and meet 61.3(e) and currency requirements.
options: Yes, BasicMed satisfies every requirement needed to fly IFR
No — BasicMed only substitutes for the medical certificate of 61.3(c); the pilot must still separately hold an instrument rating and meet 61.3(e) and currency requirements
No, because BasicMed can never be combined with IFR flight
questions.explanation: BasicMed is strictly a substitute for the 61.3(c) medical certificate; it does nothing to the separate 61.3(e) instrument-rating requirement or 61.57(c) currency — pilots sometimes conflate 'no medical needed' with 'no rating needed.'

questions.front: How long is a third-class medical certificate valid for a pilot who had not reached their 40th birthday on the date of the exam?
questions.back: 60 calendar months (5 years) from the month of the examination.
questions.explanation: 61.23(d) ties the longer 60-month duration to third-class (private/recreational/student/sport) privileges for pilots under 40 — crossing the 40th birthday drops the same class of certificate to 24 months.

questions.front: How long is a third-class medical certificate valid for a pilot who had reached their 40th birthday on or before the date of the exam?
questions.back: 24 calendar months (2 years) from the month of the examination.
questions.explanation: Age 40 is the dividing line in 61.23(d) that cuts the third-class duration in half, from 60 months down to 24 months.

questions.front: A private pilot holds an instrument rating and a current third-class medical certificate. Does 61.23 require a higher class of medical certificate for flying IFR than for the same flight VFR?
questions.back: No — the required medical class depends on the underlying pilot certificate privileges exercised (e.g., private), not on whether the flight is IFR or VFR.
options: Yes, IFR flight always requires at least a second-class medical certificate
No — the required medical class depends on the underlying pilot certificate privileges exercised (e.g., private), not on whether the flight is IFR or VFR
Yes, instrument-rated pilots must hold a first-class medical to legally file an IFR flight plan
questions.explanation: Medical certificate class under 61.23(a) tracks the certificate privileges being exercised (student/recreational/private = third class, commercial = second class, ATP = first class), not whether the operation is IFR or VFR — holding an instrument rating adds no separate medical requirement of its own.

questions.front: How often must a pilot exercising BasicMed privileges complete a comprehensive medical examination with a state-licensed physician using the Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist (CMEC)?
questions.back: Every 48 calendar months.
options: Every 24 calendar months
Every 48 calendar months
Every 60 calendar months
questions.explanation: BasicMed has two different clocks that pilots often mix up: the physician's physical exam is required every 48 months, while the free online medical education course is required every 24 months.

questions.front: Under BasicMed, how often must a pilot complete the free online medical education course?
questions.back: Every 24 calendar months.
questions.explanation: This 24-month course interval is half as frequent as the 48-month physician's exam interval — remembering the pairing (course every 2 years, exam every 4) avoids mixing the two up.

questions.front: Which set of operating limitations correctly applies to a pilot exercising BasicMed privileges under 61.113(i)?
questions.back: Up to 12,500 lbs MTOW, 7 or fewer occupants, no more than 6 passengers, below 18,000 ft MSL, and 250 KIAS or less.
options: Up to 12,500 lbs MTOW, 7 or fewer occupants, no more than 6 passengers, below 18,000 ft MSL, and 250 KIAS or less
Up to 12,500 lbs MTOW, 9 or fewer occupant seats, unlimited passengers, and no altitude restriction
Up to 6,000 lbs MTOW, but IFR flight and flight above 10,000 ft MSL are prohibited entirely
questions.explanation: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 expanded BasicMed: up to 12,500 lbs MTOW, up to 7 occupants with no more than 6 passengers, below 18,000 ft MSL, at 250 KIAS or less - and IFR flight is allowed within those limits. Answers quoting the pre-2024 6,000-lb/6-seat limits are now wrong.

questions.front: To ever become eligible for BasicMed, a pilot must have held a valid FAA medical certificate of any class issued at some point after which date?
options: January 1, 2000
There is no such requirement — any pilot may use BasicMed regardless of medical history
questions.explanation: This 'held a medical certificate after July 14, 2006' rule is BasicMed's baseline eligibility gate, set out in 61.23(c)(3) (cross-referenced by 61.113(i)) — a pilot who never held any FAA medical certificate, or whose most recent one predates that date, cannot use BasicMed.

questions.front: What are the standard alternate airport weather minimums under 14 CFR 91.169 for a precision approach versus a nonprecision approach?
questions.back: Precision approach: 600-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility (600-2). Nonprecision approach: 800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility (800-2).
questions.explanation: Memory hook: precision gets the lower number — 600 for precision, 800 for nonprecision, both with 2 miles visibility. These standard values apply only when the alternate's approach chart does not publish its own nonstandard alternate minimums.

questions.front: An airport's only published instrument approach is an RNAV (GPS) procedure with LNAV minimums only, with no vertical guidance published. For purposes of the standard alternate weather minimums in 14 CFR 91.169, this approach is treated as:
questions.back: A nonprecision approach, requiring 800-2 ceiling and visibility
options: A precision approach, requiring 600-2 ceiling and visibility
A nonprecision approach, requiring 800-2 ceiling and visibility
Not usable for alternate planning because it lacks vertical guidance
questions.explanation: Only approaches with electronic vertical guidance to precision-like minimums (ILS, LPV, GLS) qualify as precision for the 600-2 standard; an LNAV-only GPS approach has no vertical guidance, so the higher 800-2 nonprecision standard applies.

questions.front: Where would a pilot find nonstandard (higher-than-normal) alternate minimums for a particular airport?
questions.back: Published directly on that airport's instrument approach procedure chart
options: In the Airport/Facility Directory remarks section only
They are never published; pilots must call the issuing FSDO
Published directly on that airport's instrument approach procedure chart
questions.explanation: When terrain, missing lighting, or other factors require higher-than-standard alternate minimums, the FAA publishes them right on the approach chart itself rather than leaving pilots to assume the 600-2/800-2 defaults apply.

questions.front: An airport has an ILS approach with nonstandard alternate minimums of 800-2½ published on the chart. A pilot needs to file this airport as an alternate, and the forecast shows a 700-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility at the ETA. Can this airport legally be used as the alternate?
questions.back: No — the published nonstandard minimums (800-2½) apply and must be met, not the standard 600-2 for a precision approach
options: No — the published nonstandard minimums (800-2½) apply and must be met, not the standard 600-2 for a precision approach
Yes — because 700 and 3 exceed the standard 600-2 precision approach minimums
Yes — nonstandard minimums only apply to nonprecision approaches, so the ILS reverts to 600-2
questions.explanation: A common trap is defaulting to the 'precision approach = 600-2' rule of thumb without checking the chart; published nonstandard minimums always override the standard 600-2/800-2 values, regardless of approach type.

questions.front: Podunk Municipal has no published instrument approach procedure of any kind. A pilot wants to list it as the IFR alternate. The forecast for the ETA at Podunk shows a 1,500-foot broken ceiling and 4 miles visibility, and the MEA in that area is well above the field. Is Podunk legal to file as the alternate?
questions.back: Yes — the forecast allows descent from the MEA, a VFR approach, and a landing under basic VFR
options: No — an alternate must always have a published instrument approach procedure
Yes — the forecast allows descent from the MEA, a VFR approach, and a landing under basic VFR
No — basic VFR alternates require at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility regardless of MEA
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.169(c)(1) allows an airport with no instrument approach to be used as an alternate only if forecast weather permits descending from the MEA/MOCA, maneuvering to the airport, and landing using basic VFR weather minimums — there's no fixed 600-2/800-2 number for this case.

questions.front: Besides the items required on a VFR flight plan under 91.153(a), what must every IFR flight plan additionally include per 14 CFR 91.169(a), unless a specific exception applies?
questions.back: An alternate airport.
questions.explanation: 91.169(a) folds in the standard VFR flight-plan data items (aircraft ID, route, fuel, souls on board, etc.) from 91.153(a) and adds one IFR-specific requirement: naming an alternate airport, unless the destination qualifies for the exception in 91.169(b).

questions.front: A pilot with a WAAS (TSO-C145/146) GPS wants to file an airport as the IFR alternate where the only approach is an RNAV (GPS) procedure with LPV, LNAV/VNAV, and LNAV minima published. Which minima must be used when flight planning the alternate?
questions.back: LNAV or circling minima only
options: LPV minima, since the aircraft is WAAS-equipped
LNAV/VNAV minima, since it provides vertical guidance without needing SBAS augmentation
LNAV or circling minima only
questions.explanation: The FAA can't guarantee in advance that WAAS vertical guidance (LPV or LNAV/VNAV) will be available at the alternate's location and time, so flight planning for the alternate must use the more conservative LNAV or circling line — even though the pilot may fly a higher service level if it's actually available on arrival.

questions.front: A pilot using a non-WAAS (TSO-C129) GPS receiver wants to rely on a GPS-based approach for the alternate airport. What restriction applies regarding using GPS approaches at both the destination and the alternate?
questions.back: A GPS-based approach may be used to qualify either the destination or the alternate airport, but not both — if GPS is used for the destination approach, the alternate must have an approach the pilot can fly without relying on GPS (or vice versa).
questions.explanation: Because a single satellite outage or RAIM/FDE hole could remove instrument approach capability at more than one airport at once if both rely on GPS, non-WAAS users must have a non-GPS-dependent backup at one of the two airports.

questions.front: A WAAS-equipped aircraft is planning a flight where the destination has an RNAV (GPS) approach with LPV minima, and the identical approach exists at the alternate. At which airport(s) may the pilot flight-plan using the LPV minima?
questions.back: The destination airport only
options: Both the destination and the alternate airport
The destination airport only
The alternate airport only, since it needs the tighter margin
questions.explanation: LPV minima may be used for flight planning at the destination, but alternates must be planned using LNAV or circling minima regardless of WAAS equipage — a frequently missed distinction between destination and alternate planning rules.

questions.front: According to 14 CFR 91.173, what two things must a pilot have before operating an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR?
questions.back: A filed IFR flight plan and a received ATC clearance
options: A filed IFR flight plan and a received ATC clearance
A filed IFR flight plan and an assigned squawk code
An ATC clearance and a briefed alternate airport
questions.explanation: 91.173 is the foundational rule requiring both elements — filing alone doesn't authorize IFR flight; the clearance must actually be received from ATC before operating IFR in controlled airspace.

questions.front: After landing at an airport without an operating control tower at the end of an IFR flight, what is the pilot's responsibility regarding the IFR flight plan?
questions.back: The pilot must cancel the IFR flight plan with ATC or FSS, since the flight plan isn't automatically closed
options: Nothing — ATC automatically closes the flight plan once radar contact is lost on the ground
The flight plan remains open until the next IFR departure, at which point it's overwritten
The pilot must cancel the IFR flight plan with ATC or FSS, since the flight plan isn't automatically closed
questions.explanation: Without a tower to relay landing confirmation, ATC has no way to know the aircraft landed safely; if the flight plan isn't canceled, search-and-rescue procedures can be triggered once the ETA passes.

questions.front: If a pilot elects to cancel an IFR flight plan while still airborne in VMC, what must be true, and what does the pilot then assume responsibility for?
questions.back: The aircraft must be operating in VFR weather conditions; once canceled, the pilot assumes responsibility for maintaining VFR, separation from other traffic, and terrain/obstruction clearance for the remainder of the flight.
questions.explanation: Canceling IFR early can allow a more direct routing, but it trades away ATC's separation services — a pilot should only do this with a clear VFR picture ahead, not just a momentary break in the clouds.

questions.front: Which of the following is a required item on an IFR flight plan?
questions.back: Fuel on board, expressed in hours and minutes
options: The pilot's total logged instrument flight time
Fuel on board, expressed in hours and minutes
The aircraft's maximum certificated service ceiling
questions.explanation: Fuel on board tells ATC and search-and-rescue how long the flight can safely remain airborne; the pilot's flight time and the airplane's absolute ceiling are never asked for on the flight plan form.

source.section: 91.153(a)(7), incorporated into IFR flight plan requirements by 91.169(a)(1)

questions.front: If a pilot's actual route or altitude needs differ from what's on a filed but not-yet-activated IFR flight plan, what should the pilot do?
questions.back: Notify ATC or the Flight Service Station of the change as soon as practical so the flight plan on file matches the pilot's actual intentions before a clearance is issued.
questions.explanation: ATC builds the initial clearance from the filed flight plan; if the pilot silently changes plans, the clearance issued may not match what the pilot is actually able or intending to fly, causing delay or a clearance the pilot has to renegotiate.

questions.front: Why is it important for the 'number of persons on board' entered on an IFR flight plan to be accurate at the time of departure?
questions.back: Search and rescue personnel rely on that number to know how many people to look for if the aircraft becomes overdue or is involved in an accident, so the pilot must update it if it changes just before departure.
questions.explanation: This field is easy to forget to update after a last-minute passenger change, but it directly affects how a search-and-rescue response is sized and conducted.

source.section: 91.153(a)(8), incorporated into IFR flight plan requirements by 91.169(a)(1)

questions.front: What do the letters in the memory aid 'CRAFT' stand for when copying an IFR clearance?
questions.back: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, and Transponder code.
questions.explanation: CRAFT captures the five elements ATC normally states in an IFR clearance, in the order they're typically given, making it easier to copy a clearance accurately on the first read.

questions.front: A clearance reads: 'Cessna 4AB, cleared to Springfield Airport via radar vectors to Victor 123, then as filed, maintain 6,000, expect one-zero-thousand ten minutes after departure, departure frequency 125.4, squawk 4521.' What is the clearance limit in this clearance?
questions.back: Springfield Airport — the destination stated in the clearance
options: Springfield Airport — the destination stated in the clearance
Victor 123 — the airway used en route to the destination
6,000 feet — the initial altitude assigned after departure
questions.explanation: The clearance limit is the fix or airport the clearance authorizes the flight to proceed to — here it's stated right after 'cleared to'; the route, altitude, and frequency are the other, separate CRAFT elements.

questions.front: In a typical IFR departure clearance, what does the 'Frequency' item, the 'F' in CRAFT, refer to?
questions.back: The frequency to contact departure control after takeoff
options: The frequency used to file the flight plan with Flight Service
The VOR frequency for the first navigation fix
The frequency to contact departure control after takeoff
questions.explanation: ATC includes the post-departure contact frequency so the pilot knows who to check in with once airborne, distinct from any navigation frequencies used en route.

questions.front: Per AIM guidance, which parts of an ATC clearance or instruction must a pilot read back?
questions.back: Altitude assignments, headings/vectors, and runway assignments
options: The entire clearance verbatim, word for word, every time
Altitude assignments, headings/vectors, and runway assignments
Only the clearance limit and route, never the altitude
questions.explanation: These 'numbers' items are the ones most likely to cause an accident if misheard, so the AIM specifically calls for their readback as a cross-check between pilot and controller — full verbatim readback of every clearance isn't required or expected.

questions.front: What must a pilot's readback of a 'hold short of Runway 27' instruction include?
questions.back: The specific hold-short point (e.g., 'hold short of Runway 27') and the aircraft's call sign, so the controller can positively verify who acknowledged the instruction.
questions.explanation: Hold-short readbacks are treated as mandatory items because a missed hold-short instruction is a runway-incursion risk; controllers are required to obtain the readback if the pilot doesn't offer it unprompted.

questions.front: Ground control transmits: 'November 123AB, cross Runway 27 at Alpha, contact Ground point niner.' What is the pilot required to do with this instruction?
questions.back: Read back the runway crossing instruction, including the call sign, before crossing
options: Simply comply without a verbal readback, since only hold-short instructions require it
Read back only the new ground frequency, since the crossing was already implied
Read back the runway crossing instruction, including the call sign, before crossing
questions.explanation: Runway crossing clearances are treated the same as hold-short instructions for readback purposes — both directly affect runway safety, so the controller needs positive verbal confirmation before the aircraft proceeds onto the runway.

questions.front: If a pilot is unable to depart before a clearance's stated void time, what must the pilot do, and by when?
questions.back: Contact ATC as soon as possible to advise intentions; if ATC isn't contacted within 30 minutes after the void time, the flight may be treated as overdue and search-and-rescue procedures can be initiated.
questions.explanation: The 30-minute outer limit exists so ATC at a non-towered field can plan around the aircraft, such as releasing other IFR traffic, without waiting indefinitely to learn whether the flight ever departed.

source.section: 5-2-7, Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times

questions.front: Which statement about a clearance void time is correct?
questions.back: The pilot must be airborne before the stated time, or the clearance is no longer valid
options: The pilot may depart any time within the hour that contains the stated void time
The pilot must be airborne before the stated time, or the clearance is no longer valid
A void time clearance can only be issued to aircraft departing from towered airports
questions.explanation: Void times are used mainly at airports without an operating control tower or direct radio contact, so ATC can protect the airspace for the departure only up to a specific, precise time — not a broader window.

source.section: 5-2-7, Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times

questions.front: A pilot receives: 'Clearance void if not off by 1450. If not off by 1450, advise Denver Center not later than 1455 of your intentions.' The pilot is unable to depart. What must the pilot do?
questions.back: Contact Denver Center by 1455 as specifically instructed, since ATC gave an explicit callback time
options: Contact Denver Center by 1455 as specifically instructed, since ATC gave an explicit callback time
Nothing is required until 1520 (30 minutes after the void time), regardless of what ATC stated
Depart anyway before 1500, since void times allow a 10-minute grace period
questions.explanation: ATC may specify a callback time shorter than the standard 30-minute maximum; when a specific time is given in the clearance, it governs — the pilot can't default to the general 30-minute rule when ATC has already stated an earlier deadline.

source.section: 5-2-7, Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times

questions.front: When ATC issues a clearance using the phrase 'cleared to Memphis as filed,' what part of the pilot's flight plan does 'as filed' refer to?
questions.back: The route of flight only
options: The route, altitude, and departure frequency all together
Only the alternate airport listed on the flight plan
The route of flight only
questions.explanation: 'Cleared as filed' is shorthand ATC uses to avoid reading back a long route, but it never covers altitude — the controller must still state the assigned altitude separately so there's no ambiguity about the initial altitude to fly.

source.section: 5-2-6, Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared...as Filed) Procedures

questions.front: When ATC uses an abbreviated 'cleared as filed' clearance, what CRAFT element must the controller still state separately, and why?
questions.back: The altitude — 'cleared as filed' covers only the route, so the controller must always separately state the assigned altitude to ensure the pilot has an unambiguous initial altitude to fly.
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes assume 'as filed' locks in everything from the flight plan, including the requested cruise altitude, but ATC's actual assigned altitude can differ from what was filed and is never implied by 'as filed.'

source.section: 5-2-6, Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared...as Filed) Procedures

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.167(a)(3), how long must an airplane be able to fly at normal cruising speed after reaching the alternate airport (or the destination, if no alternate is required) when operating in IFR conditions?
questions.back: 45 minutes
options: 30 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
questions.explanation: 91.167(a)(3) requires a 45-minute fuel reserve at normal cruising speed for airplanes; helicopters get a lighter 30-minute reserve under the same rule, which is a common mix-up for pilots who fly both categories.

questions.front: An instrument-rated pilot plans an IFR flight in an airplane for which no alternate airport is required. Under 14 CFR 91.167, what fuel reserve must still be carried?
questions.back: Enough to fly to the destination, then continue for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
options: None — reserve fuel is only required when an alternate is filed
Enough to fly to the destination, then continue for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
Enough to fly to the destination, then continue for 30 minutes at normal cruising speed
questions.explanation: The 45-minute reserve in 91.167(a)(3) applies whether or not an alternate is required; qualifying for the weather-minima exception to filing an alternate does not waive the reserve fuel requirement.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.167, in what sequence must an airplane carry enough fuel to fly when operating in IFR conditions?
questions.back: (1) To the first airport of intended landing, (2) from there to the alternate airport if one is required, and (3) after that, for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
questions.explanation: This three-leg fuel chain is the foundation of IFR fuel planning; pilots must stack all three legs, not just plan fuel for the destination alone.

questions.front: Does 14 CFR 91.167(a)(3) require the same fuel reserve for helicopters as for airplanes operating in IFR conditions?
questions.back: No. Airplanes must carry a 45-minute reserve at normal cruising speed; helicopters need only a 30-minute reserve at normal cruising speed under the same rule.
questions.explanation: This category-specific split is easy to overlook because most instrument training focuses on the 45-minute number; rotorcraft pilots need the lower 30-minute figure instead.

questions.front: According to 14 CFR 91.171(a), how often must VOR equipment used for IFR flight be operationally checked, absent an approved maintenance procedure?
questions.back: Within the preceding 30 days
options: Within the preceding 30 days
Within the preceding 90 days
Within the preceding 24 calendar months
questions.explanation: 91.171 sets a 30-day VOR check interval, distinct from the 24-calendar-month pitot-static and transponder tests required under 91.411 and 91.413 — mixing these intervals up is a frequent knowledge-test trap.

questions.front: A pilot checks VOR receiver accuracy using a VOT (VOR test signal) transmitted at an airport. What is the maximum allowable bearing error under 14 CFR 91.171(b)?
questions.back: ±4 degrees
options: ±4 degrees
±6 degrees
±2 degrees
questions.explanation: The VOT and designated ground checkpoint methods both allow ±4°, while the airborne checkpoint and in-flight airway-radial methods allow the looser ±6° — confusing these two tolerance numbers is one of the most common VOR-check test errors.

questions.front: No VOT signal or FAA-designated VOR checkpoint (ground or airborne) is available where a pilot is based. Under 14 CFR 91.171(b), what alternate check may be used to satisfy the 30-day requirement?
questions.back: Select a point along an established VOR airway, verify position over that point, and confirm the VOR reads the published radial within ±6 degrees
options: Select a VOR radial along the centerline of an established VOR airway, fly directly over a prominent ground point on that radial, and confirm the VOR indicates the published radial within 6 degrees
Tune two VOR receivers to the same station and confirm they agree with each other within 4 degrees
Use the localizer frequency of a nearby ILS as a substitute VOR reference, with a tolerance of 4 degrees
questions.explanation: This in-flight airway check is the designated fallback when no VOT or designated checkpoint (ground or airborne) exists, and it shares the looser 6° tolerance with the airborne checkpoint method. The dual-receiver check (4°, the middle option) is a real, separate method available to any aircraft with two independent VOR receivers, not specifically tied to a missing VOT.

questions.front: For an aircraft with dual VOR receivers, how can the required 30-day VOR check be performed under 14 CFR 91.171(c), and what is the maximum allowable disagreement?
questions.back: Tune both receivers to the same VOR station and note the bearing (radial) each indicates to the station; the two indicated bearings may not differ from each other by more than 4 degrees.
questions.explanation: The dual-receiver check is convenient because it needs no VOT or ground checkpoint — it uses the aircraft's own second receiver as the reference, with the same tight 4° tolerance as a VOT check.

questions.front: What four items must be entered in the aircraft log or other permanent record after a required VOR operational check under 14 CFR 91.171(d)?
questions.back: The date of the check, the place where it was performed, the bearing error found, and the signature of the person who performed the check.
questions.explanation: All four items are required together — a bearing-error-only entry without a date, place, and signature does not satisfy 91.171(d), which examiners sometimes test by describing an incomplete logbook entry.

questions.front: Which instrument is specifically added for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d), beyond the day-VFR equipment already required by 91.205(b)?
questions.back: A gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator
options: A gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator
An outside air temperature gauge
A magnetic compass with a correction card
questions.explanation: 91.205(d) layers IFR-specific instruments on top of the day-VFR list; the magnetic compass is already a day-VFR item under 91.205(b), so it isn't newly 'added' for IFR, while an OAT gauge isn't on the base 91.205(d) list at all.

questions.front: The clock required for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d)(6) must display which of the following?
questions.back: Hours, minutes, and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation
options: Hours and minutes only, in analog or digital form
Hours, minutes, and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation
Elapsed time only, since the clock need not show time of day
questions.explanation: The seconds display supports timed approaches and holding patterns; a panel clock or watch showing only hours and minutes does not by itself satisfy 91.205(d)(6).

questions.front: An airplane is equipped with a third attitude instrument system usable through 360 degrees of pitch and roll, installed to meet the standard referenced in 14 CFR 91.205(d)(3)(i). What effect does this have on the IFR equipment list?
questions.back: The gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator is no longer required
options: The gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator is no longer required
The gyroscopic direction indicator (heading indicator) is no longer required
The sensitive altimeter requirement is waived
questions.explanation: 91.205(d)(3) exempts airplanes with a qualifying independent third attitude system from also carrying a separate rate-of-turn indicator — this is why some glass-cockpit airplanes with a standby attitude indicator omit the traditional turn coordinator, while rotorcraft get a similar exception with different pitch/roll limits.

questions.front: List the eight instruments and equipment items 14 CFR 91.205(d) adds specifically for IFR flight, beyond the day/night VFR list.
questions.back: (1) Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route flown, (2) gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator (with a third-attitude-system exception), (3) slip-skid indicator, (4) sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, (5) a clock with hours/minutes/seconds display, (6) generator or alternator of adequate capacity, (7) gyroscopic pitch-and-bank (attitude) indicator, and (8) gyroscopic direction indicator (heading indicator).
questions.explanation: Grouping these into a memorized list helps on the written test, since questions often isolate just one item and ask whether it's genuinely an IFR add-on or already required for day VFR.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.205(d)(5), what standard must an IFR aircraft's altimeter meet, beyond simply being installed and functioning?
questions.back: It must be a sensitive altimeter that is adjustable for barometric pressure (a Kollsman-window altimeter), not a fixed, non-adjustable altimeter.
questions.explanation: A non-adjustable altimeter can't be reset to current altimeter settings, which is essential for maintaining IFR altitude separation — that's why 91.205(d)(5) specifically calls out 'adjustable for barometric pressure.'

questions.front: An aircraft with no FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List has an inoperative DME, and the planned IFR route requires DME. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what must happen before the flight can proceed?
questions.back: The DME must be repaired, or the flight must avoid the route/procedures that require it — it cannot simply be placarded inoperative and flown as planned
options: The DME must be repaired, or the flight must avoid the route/procedures that require it — it cannot simply be placarded inoperative and flown as planned
The pilot may placard the DME inoperative and fly the route anyway, since DME is only advisory
A logbook entry noting the failure, without deactivation or placarding, satisfies the rule
questions.explanation: 91.213(d)(2)(iii) only allows the placard-and-go option for equipment that is NOT required by 91.205 or any other rule of Part 91 for the specific kind of flight operation being conducted; equipment the planned route actually requires does not qualify for that deferral.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.213(a), an aircraft may be dispatched with instruments or equipment inoperative if the operator holds an approved document specific to that aircraft. What is that document called?
questions.back: Minimum Equipment List (MEL)
options: Minimum Equipment List (MEL)
Standard Airworthiness Certificate
Aircraft Flight Manual Supplement
questions.explanation: An approved MEL tailored to the specific aircraft by make, model, and serial/registration number permits dispatch with certain inoperative items under 91.213(a); without one, operators must instead follow the more restrictive placard procedure in 91.213(d).

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d)(3) and (d)(4), what two things must be done to legally defer a non-required, inoperative instrument or piece of equipment when no MEL applies?
questions.back: The item must be either (1) removed from the aircraft, with the cockpit control placarded and the maintenance recorded, or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative'; and (2) a pilot or an appropriately rated mechanic must determine that the inoperative item does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft.
questions.explanation: Both steps are required together — placarding alone isn't enough without the hazard determination, and the determination alone isn't enough without physically deactivating or removing the item.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d)(2), name the categories of inoperative equipment that can never be deferred using the no-MEL placard procedure, no matter how minor the failure seems.
questions.back: Equipment that is (1) part of the VFR-day type-certification instruments/equipment, (2) indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list or Kinds of Operation Equipment List for the flight being conducted, (3) required by 91.205 or any other rule of Part 91 for the specific kind of flight operation being conducted, or (4) required to be operational by an Airworthiness Directive.
questions.explanation: These carve-outs exist because some equipment is safety-critical or legally mandated regardless of dispatch convenience — a pilot can't placard around a type-certificate item, an equipment-list item, or an AD-mandated fix just because there's no approved MEL.

questions.front: In which classes of airspace does 14 CFR 91.215 always require an operating transponder with automatic altitude reporting, regardless of altitude?
questions.back: Class A, Class B, and Class C airspace
options: Class A, Class B, and Class C airspace
Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL
Class G airspace
questions.explanation: 91.215(b)(1) requires a transponder in Class A, B, and C airspace outright, with no altitude limit, plus several other defined areas by altitude and distance covered in the rest of (b); Class G airspace is never covered by this rule.

questions.front: A glider with no engine-driven electrical system wants to operate within the lateral limits of a Class B primary airport's 30-nautical-mile Mode C veil, below 10,000 feet MSL and outside Class B airspace itself. Under 14 CFR 91.215(b)(3), is a transponder required?
questions.back: No — aircraft without an engine-driven electrical system are exempt from this requirement under these conditions
options: No — aircraft without an engine-driven electrical system are exempt from this requirement under these conditions
Yes — transponders are required for all aircraft in the Mode C veil regardless of electrical system
No — gliders are exempt from the Mode C veil at any altitude, even above 10,000 feet MSL
questions.explanation: 91.215(b)(3) carves out aircraft never certificated with an engine-driven electrical system, balloons, and gliders from the 30-nm Mode C veil transponder requirement, but only while they stay outside Class A, B, or C airspace and below the ceiling of the Class B/C airspace or 10,000 feet MSL, whichever is lower.

questions.front: How far from a Class B primary airport does the 14 CFR 91.215 transponder requirement extend outward at the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, forming what's commonly called the Mode C veil?
questions.back: 30 nautical miles
options: 20 nautical miles
30 nautical miles
40 nautical miles
questions.explanation: This 30-nm ring requires an operating transponder with altitude reporting from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL even for aircraft that never enter the Class B airspace itself, only transiting nearby.

questions.front: Above what altitude does 14 CFR 91.215 require an operating transponder in Class E airspace over the 48 contiguous states, and what is the notable exception?
questions.back: At and above 10,000 feet MSL — except for airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL, which is not covered even if it happens to sit above 10,000 feet MSL (such as over high mountainous terrain).
questions.explanation: This AGL carve-out exists so aircraft operating low over high terrain — technically above 10,000 MSL but close to the ground — aren't forced to carry a transponder they wouldn't otherwise need at that height above the surface.

questions.front: Besides Class A, B, and C airspace themselves, what two other defined areas does 14 CFR 91.215(b) require an operating transponder in, tied to Class B/C airspace?
questions.back: (1) Within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, and (2) above the ceiling of, and within the lateral boundaries of, Class B or Class C airspace, up to 10,000 feet MSL.
questions.explanation: Both extensions push the transponder requirement outward or upward from the charted Class B/C boundaries so that traffic transiting nearby is still visible to ATC's Mode C-dependent conflict alerts.

questions.front: Since what date has ADS-B Out equipment generally been required to operate in the airspace defined by 14 CFR 91.225?
questions.back: January 1, 2020
options: January 1, 2020
January 1, 2015
January 1, 2025
questions.explanation: 91.225 set January 1, 2020 as the compliance date for ADS-B Out throughout the airspace the rule covers; pilots sometimes confuse this with the unrelated 24-calendar-month transponder inspection cycle under 91.413.

questions.front: An aircraft plans to operate at FL220 in Class A airspace. Under 14 CFR 91.225(a), which ADS-B Out equipment satisfies the requirement at that altitude?
questions.back: Equipment meeting TSO-C166b or TSO-C166c (1090ES)
options: UAT (978 MHz, TSO-C154c) only
Equipment meeting TSO-C166b or TSO-C166c (1090ES)
Either 1090ES or UAT, pilot's choice
questions.explanation: 91.225(a) specifically ties Class A airspace to the 1090ES equipment standards; UAT (978 MHz) only satisfies the ADS-B Out requirement in the lower airspace covered under 91.225(b), which applies below 18,000 feet MSL, beneath Class A.

questions.front: A pilot plans to fly VFR through the airspace within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL. Under 14 CFR 91.225(d)(2), what equipment is required there in addition to the transponder already required by 91.215?
questions.back: ADS-B Out
options: ADS-B Out
ADS-B In
TCAS II
questions.explanation: 91.225(d) layers an ADS-B Out requirement onto the same airspace where 91.215 already requires a Mode C transponder, including the 30-nm Mode C veil around Class B primary airports in (d)(2); ADS-B In is never a Part 91 equipment requirement.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.225(d)(5), what Class E airspace area over water requires ADS-B Out equipment, beyond the 10,000-foot MSL shelf over the 48 contiguous states?
questions.back: Class E airspace over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 feet MSL, within 12 nautical miles of the U.S. coastline.
questions.explanation: This lower-altitude Gulf of Mexico requirement was added to support offshore helicopter traffic surveillance, since those flights often operate well below the 10,000-foot MSL threshold that applies over land.

questions.front: Off an established airway, with no published MEA, in non-mountainous terrain, what minimum obstacle clearance must a pilot maintain under IFR (except during takeoff or landing)?
questions.back: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown.
options: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 nautical miles of course
500 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 nautical miles of course
2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 nautical miles of course
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.177(a)(2) sets 1,000 ft clearance in non-mountainous areas and 2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas; test writers often swap these two numbers to catch pilots who don't tie the value to terrain type.

questions.front: While operating IFR over a designated mountainous area with no published MEA available, what minimum altitude satisfies the 91.177 obstacle clearance requirement?
questions.back: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles of the course to be flown.
options: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of course
2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of course
2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 10 NM of course
questions.explanation: Mountainous terrain doubles the required vertical clearance to 2,000 feet, but the 4 NM horizontal search distance stays the same as the non-mountainous rule — only the vertical buffer changes.

questions.front: Define Minimum Enroute Altitude (MEA) as used on IFR enroute charts.
questions.back: The lowest published altitude between radio fixes that assures acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance requirements for that route segment.
questions.explanation: MEA guarantees both obstacle clearance AND signal reception between fixes — that dual requirement is what separates it from MOCA, which only guarantees signal reception close to the VOR.

questions.front: How far from the VOR is navigation signal coverage guaranteed when flying at the Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude (MOCA)?
questions.back: Within 22 nautical miles of the VOR; beyond that distance, signal reception may not be reliable even though obstacle clearance is still assured for the entire route segment.
questions.explanation: MOCA still clears obstacles along the whole segment, but the 22 NM figure is only the reception guarantee — a classic distinction from MEA, which guarantees usable signal for the entire segment.

questions.front: An aircraft is approaching a fix beyond which the MEA increases sharply due to rising terrain. According to 91.177(b), when must the pilot reach the higher minimum altitude?
questions.back: The climb to the higher MEA must begin immediately after passing the point where it applies, except that if a Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA) is published for that fix, the pilot must already be at the MCA before crossing it.
options: Immediately after passing the fix, unless a charted Minimum Crossing Altitude requires reaching it before the fix
Within 5 nautical miles after passing the fix, regardless of any charted crossing restriction
By the next compulsory reporting point, regardless of terrain
questions.explanation: 91.177(b) normally lets the climb start right at the fix, but a charted MCA overrides that when terrain rises too fast to climb through safely after the fix — mixing up MCA with MOCA is one of the most common regulatory mix-ups on this topic.

questions.front: Under 91.177(a), what takes priority over the generic 1,000/2,000-foot obstacle clearance formula when determining the minimum IFR altitude on a federal airway?
questions.back: The minimum altitude prescribed in 14 CFR Part 95 (i.e., the charted MEA, MOCA, or MCA on the enroute chart); the 1,000/2,000-foot rule is only a fallback used when no minimum altitude has been published for that route.
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that the 1,000/2,000 ft rule always applies — it's actually the exception, used only where a route has no published minimum IFR altitude.

questions.front: In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL, on a magnetic course of 090, which cruising altitude complies with 91.179?
questions.back: 7,000 feet MSL — magnetic courses of 000 through 179 degrees use odd thousand-foot altitudes (3,000, 5,000, 7,000, and so on).
options: 7,000 feet MSL
8,000 feet MSL
6,500 feet MSL
questions.explanation: The rule is based on magnetic course, not the reverse heading; course 090 falls in the 000-179 range, so it requires an odd-thousand altitude, not an even one.

questions.front: Operating IFR outside controlled airspace on a magnetic course of 270 between 18,000 feet MSL and FL290, which flight level is appropriate?
questions.back: FL200 — magnetic courses 180 through 359 degrees use even flight levels (FL180, FL200, FL220, and so on) in this altitude band.
options: FL200
FL190
FL210
questions.explanation: The odd/even-by-course rule continues above 18,000 feet up to FL290; only above FL290 does the spacing widen to 4,000-foot intervals.

questions.front: Above FL290 in uncontrolled airspace, at what interval are cruising flight levels assigned, and what is the starting level for each course direction?
questions.back: 4,000-foot intervals: magnetic course 000-179 degrees uses FL290, 330, 370, 410...; magnetic course 180-359 degrees uses FL310, 350, 390...
questions.explanation: The vertical buffer widens to 4,000 feet above FL290 because altimetry error and traffic separation demands grow at higher altitudes, unlike the 2,000-foot spacing used below it.

questions.front: When operating IFR in controlled airspace, what altitude governs cruising flight under 91.179(a)?
questions.back: The altitude or flight level assigned by ATC — the odd/even magnetic-course rule only applies in uncontrolled airspace or when cleared to maintain 'VFR conditions on top.'
options: Whatever altitude or flight level ATC has assigned
The odd/even altitude based on magnetic course, same as uncontrolled airspace
Any altitude at least 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle
questions.explanation: A common trap is assuming the odd/even rule is universal; in controlled airspace it's entirely superseded by the ATC clearance and only resurfaces under a VFR-on-top clearance.

questions.front: If ATC issues a clearance to maintain 'VFR conditions on top' while on an IFR flight plan, which altitude rule must the pilot follow?
questions.back: The VFR cruising altitude rule of 14 CFR 91.159 — odd thousand plus 500 feet on magnetic courses 000-179, even thousand plus 500 feet on courses 180-359.
questions.explanation: This is the one case where an IFR flight in controlled airspace reverts to a VFR-style altitude selection, and it adds the +500 feet that the pure IFR odd/even rule under 91.179 does not include.

questions.front: The odd/even cruising altitude rule in 91.179 is based on which of the following?
questions.back: Magnetic course — the direction of the intended track over the ground, not the heading flown to correct for wind.
options: Magnetic course
Magnetic heading
True course
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes select an altitude off their heading indicator instead of their planned course; a strong crosswind can put heading and course in different halves of the compass, changing which altitudes are legal.

questions.front: Under 91.179(b), during what two circumstances is a pilot in uncontrolled airspace excused from strictly maintaining the odd/even cruising altitude?
questions.back: While turning, and while in a holding pattern of two minutes or less.
questions.explanation: This exception exists because momentary altitude deviations during a tight turn or a short hold are operationally unavoidable and do not create the same conflict risk as sustained level flight off the assigned altitude structure.

questions.front: Below 18,000 feet MSL, 91.121 requires the altimeter to be set to which value?
questions.back: The current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route and within 100 nautical miles of the aircraft (or, if none is available, an appropriate available station's setting).
options: The current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route within 100 NM of the aircraft
29.92 inches of mercury at all times
The elevation of the nearest airport regardless of distance
questions.explanation: The 100 NM radius is the specific number examiners test — beyond that distance, a stale or unrepresentative setting is technically noncompliant even if it is the last one the pilot received.

questions.front: At or above 18,000 feet MSL, to what value must the altimeter be set regardless of local station pressure?
questions.back: 29.92 inches of Hg (standard setting) — this common reference is what makes flight levels comparable for all aircraft operating in that airspace.
options: 29.92 inches of mercury
The current altimeter setting of the nearest station within 100 NM
Field elevation of the departure airport
questions.explanation: A single standard setting above 18,000 feet ensures consistent relative vertical separation between aircraft regardless of the actual, constantly-changing local pressure — that is the whole reason flight levels are named differently from altitudes.

questions.front: If an aircraft has no radio and cannot obtain a current altimeter setting before an IFR departure, to what should the altimeter be set per 91.121?
questions.back: The elevation of the departure airport (or the most recent altimeter setting available before departure).
questions.explanation: This fallback keeps the altimeter reasonably accurate near the departure point when no station report is obtainable, since a non-radio aircraft cannot request an updated setting en route either.

questions.front: An aircraft is descending from FL350 to 10,000 feet MSL on an IFR flight plan. At what point must the pilot transition the altimeter from 29.92 to the current local setting?
questions.back: Immediately upon descending through 18,000 feet MSL — the transition between the standard 29.92 setting and the local altimeter setting occurs exactly at that fixed altitude in either direction.
options: Immediately upon descending through 18,000 feet MSL
Only after being cleared for the approach at the destination
As soon as ATC hands off to the next facility, regardless of altitude
questions.explanation: 18,000 feet MSL is the single, fixed transition altitude everywhere in the U.S. system (unlike some countries that use a variable transition altitude); ATC typically includes the current altimeter setting with the descent clearance as a reminder.

questions.front: For an altimeter setting to satisfy 91.121 below 18,000 feet, what two conditions must the reporting station meet?
questions.back: It must be along the route of flight and within 100 nautical miles of the aircraft's position.
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be met simultaneously — a station within 100 NM but off to the side of the actual route does not satisfy the rule if a more representative station along the route exists.

questions.front: When cruising at FL200 with the altimeter set to the required 29.92, what does the indicated altitude actually represent if the real sea-level pressure is not 29.92?
questions.back: Pressure altitude — height above the standard-pressure datum, which equals true altitude only when the actual atmospheric pressure happens to be 29.92 inches Hg.
options: Pressure altitude, which may differ from true altitude
True altitude exactly, regardless of actual pressure
Density altitude corrected for temperature
questions.explanation: Above 18,000 feet everyone flies pressure altitude by design so relative separation between aircraft stays accurate, but it is easy to forget that pressure altitude is not the same as true height above sea level or terrain.

questions.front: In cold temperatures, how does true altitude compare to indicated altitude when the altimeter is correctly set to the local station pressure?
questions.back: True altitude is lower than indicated altitude — cold air is denser, compressing pressure levels closer together than standard, so the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter shows.
questions.explanation: The mnemonic 'from hot to cold, look out below' reminds pilots that flying into colder air reduces true height above terrain even though the altimeter setting itself is fully current and correct.

source.section: 7-3-1 Effect of Cold Temperature on Barometric Altimeters

questions.front: The magnitude of cold-temperature altimetry error depends primarily on which two factors?
questions.back: Temperature (colder produces greater error) and height above the elevation of the altimeter setting source (greater height above the station produces greater error).
options: How cold the temperature is and how high the aircraft is above the reporting station's elevation
The aircraft's true airspeed and the barometric trend
The magnetic variation and the altimeter's mechanical tolerance
questions.explanation: This is why the error matters most on approach at cold, terrain-challenged airports — the aircraft is close to terrain and often well above field elevation on an intermediate segment, compounding both factors at once.

source.section: 7-3-1 Effect of Cold Temperature on Barometric Altimeters

questions.front: At an airport designated as a Cold Temperature Restricted Airport, what is a pilot generally required to do when operating below the published temperature threshold?
questions.back: Apply the appropriate cold-temperature correction to the charted segment(s) — identified by a snowflake icon — or otherwise arrange for a suitable altitude with ATC when required.
options: Apply a cold-temperature altitude correction to the specified charted segment(s) or coordinate an alternative with ATC
Ignore the published minimums since jet aircraft are exempt
Add exactly 1,000 feet to every published minimum altitude on the approach
questions.explanation: The correction is not a flat, universal number — it is calculated from a table (or the aircraft's approved system) based on reported temperature and height above the station, then applied only to the specific charted segment(s), most often the final approach segment.

questions.front: How is a Cold Temperature Restricted Airport identified on an instrument approach procedure chart?
questions.back: A snowflake icon next to the airport temperature (or an accompanying note) marks it as cold-temperature restricted, along with the published threshold temperature below which the correction or restriction applies.
questions.explanation: The threshold temperature varies by airport and procedure, so pilots must read the specific chart note rather than assume a single nationwide value applies everywhere.

questions.front: A pilot flying from a warm air mass into a significantly colder air mass, with the altimeter still correctly set, is most at risk of which error?
questions.back: Flying lower than indicated — true altitude drops below indicated altitude in cold air, eroding the obstacle clearance the pilot believes is being maintained.
options: Flying lower than the altimeter indicates, reducing actual obstacle clearance
Flying higher than the altimeter indicates, wasting fuel
No altimeter error occurs as long as the setting is current
questions.explanation: Because the altimeter setting itself can be perfectly current and correct, this error is easy to miss; it is a temperature effect rather than a setting error, which is exactly why cold-temperature corrections exist as a separate procedure.

source.section: 7-3-1 Effect of Cold Temperature on Barometric Altimeters

questions.front: The current altimeter setting along the route is 29.70. Per the 91.121(b) lowest usable flight level table, what is the lowest flight level a pilot may use?
questions.back: FL185 — an altimeter setting of 29.91 through 29.42 raises the lowest usable flight level from FL180 to FL185.
options: FL185
FL180
FL190
questions.explanation: The 91.121(b) table raises the floor of usable flight levels in 500-foot bands as pressure drops below standard (29.91-29.42 -> FL185, 29.41-28.92 -> FL190, and so on). An altimeter setting of 29.70 falls in the first band below standard, so FL185 -- not FL190 -- is the lowest usable flight level.

questions.front: What is the lowest usable flight level when the current altimeter setting is 29.92 or higher?
questions.back: FL180 — standard or higher pressure allows the normal floor of the flight-level structure to be used as published.
questions.explanation: FL180 is only the 'true' floor when pressure is at or above standard; low-pressure systems push the usable floor higher per the 91.121(b) table.

questions.front: An aircraft is level at FL180 when the current altimeter setting along the route drops to 29.35. What must the pilot do?
questions.back: Request reassignment to FL190 or higher — a current altimeter setting of 29.41 through 28.92 makes FL190 the lowest usable flight level under 91.121(b), so FL180 is no longer legal to occupy.
options: Request a higher flight level from ATC, since FL180 is no longer usable at that pressure setting
Continue at FL180 since flight levels are unaffected by surface pressure changes
Descend below 18,000 feet until the pressure setting rises above 29.42
questions.explanation: The lowest-usable-flight-level table is dynamic: a deepening low-pressure system can make a previously legal flight level illegal for continued use even though nothing about the route or aircraft changed, so pilots must monitor altimeter setting reports while at high flight levels.

questions.front: An unpressurized airplane will cruise at a cabin pressure altitude of 13,500 feet MSL for a 50-minute leg. According to 14 CFR 91.211, when must the required minimum flight crew begin using supplemental oxygen?
questions.back: After spending 30 minutes at that altitude, oxygen use must begin for the remaining 20 minutes
options: Oxygen must be used for the entire 50-minute leg
No oxygen is required because 13,500 feet is below 14,000 feet MSL
After spending 30 minutes at that altitude, oxygen use must begin for the remaining 20 minutes
questions.explanation: 91.211(a)(1) only requires oxygen for the portion of time at 12,500-14,000 feet MSL that exceeds 30 minutes. Pilots often treat 14,000 feet as the only relevant threshold and forget the duration clock that applies in the 12,500-14,000 foot band.

source.section: Supplemental oxygen - flight crew duration rule

questions.front: Above what cabin pressure altitude does 14 CFR 91.211 require supplemental oxygen to be provided to every occupant on board, not just the flight crew?
questions.back: Above 15,000 feet MSL - every occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen.
questions.explanation: This is the top tier of the three-step 91.211 oxygen rule. Below 15,000 feet, only the required minimum flight crew must be using oxygen, and passengers aren't required to use what's provided.

source.section: Supplemental oxygen - all occupants above 15,000 ft

questions.front: At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet MSL, what does 14 CFR 91.211 require of the required minimum flight crew?
questions.back: Supplemental oxygen must be used continuously for the entire time at that altitude
options: Supplemental oxygen is required only after 30 minutes at that altitude
Supplemental oxygen must be used continuously for the entire time at that altitude
Oxygen must be available but its use is left to crew discretion
questions.explanation: The 30-minute grace period is unique to the lower 12,500-14,000 foot band. Above 14,000 feet there is no time allowance, and oxygen use by the flight crew is continuous.

source.section: Supplemental oxygen - continuous use above 14,000 ft

questions.front: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, what is the maximum indicated airspeed permitted for any aircraft operating below 10,000 feet MSL under 14 CFR 91.117(a)?
questions.back: 250 knots
options: 250 knots
200 knots
270 knots
questions.explanation: 250 KIAS is the baseline speed limit below 10,000 feet MSL. The lower 200-knot limit applies only in more specific, congested airspace described elsewhere in 91.117.

source.section: Aircraft speed - general limit below 10,000 ft MSL

questions.front: What airspeed restriction applies at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D surface area, per 14 CFR 91.117(b)?
questions.back: 200 knots indicated airspeed maximum, unless otherwise authorized or required by ATC.
questions.explanation: This tighter limit near the primary airport protects traffic in the pattern. It is easy to confuse with the broader 250-knot limit that applies elsewhere below 10,000 feet.

source.section: Aircraft speed - Class C/D primary airport limit

questions.front: A turbine-powered airplane is operating in the airspace that underlies a Class B airspace shelf. What indicated airspeed limit applies under 14 CFR 91.117(c)?
questions.back: 200 knots
options: 250 knots
230 knots
200 knots
questions.explanation: 91.117(c) sets a 200-knot cap underneath Class B airspace, and in VFR corridors through it, to protect slower traffic that isn't equipped or cleared to operate inside the Class B shelf itself.

source.section: Aircraft speed - airspace underlying Class B

questions.front: What exception does 14 CFR 91.117(d) provide to the airspeed limits elsewhere in that section?
questions.back: If the minimum safe airspeed for a particular operation is greater than the maximum speed otherwise prescribed, the aircraft may be operated at that minimum safe speed instead.
questions.explanation: This narrow safety valve keeps a heavy or high-performance aircraft from being forced below a safe operating speed just to comply with the numeric limits in 91.117(a)-(c).

source.section: Aircraft speed - minimum safe airspeed exception

questions.front: Once a pilot in command has accepted an ATC clearance, under what conditions may that pilot deviate from it, per 14 CFR 91.123(a)?
questions.back: Only after obtaining an amended clearance, in a genuine emergency, or in response to a TCAS resolution advisory
options: At the pilot's discretion any time a more efficient route becomes apparent
Only after obtaining an amended clearance, in a genuine emergency, or in response to a TCAS resolution advisory
Only after notifying ATC and receiving a read-back acknowledgment
questions.explanation: 91.123(a) binds the pilot to the accepted clearance except for these two narrow carve-outs. Simple efficiency or convenience is never a legal basis for deviating.

questions.front: If a pilot in command must deviate from an ATC clearance because of an emergency, what does 14 CFR 91.123(c) require afterward?
questions.back: The pilot must notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible.
questions.explanation: The notification duty is immediate and separate from any later written report the FAA might request. 'As soon as possible' means right after the emergency is under control, not after landing.

questions.front: ATC provides priority handling to a flight during an in-flight emergency, even though the pilot never actually deviated from any regulation. If the facility requests it, what does 14 CFR 91.123(d) require the pilot in command to submit?
questions.back: A detailed report of the emergency within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility
options: A detailed report of the emergency within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility
Nothing, since no rule was actually broken
A written report within 10 days to the FAA Flight Standards District Office
