questions.explanation: This requirement is easy to miss because it applies even without any rule violation. Simply receiving priority handling can trigger a 48-hour written report if the facility asks, a different obligation than the 91.3(c) report tied to an actual deviation.

source.section: Report following priority handling in an emergency

questions.front: A pilot overhears ATC issue a heading and altitude to another aircraft on the same frequency. May that pilot apply the same instructions to their own flight, under 14 CFR 91.123(e)?
questions.back: No, unless ATC specifically authorizes it - instructions issued to another aircraft for radar control may not be self-applied
options: Yes, since both aircraft are on the same ATC frequency and can be assumed to share the clearance
Yes, as long as the pilot reads back the instruction to confirm receipt
No, unless ATC specifically authorizes it - instructions issued to another aircraft for radar control may not be self-applied
questions.explanation: Radar instructions are aircraft-specific. 91.123(e) exists precisely to prevent a pilot from copying another aircraft's vector or altitude assignment, which could put two aircraft into direct conflict.

questions.front: What does 14 CFR 91.3(a) establish about a pilot in command's authority over the operation of the aircraft?
questions.back: The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft.
questions.explanation: This single sentence underlies nearly every PIC-authority question on the test. It's why the PIC, not ATC, dispatch, or company policy, has the last word on how the flight is conducted.

source.section: Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command

questions.front: During an in-flight emergency that requires immediate action, what authority does 14 CFR 91.3(b) grant the pilot in command?
questions.back: The PIC may deviate from any rule of Part 91 to the extent required to meet the emergency
options: The PIC may deviate from any rule of Part 91 to the extent required to meet the emergency
The PIC may deviate only from altitude and routing rules, not from equipment or currency requirements
The PIC must first obtain ATC's concurrence before deviating from any rule
questions.explanation: 91.3(b) is deliberately broad, covering 'any rule of this part,' because emergencies don't respect regulatory boundaries. The only real limit is that the deviation be no greater than the emergency actually requires.

questions.front: After a pilot in command uses the emergency authority in 14 CFR 91.3(b) to deviate from a regulation, what does 91.3(c) then require?
questions.back: If requested by the Administrator, the pilot in command must send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator.
questions.explanation: Unlike the fixed 48-hour deadline in 91.123(d) for priority-handling reports, 91.3(c) itself sets no deadline. The report is owed only if and when the FAA actually requests it.

questions.front: While in radar contact on an IFR flight, a pilot determines the aircraft cannot climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute. Must this be reported to ATC?
questions.back: Report it to ATC, since this is a mandatory report at all times, radar contact or not
options: No report is needed as long as radar contact is maintained
Report it to ATC, since this is a mandatory report at all times, radar contact or not
Report it only if the rate falls below 500 fpm for more than five minutes
questions.explanation: An aircraft's inability to meet a 500 fpm climb or descent rate directly affects how ATC sequences and separates traffic, so this is one of the reports required 'at all times' under AIM guidance, regardless of radar coverage.

questions.front: By how much must average true airspeed at cruising altitude differ from the speed filed in the IFR flight plan before a report to ATC is required, per AIM guidance?
questions.back: 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater.
questions.explanation: Pilots often remember only '10 knots' and forget the 5-percent alternative, which becomes the controlling number for faster aircraft. For example, at 250 knots filed, 5 percent (12.5 knots) is the trigger, not 10.

questions.front: An IFR flight's primary navigation receiver fails en route. Must this be reported to ATC, per AIM guidance on mandatory reports?
questions.back: Yes - loss of navigation, approach, or communication capability must be reported
options: Yes - loss of navigation, approach, or communication capability must be reported
No - only a complete loss of electrical power triggers a mandatory report
No - equipment failures are only reportable in a written report after landing
questions.explanation: This is one of the reports required 'at all times': loss of navigation, approach, or communication capability must be reported, not just a total electrical failure, because ATC needs to know exactly what services the aircraft can still receive.

questions.front: What information must a pilot report to ATC upon reaching a clearance limit or an assigned holding fix, per AIM guidance?
questions.back: The time and the altitude (or flight level) upon reaching the holding fix or clearance limit.
questions.explanation: This report tells ATC precisely when the aircraft entered the hold, which is essential for sequencing and for issuing further clearance beyond that fix.

questions.front: An IFR flight is not in radar contact and has not been asked to make ADS-B position reports. Approaching a non-precision approach, what additional report is required as the aircraft passes the final approach fix inbound?
questions.back: Report leaving the final approach fix inbound, including the time
options: No additional report is required beyond the standard reports made at all times
Report leaving the final approach fix inbound, including the time
Report only if the missed approach point will double as a compulsory reporting point
questions.explanation: When not in radar contact, AIM guidance adds reports beyond the 'at all times' list. Leaving the FAF (or outer marker on a precision approach) inbound is one, since it's the only way a non-radar controller can track approach progress.

questions.front: Without radar contact, by how much must a pilot's estimated time of arrival at the next compulsory reporting point change before it must be reported to ATC?
questions.back: More than 2 minutes - a revised ETA must be given (3 minutes applies specifically to North Atlantic (NAT) operations).
questions.explanation: This threshold keeps non-radar sequencing accurate without burdening the frequency with reports for trivial ETA shifts. Many pilots misremember this as a flat 3-minute rule, but current AIM guidance sets the general threshold at 2 minutes, reserving 3 minutes for North Atlantic tracks.

questions.front: Which of the following must always be reported to ATC, whether or not the aircraft is in radar contact?
questions.back: Executing a missed approach
options: Descending through a cloud layer during the approach
Switching from one VOR frequency to another en route
Executing a missed approach
questions.explanation: A missed approach is one of the events that must be reported 'at all times' per AIM guidance, since ATC must immediately know to reissue instructions or sequence a new approach attempt.

questions.front: A pilot is cleared to operate 'VFR-on-top' and changes cruising altitude. What must be reported to ATC, per AIM guidance on mandatory reports?
questions.back: The altitude change - any change in altitude made while operating VFR-on-top must be reported.
questions.explanation: Because a VFR-on-top clearance lets the pilot select altitude within regulatory limits, ATC has no other way to know the aircraft's current altitude unless each change is reported.

questions.front: An IFR flight in IMC suddenly needs an immediate turn and climb off its assigned route to avoid terrain-obscuring weather, and no radio contact with ATC has yet been made. What is the correct order of actions under 14 CFR 91.3 and 91.123?
questions.back: The pilot in command may deviate immediately as the emergency requires, then notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible
options: The pilot in command may deviate immediately as the emergency requires, then notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible
The pilot must first declare an emergency on frequency before any deviation is legally permitted
The pilot may deviate only if the new flight path stays within the originally assigned altitude
questions.explanation: 91.3(b) authorizes the deviation the instant the emergency demands it; there is no requirement to make radio contact first. 91.123(c) then requires notifying ATC as soon as possible afterward, not before.

questions.front: An IFR flight in radar contact encounters a sudden 40-knot windshear reported by no other aircraft and not included in any forecast. The pilot elects not to declare an emergency. Does 14 CFR 91.183 still require reporting this to ATC?
questions.back: Yes - information relating to the safety of flight must be reported regardless of whether an emergency is declared
options: No - only PIREPs filed with Flight Service satisfy this requirement, not a report to ATC
Yes - information relating to the safety of flight must be reported regardless of whether an emergency is declared
No - since the flight remains in radar contact, ATC will detect the hazard independently
questions.explanation: 91.183 requires reporting unforecast weather encountered and any other information relating to the safety of flight at all times. This obligation is independent of whether the pilot ever declares an emergency, and radar contact does not let ATC 'see' windshear the way a pilot report does.

source.section: IFR operations - safety of flight information report

questions.front: Without radar contact, what report must a pilot make immediately upon leaving an assigned holding fix?
questions.back: Report leaving the holding fix (or point), in addition to the standard time/altitude report made upon reaching it.
questions.explanation: This report is part of the 'at all times' list of additional reports in AIM guidance, so it applies whether or not the aircraft is in radar contact. It bookends the earlier 'reaching the holding fix' report so a controller can track exactly when the aircraft resumed its route.

questions.front: When making a required position report at a compulsory reporting point without radar contact, which of these items must the pilot include, per AIM guidance?
questions.back: Aircraft identification, position, time, altitude, and the ETA and name of the next reporting point
options: Type of aircraft and equipment suffix only
Aircraft identification, position, time, altitude, and the ETA and name of the next reporting point
Fuel remaining and number of souls on board
questions.explanation: A standard non-radar position report follows a set format: identification, position, time, altitude/flight level, ETA at and name of the next reporting point, plus the name of the fix after that, so ATC can build a mental picture of the flight's progress without radar.

questions.front: Which pilots are legally bound by the specific takeoff visibility minimums published under 14 CFR 91.175(f)?
questions.back: Pilots operating under 14 CFR Parts 121, 125, 129, or 135.
options: Pilots operating under 14 CFR Parts 121, 125, 129, or 135
Every IFR pilot, including those flying under Part 91 general operating rules
Only pilots flying turbine-powered aircraft, regardless of the operating part
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.175(f) takeoff minimums apply only to commercial/commuter operators; a Part 91 pilot flying for personal or business purposes is not bound by them, though departing below standard minimums is strongly discouraged. This split is a frequent trap on the written test.

questions.front: Under the default takeoff minimums of 14 CFR 91.175(f), what flight visibility applies to a non-helicopter aircraft with two engines or fewer, versus one with more than two engines, when no other minimums are published for the airport?
questions.back: 1 statute mile flight visibility for aircraft with two engines or fewer; 1/2 statute mile for aircraft with more than two engines. (Helicopters also default to 1/2 statute mile.)
questions.explanation: These are the fallback numbers used only when an airport has no published takeoff minimums of its own; more engines effectively buys a lower default because of the engine-out performance margin built into the rule.

questions.front: A Part 91 pilot not operating for compensation plans an IFR departure from an airport reporting 1/4 statute mile visibility, with no takeoff minimums published for that field. Is the departure legal?
questions.back: Yes — 14 CFR 91.175(f) takeoff minimums do not apply to Part 91 operations.
options: Yes — 14 CFR 91.175(f) takeoff minimums do not apply to Part 91 operations
No — 1 statute mile is the legal floor for every IFR takeoff regardless of operating rules
No — the pilot must have at least the visibility required for the published landing minimums to depart
questions.explanation: Legality and prudence are different things here: nothing in 14 CFR prohibits a Part 91 pilot from departing in near-zero visibility, but doing so removes any margin for an engine or system failure right after liftoff.

questions.front: Where would a pilot find the specific published takeoff minimums and any obstacle departure procedure for an airport that has one on file?
questions.back: In the Terminal Procedures Publication under that airport's 'Takeoff Minimums and (Obstacle) Departure Procedures' listing — approach and departure charts flag this with a black triangle 'T' symbol directing the pilot to look it up.
questions.explanation: The 'T' symbol is easy to overlook on the chart; it doesn't state the minimums itself, it just signals that non-standard takeoff minimums or an ODP exist and must be checked separately in the Terminal Procedures Publication.

source.section: AIM 5-2-9 – Instrument Departure Procedures (DP): Obstacle Departure Procedures (ODP), SIDs, and DVAs

questions.front: For a helicopter with no other takeoff minimums prescribed, what default flight visibility applies under 14 CFR 91.175(f)?
questions.back: 1/2 statute mile.
options: 1/2 statute mile
1 statute mile
1/4 statute mile
questions.explanation: Helicopters share the same 1/2-mile default as multi-engine airplanes with more than two engines, reflecting their generally lower approach and go-around speeds.

questions.front: A Part 135 charter departs an airport with no published takeoff minimums, flying a three-engine turboprop. What minimum flight visibility does 14 CFR 91.175(f) require?
questions.back: 1/2 statute mile.
options: 1/2 statute mile
1 statute mile
3/4 statute mile
questions.explanation: The default splits at 'two engines or fewer' (1 SM) versus 'more than two engines' (1/2 SM); three engines falls in the lower-visibility category, which trips up pilots who assume more engines always means a higher minimum.

questions.front: Before descending below the DA or MDA on an instrument approach, what must be true according to 14 CFR 91.175(c)?
questions.back: Flight visibility is not less than that prescribed for the procedure, the aircraft is continuously in a position to land using normal maneuvers, and a required visual reference for the runway is distinctly visible and identifiable.
options: Flight visibility is not less than that prescribed for the procedure, the aircraft is continuously in a position to land using normal maneuvers, and a required visual reference for the runway is distinctly visible and identifiable
The ground visibility reported by ATC must be at or above the published minimum, regardless of what the pilot can see
The RVR reported by the tower must equal or exceed the charted minimum before any descent below MDA is permitted
questions.explanation: It's the pilot's own flight visibility — not a reported ground visibility or RVR figure — that legally controls the descent decision; reported values are only guidance for planning and missed-approach point calls.

questions.front: Name at least four of the visual references a pilot may use, under 14 CFR 91.175(c), to continue descending below DA or MDA to land.
questions.back: Any four of: the runway threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), the visual glideslope indicator (e.g., VASI or PAPI), the touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings, touchdown zone lights, the runway or runway markings, runway lights, or the approach light system.
questions.explanation: The regulation lists ten qualifying references; distinctly seeing just one of them satisfies the visual-reference requirement — the pilot doesn't need the whole runway environment in sight. Note the current rule text says 'visual glideslope indicator,' which covers VASI, PAPI, and similar systems, not just VASI specifically.

source.section: 91.175(c)(3) – Visual references for descent below DA/MDA

questions.front: Using only the approach light system as the visual reference during an approach, below what height must a pilot also see red terminating bars or red side row bars before continuing the descent?
questions.back: 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation.
options: 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation
200 feet above the touchdown zone elevation
50 feet above the touchdown zone elevation
questions.explanation: Approach lights alone can get you down to 100 feet above TDZE; below that, the rule requires seeing the red terminating or side row bars so you're confirming the actual runway threshold, not just misjudging a string of lights.

source.section: 91.175(c)(3)(i) – Visual reference using the approach light system

questions.front: Which type of visibility legally governs whether a pilot may descend below DA/MDA on an instrument approach — reported ground visibility or flight visibility?
questions.back: Flight visibility, as observed by the pilot from the cockpit while airborne; it must meet or exceed the visibility prescribed for the procedure regardless of what ground visibility or RVR ATC reports.
questions.explanation: Reported ground visibility (via ATIS, tower, or RVR) is used for planning and for legally beginning the approach; only what the pilot can actually see determines whether descent below minimums may continue.

questions.front: An ILS approach has a published minimum of RVR 4000, but the RVR system is out of service and ground visibility of 3/4 statute mile is reported instead. What does 14 CFR 91.175(h) allow?
questions.back: The pilot may use the reported 3/4 statute mile ground visibility, since it is the comparable value to RVR 4000.
options: The pilot may use the reported 3/4 statute mile ground visibility, since it is the comparable value to RVR 4000
The approach may not be flown at all because RVR is unavailable and no substitution is permitted
The pilot must instead use 1/2 statute mile, the standard substitute value whenever RVR is inoperative
questions.explanation: 91.175(h) contains a conversion table between RVR and statute-mile visibility for exactly this situation — RVR 4000 converts to 3/4 SM — so an inoperative RVR readout doesn't automatically ground the approach.

source.section: 91.175(h) – Comparable values of RVR and ground visibility

questions.front: During the circling portion of an instrument approach, what must remain true about the aircraft's position relative to the runway at all times below MDA?
questions.back: The aircraft must remain continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made using normal maneuvers.
options: The aircraft must remain continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made using normal maneuvers
The aircraft may maneuver anywhere within Class E airspace as long as the runway environment stays in sight
The aircraft must stay within exactly 1 statute mile of the runway threshold throughout the circle
questions.explanation: There's no single fixed-mile number written into 91.175 for circling — protected radii actually vary by approach category and MDA under TERPS — so an option quoting one specific mile value is a giveaway distractor rather than the actual rule.

questions.front: If a pilot descending below DA or MDA loses the required visual references or is no longer in a position to land using normal maneuvers, what is the pilot required to do?
questions.back: Execute the missed approach procedure immediately — continuing the approach once the 91.175(c) conditions are no longer met is not permitted.
questions.explanation: 91.175(e) explicitly requires an immediate missed approach whenever the 91.175(c) conditions are not met, whether that occurs while below MDA or upon arrival at the missed approach point; losing sight of the runway environment at 200 feet still means going missed, even if it was visible a moment earlier.

questions.front: What must every aircraft, whether operating IFR or VFR, obtain from ATC before entering Class B airspace?
questions.back: An explicit ATC clearance to enter.
options: An explicit ATC clearance to enter
Two-way radio contact acknowledgment only, as with Class C
A discrete transponder code issued by the nearest flight service station
questions.explanation: Class B is unique among B/C/D in requiring a clearance — not just radio contact — for entry by any aircraft; for an IFR flight this clearance is normally already embedded in the enroute IFR clearance and routing.

questions.front: Does an aircraft's active IFR clearance also satisfy the entry requirements for Class C and Class D airspace, or is a separate authorization needed?
questions.back: An active IFR clearance satisfies entry into Class C and Class D airspace; no separate radio call or clearance is needed beyond maintaining normal ATC communication, since the IFR clearance already puts the aircraft in continuous contact with ATC.
questions.explanation: VFR pilots must establish two-way radio contact themselves before entering Class C/D; IFR pilots already exceed that bar simply by being on an active clearance and frequency.

questions.front: A VFR pilot must establish two-way radio communication before entering Class C airspace. What is the equivalent burden placed on an IFR flight entering the same airspace?
questions.back: None beyond maintaining the ATC clearance and assigned frequency already in effect.
options: None beyond maintaining the ATC clearance and assigned frequency already in effect
The IFR pilot must still make a separate initial call requesting permission to enter, apart from the clearance
IFR flights are exempt from all Class C radar services once inside the boundary
questions.explanation: Being 'IFR' already implies continuous, positive ATC contact, so the VFR-specific 'establish two-way radio communications' requirement has nothing left to add for an IFR flight.

questions.front: An IFR flight has been cleared for the ILS to a Class D airport by the approach control facility but has not yet talked to the airport's control tower. What must happen before landing?
questions.back: The pilot must contact the tower and receive a landing clearance, since only the tower can authorize landing within the Class D surface area.
options: The pilot must contact the tower and receive a landing clearance, since only the tower can authorize landing within the Class D surface area
Nothing further — the approach clearance from approach control already authorizes the landing
The pilot must broadcast in the blind on CTAF rather than switch to tower frequency, since tower is for VFR traffic only
questions.explanation: Approach control's clearance gets you established on the approach; it's a separate authorization from the tower's landing clearance, and approach normally hands the pilot off to tower well before the runway.

questions.front: What typically happens to the airspace classification and instrument approach procedures at a Class D airport when its part-time control tower closes for the night?
questions.back: The surface area typically reverts to Class E (or Class G, as published in the Chart Supplement) for that airport, and pilots can still fly published instrument approaches using non-towered procedures such as a clearance void time or canceling IFR in the air or after landing.
questions.explanation: A closed tower doesn't close the airport to IFR traffic — it just shifts how clearances and separation are handled, from the tower to the pilot and the controlling ARTCC or approach facility.

questions.front: How does a pilot typically obtain an IFR clearance to fly an approach into a Class D airport whose part-time tower is currently closed?
questions.back: Through clearance delivery from the controlling ARTCC or approach facility, often including a clearance void time or instructions to cancel IFR in the air or on landing.
options: Through clearance delivery from the controlling ARTCC or approach facility, often including a clearance void time or instructions to cancel IFR in the air or on landing
The approach cannot legally be flown IFR until the tower reopens
By self-announcing on the tower frequency, which remains staffed remotely by the ARTCC at all times
questions.explanation: This is the same basic technique used at any non-towered field for an IFR clearance — void times or airborne cancellation — just applied temporarily to a field that normally has a tower.

questions.front: Who holds final authority to accept or decline a land-and-hold-short (LAHSO) clearance issued by ATC?
questions.back: The pilot in command.
options: The pilot in command
The air traffic controller, since compliance is mandatory once assigned
The company dispatcher, prior to departure
questions.explanation: LAHSO is offered, not imposed — the PIC can decline it outright or, if a safe stop is no longer assured, execute a rejected landing and promptly notify the controller, and ATC must have an alternative plan ready either way.

source.section: AIM 4-3-11 – Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)

questions.front: What must a pilot know before accepting a land-and-hold-short (LAHSO) clearance to a runway with an intersecting-runway hold-short point?
questions.back: The Available Landing Distance (ALD) to the hold-short point and the aircraft's required landing distance for the conditions — the pilot must confirm the ALD is sufficient to stop safely before accepting.
questions.explanation: ALD is shorter than the full runway length, so a distance that's comfortably legal for a normal full-length landing can still be inadequate for a LAHSO clearance on that same runway.

source.section: AIM 4-3-11 – Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)

questions.front: A pilot has accepted a LAHSO clearance but realizes on short final that a safe stop before the hold-short point is no longer assured. What is the correct action?
questions.back: Advise ATC as early as possible and be prepared to go around, treating the earlier acceptance as no longer valid.
options: Advise ATC as early as possible and be prepared to go around, treating the earlier acceptance as no longer valid
Continue as cleared, since an accepted LAHSO clearance cannot be withdrawn once given
Land and immediately exit at the nearest taxiway regardless of the hold-short point to clear the runway quickly
questions.explanation: A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing — if a go-around becomes necessary after accepting LAHSO, the pilot should maintain safe separation and promptly notify the controller, rather than trying to force a stop that isn't going to happen.

source.section: AIM 4-3-11 – Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)

questions.front: What does the acronym LAHSO stand for in ATC terminology?
questions.back: Land And Hold Short Operations.
questions.explanation: It describes an ATC clearance requiring a landing aircraft to stop before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or other designated point on the landing runway.

source.section: AIM 4-3-11 – Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)

questions.front: A pilot without an instrument rating requests a Special VFR clearance to depart a Class D surface area 30 minutes after sunset. Is this permitted?
questions.back: No — Special VFR between sunset and sunrise requires the pilot to hold an instrument rating and the aircraft to be equipped for IFR flight.
options: No — Special VFR between sunset and sunrise requires the pilot to hold an instrument rating and the aircraft to be equipped for IFR flight
Yes — Special VFR at night only requires 1 statute mile visibility and remaining clear of clouds, regardless of pilot certification
Yes — as long as the tower controller verbally approves the request
questions.explanation: 91.157(b)(4) tightens the daytime Special VFR rules specifically for night operations, closing a loophole that would otherwise let a VFR-only pilot end up in marginal weather after dark with no instrument training to fall back on.

questions.front: What two additional requirements apply, beyond the standard Special VFR conditions, for operating Special VFR at night under 14 CFR 91.157?
questions.back: The pilot must hold an instrument rating (meet the applicable requirements for instrument flight under Part 61), and the aircraft must be equipped for IFR flight per 14 CFR 91.205(d).
questions.explanation: Both the person and the machine have to be IFR-capable at night — the rule doesn't just ask for a rated pilot in any airplane, or an IFR-equipped airplane flown by any pilot.

questions.front: An instrument-rated pilot is flying a rental airplane that lacks the equipment required for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d). The pilot requests Special VFR at night in Class D airspace. Why would ATC be correct to deny it?
questions.back: Because both pilot qualification and aircraft IFR equipment are required for night Special VFR — the pilot's rating alone isn't enough.
options: Because both pilot qualification and aircraft IFR equipment are required for night Special VFR — the pilot's rating alone isn't enough
Because ATC never issues Special VFR clearances after sunset under any circumstances
Because Special VFR is authorized only in Class B airspace after dark, not Class D
questions.explanation: This pairs the two-part test from 91.157(b)(4): an instrument-rated pilot in a VFR-only-equipped airplane still fails the requirement, since the airplane itself must meet 91.205(d).

questions.front: What two conditions must be present for structural icing to occur in flight?
questions.back: Visible moisture (clouds or precipitation) and an aircraft surface temperature at or below freezing (0°C).
questions.explanation: Both conditions are required: supercooled visible moisture strikes a below-freezing airframe and freezes on contact.

questions.front: Which conditions are most favorable for the formation of radiation fog?
questions.back: Clear skies, light or calm wind, and moist air over low, flat terrain at night.
options: Clear skies, calm winds, and moist air over low-lying terrain at night
Warm moist air moving over a colder surface with moderate winds
Overcast skies and gusty winds behind a cold front
questions.explanation: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools rapidly on clear, calm nights and chills moist air to its dew point. Warm air over a cold surface produces advection fog instead.

questions.front: What are the two most abundant gases in Earth's atmosphere by volume, and roughly what percentage does each make up?
questions.back: Nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%)
options: Nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%)
Oxygen (about 78%) and nitrogen (about 21%)
Nitrogen (about 78%) and carbon dioxide (about 21%)
questions.explanation: Dry air is roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% trace gases such as argon and carbon dioxide. A common mix-up is assuming oxygen is the dominant gas, when nitrogen actually makes up the largest share.

questions.front: List the five main layers of the atmosphere from the surface upward, and identify which one contains essentially all weather.
questions.back: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere (lowest to highest). The troposphere contains essentially all weather phenomena.
questions.explanation: Weather is confined to the troposphere because that's where most water vapor and vertical mixing occur; the stratosphere above the tropopause is far more stable and stratified, which is why jet aircraft cruise near its base to get above most weather. The outermost layer, the exosphere, is where atoms and molecules escape into space and satellites orbit the Earth.

questions.front: A flight near the equator finds the tropopause considerably higher than a flight at the same time of year near the poles. What primarily accounts for this difference in tropopause height with latitude?
questions.back: Warmer surface and air temperatures near the equator cause the troposphere to extend to a greater height than the colder polar troposphere
options: Warmer surface and air temperatures near the equator cause the troposphere to extend to a greater height than the colder polar troposphere
The Coriolis force is strongest at the equator, which mechanically pushes the tropopause upward
Ozone concentrations are highest over the equator, which raises the base of the stratosphere
questions.explanation: The troposphere is thickest where it's warmest, so a warm, expanded equatorial air column pushes the tropopause much higher than the shallow, cold polar troposphere. Coriolis force is actually zero at the equator, which rules out that distractor.

source.section: The Earth's Atmosphere - Vertical Structure, Troposphere (4.3.1)

questions.front: What is the tropopause, and why is its variability important to instrument pilots operating in the flight levels?
questions.back: The tropopause is the transition layer between the troposphere and stratosphere, marked by temperature leveling off instead of continuing to decrease with height. It matters to pilots because its altitude varies with latitude and season (higher over the tropics, lower over the poles), and it often coincides with the strongest jet stream winds and associated clear air turbulence.
questions.explanation: Because the tropopause height is not fixed, pilots can't assume a single altitude for jet stream or CAT avoidance - it must be checked for the specific route and season using winds and temperatures aloft data.

source.section: The Earth's Atmosphere - Vertical Structure, Troposphere (4.3.1); Turbulence - Clear-Air Turbulence (19.2.3.2.1)

questions.front: What are the standard sea-level pressure and temperature values that define the ICAO standard atmosphere?
questions.back: 29.92 inches of mercury (1013.25 hPa/mb) and 15°C (59°F) at sea level.
questions.explanation: These reference values are the baseline for pressure altitude, altimeter calibration, and every departure-from-standard calculation a pilot makes, such as density altitude.

source.section: The Earth's Atmosphere - The Standard Atmosphere (4.4)

questions.front: In the standard atmosphere, at approximately what average rate does temperature decrease with altitude throughout the troposphere?
questions.back: 2°C (3.5°F) per 1,000 feet
options: 2°C (3.5°F) per 1,000 feet
3°C (5.4°F) per 1,000 feet
1°C (1.8°F) per 1,000 feet
questions.explanation: This is the standard (environmental) lapse rate used to define the standard atmosphere model, and it differs from the dry adiabatic lapse rate of 3°C per 1,000 feet that applies to an individual rising air parcel - mixing the two up is a frequent test trap.

source.section: The Earth's Atmosphere - The Standard Atmosphere (4.4)

questions.front: An aircraft is flying at a constant indicated altitude through air that is colder than standard for that pressure altitude, with the altimeter set correctly for local pressure. How does the aircraft's true altitude compare to its indicated altitude, and what memory aid applies?
questions.back: True altitude is lower than indicated altitude - 'from hot to cold, look out below'
options: True altitude is lower than indicated altitude - 'from hot to cold, look out below'
True altitude is higher than indicated altitude, since colder air causes the altimeter to under-read
True and indicated altitude are unaffected by temperature as long as the altimeter setting is correct
questions.explanation: Colder-than-standard air is denser, compressing pressure levels closer together, so the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter indicates even with a correct altimeter setting, since that setting only corrects for surface pressure, not the temperature profile above it.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Altimeter Setting (8.4.1.2.1)

questions.front: At what altitude does the tropopause occur in the standard atmosphere, and what is the standard temperature at that altitude?
questions.back: Approximately 36,089 feet MSL, where the standard temperature is -56.5°C.
questions.explanation: This is the reference altitude used to define the top of the standard troposphere; above it, temperature stays essentially constant through the lower stratosphere in the standard atmosphere model.

source.section: The Earth's Atmosphere - The Standard Atmosphere (4.4)

questions.front: Define a temperature inversion.
questions.back: A layer of the atmosphere in which temperature increases with height instead of the normal decrease - meaning warmer air overlies cooler air.
questions.explanation: The word 'inversion' literally means the normal temperature-altitude relationship is inverted; because the warm air is already on top, an inversion layer is extremely stable and strongly resists vertical mixing.

questions.front: Haze, smoke, and moisture are often observed concentrated in a shallow layer near the surface beneath a temperature inversion. What property of the inversion layer explains this?
questions.back: The inversion layer is extremely stable, which suppresses vertical mixing and traps particulates and moisture beneath it
options: The inversion layer is extremely stable, which suppresses vertical mixing and traps particulates and moisture beneath it
The inversion layer accelerates surface winds, which stirs particulates upward through the layer and disperses them
The inversion layer has a lapse rate steeper than the dry adiabatic rate, forcing particulates to rise rapidly
questions.explanation: Because temperature increases with height in an inversion, rising air quickly becomes colder and denser than its surroundings, so vertical currents are strongly suppressed and anything below the inversion - smoke, haze, or moisture - stays trapped near the surface.

questions.front: What causes a subsidence inversion, and where are these commonly located?
questions.back: A subsidence inversion forms when a deep layer of air slowly sinks within a high-pressure system and warms adiabatically as it is compressed; because the upper part of the sinking layer warms more than the air near the surface, an inversion develops aloft. These are common under large, slow-moving high-pressure systems, including the subtropical highs.
questions.explanation: Subsidence inversions are distinguished from frontal inversions - which form at a boundary between air masses - by their cause: sinking, compressing air in a high rather than one air mass overriding another.

source.section: Vertical Motion and Clouds - Common Sources of Vertical Motion, Frictional Effects (12.4.2); Tropical Weather - Subtropical High-Pressure Belts (17.2.1)

questions.front: Warm air gradually overrunning a shallow layer of colder air along a frontal surface, such as ahead of an approaching warm front, typically produces what kind of temperature inversion?
questions.back: A frontal inversion
options: A frontal inversion
A subsidence inversion
A convective inversion
questions.explanation: A frontal inversion forms right at the sloped boundary where warmer air rides up and over a colder air mass; it's distinguished from a subsidence inversion, which instead forms from sinking, compressing air in a high-pressure system with no frontal boundary involved.

questions.front: A pilot receives a briefing noting a well-defined low-level temperature inversion is present near the surface. Which hazard is most directly and classically associated with flying through this type of layer?
questions.back: An abrupt change in wind speed and/or direction (low-level wind shear) across the inversion layer
options: An abrupt change in wind speed and/or direction (low-level wind shear) across the inversion layer
Increased convective turbulence throughout the inversion, since warm air rising through it causes strong updrafts
Rapidly decreasing visibility caused by an increased lapse rate that promotes vertical mixing of moisture
questions.explanation: Because an inversion is extremely stable, it suppresses convective turbulence rather than promoting it, and it reduces rather than increases vertical mixing - the classic inversion hazard is instead a sharp wind shear across the top of the layer, which can catch pilots off guard on approach or climb-out.

source.section: Turbulence - Wind Shear Turbulence, Temperature Inversion (19.2.3.1)

questions.front: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, and to what does it apply?
questions.back: Approximately 3°C (5.4°F) per 1,000 feet - the rate at which an unsaturated (dry) air parcel cools as it rises and expands, or warms as it descends and compresses, assuming no heat exchange with the surrounding air.
questions.explanation: This applies to an individual rising or sinking parcel of unsaturated air, not to the surrounding environment as a whole - don't confuse it with the standard (environmental) lapse rate of 2°C per 1,000 feet, which describes the average state of the atmosphere itself.

source.section: Vertical Motion and Clouds - Vertical Motion Effects on an Unsaturated Air Parcel (12.2)

questions.front: Why does a rising saturated air parcel cool more slowly with altitude than a rising unsaturated air parcel?
questions.back: Condensation of water vapor within the saturated parcel releases latent heat, which partly offsets the cooling caused by expansion
options: Condensation of water vapor within the saturated parcel releases latent heat, which partly offsets the cooling caused by expansion
A saturated parcel contains less water vapor than a dry parcel, so it expands less as it rises
A saturated parcel is denser than a dry parcel, so it rises more slowly and picks up more frictional heating
questions.explanation: As water vapor condenses into cloud droplets, it releases the latent heat that was stored when it evaporated, warming the parcel and slowing its cooling rate - this is why the moist adiabatic lapse rate is always less than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.

source.section: Vertical Motion and Clouds - Vertical Motion Effects on a Saturated Air Parcel (12.3)

questions.front: At a given location, the environmental (existing) lapse rate is measured at 4°C per 1,000 feet, which is steeper than the dry adiabatic lapse rate. How is this atmosphere classified, and what happens to a parcel of air that gets displaced upward?
questions.back: Absolutely unstable - the displaced parcel stays warmer than its surroundings at every altitude and keeps rising on its own
options: Absolutely unstable - the displaced parcel stays warmer than its surroundings at every altitude and keeps rising on its own
Absolutely stable - the displaced parcel cools faster than its surroundings and sinks back to its original level
Conditionally unstable - the parcel only continues rising once it becomes saturated
questions.explanation: When the environmental lapse rate exceeds the dry adiabatic rate, a lifted parcel - whether saturated or not - cools slower than the air around it cools with height, so it remains buoyant and continues rising unaided; this is the steepest, most unstable of the three classic stability categories.

source.section: Atmospheric Stability - Stability Types, Absolute Instability (13.3.3)

questions.front: What does it mean for the atmosphere to be 'conditionally unstable,' and what is the condition that name refers to?
questions.back: It means the environmental lapse rate lies between the dry adiabatic and moist (saturated) adiabatic lapse rates: the air is stable with respect to an unsaturated parcel but unstable with respect to a saturated parcel. The 'condition' is that the parcel must become saturated, usually by being lifted, before it can rise on its own.
questions.explanation: This is a middle-ground stability case: a lifted dry parcel resists rising, but once it's forced up far enough to reach its saturation point, further lifting can make it buoyant and self-sustaining - important for understanding why forced lifting from fronts or terrain can trigger deep convection.

source.section: Atmospheric Stability - Stability Types, Conditional Instability (13.3.4)

questions.front: Which combination of flight conditions and cloud types is most characteristic of a stable air mass?
questions.back: Smooth air, stratiform clouds, and steady, continuous precipitation or drizzle
options: Smooth air, stratiform clouds, and steady, continuous precipitation or drizzle
Turbulence, cumuliform clouds, and showery, intermittent precipitation
Poor surface visibility from strong vertical mixing, with excellent visibility aloft in towering clouds
questions.explanation: Stable air resists vertical motion, so it spreads moisture horizontally into flat, layered stratiform clouds with smooth flight conditions and steady precipitation; the second option actually describes an unstable air mass, and students commonly flip the two when memorizing this table.

questions.front: In the Northern Hemisphere, in which direction does surface wind circulate around a high-pressure system?
questions.back: Clockwise and outward, away from the center
options: Clockwise and outward, away from the center
Counterclockwise and outward, away from the center
Clockwise and inward, toward the center
questions.explanation: Air diverges from a high and, deflected to the right by the Coriolis force in the Northern Hemisphere, circulates clockwise; a low is the mirror image - counterclockwise and converging inward - a pairing worth memorizing together.

questions.front: What kind of weather is typically associated with a surface high-pressure system, and what mechanism produces it?
questions.back: Generally fair weather with clear to scattered skies, because air subsides (sinks) within a high-pressure system; as it sinks it is compressed and warmed adiabatically, which inhibits condensation and cloud formation.
questions.explanation: The sinking, warming, drying motion inside a high is the opposite of the rising, cooling, condensing motion inside a low - understanding this cause-and-effect is more useful than just memorizing 'highs are good weather.'

source.section: Vertical Motion and Clouds - Common Sources of Vertical Motion, Frictional Effects (12.4.2)

questions.front: Why are surface low-pressure systems typically associated with clouds and precipitation?
questions.back: Surface winds converge into the low and are forced to rise, cooling adiabatically until moisture condenses
options: Surface winds converge into the low and are forced to rise, cooling adiabatically until moisture condenses
Air subsides within the low, compressing and cooling until it reaches its dew point
The pressure gradient around a low is too weak to sustain any wind, allowing moisture to stagnate and condense in place
questions.explanation: Convergence forces air upward, and rising air cools by adiabatic expansion; once it cools to its dew point, clouds and precipitation result - the direct opposite of the sinking, drying motion found in a high.

source.section: Vertical Motion and Clouds - Common Sources of Vertical Motion, Frictional Effects (12.4.2)

questions.front: What happens to an aircraft's true altitude when flying at a constant indicated altitude from an area of higher atmospheric pressure into an area of lower pressure without resetting the altimeter, and what memory aid describes this?
questions.back: True altitude decreases even though indicated altitude stays the same - the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter shows. The memory aid is 'high to low, look out below.'
questions.explanation: An uncorrected altimeter is still referenced to the higher pressure it was set to, so as actual outside pressure drops, the airplane must descend further than the altimeter reflects to reach any given pressure level, silently eroding obstacle clearance.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Altimeter Setting (8.4.1.2.1)

questions.front: An aircraft holds a constant indicated altitude while flying from a region where the altimeter setting is 30.24 in Hg toward a region where the setting is 29.68 in Hg, and the pilot never updates the altimeter. What happens to the aircraft's true altitude, and why?
questions.back: True altitude decreases below indicated altitude, because the uncorrected altimeter over-reads once actual pressure has dropped
options: True altitude decreases below indicated altitude, because the uncorrected altimeter over-reads once actual pressure has dropped
True altitude increases above indicated altitude, because lower pressure aloft causes the altimeter to under-read
True altitude stays equal to indicated altitude, since altimeter setting changes only matter below the transition altitude
questions.explanation: Actual pressure has dropped roughly half an inch of mercury without the altimeter being updated, so the instrument reads higher than the aircraft's true height - a clear illustration of why 'high to low, look out below' is a critical habit, not just a mnemonic, since the error grows continuously as pressure falls.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Altimeter Setting (8.4.1.2.1)

questions.front: How is density altitude defined?
questions.back: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
options: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
Indicated altitude corrected for nonstandard pressure
True altitude corrected for humidity and wind
questions.explanation: Density altitude represents the altitude in the standard atmosphere that corresponds to the air's actual density - it's a performance metric, not a height above any surface, and it's easy to confuse with pressure altitude, which reflects only the 29.92 in Hg calibration, not temperature.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Density Altitude (8.4.1.5)

questions.front: Compared to a standard day, how does a high density altitude condition (hot temperature and/or high field elevation) generally affect aircraft takeoff and climb performance?
questions.back: Takeoff roll lengthens, climb rate decreases, and engine and propeller efficiency are reduced
options: Takeoff roll lengthens, climb rate decreases, and engine and propeller efficiency are reduced
Takeoff roll shortens, climb rate increases, and engine and propeller efficiency improve
Performance is essentially unchanged, since density altitude affects only true airspeed indications, not power output
questions.explanation: Less-dense air means the wings produce less lift at a given speed, the propeller bites less air per revolution, and a normally-aspirated engine makes less power - all of which degrade performance, which is why 'high, hot, and humid' is the classic hazard combination pilots are taught to respect.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Density Altitude (8.4.1.5)

questions.front: How does high relative humidity affect density altitude, compared to dry air at the same temperature and pressure altitude?
questions.back: High humidity increases density altitude slightly, because water vapor molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace, making moist air less dense
options: High humidity increases density altitude slightly, because water vapor molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace, making moist air less dense
High humidity decreases density altitude, because water vapor adds mass to the air and makes it denser
Humidity has no measurable effect on density altitude - only temperature and pressure altitude matter
questions.explanation: Water vapor has a lower molecular weight than the nitrogen and oxygen it displaces, so humid air is actually less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure - a counterintuitive fact that adds to density altitude and is often overlooked next to temperature and elevation. The Aviation Weather Handbook notes this humidity effect is real but comparatively small next to temperature's influence on density altitude.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Density, Water Vapor's Effects on Density (8.3.5)

questions.front: What three factors are used to determine density altitude, and how does each one affect it?
questions.back: Pressure altitude, outside air temperature, and humidity. Density altitude increases with higher pressure altitude, higher temperature, and higher humidity, and decreases as any of those three factors decreases.
questions.explanation: Remembering all three factors matters, though temperature has by far the greatest effect on density altitude - the Aviation Weather Handbook notes that humidity's contribution, while real (moist air is less dense), is generally negligible by comparison. Even so, humid, high-elevation, hot-day departures can produce a density altitude thousands of feet above field elevation, eroding the performance margins a pilot planned for.

source.section: Atmospheric Pressure and Altimetry - Altimetry, Density Altitude (8.4.1.5); Density, Water Vapor's Effects on Density (8.3.5)

questions.front: A pilot notices that deserts cluster near 30° North and South latitude worldwide, while stormy, wet weather is common near 50°-60° latitude. Which feature of the general circulation explains this pattern?
questions.back: Sinking air near 30° latitude, at the Hadley/Ferrel cell boundary, creates high pressure there, while rising air near 50°-60° creates the low-pressure storm track.
options: The Intertropical Convergence Zone shifts seasonally between 30° and 60° latitude, causing alternating wet and dry belts.
Sinking air near 30° latitude, at the Hadley/Ferrel cell boundary, creates high pressure there, while rising air near 50°-60° creates the low-pressure storm track.
Land and sea breeze circulations dominate at 30° latitude, blocking moisture from reaching the interior.
questions.explanation: The three-cell model places semi-permanent high pressure (sinking, fair, dry air) near 30°N/S at the Hadley/Ferrel boundary, and low pressure (rising, stormy air) near 50°-60°N/S at the Ferrel/Polar boundary — which is exactly why most of the world's deserts sit near 30° latitude.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.3 Rotating Earth Circulation System

questions.front: Name the three circulation cells that make up the Northern Hemisphere's general circulation, from equator to pole.
questions.back: Hadley cell (equator to about 30° latitude), Ferrel cell (about 30° to 60° latitude), and Polar cell (about 60° to the pole).
questions.explanation: Each cell is a separate convective loop; together they replace the simple single-cell circulation that would exist on a non-rotating Earth, and the boundaries between them mark the semi-permanent surface pressure belts.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.3 Rotating Earth Circulation System

questions.front: In the Polar cell, what is the general surface wind direction, and what causes it?
questions.back: Easterly, because air sinking at the poles diverges outward and is deflected by the Coriolis force.
options: Westerly, because the Polar cell mirrors the mid-latitude Ferrel cell circulation.
Variable and calm, because Coriolis force is strongest at the poles and cancels the pressure gradient.
Easterly, because air sinking at the poles diverges outward and is deflected by the Coriolis force.
questions.explanation: As air sinks over the poles and spreads outward toward lower latitudes, the Coriolis force deflects it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, producing the polar easterlies — the opposite direction from the mid-latitude Ferrel cell's poleward surface flow.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.3 Rotating Earth Circulation System

questions.front: Why do jet stream winds generally flow from west to east around the globe?
questions.back: Air conserves its eastward momentum as it moves poleward, while the surface beneath it rotates more slowly, so it accelerates eastward relative to the ground.
options: Air conserves its eastward momentum as it moves poleward, while the surface beneath it rotates more slowly, so it accelerates eastward relative to the ground.
The pressure gradient force between the semi-permanent subtropical high-pressure belt and the polar low-pressure trough always points from west to east.
Friction between the fast-moving jet core and the slower tropopause air below drags the entire wind field eastward as the Earth rotates.
questions.explanation: A point on the equator moves faster relative to the Earth's axis than a point at higher latitude; air conserving its eastward momentum as it moves poleward therefore ends up moving faster eastward than the ground beneath it — the same underlying principle that produces the surface Coriolis effect.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.4.1 Direction of Wind Flow

questions.front: What altitude range and maximum speed can jet stream winds reach, according to the Aviation Weather Handbook?
questions.back: Jet streams are typically found between about FL200 and FL450, with speeds that can exceed 275 mph (about 239 knots).
questions.explanation: Jet stream speeds are typically highest in winter because the temperature contrast between hot and cold air masses is then most pronounced — the same temperature-gradient relationship that determines jet stream strength year-round.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.4.2 Location

questions.front: A pilot is briefed on two jet stream cores: one near 30°N and one near 50°-60°N. Which one is the polar front jet?
questions.back: The one near 50°-60°N, since it forms along the boundary between the Ferrel and Polar cells.
options: The one near 30°N, since it forms along the boundary between the Hadley and Ferrel cells.
The one near 50°-60°N, since it forms along the boundary between the Ferrel and Polar cells.
Both are polar front jets; the subtropical jet only exists in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.explanation: The polar (front) jet sits at roughly 50°-60° latitude where the Ferrel and Polar cells meet and temperature contrast is greatest; the subtropical jet, near 30° latitude, forms at the Hadley/Ferrel boundary instead — mixing up the two locations is a common written-exam error.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.4.2 Location

questions.front: In which season are jet streams strongest, and why?
questions.back: Winter, because the temperature contrast between warm and cold air masses is most pronounced then, and jet stream strength increases with the temperature gradient.
questions.explanation: Stronger temperature gradients produce stronger pressure gradients aloft, which drive faster winds — the same relationship that makes jet streams track the boundary between hot and cold air year-round.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.4 Jet Streams

questions.front: How does the jet stream's position over North America typically change from winter to summer?
questions.back: It shifts northward, moving into Canada by summer, then moves back south into the United States as autumn approaches.
options: It stays anchored near 40°N latitude throughout the year, since jet position is fixed by tropopause height, not season.
It shifts southward into the Gulf of Mexico in summer to follow the strongest surface heating.
It shifts northward, moving into Canada by summer, then moves back south into the United States as autumn approaches.
questions.explanation: The jet stream tracks the sun's seasonal migration and the associated shift in the polar front, moving north in spring/summer and returning south in autumn/winter — which is why strong jet-stream headwinds and turbulence over the lower 48 states are more common in winter.

source.section: Chapter 9, Global Circulations and Jet Streams, Section 9.4.2 Location

questions.front: On a calm, sunny summer afternoon at a coastal airport, which way does the sea breeze typically flow, and what causes it?
questions.back: From sea to land, because faster-heating land creates lower surface pressure that draws in cooler marine air.
options: From sea to land, because faster-heating land creates lower surface pressure that draws in cooler marine air.
From land to sea, because warm air over the ocean rises and pulls surface air offshore.
From sea to land, but only when a synoptic-scale front happens to be passing through the area.
questions.explanation: Land has a lower heat capacity than water, so it warms faster during the day; the resulting pressure gradient (low over the warm land, high over the cooler water) drives low-level wind onshore — a purely local, diurnal circulation unrelated to frontal passage.

questions.front: Compare the typical timing and relative strength of a land breeze versus a sea breeze at the same coastal location.
questions.back: A land breeze blows from land to sea, forms at night into early morning, and is usually weaker than the daytime sea breeze.
questions.explanation: Nighttime radiational cooling produces a smaller land-water temperature contrast than daytime heating does, so the land breeze's pressure gradient — and thus its wind speed — is typically weaker than the sea breeze's.

questions.front: A narrow peninsula experiences unusually vigorous thunderstorm development during late morning or early afternoon on an otherwise unremarkable summer day. What coastal wind effect best explains this?
questions.back: Sea breezes forming along both shores of the peninsula converge near its center, producing stronger lift than either sea breeze front alone.
options: The peninsula blocks the prevailing sea breeze entirely, forcing air to rise mechanically over the high terrain.
Sea breezes forming along both shores of the peninsula converge near its center, producing stronger lift than either sea breeze front alone.
A single, unusually strong sea breeze front stalls over the peninsula because land breezes cannot form on narrow landmasses.
questions.explanation: When sea breezes develop along opposite shores of a narrow peninsula or island, they converge near the center, and this added convergence and lift — beyond what a single sea breeze front provides — can be enough to trigger showers and thunderstorms if the air is sufficiently moist and unstable.

source.section: Chapter 10, Wind, Section 10.6.1.2 Effects of Coastline Shape

questions.front: What two conditions must a region have in order to serve as a good air mass source region?
questions.back: It must have a fairly uniform surface, so the air acquires consistent properties, and weather systems must be light or stagnant enough for the air to remain over the region long enough to take on the temperature and moisture characteristics of the surface below.
questions.explanation: This is exactly why the continental United States is a poor air mass source region — frequent passage of weather disturbances disrupts any chance for air to stagnate and equilibrate with the surface beneath it.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.2 Air Masses

questions.front: An air mass is labeled 'mT.' What does this tell you about its source region and characteristics?
questions.back: It formed over water at low latitude, so it is warm and moist.
options: It formed over land at high latitude, so it is cold and dry.
It formed over water at high latitude, so it is cool and moist.
It formed over water at low latitude, so it is warm and moist.
questions.explanation: The first letter describes moisture — continental (c) for dry, land-formed air, or maritime (m) for moist, water-formed air — and the second letter describes temperature (Arctic, Polar, or Tropical); 'mT' therefore means maritime tropical, the classic warm, moist Gulf of Mexico source air mass.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.2.1 Air Mass Classification

questions.front: What are the temperature and moisture characteristics of a continental polar (cP) air mass, and where does it typically originate?
questions.back: Cold and dry; it typically originates over the snow-covered interior of Canada and Alaska.
questions.explanation: The 'c' (continental) indicates it formed over land and is therefore dry, while 'P' (polar) indicates it formed at high latitude and is therefore cold — cP air commonly brings clear, cold weather to the northern U.S. in winter.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Sections 11.2.1.3 (Five Air Masses) and 11.2.2 (Air Mass Modification)

questions.front: Which air mass is the primary source of moisture for precipitation over the Gulf Coast and eastern United States during summer?
questions.back: Maritime tropical (mT) air moving north from the Gulf of Mexico and the tropical Atlantic.
options: Maritime tropical (mT) air moving north from the Gulf of Mexico and the tropical Atlantic.
Continental tropical (cT) air pumped north off the Mexican Plateau and southwestern deserts.
Maritime polar (mP) air moving south out of the North Pacific and North Atlantic.
questions.explanation: mT air carries the warmth and abundant moisture of tropical ocean surfaces; cT air, by contrast, is hot and dry and can produce drought if it stagnates over the Midwest, which is why confusing the two 'tropical' air masses is a common exam trap.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.2.2 Air Mass Modification

questions.front: In late autumn, cold, dry, stable continental polar air flows across one of the still-unfrozen Great Lakes. What typically happens to the air mass's stability and cloud cover as it crosses the lake?
questions.back: The air is warmed and moistened from below, stability decreases, and shallow cumuliform clouds with heavy lee-side snow showers develop.
options: The air is cooled and dried further, stability increases, and the lake shore stays clear while snow falls only over open water.
The air is warmed and moistened from below, stability decreases, and shallow cumuliform clouds with heavy lee-side snow showers develop.
The air mass properties are unchanged, because a single lake is too small to modify an entire continental air mass.
questions.explanation: This is the lake-effect process: relatively warm, ice-free lake water heats and moistens the base of the cold, dry, stable air mass moving over it, decreasing its stability and generating convective clouds that can dump heavy snow on the lee shore.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.2.2.1 Lake Effect

questions.front: What is the typical forward speed range of a warm front?
questions.back: About 10 to 25 mph.
questions.explanation: Warm fronts move slowly because the warm air must gradually override the retreating cooler, denser air ahead of it along a gentle frontal slope — contrast this with cold fronts, which typically move nearly twice as fast.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.1 Warm Front

questions.front: Several hours before a warm front reaches an airport, what trend should a pilot expect in cloud type, wind, and barometric pressure?
questions.back: Lowering cirriform and stratiform clouds, wind from the south-southeast, and barometric pressure that continues to fall.
options: Building towering cumulus clouds, gusty variable wind, and barometric pressure that bottoms out and then rises quickly.
Clearing skies, a wind shift to the northwest, and rapidly rising barometric pressure.
Lowering cirriform and stratiform clouds, wind from the south-southeast, and barometric pressure that continues to fall.
questions.explanation: The other two options both describe cold front passage, not the approach of a warm front — a classic mix-up. Ahead of a warm front, expect a lowering, thickening deck of cirriform then stratiform clouds, a south-southeasterly wind, and steadily falling pressure.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.1 Warm Front

questions.front: Why do warm fronts typically produce widespread stratiform clouds and steady precipitation rather than the showery, convective weather associated with cold fronts?
questions.back: The warm air overrides the retreating cold air along a gentle slope, producing gradual, broad-scale lift instead of abrupt lift.
options: The warm air overrides the retreating cold air along a gentle slope, producing gradual, broad-scale lift instead of abrupt lift.
Warm fronts are always associated with unstable air, which spreads precipitation over a wider area than stable air does.
Warm fronts move faster than cold fronts, so precipitation gets smeared out over a larger area ahead of the front.
questions.explanation: A warm front's gentle slope lifts warm air gradually over a large area, favoring widespread stratiform cloud decks and steady precipitation when the rising air is stable — the opposite of a cold front's steep slope, which forces abrupt lift and narrow bands of showers or thunderstorms.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.1 Warm Front

questions.front: How fast does a typical cold front move across the ground, and what is the fastest speed an extreme cold front has been recorded moving?
questions.back: Typically 25 to 30 mph, though extreme cold fronts have been recorded moving as fast as 60 mph.
questions.explanation: Cold, dense air acts like a snowplow at the surface, and fast-moving cold fronts are driven by strong pressure gradients behind them — the faster the front, the steeper and more violent the associated weather along its leading edge tends to be.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.2 Cold Front

questions.front: During the passage of a cold front, what should a pilot expect to observe?
questions.back: Poor visibility with gusty, variable wind, a rapid drop in temperature and dewpoint, and pressure bottoming out before it begins to rise.
options: Steadily improving visibility, a steady south-southwest wind, and pressure that levels off and then slowly falls.
Poor visibility with gusty, variable wind, a rapid drop in temperature and dewpoint, and pressure bottoming out before it begins to rise.
Stratiform clouds with drizzle, light and variable wind, and a dewpoint that stays steady throughout the passage.
questions.explanation: The other two options both describe warm front passage — the giveaway is the steady, gradual wind and pressure trend versus the abrupt, gusty, rapidly changing conditions of a real cold front passage.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.2 Cold Front

questions.front: A fast-moving cold front is overtaking a mass of unstable, warm air. Which hazard is most specifically associated with this scenario, and what causes it?
questions.back: A continuous line of thunderstorms, or squall line, forming along or ahead of the front due to its steep slope and rapid speed.
options: Widespread stratiform icing extending 100 miles or more ahead of the front because of its gentle overriding slope.
A slow-moving, stationary line of drizzle and fog hugging the surface for a day or more behind the front.
A continuous line of thunderstorms, or squall line, forming along or ahead of the front due to its steep slope and rapid speed.
questions.explanation: Friction between the ground and a fast-moving cold front steepens its frontal surface even further, concentrating lift into a narrow zone; if the overtaken air is unstable, this can organize into a squall line, which is a serious hazard because of its intensity and speed.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.2 Cold Front

questions.front: What defines a stationary front, and how long can its associated weather persist?
questions.back: A stationary front forms where the opposing forces of two air masses are relatively equal, so the boundary between them stops advancing; its weather, a mixture of what would be found along a warm front and a cold front, can persist for days.
questions.explanation: Because neither air mass is winning the push, the front doesn't advance, and pilots can be stuck with the same marginal weather for an extended period until the pressure pattern changes enough to move the front.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.3 Stationary Front

questions.front: In a warm front occlusion, the air ahead of the original warm front is colder than the air behind the overtaking cold front. What happens as a result, and how does the associated weather compare to a cold front occlusion?
questions.back: The cold front rides up and over the warm front aloft; if the lifted air is unstable, the weather is more severe than a cold front occlusion.
options: The cold front rides up and over the warm front aloft; if the lifted air is unstable, the weather is more severe than a cold front occlusion.
The cold front undercuts the warm front at the surface exactly as in a cold front occlusion, producing identical weather regardless of which air is colder.
The two fronts cancel each other out, and the occlusion dissipates without producing significant weather.
questions.explanation: Which type of occlusion forms depends on which air mass is coldest, not simply which front is faster. In a warm front occlusion the coldest air is ahead of the warm front, so the invading cold front rides up and over it rather than undercutting it, and if the lifted air is unstable this tends to produce more severe weather, including embedded thunderstorms.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.4 Occluded Front

questions.front: As an occluded front approaches and then passes an airport, what sequence of frontal weather should a pilot expect?
questions.back: Warm-front-type weather prevails as the occlusion approaches, immediately followed by cold-front-type weather as the occlusion passes, because the occluded front combines the characteristics of both fronts.
questions.explanation: An occluded front forms when a faster cold front catches up to and overtakes a warm front, so its passage effectively delivers both frontal weather sequences back-to-back rather than just one.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model, Section 11.3.4 Occluded Front

questions.front: A pilot assumes that any squall line must be attached to a cold front. Why is this assumption incorrect?
questions.back: A squall line is a non-frontal, narrow band of thunderstorms that often forms ahead of a cold front but can also develop far from any front.
options: Squall lines only form along stationary fronts, never along cold fronts, so the pilot has the wrong front type in mind.
A squall line is a non-frontal, narrow band of thunderstorms that often forms ahead of a cold front but can also develop far from any front.
Squall lines are just another name for a cold front's leading edge, so the pilot's assumption is actually correct.
questions.explanation: Squall lines commonly develop ahead of fast-moving cold fronts, which is why they're often associated with them, but the handbook specifically classifies them as non-frontal — they can form in unstable air well away from any frontal boundary, so a pilot cannot assume a front must be nearby.

source.section: Chapter 22, Thunderstorms, Multicell Line Thunderstorm (Squall Line) discussion

questions.front: Why are squall lines considered one of the most hazardous weather phenomena for pilots to deal with in flight?
questions.back: A squall line can extend laterally for hundreds of miles and is usually too tall to fly over, too dangerous to fly through or under, and difficult to circumnavigate, making it an effective barrier to air traffic.
questions.explanation: Unlike an isolated cell that a pilot might deviate around easily, a squall line's sheer length and continuity of intense convection often leave no safe gap nearby, forcing significant deviations or a divert/delay decision.

source.section: Chapter 22, Thunderstorms, Multicell Line Thunderstorm (Squall Line) discussion

questions.front: Under the AIM's PIREP turbulence-reporting criteria, which description matches 'light' turbulence intensity?
questions.back: Occupants feel a slight strain against their seat belts, and unsecured objects may be displaced slightly
options: Occupants feel a slight strain against their seat belts, and unsecured objects may be displaced slightly
Occupants are forced violently against the seat belts, and walking is impossible
There is a definite strain against the seat belt and unsecured objects are dislodged
questions.explanation: Light turbulence causes only momentary, slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude. The distinction most pilots blur is light vs. moderate: if objects are merely displaced, call it light; once objects are dislodged and walking is difficult, it's moderate.

questions.front: Recall the AIM definition of 'severe' turbulence for PIREP reporting purposes.
questions.back: Large, abrupt changes in altitude and/or attitude occur, often with large variations in indicated airspeed; the aircraft may be momentarily out of control; occupants are forced violently against their seat belts.
questions.explanation: Severe turbulence is the threshold at which control authority is momentarily lost — that word 'control' is what separates it from moderate turbulence, where the aircraft stays in positive control the whole time.

questions.front: A pilot reports that unsecured objects were dislodged from their seats, walking in the cabin was difficult, but the aircraft never went out of control. Which PIREP turbulence intensity should be reported?
questions.back: Moderate
options: Severe
Moderate
Light
questions.explanation: Moderate turbulence dislodges unsecured objects and makes walking difficult, but the aircraft stays under positive control throughout — losing control, even momentarily, is what pushes a report into the severe category.

questions.front: What intensity descriptor should a pilot append to a PIREP when reporting turbulence encountered above 15,000 feet MSL in clear air, unassociated with clouds or convective activity?
