questions.back: CAT (clear air turbulence), reported along with the standard intensity level (e.g., 'moderate CAT').
questions.explanation: The AIM specifically calls out CAT for high-altitude turbulence not tied to clouds; using that term in a PIREP helps other crews and forecasters distinguish it from convective or mechanical turbulence.

questions.front: During cruise at FL350 a crew reports large, abrupt pitch and roll excursions, a momentary loss of positive control, and airspeed fluctuating by 20 knots, with no structural damage. How should this turbulence be classified in the PIREP?
questions.back: Severe
options: Extreme
Moderate
Severe
questions.explanation: Momentary loss of control with large, abrupt attitude and airspeed changes is the textbook description of severe turbulence. Extreme turbulence goes a step further — the aircraft becomes practically impossible to control and may sustain structural damage, which did not happen here.

questions.front: What smooth, lens-shaped stationary cloud forms at the crests of a mountain wave and signals wave activity aloft?
questions.back: Altocumulus standing lenticular (ACSL) cloud — it forms at the wave crest and stays fixed in place relative to the terrain even though strong winds are blowing through it.
questions.explanation: Lenticular clouds mark the rising portion of each wave crest downwind of a ridge; air condenses on the windward side of the wave and evaporates on the lee side, so the cloud shape appears stationary even as the air moves rapidly through it.

source.section: Chapter 16, Mountain Weather — 16.2.7 Visual Indicators of Orographic Wind Fields

questions.front: Ragged, turbulent rotor clouds forming at or below ridge-crest level beneath a mountain wave typically indicate what?
questions.back: Severe to extreme turbulence in the rotor circulation
options: Severe to extreme turbulence in the rotor circulation
A weakening wave system with only light chop expected
Icing conditions only, with negligible turbulence
questions.explanation: Rotor clouds mark a horizontal vortex of violently rotating air beneath the wave crest; this is among the most turbulent phenomena in the atmosphere, which is why pilots are cautioned to avoid the area under lenticular clouds near mountains.

source.section: Chapter 16, Mountain Weather — 16.2.5 Persistent Horizontal Roll Vortices (Rotors)

questions.front: What approximate wind speed and crossing angle over a ridge favor the development of a mountain wave?
questions.back: Wind of about 15 knots or greater blowing across the ridge at an intersection angle of at least 30 degrees to the ridge line (i.e., not blowing nearly parallel to the range).
questions.explanation: Both criteria matter: wind that is too weak, or that runs nearly parallel to the ridge line, won't set up the standing-wave oscillation that produces downstream turbulence and rotor circulation on the lee side.

questions.front: When crossing a mountain ridge in conditions favorable for mountain wave turbulence, what technique reduces risk if severe turbulence or downdrafts are encountered?
questions.back: Approach the ridge at about a 45-degree angle, allowing a quick turn away from rising terrain
options: Cross the ridge perpendicular and at the lowest safe altitude to minimize exposure time
Approach the ridge at about a 45-degree angle, allowing a quick turn away from rising terrain
Fly directly downwind of the ridge to use the tailwind to climb over it faster
questions.explanation: Crossing at an angle, rather than head-on, lets a pilot who encounters severe downdrafts turn away from rising terrain without a full 180-degree reversal, a maneuver that costs precious altitude when descending air already exceeds the airplane's climb capability.

questions.front: A pilot notices a single band of lenticular clouds stacked directly over and just downwind of a ridge, with no organized wave clouds farther downstream. Compared to a long train of several lenticular bands extending many miles downwind, this pattern is most consistent with which type of mountain wave?
questions.back: A vertically propagating mountain wave, whose energy radiates upward rather than trapping in a horizontal train
options: A vertically propagating mountain wave, whose energy radiates upward rather than trapping in a horizontal train
A trapped lee wave, which by definition produces a long series of wave crests far downwind
Mechanical turbulence with no organized wave structure at all
questions.explanation: Trapped lee waves form a repeating downwind train of wave crests (and lenticular clouds) that can extend 100+ miles, while a vertically propagating wave stays fairly close to the ridge and sends its energy upward, sometimes into the stratosphere — the horizontal cloud pattern is the clue distinguishing the two.

source.section: Chapter 16, Mountain Weather — 16.2.3 Vertically Propagating Mountain Waves / 16.2.4 Trapped Lee Waves

questions.front: Low-level wind shear (LLWS) is best defined as which of the following?
questions.back: A sudden change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance near the surface
options: A gradual, steady increase in headwind component as an aircraft climbs through the first 5,000 feet
Any turbulence encountered while below the freezing level in stratiform clouds
A sudden change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance near the surface
questions.explanation: The defining feature of wind shear is abruptness over a short distance, horizontal or vertical. A gradual wind change, by contrast, is easy for an aircraft and its autopilot to compensate for and is not considered hazardous shear.

questions.front: What is the recommended pilot response upon recognizing a wind shear or microburst encounter during approach or departure?
questions.back: Apply maximum available thrust/power immediately, establish and hold the recommended nose-up pitch attitude (fly pitch, not airspeed), and do not change the flap or gear configuration until clear of the shear.
questions.explanation: Airspeed indications lag and can be unreliable during a shear encounter, so the escape maneuver is flown on pitch attitude and full power rather than chasing the airspeed indicator, which invites over-controlling at the worst possible moment.

source.section: Chapter 26, Advisories — 26.8 Low-Level Wind Shear (LLWS)/Microburst Advisories

questions.front: The Low-Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWAS), installed at many towered airports, is designed primarily to detect wind shear generated by which phenomenon?
questions.back: Thunderstorm outflow and gust fronts, including microbursts, near the airport surface
options: Clear air turbulence associated with the jet stream at cruise altitudes
Thunderstorm outflow and gust fronts, including microbursts, near the airport surface
Wingtip vortices from departing heavy aircraft
questions.explanation: LLWAS uses a network of surface anemometers around the airfield to detect the sudden wind shifts caused by convective outflow so towers can issue wind shear alerts; it has no ability to sense clear air turbulence aloft or wake vortices.

source.section: Chapter 26, Advisories — 26.8 Low-Level Wind Shear (LLWS)/Microburst Advisories

questions.front: On a stabilized ILS approach, a pilot notices indicated airspeed suddenly increase 15 knots above target with no power change, followed by the aircraft rising above glideslope. What hazard do these fluctuations suggest, and what should the pilot do?
questions.back: These are classic indications of wind shear — the initial airspeed/altitude gain from an increasing headwind is often followed by the opposite: a performance-decreasing shear (decreasing headwind or tailwind) and possible downdraft. The pilot should discontinue the approach and fly the wind shear escape maneuver (full power, target pitch attitude) rather than attempting to salvage the landing.
questions.explanation: Many crews are tempted to reduce power to correct the initial 'high and fast' deviation, which is exactly wrong — that deviation is often the leading edge of a shear that reverses into a performance-decreasing headwind loss or downdraft moments later.

questions.front: A strong, shallow nocturnal temperature inversion topped by a low-level jet of 40+ knots is a classic setup for what hazard, even with no thunderstorms present?
questions.back: Significant wind shear between the calm surface air and the jet just above it
options: Significant wind shear between the calm surface air and the jet just above it
Widespread structural icing due to supercooled large droplets
Clear air turbulence at flight levels above 30,000 feet
questions.explanation: On clear, calm nights, radiational cooling can decouple the light surface wind from the much stronger flow just a few hundred feet up, creating a sharp shear layer at the top of the inversion — this non-convective wind shear catches pilots off guard because there's no thunderstorm to warn them.

questions.front: Recall the approximate horizontal diameter and total lifespan of a typical microburst.
questions.back: About 2.5 miles (roughly 1 to 4 km) or less in diameter at the surface, with a total life cycle of only about 5 to 15 minutes from onset to dissipation.
questions.explanation: Its small size and short life are exactly why microbursts are so dangerous — one can form and impact final approach before it's ever detected or reported, and it's often gone by the time the next aircraft passes the same spot.

questions.front: An aircraft flying through a microburst on final approach first experiences an increasing headwind (and rising performance). What does it typically encounter in the second half of the shear?
questions.back: A decreasing headwind that becomes a tailwind, plus a strong downdraft — both performance-decreasing
options: A second, stronger increasing headwind that further increases performance
Calm, undisturbed air with no further hazard
A decreasing headwind that becomes a tailwind, plus a strong downdraft — both performance-decreasing
questions.explanation: A microburst encounter is a two-phase trap: the initial headwind gain (performance-increasing shear) can lull a pilot into reducing power right before the outflow reverses to a tailwind plus downdraft (performance-decreasing shear) that can drive the aircraft toward the ground.

questions.front: What downdraft rate can a strong microburst produce, and roughly how soon after the outflow reaches the surface does peak wind intensity occur?
questions.back: Downdrafts can exceed 6,000 feet per minute, with peak wind intensity typically occurring within about 5 minutes after the outflow first strikes the surface.
questions.explanation: That descent rate is well beyond the climb performance of virtually any aircraft, which is why the only survivable response is to avoid a microburst rather than try to fly through it; the short time-to-peak also means a PIREP from the aircraft just ahead may already be stale.

questions.front: In a dry, high-based convective environment, which visual cue commonly precedes a dry microburst?
questions.back: Virga (precipitation evaporating before reaching the ground) hanging beneath a high cloud base
options: Virga (precipitation evaporating before reaching the ground) hanging beneath a high cloud base
A well-developed rain shaft reaching the surface with heavy rain
A rainbow forming opposite the sun beneath the cloud
questions.explanation: In a dry microburst, evaporative cooling of falling precipitation, seen as virga, chills and accelerates the air downward before any rain reaches the ground — unlike a wet microburst, which is accompanied by heavy rain at the surface.

questions.front: An aircraft on short final at 400 feet AGL suddenly loses 20 knots of airspeed and begins sinking below glideslope as it enters a microburst outflow. What is the correct immediate response?
questions.back: Apply maximum thrust and fly the recommended nose-up pitch attitude for a wind shear escape, without changing the flap configuration
options: Reduce pitch to regain the lost airspeed before adding power, then reconfigure flaps for a go-around
Apply maximum thrust and fly the recommended nose-up pitch attitude for a wind shear escape, without changing the flap configuration
Continue the approach at idle power since the tailwind component will soon reverse back to a headwind
questions.explanation: In a low-altitude microburst encounter there is no time to trade pitch for airspeed — full power and a fixed escape pitch attitude, flown immediately, gives the best chance of clearing the downdraft; reconfiguring flaps or waiting for the shear to reverse can cost the altitude margin needed to survive it.

source.section: Chapter 26, Advisories — 26.8 Low-Level Wind Shear (LLWS)/Microburst Advisories

questions.front: Define clear air turbulence (CAT) as used in aviation weather reporting.
questions.back: Turbulence encountered in air with no significant cloudiness and away from convective activity, most often at flight levels above 15,000 feet MSL and frequently associated with the strong wind shear near jet streams.
questions.explanation: The 'clear air' in the name is literal — CAT gives no visual warning the way a cumulonimbus tower would, which is exactly what makes it hazardous to unsuspecting crews.

questions.front: Clear air turbulence is most frequently encountered in which location relative to a jet stream?
questions.back: In the zones of strong wind shear near the jet core, especially on its cold, poleward side
options: In the zones of strong wind shear near the jet core, especially on its cold, poleward side
Well below the jet stream, near the surface where friction is greatest
Only directly inside the visible cirrus shield that often accompanies the jet
questions.explanation: CAT forms where wind speed and/or direction change sharply over a short distance; the tightest gradients are typically found along the cold, poleward side of the jet stream and near the tropopause, not at the surface or only inside visible cirrus.

questions.front: Why can't airborne weather radar be used to detect clear air turbulence ahead of the aircraft?
questions.back: Airborne radar detects precipitation, and CAT occurs in clear air with nothing to reflect the beam
options: CAT only occurs below the altitudes at which airborne weather radar operates
Airborne radar is disabled automatically above 15,000 feet to prevent false returns
Airborne radar detects precipitation, and CAT occurs in clear air with nothing to reflect the beam
questions.explanation: Weather radar works by bouncing energy off water or ice particles; since CAT by definition happens in cloud-free air, there is nothing for the radar to reflect off, so PIREPs and turbulence forecast products remain the primary tools for anticipating it.

questions.front: Under what combination of aircraft weight, configuration, and speed is wingtip vortex (wake turbulence) strength the greatest?
questions.back: Heavy, Clean, and Slow (HCS) — the generating aircraft is at a high gross weight, in a clean configuration (flaps up), and flying slowly, all of which require a high angle of attack and produce the strongest trailing vortices.
questions.explanation: Remember it as 'Heavy, Clean, Slow' — each factor independently raises the lift coefficient (and thus vortex strength) the wing must generate, so an aircraft that is heavy and clean and slow produces the worst-case wake.

questions.front: As wingtip vortices descend behind a large aircraft, what typically happens to their sink rate as they approach the ground?
questions.back: They slow their descent, level off within about 100–200 feet of the surface, and drift laterally
options: They slow their descent, level off within about 100–200 feet of the surface, and drift laterally
They accelerate downward continuously until they dissipate at ground level
They immediately stop sinking at rotation altitude and remain fixed at that height
questions.explanation: Vortices sink at a few hundred feet per minute initially, but as they near the ground they level off and begin to drift horizontally — with a light crosswind, the upwind vortex can stall over the touchdown zone rather than moving away, which is why a light quartering tailwind is considered particularly hazardous.

questions.front: When cleared to land behind a heavy aircraft on the same runway under IFR, what technique helps a pilot avoid its wake turbulence?
questions.back: Stay at or above the preceding aircraft's final approach flight path and plan to land beyond its touchdown point
options: Descend below the preceding aircraft's glidepath to stay clear of its wake, which sinks upward behind the aircraft
Stay at or above the preceding aircraft's final approach flight path and plan to land beyond its touchdown point
Land well before the preceding aircraft's touchdown point so as to be clear of it before its vortices develop
questions.explanation: Because vortices sink and drift, the safest zone is above the generating aircraft's flight path and beyond where it touched down; ATC wake turbulence separation reduces the risk, but on a visual or converging approach the pilot bears final responsibility for maintaining that clearance.

questions.front: On an IFR flight, ATC issues wake turbulence separation and a cautionary advisory, but the pilot still experiences a brief uncommanded roll from a preceding heavy aircraft's wake. Who bears ultimate responsibility for wake turbulence avoidance, and what should a concerned pilot do beforehand?
questions.back: The pilot-in-command bears ultimate responsibility for wake turbulence avoidance, regardless of ATC separation or cautionary advisories issued. If the assigned spacing seems insufficient, the pilot should request additional spacing, a different runway, or a delay from ATC before accepting the clearance.
questions.explanation: ATC wake turbulence separation minima and 'caution wake turbulence' advisories are aids, not guarantees — the AIM is explicit that avoiding wake turbulence is the pilot's responsibility, since only the pilot can judge conditions, like a light quartering tailwind, that standard procedures don't fully account for.

questions.front: What does the temperature–dewpoint spread reported in a METAR primarily indicate about the air near the surface?
questions.back: How close the air is to being saturated with moisture.
options: How close the air is to being saturated with moisture
The current barometric pressure trend at the station
The strength and direction of the surface wind
questions.explanation: The spread is temperature minus dewpoint; a small spread means the air holds nearly all the water vapor it can at that temperature (high relative humidity), while a large spread means the air is relatively dry. It says nothing directly about pressure or wind.

questions.front: A pilot notices the temperature–dewpoint spread at an airport has been steadily narrowing over the past few hours while the sky remains mostly clear. What does this trend suggest?
questions.back: The air is nearing saturation, so cloud or fog is becoming more likely to form.
options: A frontal passage has just occurred at this station
The air is becoming noticeably drier than it was
The air is nearing saturation, so cloud or fog is more likely
questions.explanation: A narrowing spread means relative humidity is rising toward 100%; once temperature and dewpoint converge, the air is saturated and visible moisture can form. A narrowing spread alone does not confirm that a front has passed.

questions.front: Which altitude range and composition characterize the low cloud family?
questions.back: Surface to about 6,500 feet AGL, composed mainly of water droplets, including stratus, stratocumulus, and cumulus.
options: 6,500 to 20,000 feet AGL, composed mainly of ice crystals
Surface to about 6,500 feet AGL, composed mainly of water droplets
Above 20,000 feet AGL, composed mainly of ice crystals
questions.explanation: Low clouds form in the warmer air near the surface, so they're built of liquid water droplets rather than ice — which is why the low cloud family is the primary source of structural icing.

source.section: Chapter 12, Vertical Motion and Clouds (Cloud Levels, Table 12-3); Appendix A, Cloud Types

questions.front: What altitude range defines the middle cloud family, and what prefix identifies its cloud types?
questions.back: Roughly 6,500 to 23,000 feet AGL in temperate latitudes (the exact range varies with latitude); middle clouds carry the prefix 'alto-' (altocumulus, altostratus).
questions.explanation: The 'alto' prefix is a quick memory cue for the middle layer, distinguishing it from 'cirro-' (high clouds) and the unprefixed low cloud names.

source.section: Chapter 12, Vertical Motion and Clouds (Cloud Levels, Table 12-3)

questions.front: High clouds such as cirrus and cirrostratus are composed almost entirely of ice crystals. What is the main practical significance of this for a pilot?
questions.back: They rarely cause structural icing, but their pattern can signal weather developing well ahead of the route.
options: They rarely cause icing, but can signal weather developing well ahead
They pose a significant structural icing hazard to aircraft flying through them
They always mark an area of severe turbulence directly beneath the cloud
questions.explanation: Structural icing requires supercooled liquid water, and ice crystals mostly bounce off airframes. Cirrus thickening ahead of a route is instead a classic early sign of an approaching weather system, not proof of turbulence below.

questions.front: Increasing and thickening cirrus clouds streaming ahead of an aircraft's route most likely indicate which of the following?
questions.back: A warm front, or the weather system ahead of it, may be approaching — cirrus thickening into cirrostratus is a classic overrunning signature that precedes a warm front's surface position.
options: A dry cold front has just passed through the area
Convective activity is imminent within the next hour
A warm front (or its associated weather) may be approaching
questions.explanation: Cirriform clouds are noted as a typical sign of an approaching warm front well ahead of the surface front, giving pilots advance notice before precipitation reaches the airport. A dry cold front passage and imminent convective activity are not consistent with simply increasing, thickening cirrus.

source.section: Chapter 11, Air Masses, Fronts, and the Wave Cyclone Model

questions.front: Smooth, lens-shaped clouds observed standing nearly stationary downwind of a mountain range most directly indicate the presence of what phenomenon?
questions.back: Mountain wave activity, which can produce severe turbulence and strong up- and downdrafts even in clear air.
options: A slow-moving warm front approaching from the west
Mountain wave activity, with possible severe turbulence
Localized radiation fog forming in the valley below
questions.explanation: Altocumulus standing lenticular clouds form as stable air flows over a mountain and oscillates downstream; their smooth, stacked, lens shape is a visual warning of mountain wave turbulence rather than frontal weather.

questions.front: Mammatus clouds hanging from the underside of an anvil are most closely associated with which condition?
questions.back: A severe or decaying thunderstorm; the pouch-like clouds form from sinking, cooled air in the storm's outflow and downdraft.
options: A severe or decaying thunderstorm, warranting continued caution for turbulence
A weakening stratus deck producing only light drizzle
Stable air with no significant hazard to flight
questions.explanation: Mammatus are often mistaken for a sign the storm has passed and is now harmless, but the turbulence and downdrafts that produced them can persist even as the parent cell weakens.

questions.front: A cloud layer with a flat, uniform, sheet-like appearance rather than a puffy, heaped one most directly tells a pilot that the air in that layer is:
questions.back: Stable — stratiform (sheet-like) clouds form in stable air that resists vertical motion, while cumuliform (heaped) clouds form in unstable air.
options: Unstable, with active vertical currents throughout
Saturated at every altitude below the cloud base
Stable, resisting vertical motion
questions.explanation: Stable air resists lifting, so any moisture that does condense spreads out horizontally into layers rather than building upward, which is the opposite of the towering look produced by unstable, rising air.

questions.front: What does the vertical development of a towering cumulus cloud indicate about the air mass it's growing in?
questions.back: Strong vertical (convective) currents and an unstable air mass, with turbulence, icing, and possible precipitation likely within and near the cloud.
questions.explanation: Towering cumulus marks active convection; it's a visual cue to expect a bumpy ride and to treat the cloud as a potential building thunderstorm cell if growth continues.

questions.front: What primarily distinguishes advection fog from other fog types in terms of the wind needed for it to form?
questions.back: A light to moderate wind is needed to carry warm, moist air over a colder surface until it cools to saturation.
options: Advection fog only forms in completely still air over open water
A light to moderate wind is needed to carry warm, moist air over a colder surface
Advection fog requires little or no wind, just like radiation fog
questions.explanation: Unlike radiation fog, which needs calm winds under a clear, still night sky, advection fog depends on horizontal air movement — that's the 'advection' in its name.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: Give a classic real-world setting where advection fog commonly forms.
questions.back: Warm, moist air moving over a colder surface — for example, moist ocean air moving over cooler coastal waters or land, or moist air blowing across snow-covered ground; coastal areas are especially prone to it.
questions.explanation: Coastal airports see frequent advection fog because onshore winds regularly push warm, moist air over cold water or cold land, cooling it to saturation as it travels.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: Upslope fog forms primarily through which process?
questions.back: Moist, stable air is mechanically lifted up sloping terrain and cools adiabatically until it reaches saturation.
options: Moist, stable air is forced up sloping terrain and cools adiabatically to saturation
Cold air drains downhill overnight and pools in a low valley
Rain falling from a cloud deck evaporates into the air near the ground
questions.explanation: Because the lifting is mechanical, driven by wind pushing air uphill rather than by radiational cooling, upslope fog needs both a moisture source and wind — and can form even under an overcast sky, unlike radiation fog.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: What two ingredients are necessary for upslope fog to form?
questions.back: Moist, stable air and a wind component that carries that air up sloping terrain, cooling it adiabatically to the saturation point.
questions.explanation: Both a moisture source and rising terrain with wind to drive the air uphill are required — remove either the wind or the slope and the mechanism disappears.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: Steam fog (sometimes called sea smoke) typically forms under which condition?
questions.back: Cold air moves across relatively warm water, and evaporation from the water surface quickly saturates the cold air just above it.
options: Warm, moist air moves across a colder body of water
Rain falls from a warm cloud deck into a shallow layer of cold surface air
Cold, dry air moves across a relatively warm body of water
questions.explanation: This is essentially the reverse setup from advection fog: here the water is the warm source and the air is cold, so moisture evaporating off the surface condenses almost immediately into rising wisps of fog.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: What hazard is most closely associated with flying through steam fog over open water, and why does it occur?
questions.back: Low-level turbulence and possible airframe icing, because the air directly above the relatively warm water is highly unstable and quickly saturated with moisture evaporating into the cold air above.
questions.explanation: Steam fog signals an unstable, moisture-rich layer right at the surface — a hazard particularly noted in cold-lake and arctic operations where 'sea smoke' forms.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: Frontal (precipitation-induced) fog most commonly develops when:
questions.back: Warm rain falling through cooler surface air evaporates and adds moisture, raising the dewpoint until the air becomes saturated and fog forms.
options: A cold front pushes a wall of dust and dry air ahead of it
Relatively warm rain falls through cooler surface air and evaporates, raising the dewpoint to saturation
Clear skies and calm winds let the surface radiate heat away overnight
questions.explanation: Unlike other fog types that form by cooling the air down to its dewpoint, frontal/precipitation-induced fog forms by raising the dewpoint through added moisture — that's why it's commonly seen ahead of warm fronts and along slow-moving cold fronts with steady rain.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: What is the term for fog that forms when falling rain evaporates into and saturates the cooler air near the surface, and where is it most commonly encountered?
questions.back: Precipitation-induced (frontal) fog; it's most commonly encountered ahead of a warm front or along a slow-moving cold front where rain is falling into cooler surface air.
questions.explanation: This fog type is unusual among fog types in forming by adding moisture (raising the dewpoint) rather than by cooling the air down to it.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility

questions.front: An aircraft encounters freezing rain during a descent through 4,000 feet. What does this observation most reliably tell the pilot about the temperature structure of the atmosphere above?
questions.back: There is a warm layer aloft — a temperature inversion — where snow melted into rain, sitting above a shallow subfreezing layer near the surface that the raindrops did not have time to refreeze in before reaching the aircraft.
options: A layer of above-freezing air aloft sits over a shallow subfreezing layer near the surface
The entire column of air from the surface upward is below freezing
The freezing level is at the surface and it gets colder steadily with altitude
questions.explanation: Freezing rain is direct evidence of an inversion: without a warm layer aloft to melt falling snow into liquid, there would be no supercooled raindrops to freeze on contact — a classic overrunning (warm front) signature.

questions.front: Besides confirming supercooled liquid precipitation, what does a pilot report of freezing rain reveal about the vertical temperature profile, and why does that matter operationally?
questions.back: It reveals a temperature inversion — a layer of above-freezing air aloft sitting over a shallow subfreezing layer at the surface. Operationally this matters because climbing does not automatically escape the icing (the warm layer may hold supercooled drops too); the safer escape is often to find air that is above freezing all the way to the surface, or to stay below a very thin subfreezing layer.
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes assume climbing always escapes icing, but with freezing rain the worst icing is often just above the surface layer, right in the melting/refreezing zone — recognizing the inversion is what should drive the escape decision.

questions.front: Ice pellets (sleet) are being reported at the surface at an airport along your route. What should this tell you about conditions at some higher altitude nearby?
questions.back: Freezing rain is likely occurring higher up, at an altitude where the subfreezing layer is too thin for the melted snow to fully refreeze before reaching that level.
options: The entire atmosphere above the airport is at or below freezing
Ice pellets confirm that no warm layer exists anywhere in the column
Freezing rain is likely occurring higher up, where the subfreezing layer is thinner
questions.explanation: Ice pellets and freezing rain share the same setup — snow melting in a warm layer aloft — the only difference is how deep the subfreezing layer near the surface is. A pilot climbing through a column where ice pellets are reported at the surface should expect freezing rain on the way up.

questions.front: What single structural difference in the atmosphere determines whether snow that melts in a warm layer aloft reaches the ground as freezing rain versus ice pellets?
questions.back: The depth of the subfreezing layer near the surface: a shallow subfreezing layer leaves the melted drops liquid (supercooled), producing freezing rain, while a deeper subfreezing layer gives the drops time to refreeze into ice pellets before reaching the ground.
questions.explanation: Both precipitation types start identically, with snow melting in a warm layer aloft, so the surface report tells you how deep the near-surface cold layer is, not how much warm air exists above.

questions.front: What is virga, and how does it differ from ordinary rain or snow reaching the ground?
questions.back: Precipitation (rain or snow) that falls from a cloud but evaporates or sublimates before it reaches the ground.
options: A thin ice-crystal cloud layer that forms ahead of a warm front
Precipitation that falls from a cloud base but evaporates before reaching the surface
Freezing rain that falls through a shallow layer of subfreezing air
questions.explanation: Virga is easy to spot visually as streaks or wisps trailing beneath a cloud base that fade out before touching the ground — it signals dry air below cloud base.

source.section: Appendix A, Cloud Types (Cumulus, footnote on virga)

questions.front: What hazard can virga produce beneath a convective cloud, and why?
questions.back: Strong, localized downdrafts, potentially a microburst — as the falling precipitation evaporates it cools the surrounding air, which becomes denser and accelerates downward toward the surface.
questions.explanation: Virga is especially dangerous in dry climates where 'dry microbursts' form under high-based convective clouds with little or no rain reaching the ground, catching pilots off guard because there's no visible rain shaft to warn them.

source.section: Appendix A, Cloud Types; Chapter 22, Thunderstorms (Downburst and Microburst)

questions.front: Drizzle — small, uniformly sized water droplets falling slowly — typically originates from which type of cloud, and what does that reveal about the air mass?
questions.back: Stratus clouds, which indicates a stable air mass with little vertical motion.
options: Stratus clouds, indicating a stable air mass
Cumulonimbus clouds, indicating a highly unstable air mass
Cirrostratus clouds, indicating a very dry upper atmosphere
questions.explanation: Stable air lacks the vertical currents needed to build larger raindrops, so precipitation from stratiform clouds stays small and falls as drizzle — often paired with low ceilings and poor visibility.

source.section: Chapter 18, Weather and Obstructions to Visibility (Precipitation); Appendix A, Cloud Types (Stratus)

questions.front: During an instrument approach, ATIS reports light ice pellets and a surface temperature of −2°C. As you fly the approach and later execute a climbing missed approach, what icing condition should you specifically anticipate, and why?
questions.back: Anticipate freezing rain (supercooled drops) in a warm layer above the surface subfreezing layer as you climb. Ice pellets at the surface mean snow melted aloft and the near-surface cold layer only partially refroze it, so a layer of liquid, supercooled precipitation still exists somewhere above you, capable of rapid airframe ice accumulation during the climb.
questions.explanation: It's tempting to read 'ice pellets' as a comparatively benign, already-frozen precipitation type, but the same temperature profile that produces ice pellets at the surface routinely has freezing rain in the melting layer just above it — the layer a climbing missed approach must pass through.

questions.front: What are the three stages of a thunderstorm's life cycle, and which stage is dominated by continuous updrafts with no precipitation yet reaching the ground?
questions.back: The three stages are the towering cumulus (developing), mature, and dissipating stages. The towering cumulus stage is dominated by continuous updrafts, with the cloud still building and no precipitation reaching the surface.
questions.explanation: The towering cumulus stage is essentially 'all updraft' — recognizing it matters because turbulence and icing can already be significant even though radar/visual precipitation cues haven't appeared yet.

source.section: Thunderstorms – Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm (Towering Cumulus Stage)

questions.front: By definition, what event marks the beginning of a thunderstorm's mature stage?
questions.back: Precipitation begins falling from the cloud base and reaches the surface.
options: Precipitation begins falling from the cloud base and reaches the surface
The cloud top first penetrates the tropopause and forms an anvil
Lightning is first detected within the cell
questions.explanation: The onset of precipitation at the surface is the textbook dividing line between the towering cumulus and mature stages — it signals downdrafts have joined the updrafts, producing the storm's most violent turbulence, hail, and gust fronts.

source.section: Thunderstorms – Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm (Mature Stage)

questions.front: What single change in vertical air motion defines a thunderstorm cell's transition into its dissipating stage?
questions.back: Downdrafts spread throughout the entire cell and updrafts cease. Once downdrafts dominate the whole cloud, the storm has entered the dissipating stage; rainfall decreases while an anvil (cirrus) top may remain.
questions.explanation: Because updrafts fuel the storm's moisture supply, once downdrafts take over the entire cell there's nothing left to sustain growth — this is why the dissipating stage brings decreasing rain even though the cloud may still look large.

source.section: Thunderstorms – Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm (Dissipating Stage)

questions.front: During which stage of a thunderstorm's life cycle are hazards such as heavy rain, hail, frequent lightning, and severe turbulence typically at their worst?
questions.back: The mature stage
options: The mature stage
The towering cumulus stage
The dissipating stage
questions.explanation: The mature stage has strong updrafts and downdrafts coexisting side by side, producing the storm's peak turbulence, hail growth, lightning frequency, and gust-front outflow — a handy hook is 'mature means maximum.'

source.section: Thunderstorms – Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm (Mature Stage)

questions.front: What three basic ingredients must be present simultaneously for a thunderstorm to form?
questions.back: (1) Sufficient water vapor/moisture, (2) an unstable (conditionally unstable) lapse rate, and (3) a lifting mechanism to raise the moist air to its level of free convection.
questions.explanation: All three are required at once — moisture alone just makes clouds or fog, instability alone does nothing without a trigger, and lift alone in stable or dry air produces no convection.

questions.front: A cold front is advancing into a moist air mass that has a stable temperature lapse rate. Which condition needed for thunderstorm development is missing along the front?
questions.back: An unstable lapse rate
options: An unstable lapse rate
A source of lift
Sufficient low-level moisture
questions.explanation: The front already supplies lift and the air mass already has moisture, so the missing ingredient is instability — without a lapse rate that lets a lifted parcel stay warmer than its surroundings, rising air won't accelerate into a thunderstorm.

questions.front: Which of the following is an example of the 'lifting action' required for thunderstorm formation?
questions.back: Convective heating, orographic lift, or frontal lifting
options: Convective heating, orographic lift, or frontal lifting
A temperature inversion capping the boundary layer
High relative humidity throughout the troposphere
questions.explanation: Lift is the trigger that gets a parcel moving upward to its level of free convection; an inversion actually suppresses lift (it's a cap, not a trigger), and humidity alone supplies moisture, not lift.

questions.front: Why are embedded thunderstorms considered especially hazardous for IFR flight?
questions.back: They are hidden within larger cloud layers, so pilots cannot see and avoid them visually
options: They are hidden within larger cloud layers, so pilots cannot see and avoid them visually
They only occur in perfectly clear air, making them hard to detect by any means
They never produce turbulence or icing, only lightning
questions.explanation: Because embedded cells are buried in stratiform cloud decks, visual avoidance is impossible; pilots must rely on airborne weather radar, satellite/datalink imagery, or ATC/PIREP reports to route around them.

questions.front: What synoptic setup can produce embedded thunderstorms, and what tool is generally needed to detect them?
questions.back: Embedded thunderstorms can develop within widespread stratiform cloud layers — for example, where unstable, moist air is forced aloft during a warm-front-type occlusion — so they are hidden from view; because they're obscured from sight, airborne weather radar (or satellite/datalink weather) is typically needed to detect and avoid them.
questions.explanation: Since a stratus deck can completely mask a buried cumulonimbus cell, radar returns — not the pilot's eyes — become the primary avoidance tool in this scenario. The Aviation Weather Handbook notes that when the air forced aloft during a warm-front-type occlusion is unstable, embedded thunderstorms are likely.

source.section: Fronts – Occluded Front; Thunderstorms – Embedded Thunderstorms

questions.front: According to the AIM, by how many nautical miles should a pilot avoid a thunderstorm cell that has been identified as severe or is producing an intense radar echo?
questions.back: At least 20 NM
options: At least 20 NM
At least 5 NM
At least 50 NM
questions.explanation: The 20 NM rule accounts for hail, turbulence, and lightning that can extend well beyond the visible or radar-painted edge of a severe cell — a number worth memorizing verbatim for the written test.

questions.front: What vertical clearance rule does the AIM recommend when overflying the top of a known or suspected severe thunderstorm?
questions.back: Clear the top by at least 1,000 feet of altitude for each 10 knots of wind speed at the cloud top (for example, 5,000 feet of clearance if the wind at the top is 50 knots).
questions.explanation: Stronger winds aloft mean a larger area of turbulent outflow and wave-like disturbance downwind of the towering cell, so the required buffer scales directly with the top-level wind speed rather than being a fixed number.

questions.front: A pilot sees clear sky beneath the anvil of a distant thunderstorm and considers flying under it to save time. Why does the AIM advise against this?
questions.back: Severe to extreme clear-air turbulence (CAT) can exist in the seemingly clear air beneath the anvil
options: Severe to extreme clear-air turbulence (CAT) can exist in the seemingly clear air beneath the anvil
Radio communications always fail directly beneath any anvil cloud formation
Every anvil cloud contains an invisible embedded tornado underneath it
questions.explanation: The AIM states verbatim: 'Don't attempt to fly under the anvil of a thunderstorm — there is a potential for severe and extreme clear air turbulence.' Clear air beneath an anvil is not a guarantee of smooth air, since the turbulence can extend well beyond the visible cloud edge.

questions.front: Which type of structural ice has a rough, milky-white, opaque appearance and forms when small supercooled droplets freeze almost instantly on contact?
questions.back: Rime ice
options: Rime ice
Clear ice
Mixed ice
questions.explanation: Small droplets, typical of stratiform clouds, freeze on impact before they can spread out, trapping air bubbles — that trapped air is what gives rime ice its opaque, milky look and rough texture.

source.section: Icing – Types of Structural Icing (Rime Ice)

questions.front: What droplet and cloud conditions produce clear (glaze) ice, and why is it generally more hazardous than rime ice of the same thickness?
questions.back: Clear ice forms from large supercooled water droplets, typically in cumuliform clouds or freezing rain, which spread out and flow back before freezing solid. It is smooth, dense, hard, and adheres tightly — adding significant weight and disrupting airfoil shape more severely, while being harder to see and remove, than the lighter, more brittle rime ice.
questions.explanation: Because clear ice is transparent and conforms closely to the airfoil, pilots often underestimate how much has accumulated, while its density and strong bond make mechanical removal (boots) less effective — a common trap on the written exam.

source.section: Icing – Types of Structural Icing (Clear Ice)

questions.front: An aircraft accumulates ice with alternating rough, opaque patches and smooth, clear patches during the same encounter. What type of icing is this?
questions.back: Mixed ice
options: Mixed ice
Frost
Trace ice
questions.explanation: Mixed ice results when an aircraft flies through a combination of small and large supercooled droplets, or through snow/ice crystals mixed with liquid droplets, depositing a combination of clear and rime characteristics in the same layer.

source.section: Icing – Types of Structural Icing (Mixed Ice)

questions.front: A pilot must decide which of two reported icing encounters poses the greater threat: one producing rough, opaque rime ice, and one producing smooth, clear ice of similar reported thickness. Which is generally more hazardous, and why?
questions.back: The clear ice encounter — it tends to form aerodynamic 'horns' near the leading edge that disrupt airflow over a much larger area of the airfoil than rime ice, while being dense and transparent, making it harder to recognize and remove
options: The clear ice encounter — it forms leading-edge ice 'horns' that disrupt a much larger area of airflow and is harder to recognize and remove
The rime ice encounter, because its rough texture always accumulates faster than clear ice
Both pose exactly equal hazard because icing severity depends only on thickness, not ice type
questions.explanation: Rime ice looks scarier because it's rough and opaque, but clear ice tends to form horn-shaped ridges near the leading edge that disrupt a much larger area of airflow than rime ice — increasing drag dramatically — and because it's transparent and dense, a pilot may not recognize how much has accumulated or easily remove it. This is exactly the misconception the exam likes to test.

source.section: Icing – Types of Structural Icing (Clear Ice)

questions.front: In PIREP icing-intensity terminology, what does 'trace' icing mean?
questions.back: Ice becomes perceptible, and the rate of accumulation is only slightly greater than the rate of sublimation. It is not hazardous even without deicing/anti-icing equipment, unless encountered for an extended period (over one hour).
questions.explanation: Trace icing is the baseline category — barely detectable and not a threat by itself, but still worth reporting since conditions can rapidly intensify further along the route.

questions.front: A PIREP describes icing such that 'even short encounters become potentially hazardous, and use of deicing/anti-icing equipment or flight diversion is necessary.' Which icing intensity does this describe?
questions.back: Moderate
options: Moderate
Trace
Severe
questions.explanation: The key phrase for moderate icing is that diversion 'is necessary' but equipment can still control it, whereas severe icing is defined by deicing/anti-icing equipment failing to control the hazard, requiring immediate diversion — a distinction commonly confused on the exam.

questions.front: Per PIREP icing-intensity definitions, which statement best distinguishes 'light' icing from 'trace' icing?
questions.back: Light icing needs occasional equipment use past about an hour; trace is barely perceptible
options: Light icing needs occasional equipment use past about an hour; trace is barely perceptible
Light icing only occurs in clear air; trace icing only occurs in clouds
Light icing always demands an immediate diversion; trace icing never does
questions.explanation: The four PIREP categories — trace, light, moderate, severe — form a ladder of increasing accumulation rate and increasing need for active equipment use or diversion; memorizing the defining phrase for each avoids mixing them up.

questions.front: What is the definition of 'freezing level' in aviation weather?
questions.back: The lowest altitude in the atmosphere at which the outside air temperature reaches 0°C (32°F).
questions.explanation: Freezing level is a key reference point for icing planning — supercooled liquid water can exist below it, but only air at or below 0°C can actually freeze that water onto an airframe.

questions.front: Relative to the freezing level, where is clear (glaze) icing most likely to be encountered in cumuliform clouds?
questions.back: Close to the freezing level, where droplets are largest and temperatures are only slightly below 0°C
options: Close to the freezing level, where droplets are largest and temperatures are only slightly below 0°C
Far above the freezing level, in the coldest part of the cloud where temperatures are below -30°C
Only below the freezing level, in air that is entirely above 0°C
questions.explanation: Large supercooled droplets exist mainly in the relatively warmer part of a cumuliform cloud near the freezing level; higher up, droplets are smaller and often already glaciated, which favors rime rather than clear ice.

source.section: Icing – Freezing Level and Icing Type

questions.front: A temperature inversion places a layer of air warmer than 0°C aloft, sitting above a subfreezing layer near the surface, and rain falls from the warm layer down through the cold surface layer. What hazardous icing condition does this produce?
questions.back: Freezing rain — drops stay liquid until they strike the subfreezing surface below
options: Freezing rain — drops stay liquid until they strike the subfreezing surface below
Rime ice only, because all precipitation above the surface layer is already frozen
No icing hazard, since surface air is below freezing and precipitation cannot reach the ground as liquid
questions.explanation: This 'warm layer aloft over cold layer below' setup means multiple freezing levels exist in the same sounding; the rain stays liquid (or becomes supercooled) through the subfreezing layer and freezes instantly on contact with a cold surface, producing some of the most severe icing encountered in flight.

source.section: Icing – Freezing Rain and Multiple Freezing Levels

questions.front: What flight-control action most commonly triggers or reveals a tailplane (horizontal stabilizer) stall in icing conditions, and why?
questions.back: Extending flaps — flap extension increases the downwash angle striking the horizontal stabilizer, which increases the tailplane's local angle of attack. If ice has already eroded the tailplane's stall margin, this added angle of attack can trigger an abrupt, uncommanded nose-down pitch.
questions.explanation: Tailplane icing is dangerous precisely because it tends to show up during a normally routine configuration change, such as flap extension on approach, catching pilots off guard at low altitude.

questions.front: During an approach in icing conditions, a pilot extends flaps and experiences a sudden, uncommanded nose-down pitch along with a lightening of elevator control force — classic signs of a tailplane stall. What is the correct initial control response?
questions.back: Pull aft on the controls, the opposite of the forward-push used to recover from a normal wing stall
options: Pull aft on the controls, the opposite of the forward-push used to recover from a normal wing stall
Push forward on the controls and add full power, exactly as in a normal wing-stall recovery
Release all back pressure and let the aircraft find its own trimmed airspeed
questions.explanation: Because the stall is happening on the tail, not the wing, the usual 'push forward to reduce angle of attack' response actually worsens a tailplane stall; pilots must react opposite of habit, which is why this reversal is one of the most tested tailplane-icing facts.

questions.front: What is the fundamental operational difference between an aircraft's anti-ice systems and its deice systems?
questions.back: Anti-ice prevents ice formation and is used before entering icing conditions; deice removes ice after it forms
options: Anti-ice prevents ice formation and is used before entering icing conditions; deice removes ice after it forms
Anti-ice systems are only found on turbine aircraft; deice only on piston aircraft
Anti-ice and deice both remove existing ice, but deice works faster
questions.explanation: A simple memory hook: 'anti-' means against/before (prevention), 'de-' means undo/after (removal) — heated leading edges and TKS weeping-wing fluid are typically anti-ice, while pneumatic boots are the classic deice example.

source.section: Icing – Ice Protection Systems (Anti-Ice and Deice)

questions.front: How do pneumatic deice boots physically remove ice, and per current FAA guidance, when should a pilot activate them relative to the onset of ice accumulation?
questions.back: Pneumatic boots are rubber membranes on the leading edge that inflate using engine bleed-air or vacuum-pump pressure, cracking and breaking the bonded ice so it sheds into the airstream, then deflate to reset for the next cycle. Current FAA guidance recommends activating them at the first sign of ice accumulation (per the aircraft's AFM), rather than waiting for ice to build up first.
questions.explanation: Older folklore warned that early boot cycling could cause 'ice bridging,' but modern boot designs and FAA guidance have discredited that concern for most aircraft — waiting only lets more ice accumulate before the first cycle.

questions.front: A METAR remark reads 'PK WND 28045/1855'. What does this indicate?
questions.back: The peak wind since the last METAR was 280° true at 45 knots, occurring at 1855Z.
options: The peak wind since the last METAR was 280° true at 45 knots, occurring at 1855Z
The forecast peak wind for the next hour is 280° at 45 knots, valid at 1855Z
Wind is expected to shift to 280° and gust to 45 knots by 1855Z local time
questions.explanation: PK WND reports the peak wind speed observed since the last METAR, coded as true direction/speed followed by the time of occurrence in Zulu — it is an observed value, not a forecast, is included whenever the peak speed exceeds 25 knots, and appears only in the remarks section.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, METAR/SPECI – Remarks Section (Peak Wind)

questions.front: In METAR/SPECI cloud reports, how many eighths (oktas) of sky coverage do the abbreviations FEW, SCT, BKN, and OVC each represent?
questions.back: FEW = 1–2 oktas, SCT (scattered) = 3–4 oktas, BKN (broken) = 5–7 oktas, OVC (overcast) = 8 oktas (sky completely covered).
questions.explanation: Sky cover in U.S. METARs is reported in eighths of the sky dome using only these four contraction bands (plus SKC/CLR for 0 oktas); a ceiling exists only where the lowest BKN or OVC layer is reported.

questions.front: A METAR reports 'VV004' in the sky condition group. What does this tell a pilot?
questions.back: The vertical visibility into a surface-based obscuration is 400 feet.
options: The highest broken cloud layer's base is 400 feet AGL
The vertical visibility into a surface-based obscuration is 400 feet
The reported visibility is 4 statute miles restricted by haze
questions.explanation: VV followed by three digits denotes an indefinite ceiling caused by a surface-based obscuration such as fog; unlike BKN/OVC there's no discrete cloud base, only a vertical visibility reading upward from the surface.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, METAR/SPECI – Sky Condition (Vertical Visibility)

questions.front: In the METAR remarks section, what does a 5-digit pressure tendency group such as '52013' tell a pilot?
questions.back: It reports the 3-hour pressure tendency: the digit right after the '5' is a code (0–8) describing the character of the pressure change (steady, rising, falling, or reversing) over the past 3 hours, and the final three digits give the net change in tenths of a hectopascal (013 = 1.3 hPa).
questions.explanation: A rapidly falling pressure trend in this group can be an early clue to approaching weather that isn't captured anywhere else in the body of the METAR.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, METAR/SPECI – Remarks Section (Pressure Tendency)

questions.front: Which of the following always triggers issuance of a SPECI (special) observation between scheduled hourly METARs?
questions.back: A tornado, funnel cloud, or waterspout is observed forming or dissipating.
options: The temperature changes by more than 5°F within the hour
The wind direction shifts 10° while sustained speed stays under 15 knots
A tornado, funnel cloud, or waterspout is observed forming or dissipating
questions.explanation: SPECI criteria are tied to operationally significant changes — tornadic activity, sudden ceiling/visibility drops, large wind shifts, onset of thunderstorms or freezing precipitation — not routine minor fluctuations like small temperature swings or shallow wind shifts, which are common wrong-answer traps.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, METAR/SPECI – Aviation Selected Special Weather Report (SPECI)

questions.front: In a TAF, what does the change indicator 'TEMPO' signify?
questions.back: Temporary fluctuations lasting less than an hour at a time, affecting less than half the period.
options: Temporary fluctuations lasting less than an hour at a time, affecting less than half the period
A gradual change expected to be complete by the end of the time group
A temporary forecast that will be replaced by an amended TAF within the hour
questions.explanation: TEMPO is easy to confuse with BECMG: TEMPO describes brief, intermittent conditions like gusty showers, while BECMG describes a one-time, gradual, and lasting change for the rest of the period.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) – Change Indicators

questions.front: What does the TAF change indicator 'BECMG' mean, and over what time span does the change typically occur?
questions.back: BECMG (becoming) indicates a gradual, lasting change expected within the given time window (e.g., BECMG 1416 = the change occurs sometime between 1400Z and 1600Z); the window is normally about 2 hours and never exceeds 4 hours.
questions.explanation: Unlike TEMPO's brief fluctuations, BECMG describes a permanent shift to new prevailing conditions once the transition window closes.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) – Change Indicators

questions.front: In a TAF, what does an 'FM' group represent, and how is its time coded?
questions.back: FM marks a rapid, significant change to a new, relatively steady set of conditions expected to last an hour or more; it's followed by a six-digit day-hour-minute group (FMddhhmm), and everything after it supersedes the previous forecast conditions.
questions.explanation: Unlike BECMG's gradual transition window, FM specifies one precise start time (to the minute) for an abrupt change, and everything before the FM group becomes irrelevant once that time arrives.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) – Change Indicators (FM)

questions.front: What do the report type identifiers 'UA' and 'UUA' mean at the start of a PIREP, and how do they differ?
questions.back: UA identifies a routine pilot report; UUA identifies an urgent pilot report — one containing hazardous weather information such as severe turbulence, severe icing, or low-level wind shear.
questions.explanation: Urgent PIREPs (UUA) get priority handling and rapid dissemination to other pilots and ATC because they describe conditions that pose an immediate hazard to flight.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, Aircraft Observations and Reports – Pilot Weather Reports (PIREP)

questions.front: A PIREP includes '/TB MOD-SEV'. How should this be interpreted?
questions.back: The pilot experienced turbulence intensity ranging from moderate to severe.
options: Moderate turbulence lasted briefly while severe turbulence was only forecast
Moderate turbulence was reported below the aircraft, severe turbulence above it
The pilot experienced turbulence intensity ranging from moderate to severe
questions.explanation: The /TB field uses standard intensity terms (LGT, MOD, SEV, EXTM), sometimes given as a range like MOD-SEV when intensity varied during the encounter — it reports what was actually experienced, not a forecast.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, Aircraft Observations and Reports – Pilot Weather Reports (PIREP), Turbulence Reporting

questions.front: A PIREP contains the element '/IC MOD RIME 080-100'. What does this describe?
questions.back: Moderate rime icing encountered between 8,000 and 10,000 feet.
options: Moderate rime icing encountered between 8,000 and 10,000 feet
A 10% probability of moderate icing forming above 8,000 feet
Rime icing that reduced indicated airspeed by 100 knots
questions.explanation: The /IC field lists intensity first (TRACE, LGT, MOD, SEV), then type (RIME, CLEAR, MIXED), followed by the altitude range where it occurred — reversing that order, or mistaking it for a probability, is a common error.

source.section: Chapter 24 – Observations, Aircraft Observations and Reports – Pilot Weather Reports (PIREP), Icing Reporting

questions.front: Which pilot report should be classified and transmitted as an urgent PIREP (UUA) rather than a routine one?
questions.back: Severe icing encountered in cloud at 8,000 feet.
options: A smooth ride with occasional light chop in cruise flight
Severe icing encountered in cloud at 8,000 feet
Scattered clouds at 4,500 feet with 10 miles of visibility
questions.explanation: Urgent PIREP criteria are reserved for hazards that could endanger other aircraft — severe or extreme turbulence, severe icing, tornadoes, hail, low-level wind shear, and volcanic ash — while routine sky and ride reports, however useful, are filed as UA.

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, Pilot Weather Reports (PIREPs)

questions.front: What hazards does AIRMET Sierra advise pilots of?
questions.back: IFR conditions (ceilings below 1,000 feet and/or visibility below 3 statute miles affecting a wide area) and/or extensive mountain obscuration.
questions.explanation: The three AIRMET types are easy to remember by letter: Sierra = Sky (IFR/mountain obscuration), Tango = Turbulence (and strong surface wind/LLWS), Zulu = freeZing (icing/freezing level).

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, In-Flight Aviation Weather Advisories (AIRMET)

questions.front: AIRMET Tango is issued for which combination of hazards?
questions.back: Moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or greater, and nonconvective low-level wind shear.
options: Severe turbulence associated with embedded or line thunderstorms and surface hail
Moderate icing conditions and the height of the freezing level across the forecast area
Moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or greater, and nonconvective low-level wind shear
questions.explanation: Severe turbulence tied to thunderstorms instead appears in a Convective SIGMET, and icing/freezing-level information belongs to AIRMET Zulu — Tango is specifically the 'moderate turbulence and strong wind' AIRMET.

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, In-Flight Aviation Weather Advisories (AIRMET)

questions.front: What does AIRMET Zulu report?
questions.back: Moderate icing (other than in convective clouds) and the height of the forecast freezing level.
questions.explanation: Zulu = freeZing — it covers moderate icing plus the forecast freezing-level altitude; severe icing instead requires a SIGMET.

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, In-Flight Aviation Weather Advisories (AIRMET)

questions.front: A dispatcher learns that severe turbulence and severe airframe icing are forecast along a route, unrelated to any thunderstorm activity. Which advisory product would contain this information?
questions.back: A SIGMET.
options: A SIGMET
A Convective SIGMET
AIRMET Tango
questions.explanation: Convective SIGMETs are reserved specifically for thunderstorm-related hazards (surface wind ≥50kt, hail ≥3/4 in., tornadoes, embedded or line thunderstorms); non-convective severe turbulence or icing is issued as a plain SIGMET, while AIRMETs cover only the moderate-intensity versions of these hazards.

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, In-Flight Aviation Weather Advisories (SIGMET/Convective SIGMET)

questions.front: What is the primary purpose of a Center Weather Advisory (CWA)?
questions.back: An unscheduled nowcast, valid up to 2 hours, for hazards meeting or approaching AIRMET/SIGMET criteria within an ARTCC's airspace.
options: A scheduled product that replaces AIRMETs and SIGMETs every 6 hours for a Center's airspace
An unscheduled nowcast, valid up to 2 hours, for hazards meeting or approaching AIRMET/SIGMET criteria within an ARTCC's airspace
A 12- to 24-hour outlook used for strategic flight planning into a Center's airspace
questions.explanation: CWAs are tactical bridge products — they supplement, not replace, the scheduled AIRMET/SIGMET system, and their short 2-hour validity reflects their nowcast nature rather than serving as a planning tool.

source.section: Chapter 7, Section 1 – Meteorology, In-Flight Aviation Weather Advisories (Center Weather Advisory)

questions.front: What did the Graphical Forecast for Aviation (GFA) replace for the contiguous United States?
questions.back: The textual Area Forecast (FA).
options: The Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart
The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF)
The textual Area Forecast (FA)
questions.explanation: The FA was retired for the Lower 48 once the GFA's graphical depiction of ceiling/visibility, clouds, precipitation, and other elements became the standard planning tool at aviationweather.gov.

source.section: Chapter 28 – Aviation Weather Tools, Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) Tool

questions.front: What advantage does the Graphical Forecast for Aviation (GFA) offer over the textual Area Forecast (FA) it replaced?
questions.back: It presents forecast ceiling, visibility, clouds, precipitation/weather, icing, turbulence, and wind information graphically across the whole contiguous U.S., letting a pilot visualize conditions along a route at a glance instead of reading dense regional text.
questions.explanation: Because it's a set of interactive graphics rather than a wall of text describing sky/weather/obstructions for large regions, the GFA lets a pilot see forecast trends along a specific route far more quickly than the old FA text did.

source.section: Chapter 28 – Aviation Weather Tools, Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) Tool

questions.front: Within how many feet of a reporting station's elevation are wind values omitted from the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FB)?
questions.back: Within 1,500 feet of the station's elevation — no wind data is forecast for altitudes that close to the ground at that station.
questions.explanation: This prevents the forecast from providing misleading low-altitude wind data that surface friction and terrain effects would make unreliable that close to the ground.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Winds and Temperatures Aloft – FB Wind and Temperature Aloft Forecast

questions.front: On a Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast, why might the temperature value be blank for the 3,000-foot level at a particular station?
questions.back: Temperature is never forecast for a level within 2,500 feet of the station's elevation.
options: Temperature is never forecast for a level within 2,500 feet of the station's elevation
Temperatures are only forecast at flight levels above 18,000 feet
The temperature was omitted because it was forecast to be below freezing
questions.explanation: This is a distinct, larger buffer than the 1,500-foot rule used for omitting wind data — mixing up the two thresholds is a common test mistake.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Winds and Temperatures Aloft – FB Wind and Temperature Aloft Forecast

questions.front: In the coded groups of a Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast, how do you decode a wind group whose two-digit direction code is 51 or greater (indicating a forecast speed of 100 knots or more)?
questions.back: Subtract 50 from the two-digit direction code and add 100 to the coded wind speed.
options: Subtract 50 from the two-digit direction code and add 100 to the coded wind speed
Add 50 to the two-digit direction code and add 100 to the coded wind speed
Replace the direction group with '99' to flag a triple-digit speed
questions.explanation: For example, a coded group of 7319 decodes to wind from 230° true at 119 knots (73 − 50 = 23 → 230°, 19 + 100 = 119 kt); a direction-code value of 51 or greater is the tell that speed exceeds 100 knots. Encoding a forecast for transmission simply reverses the offsets: add 50 to the direction and subtract 100 from the speed.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Winds and Temperatures Aloft – FB Wind and Temperature Aloft Forecast (Decoding)

questions.front: Are wind directions given in the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast referenced to true north or magnetic north?
questions.back: True north — pilots must apply the local magnetic variation if they want to compare it to magnetic-referenced instruments or charts.
questions.explanation: This true-vs-magnetic distinction is a classic trap: surface wind in a METAR/ATIS is reported relative to true north in the raw code (though tower/ATIS wind read to pilots is converted to magnetic for runway alignment), and the winds aloft forecast likewise uses true north throughout.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Winds and Temperatures Aloft – FB Wind and Temperature Aloft Forecast

questions.front: On a surface analysis or prognostic chart, a frontal line shows alternating triangle (barb) and semicircle (bump) symbols on the SAME side of the line. What type of front is this?
questions.back: An occluded front.
options: A stationary front
A dry line
An occluded front
questions.explanation: A stationary front instead places triangles on one side and semicircles on the opposite side, each pointing away from the other — the 'same side' detail is what distinguishes an occluded front from a stationary one.

source.section: Chapter 25 – Analysis, Weather Charts – Surface Analysis Chart

questions.front: On the Surface Weather Prognostic Chart, a scalloped (dotted) outline enclosing a shaded area typically depicts what?
questions.back: The forecast area and type of precipitation.
options: The forecast area and type of precipitation
An area of forecast clear air turbulence
The boundary of a Class B surface area
questions.explanation: Surface prog charts combine frontal positions and pressure centers with these scalloped precipitation outlines so a pilot can see, at a glance, where along a route both frontal weather and precipitation are expected.

source.section: Chapter 27 – Forecasts, Short-Range Surface Prognostic (Prog) Charts

questions.front: What does the Minimum En Route Altitude (MEA) on an IFR en route chart guarantee?
questions.back: Acceptable navigational signal coverage and obstacle clearance requirements for the route segment.
options: Acceptable navigation signal coverage and required obstacle clearance for the segment
Obstacle clearance only; navigation reception is guaranteed by the MOCA
Radar coverage and two-way communications with ATC for the segment
questions.explanation: The MEA assures both obstacle clearance and nav signal coverage. The MOCA assures obstacle clearance but VOR reception only within 22 NM.

source.section: 5-6, Pilot/Controller Glossary — Minimum En Route IFR Altitude

questions.front: What does the MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) guarantee, and what is its navigation limitation?
questions.back: Required obstacle clearance for the entire route segment, but acceptable VOR navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of the VOR.
questions.explanation: Compare with the MEA, which guarantees both obstacle clearance and nav signal coverage for the whole segment.

source.section: Pilot/Controller Glossary — Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude

questions.front: On an IFR en route low altitude chart, a Victor airway is depicted as being how wide when the two defining VOR/VORTAC facilities are 102 nautical miles or less apart?
questions.back: 4 NM either side of the centerline, for a total width of 8 NM
options: 4 NM either side of the centerline, for a total width of 8 NM
3 NM either side of the centerline, for a total width of 6 NM
10 NM either side of the centerline, for a total width of 20 NM
questions.explanation: Standard VOR Federal Airways are 8 NM wide (4 NM each side of centerline) whenever the defining NAVAIDs are 102 NM or less apart; beyond that spacing the boundaries diverge along radials 4.5° either side of centerline. Confusing this width figure with obstacle-clearance distances used elsewhere on the chart is a common error.

source.section: 5-3-4/5-3-5 Airways and Route Systems / Airway or Route Course Changes – Federal Airway Width (4 NM either side of centerline)

questions.front: What is a Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA), and how is it identified on an en route low altitude chart?
questions.back: The MCA is the lowest altitude at certain fixes at which an aircraft must cross when proceeding in the direction of a higher MEA. It is charted next to the fix as an altitude value with a flag symbol and an arrow showing the direction of flight to which it applies.
questions.explanation: MCAs let aircraft climb gradually to a higher MEA ahead rather than needing an unrealistic climb right at the fix; the arrow matters because the restriction only applies when flying that direction across the fix.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA)

questions.front: A Minimum Reception Altitude (MRA) is published at an intersection primarily to ensure what?
questions.back: That the pilot can reliably receive the off-course NAVAID signal used to identify the intersection
options: That the pilot can reliably receive the off-course NAVAID signal used to identify the intersection
That the aircraft remains above all charted obstacles within 22 nautical miles of the intersection
That the aircraft stays clear of the floor of overlying Class A airspace at that intersection
questions.explanation: MRA is published only when the MEA is too low for reliable reception of the cross-radial or DME that defines the fix; it has nothing to do with obstacle clearance, which the MEA already guarantees. Mixing MRA up with obstacle-clearance altitudes is a classic trap.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Minimum Reception Altitude (MRA)

questions.front: What does Maximum Authorized Altitude (MAA) represent on a Federal airway, and why is it published?
questions.back: MAA is the highest altitude on a route segment for which an MEA is designated at which reliable reception of the defining NAVAID signals is still assured; above it, co-channel interference from another facility transmitting on the same frequency can make the signal unreliable.
questions.explanation: MAA is a signal-integrity limit, not a terrain or airspace limit — pilots sometimes assume it relates to the 18,000-foot floor of Class A airspace, but it is charted independently of that boundary.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Maximum Authorized Altitude (MAA)

questions.front: The Off-Route Obstruction Clearance Altitude (OROCA) charted in each latitude/longitude quadrangle of a low altitude en route chart provides what obstacle clearance buffer?
questions.back: 1,000 feet in non-mountainous terrain and 2,000 feet in designated mountainous terrain
options: 1,000 feet in non-mountainous terrain and 2,000 feet in designated mountainous terrain
1,000 feet everywhere within the contiguous United States
500 feet in non-mountainous terrain and 1,000 feet in designated mountainous terrain
questions.explanation: OROCA uses the same 1,000/2,000-ft buffer split as other obstruction-clearance altitudes, but it's computed for an entire lat/long quadrangle rather than along a specific route, so it typically reads far more conservative than an MEA in that same area.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Off Route Obstruction Clearance Altitude (OROCA)

questions.front: Besides obstacle clearance, what two things does OROCA NOT guarantee, and why does that matter for IFR flight planning?
questions.back: OROCA does not guarantee acceptable NAVAID signal coverage or two-way radio communications coverage. A pilot flying at the OROCA off established routes may be too low for reliable navigation or ATC contact even though obstacle clearance is assured.
questions.explanation: Pilots often treat OROCA like an MEA, but MEAs also guarantee signal reception — OROCA is obstacle clearance only, so assuming you can navigate or talk to ATC at that altitude off-route is unsafe.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Off Route Obstruction Clearance Altitude (OROCA)

questions.front: Absent any other charted indication, where does the changeover point (COP) between two NAVAIDs defining a straight airway segment normally occur?
questions.back: At the midpoint between the two facilities
options: At the midpoint between the two facilities
At the facility with the stronger published service volume
35 NM from the departure facility regardless of segment length
questions.explanation: The default COP is the geographic midpoint of the segment, which is why it's normally left uncharted; a COP flag is only printed when the changeover point deviates from that midpoint.

questions.front: How is a nonstandard changeover point (COP) depicted on an en route low altitude chart, and what information does the symbol include?
