questions.back: A nonstandard COP is shown by a flag-like symbol placed along the airway with a mileage figure indicating the distance from the facility behind the aircraft to that point.
questions.explanation: The chart only prints a COP flag when the changeover point is NOT the simple midpoint — commonly because one facility's signal is weaker or shadowed by terrain in that direction.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Changeover Points

questions.front: On an en route low altitude chart, a filled (solid black) triangle at a fix indicates what type of reporting point?
questions.back: A compulsory reporting point
options: A compulsory reporting point
A non-compulsory (on-request) reporting point
A military training route entry point
questions.explanation: Solid triangles mark compulsory reporting points, where a position report must be made unless ATC has issued radar contact; the same triangle drawn as an open outline marks a non-compulsory point reported only if requested.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Reporting Points

questions.front: What is the practical difference in pilot responsibility between a compulsory and a non-compulsory (on-request) reporting point when not in radar contact?
questions.back: At a compulsory reporting point the pilot must report position to ATC without being asked; at a non-compulsory reporting point the pilot reports only if ATC specifically requests it.
questions.explanation: Both fixes look nearly identical on the chart except for the triangle being solid (compulsory) versus open (on-request) — missing that fill difference is a common symbol-reading error.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Reporting Points

questions.front: What distinguishes an IR (IFR Military Training Route) from a VR (VFR Military Training Route) as depicted on an en route low altitude chart?
questions.back: IR routes are flown under IFR flight plans while VR routes are flown under VFR, regardless of weather conditions encountered
options: IR routes are flown under IFR flight plans while VR routes are flown under VFR, regardless of weather conditions encountered
IR routes are only found east of the Mississippi River while VR routes are only found west of it
IR routes never go below 1,500 feet AGL while VR routes always do
questions.explanation: The IR/VR designation tells you which flight rules govern military traffic on that route, not the altitude flown or geographic region — both IR and VR routes can include high-speed, low-altitude segments.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Military Training Routes

questions.front: What does a four-digit Military Training Route number (for example, VR1206) tell a pilot about the route?
questions.back: No segment of the route is above 1,500 feet AGL — the entire route is flown at or below 1,500 feet AGL.
options: No segment of the route is above 1,500 feet AGL
The route is restricted to daylight hours only
The route is flown exclusively by rotary-wing aircraft
questions.explanation: MTR digit count is a quick clue to a route's altitude structure: four-digit numbers (e.g., VR1007) mean no segment of the route is above 1,500 feet AGL, and these routes are generally developed to be flown under VFR. Routes identified by three or fewer digits (e.g., IR21) include at least one segment above 1,500 feet AGL and are developed to be flown, to the maximum extent possible, under IFR.

questions.front: An en route low altitude chart shows a dotted boundary line labeled with an adjacent center's name crossing your planned route. What does this line represent, and what is its practical significance to an IFR pilot?
questions.back: An ARTCC boundary — the pilot should expect a handoff to a different controlling facility and frequency
options: An ARTCC boundary — the pilot should expect a handoff to a different controlling facility and frequency
The lateral limit of a Military Operations Area, requiring clearance to cross
The edge of a Temporary Flight Restriction, which cannot be crossed without prior authorization
questions.explanation: ARTCC boundaries are printed as a boundary line labeled with the adjoining center's name; the main operational impact is an expected frequency change/handoff rather than any airspace-crossing restriction.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – ARTCC Boundaries

questions.front: How are Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) boundaries depicted on an en route low altitude chart?
questions.back: As a boundary line along the boundary, labeled with the name of the adjoining ARTCC (or sector) on each side of the line.
questions.explanation: The boundary line can be mistaken for other line symbology on the chart, but the printed center name alongside it is the giveaway that it marks an ATC facility boundary, not an airspace or obstacle feature.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – ARTCC Boundaries

questions.front: A note near a VOR on an en route low altitude chart reads 'UNUSABLE 040°-090° BYD 30 NM.' What must a pilot do with this information?
questions.back: Avoid relying on that VOR's signal on radials between 040° and 090° beyond 30 NM from the station
options: Avoid relying on that VOR's signal on radials between 040° and 090° beyond 30 NM from the station
Avoid flying within 30 NM of the VOR on any radial between 040° and 090°
Treat the entire VOR as out of service until the notice is removed from the chart
questions.explanation: Unusable-radial notes identify a specific radial range and often a distance beyond which that segment of the signal is unreliable — the rest of the VOR's coverage remains normal, so the whole station shouldn't be discounted.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – NAVAID Standard Service Volume (SSV) / Restricted Service Notes

questions.front: What does a boxed 'G' appearing with an MEA value on an en route low altitude chart mean, and what must an aircraft have to use that MEA?
questions.back: It denotes a GNSS MEA — an MEA established using satellite (GPS/RNAV) navigation because conventional NAVAID signal coverage doesn't support the route's obstruction-clearance altitude. The aircraft must be equipped and authorized for IFR GPS/RNAV navigation to use it.
questions.explanation: A conventional (non-GPS) MEA may not exist, or may be substantially higher, on that same segment; pilots without a suitable IFR-approved GPS cannot legally use the lower GNSS MEA.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – GNSS MEA

questions.front: On an en route low altitude chart, how is a VOR Federal Airway labeled to distinguish it from other route types?
questions.back: With the prefix 'V' followed by a number (e.g., V16)
options: With the prefix 'V' followed by a number (e.g., V16)
With the prefix 'J' followed by a number (e.g., J16)
With the prefix 'Q' followed by a number (e.g., Q16)
questions.explanation: 'V' identifies a VOR Federal (Victor) airway on low altitude charts; 'J' marks jet routes on high altitude charts, and 'Q'/'T' prefixes mark RNAV routes — mixing these up is an easy mistake when different route types share a chart area.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Airways/Route System

questions.front: What two chart elements are combined to depict a Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA) restriction at a fix?
questions.back: The MCA altitude value paired with a small arrow (or flag) showing the direction of flight to which the restriction applies.
questions.explanation: Because an MCA only matters when flying toward the higher MEA ahead, the directional arrow is essential — without it a pilot could mistakenly apply the restriction on a flight in the opposite direction, where it doesn't apply.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA)

questions.front: An aircraft is flying an airway at its current MEA of 5,000 feet. Ahead, a fix is charted with an MCA of 8,000 feet for aircraft proceeding in the direction of flight, after which the MEA rises to 9,000 feet. What must the pilot do?
questions.back: Begin the climb early enough to cross the fix at or above 8,000 feet, then continue climbing to at least 9,000 feet after the fix
options: Begin the climb early enough to cross the fix at or above 8,000 feet, then continue climbing to at least 9,000 feet after the fix
Remain at 5,000 feet until reaching the fix, then climb immediately to 9,000 feet after crossing it
Climb to 9,000 feet immediately upon receiving the clearance, since the MCA is only advisory
questions.explanation: An MCA is a hard crossing restriction, not advisory — the pilot must plan the climb so the aircraft is at or above the MCA by the fix, since a normal climb gradient may not get the aircraft there in time if the climb is delayed until reaching it.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA)

questions.front: What must a pilot do when an en route low altitude chart notes that a NAVAID's signal is unusable on certain radials or beyond a certain distance?
questions.back: The pilot must not rely on that NAVAID for navigation guidance within the specified unusable radial range or distance, and should use an alternate NAVAID, GPS, or another means to determine position and course in that area.
questions.explanation: These notes exist because the station's signal has been flight-checked and found unreliable in that specific radial/distance range; the rest of the station's coverage remains fully usable, so the whole NAVAID shouldn't be discarded.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – NAVAID Standard Service Volume (SSV) / Restricted Service Notes

questions.front: Why is a Maximum Authorized Altitude (MAA) published on some airway segments?
questions.back: Above that altitude, another facility transmitting on the same frequency can interfere with reliable reception of the defining NAVAID
options: Above that altitude, another facility transmitting on the same frequency can interfere with reliable reception of the defining NAVAID
Above that altitude, the airway passes into Class A airspace where VOR airways are not authorized
Above that altitude, terrain and obstacles are no longer adequately surveyed
questions.explanation: MAA protects against co-channel signal interference, not terrain or airspace class — assuming it's tied to the 18,000-foot floor of Class A airspace is a common wrong guess.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Airway/Route Data: Maximum Authorized Altitude (MAA)

questions.front: What is the basic purpose of a changeover point (COP) charted along a Victor airway?
questions.back: It marks where the pilot should switch the navigation receiver from the facility behind the aircraft to the facility ahead for the most reliable signal
options: It marks where the pilot should switch the navigation receiver from the facility behind the aircraft to the facility ahead for the most reliable signal
It marks the point where the pilot must report position to ATC without being asked
It marks the boundary between two adjacent ARTCCs' airspace
questions.explanation: COP is purely a navigation-guidance handoff point between two ground stations; it has nothing to do with ATC reporting requirements or ARTCC facility boundaries, which are separate chart symbols entirely.

questions.front: Charted intersections and waypoints on en route low altitude charts are assigned pronounceable names using what convention?
questions.back: Five letters, chosen to be unique and easily spoken over the radio
options: Five letters, chosen to be unique and easily spoken over the radio
Three letters, matching the ICAO identifier of the nearest airport
Four letters, matching the identifier of the defining NAVAID
questions.explanation: The five-letter convention keeps fix names distinguishable from three-letter NAVAID identifiers and four-letter ICAO airport codes, reducing the chance ATC and pilots confuse a fix name with a station or airport during a readback.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – Reporting Points and Fixes

questions.front: How is the OROCA value displayed within each latitude/longitude quadrangle on an en route low altitude chart, and what does the number represent?
questions.back: It's printed as a bold number in the middle of the grid formed by ticked lines of latitude and longitude, expressed in hundreds of feet MSL (for example, '97' means 9,700 feet).
questions.explanation: Because OROCA is computed for an entire lat/long grid rather than a specific route, it tends to read noticeably higher than nearby MEAs — pilots sometimes mistake it for a route altitude rather than the conservative off-route figure it actually is.

source.section: IFR Enroute Terms – Off Route Obstruction Clearance Altitude (OROCA)

questions.front: A Military Training Route is charted with the designation 'VR21' (only two digits — three or fewer digits). What does this digit count indicate about where this route is flown?
questions.back: The route includes one or more segments above 1,500 feet AGL.
options: The route includes one or more segments above 1,500 feet AGL
The route is flown entirely below 1,500 feet AGL
The digit count reflects the route's length in tens of nautical miles, not its altitude
questions.explanation: Routes identified by three or fewer digits (e.g., IR21, VR21) include at least one segment above 1,500 feet AGL and are developed to be flown, to the maximum extent possible, under IFR. It's the four-digit routes (e.g., VR1007) that have no segment above 1,500 feet AGL and are generally flown under VFR — the opposite of a common misconception.

questions.front: Two VOR facilities defining a straight Victor airway segment are 120 NM apart, but the facility behind the aircraft has a weaker signal in that direction. The chart shows a COP flag reading '35 NM' near the rear facility. What does this tell the pilot, and why isn't the COP simply at the 60 NM midpoint?
questions.back: The pilot should switch navigation receivers to the forward facility after 35 NM from the rear facility, well short of the 60 NM midpoint, because a nonstandard COP is charted whenever reception reliability — not simple geometry — dictates where the changeover should actually occur.
questions.explanation: This is exactly why nonstandard COPs get printed at all — the default midpoint assumption only holds when both facilities provide equally reliable signal to that midpoint; when they don't, the charted mileage overrides the geometric halfway point.

questions.front: While planning a flight along a Victor airway segment, a pilot notices the published MEA has a boxed 'G' next to it and no separate conventional MEA is charted for that segment. The aircraft has no IFR-approved GPS/RNAV equipment. What does this mean for the flight?
questions.back: The pilot cannot use that MEA and must find an alternate route or altitude the aircraft is equipped for
options: The pilot cannot use that MEA and must find an alternate route or altitude the aircraft is equipped for
The pilot may still fly the segment at the charted MEA using VOR/DME alone, since the 'G' is only advisory
The pilot must contact ATC to request a temporary waiver before using the segment
questions.explanation: A GNSS MEA with no conventional alternative means ground-based signal coverage doesn't support any lower altitude on that segment — an aircraft without suitable GPS/RNAV isn't equipped to use that MEA and needs a different routing or altitude, not a waiver.

source.section: En Route Low Altitude Charts – GNSS MEA

questions.front: While flying IFR, at what point is a pilot required to report a change in true airspeed to ATC?
questions.back: Report any time cruise TAS varies from the filed value by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater — this is one of the reports required 'at all times,' regardless of whether the flight is in radar contact.
options: Any time cruise TAS varies from the flight-plan value by more than 10 percent, regardless of knots
Any time cruise TAS varies from the flight-plan value by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater
Only when ATC specifically requests an updated TAS after a reporting point
questions.explanation: ATC and pilots rely on filed TAS to predict position and compute ETAs for reporting points and separation planning, so a significant unreported speed change can throw off those estimates. The AIM lists this among the reports required at all times, not just when out of radar contact. The memory hook is '5-and-10': five percent OR ten knots, whichever is the larger number.

questions.front: How is groundspeed related to true airspeed during en route flight planning?
questions.back: Groundspeed equals true airspeed corrected for the wind component along the aircraft's track — a headwind component subtracts from TAS to yield a lower groundspeed, and a tailwind component adds to TAS to yield a higher groundspeed.
questions.explanation: TAS describes motion through the air mass; groundspeed describes motion over the earth, so the two are equal only in dead-calm wind. This distinction drives every ETE and fuel calculation in flight planning.

source.section: Chapter 2, En Route Operations – Speed and Time Planning

questions.front: An airplane is flying with a true airspeed of 140 knots directly into a 20-knot headwind component. What groundspeed should the pilot use for time and fuel planning?
questions.back: 120 knots (TAS minus the headwind component).
options: 140 knots
160 knots
120 knots
questions.explanation: A direct headwind subtracts fully from TAS to give groundspeed; using the unadjusted 140-knot TAS instead would make every downstream ETE and fuel-remaining calculation optimistic.

source.section: Chapter 2, En Route Operations – Speed and Time Planning

questions.front: Using the standard 3-to-1 descent planning rule, approximately how far from a crossing restriction should a pilot begin a descent that must lose 12,000 feet?
questions.back: About 36 NM (12, in thousands of feet, multiplied by 3).
options: 24 NM
12 NM
36 NM
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is: multiply the altitude to lose, in thousands of feet, by 3 to get the distance in nautical miles needed at a normal descent gradient. Using a multiplier of 2, or forgetting to multiply at all, are the two most common errors.

questions.front: A flight is planning a standard 3-degree descent gradient at a groundspeed of 150 knots. What descent rate approximates that gradient?
questions.back: About 750 feet per minute (groundspeed multiplied by 5).
options: 450 fpm
750 fpm
questions.explanation: For a 3-degree path, descent rate in feet per minute is approximately groundspeed multiplied by 5 — the same relationship used to fly a 3-degree glidepath. Multiplying by 3 instead, mixing it up with the distance rule, is the classic error.

questions.front: What is the basic formula for computing estimated time en route (ETE) for an IFR route segment?
questions.back: ETE = distance (NM) divided by groundspeed (kt); the decimal-hour result is multiplied by 60 to convert to minutes for flight-plan and position-report entries.
questions.explanation: This single relationship underlies every ETA, fuel-remaining, and reporting-point calculation a pilot makes en route — it is only as accurate as the groundspeed estimate feeding it.

source.section: Chapter 2, En Route Operations – Speed and Time Planning

questions.front: A pilot plans a 350 NM IFR leg at a forecast groundspeed of 140 knots in an airplane that burns 15 gallons per hour at cruise power. Approximately how much fuel will the cruise portion of this leg consume?
questions.back: About 37.5 gallons (2.5 hours of flight time multiplied by 15 GPH).
options: 37.5 gallons
45 gallons
30 gallons
questions.explanation: First convert distance and groundspeed to time (350 divided by 140 equals 2.5 hours), then multiply by fuel flow. Skipping the time step and manipulating distance directly against fuel flow is the error behind the wrong distractors.

questions.front: What does 'endurance' mean in the context of IFR fuel planning, as distinct from range?
questions.back: Endurance is the maximum amount of time an aircraft can remain airborne on its usable fuel supply at a given power setting; range is the maximum distance it can travel on that fuel, which also depends on groundspeed.
questions.explanation: Endurance is measured in time, range in distance — mixing the two up is a common planning error, especially when estimating how long a holding pattern can be sustained before fuel becomes a factor.

questions.front: On an ICAO IFR flight plan, entering the letter 'G' in the equipment field (Item 10a) indicates what capability?
questions.back: GNSS/GPS navigation equipment is installed and approved for the route to be flown.
options: VHF communications only, no navigation equipment
GNSS/GPS equipment approved for the route to be flown
Ground-based DME/VOR equipment only
questions.explanation: ICAO equipment codes are letter-based rather than the old domestic slash suffixes; 'G' is one of the most common entries now that GPS is standard equipment, and it is normally paired with a PBN/ entry in Item 18 describing the specific navigation specification.

source.section: Appendix 4 – FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan (Item 10a Equipment Codes)

questions.front: In an ICAO flight plan, where does a pilot enter the aircraft's specific RNAV/RNP performance-based navigation capability, and what is that entry called?
questions.back: In Item 18 (Other Information), using the entry 'PBN/' followed by codes identifying the specific navigation specifications (such as RNAV or RNP capability) the aircraft and its avionics are approved for.
questions.explanation: The equipment letter in Item 10a (like 'G' or 'R') only signals that PBN-capable equipment is aboard; the PBN/ entry in Item 18 is what actually tells ATC which navigation specification — RNAV 1, RNP APCH, and so on — the aircraft is approved to fly.

source.section: Appendix 4 – FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan (Item 18 PBN/ Entry)

questions.front: In the surveillance equipment portion of an ICAO flight plan (Item 10b), what does the letter 'S' represent?
questions.back: A Mode S transponder capable of both pressure-altitude reporting and aircraft identification.
options: A Mode C transponder with altitude reporting only, no identification feature
Satellite-based ADS-B receive capability only, without a transponder
A Mode S transponder with altitude reporting and aircraft identification
questions.explanation: The ICAO surveillance codes step up in capability from 'N' (nil) through 'A' and 'C' transponder codes to 'S' and beyond; mixing up which letter includes identification versus altitude-only is a common filing mistake.

source.section: Appendix 4 – FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan (Item 10b Surveillance Equipment Codes)

questions.front: Which ICAO equipment letter, entered in Item 10a of an IFR flight plan, indicates the aircraft is approved for Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum (RVSM) operations?
questions.back: The letter 'W'.
questions.explanation: RVSM approval lets an aircraft operate in the FL290–FL410 airspace block using 1,000-foot vertical separation instead of 2,000 feet; omitting the 'W' when the aircraft is actually equipped can cause a flight plan to be rejected for a high-altitude routing.

source.section: Appendix 4 – FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan (Item 10a Equipment Codes)

questions.front: What does entering the letter 'R' in the equipment field (Item 10a) of an ICAO flight plan tell ATC?
questions.back: That the aircraft/pilot combination is approved for the performance-based navigation (PBN) required for the route, procedure, or airspace to be flown, with the specific navigation specification then detailed in the PBN/ entry of Item 18.
questions.explanation: 'R' is a broad flag that PBN approval exists; it always needs the companion PBN/ entry in Item 18 to say exactly which RNAV or RNP specification applies, so the two entries work as a pair.

source.section: Appendix 4 – FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan (Item 10a Equipment Codes)

questions.front: What is the purpose of a 'preferred IFR route,' and where can a pilot find one for a specific city pair?
questions.back: Preferred IFR routes are routes established between busier terminals to distribute traffic and reduce route-coordination workload for ATC; they are published in the Chart Supplement (and referenced in the AIM) and should be used for flight planning whenever one exists for the intended city pair.
questions.explanation: Filing a preferred route instead of a random direct route often speeds up clearance delivery, since it is a routing ATC facilities have already coordinated with each other in advance.

questions.front: What best describes a Tower En Route Control (TEC) route?
questions.back: An IFR route between two terminal areas that stays within approach control (TRACON) airspace and is handled tower-to-tower without an ARTCC handoff.
options: An IFR route between two terminal areas worked entirely by approach control facilities, without ARTCC handoff
A VFR flight-following service that control towers provide to aircraft remaining clear of clouds and in radio contact
A published IFR route usable only above the floor of the overlying Class A airspace at FL180 and higher
questions.explanation: TEC is attractive on shorter IFR flights within congested terminal complexes because it avoids the extra coordination step of a center, which can mean a faster, more predictable clearance; it is entirely an IFR concept despite the misleading resemblance to VFR flight following.

source.section: Chapter 4, Section 1 – Tower En Route Control (TEC)

questions.front: Why do busy metropolitan areas publish Tower En Route Control (TEC) routes as an alternative to normal center-handled IFR routings?
questions.back: TEC routes let approach control facilities hand an IFR flight directly to the next approach control facility, bypassing the Air Route Traffic Control Center; this reduces coordination workload and often produces faster clearances for flights that stay within the terminal-area altitude structure of the region.
questions.explanation: TEC works best for shorter trips between airports served by adjoining TRACONs — it is a route-selection tool used during flight planning, filed just like any other IFR route.

source.section: Chapter 4, Section 1 – Tower En Route Control (TEC)

questions.front: How far in advance of the proposed departure time should a pilot file an IFR flight plan?
questions.back: At least 30 minutes before the proposed departure time, to give ATC/FSS time to process the flight plan and have the clearance ready.
questions.explanation: Filing right at push-back time risks a delay while the system processes the plan; the 30-minute cushion is the standard planning guidance for domestic IFR flights.

questions.front: A pilot's actual departure will be considerably later than the proposed departure time entered on the filed IFR flight plan. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Contact ATC/FSS to amend the proposed departure time before it becomes stale.
options: Nothing — ATC automatically holds every filed flight plan indefinitely until it is activated
Contact ATC or FSS to update the proposed departure time before the flight plan goes stale
File an entirely new flight plan under a different call sign to avoid confusing the system
questions.explanation: Flight plans are not held forever; a stale departure time can cause the plan to be purged, leaving no clearance on file when the pilot actually calls for one. A quick call to update the time avoids that surprise.

source.section: Chapter 5, Section 1 – Change in Proposed Departure Time

questions.front: Unless the approach chart specifies otherwise, what are the standard alternate minimums for a civil airport whose only approach is a nonprecision procedure?
questions.back: An 800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility.
options: 600-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility
200-foot ceiling and 1/2 statute mile visibility
800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility
questions.explanation: Standard alternate minimums are 600-2 for an airport with at least one precision approach and 800-2 for nonprecision only; both are noticeably higher than typical straight-in landing minimums (like 200-1/2), which many pilots mistakenly substitute.

questions.front: What does a black triangle enclosing the letter 'A' printed in the minimums section of an instrument approach chart mean?
questions.back: Nonstandard alternate minimums apply for that airport, and the pilot must check the alternate minimums listing for the actual values.
options: The airport has nonstandard alternate minimums; the pilot must look up the specific values
The airport may never be used as a filed alternate under any weather conditions
Only Category II or III alternate minimums are published for that runway
questions.explanation: The triangle 'A' flags that the standard 600-2/800-2 minimums do not apply and different values are published elsewhere; that is a different symbol from a triangle with 'NA', which means the airport cannot be filed as an alternate at all.

questions.front: Below 18,000 feet MSL in uncontrolled airspace, what altitude rule applies to an IFR flight not on a specific ATC-assigned altitude?
questions.back: Odd thousands of feet MSL (such as 5,000, 7,000, 9,000) for magnetic courses of 0 through 179 degrees, and even thousands of feet MSL (such as 6,000, 8,000, 10,000) for magnetic courses of 180 through 359 degrees.
questions.explanation: This is the IFR cruising altitude rule for uncontrolled airspace — no plus-or-minus-500-foot offset is added, unlike the VFR cruising altitude rule that applies to the same courses; confusing the two is the most common mistake on this topic. (In controlled airspace, an IFR flight instead maintains whatever altitude ATC assigns.)

source.section: 91.179(b) – IFR Cruising Altitude or Flight Level (Uncontrolled Airspace)

questions.front: An IFR flight over uncontrolled airspace, below 18,000 feet MSL, is on a magnetic course of 250 degrees and has not been assigned a specific altitude by ATC. Which altitude complies with the standard IFR cruising altitude rule?
questions.back: 8,000 feet (an even thousand, since the magnetic course is between 180 and 359 degrees).
options: 9,000 feet
8,000 feet
8,500 feet
questions.explanation: Courses of 180 through 359 degrees use even thousands under IFR; 9,000 feet would be correct for the opposite course range, and 8,500 feet applies the VFR/VFR-on-top plus-500 offset rule instead, which does not apply here.

source.section: 91.179(b) – IFR Cruising Altitude or Flight Level (Uncontrolled Airspace)

questions.front: A pilot on an IFR flight plan is cleared to 'maintain VFR conditions on-top' while flying a magnetic course of 070 degrees below 18,000 feet MSL. Which altitude satisfies the applicable cruising altitude rule?
questions.back: 9,500 feet (an odd thousand plus 500 feet, per the VFR cruising altitude rule).
options: 9,000 feet
8,500 feet
9,500 feet
questions.explanation: A VFR-on-top clearance requires the pilot to select an altitude under the VFR cruising altitude rule (odd/even thousands plus 500 feet), not the standard IFR odd/even-thousand rule — 9,000 feet would be the answer if this were a normal IFR-assigned altitude instead.

source.section: 91.179(a) – IFR Cruising Altitude or Flight Level (VFR conditions on-top)

questions.front: Is a pilot cleared to 'maintain VFR-on-top' still flying under IFR, or has the flight effectively become VFR?
questions.back: The flight remains an IFR operation on an IFR clearance; the pilot must still comply with IFR flight plan procedures (position reports, clearance requirements) and must remain in VFR weather conditions at all times — the clearance only changes how the cruising altitude is selected, not the underlying flight rules.
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that 'VFR-on-top' means the pilot has effectively canceled IFR; in fact the IFR clearance and its obligations stay in force, and if VFR conditions can no longer be maintained the pilot must request an alternate clearance rather than simply continuing.

questions.front: A flight is cleared to maintain VFR-on-top. Regardless of the altitude chosen under the VFR cruising altitude rule, below what may the pilot not descend?
questions.back: The minimum IFR altitude (such as the MEA or another published minimum) that provides obstacle clearance for that segment.
options: The minimum IFR altitude required for obstacle clearance on that segment
Whatever altitude the pilot judges safe by outside visual reference
1,000 feet AGL, the standard VFR cross-country altitude minimum
questions.explanation: VFR-on-top does not suspend the IFR obstacle-clearance floor; a pilot cannot descend below the minimum IFR altitude just because the flight happens to be in VFR conditions on top of a cloud layer.

source.section: Chapter 4, Section 4 – IFR Clearance VFR/VFR-on-top (Minimum IFR Altitudes)

questions.front: An airplane must lose 9,000 feet before reaching an initial approach fix, and the pilot expects an average descent groundspeed of 180 knots. Using standard planning rules of thumb, approximately how many minutes before the fix should descent begin?
questions.back: About 9 minutes.
options: 27 minutes
9 minutes
15 minutes
questions.explanation: First find the distance with the 3-to-1 rule (9, in thousands of feet, times 3 equals 27 NM), then convert that distance to time at the planned groundspeed (27 NM divided by 180 kt equals 0.15 hour, or 9 minutes); mistaking the 27 NM distance figure for a time value is the trap this kind of question sets.

questions.front: When ATC includes a Standard Instrument Departure (SID) as part of an IFR clearance and the pilot accepts it, what is the pilot's obligation?
questions.back: The pilot must fly the SID exactly as published unless subsequently amended by ATC.
options: The pilot must fly the SID exactly as published unless subsequently amended by ATC
The pilot may substitute a different departure route without telling ATC as long as the aircraft joins the filed route by the first en route fix
SID routing is advisory only and pilots may disregard it once airborne in VMC
questions.explanation: Once a pilot accepts a SID as part of an IFR clearance, compliance is mandatory like any other ATC clearance; a pilot who cannot fly it must decline before departure rather than improvise en route.

questions.front: What should a pilot do before an IFR departure if they cannot comply with the SID or ODP that would normally be included in their clearance?
questions.back: Notify ATC in advance — typically by placing "NO SID" (or "NO DP") in the remarks section of the IFR flight plan, or advising ATC directly — so a different departure routing can be built.
questions.explanation: ATC assumes a filed or assigned departure procedure can be flown as published; the "NO SID" notation is how a pilot flags an inability to comply before the fact rather than after taking the clearance.

questions.front: A Part 91 pilot departs IFR from an airport with a published Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP) but is not assigned the ODP, a SID, or specific departure headings by ATC. Who is responsible for obstacle clearance during the climb?
questions.back: The pilot — responsibility stays with the pilot unless an ODP, SID, or DVA vector was filed or assigned.
options: ATC, because radar coverage begins at the departure end of the runway
The pilot — responsibility stays with the pilot unless an ODP, SID, or DVA vector was filed or assigned
No one — standard takeoff minimums alone guarantee obstacle clearance regardless of routing
questions.explanation: ODPs are not mandatory under Part 91 unless ATC assigns one, but skipping it shifts full obstacle-avoidance responsibility to the pilot — many pilots wrongly assume ATC or 'standard minimums' automatically cover them.

questions.front: What climb gradient is assumed to provide obstacle clearance on an IFR departure when no higher gradient is published?
questions.back: 200 feet per nautical mile (the standard climb gradient), climbing from the departure end of the runway to the MEA, MOCA, or minimum IFR altitude.
questions.explanation: 200 ft/NM is the default TERPS design gradient; if terrain or obstacles require more, the procedure explicitly publishes a higher minimum climb gradient for that runway.

source.section: Chapter 1, Departure Procedures - Obstacle Clearance Criteria

questions.front: A departure procedure requires a minimum climb gradient of 300 feet per nautical mile to 4,000 feet. At a groundspeed of 120 knots, approximately what climb rate in feet per minute satisfies this requirement?
questions.back: 600 feet per minute (300 ft/NM x 120 kt / 60 = 600 fpm).
options: 400 feet per minute
600 feet per minute
900 feet per minute
questions.explanation: Climb gradient (ft/NM) converts to climb rate (fpm) by multiplying by groundspeed in knots and dividing by 60; the same gradient requires a different fpm depending on how fast the aircraft is moving.

questions.front: Why can two different aircraft flying the same charted climb-gradient requirement need different vertical speeds in feet per minute to comply?
questions.back: Climb gradient is fixed distance-based (ft/NM), so the fpm needed changes with each aircraft's groundspeed.
options: Climb gradient is fixed distance-based (ft/NM), so the fpm needed changes with each aircraft's groundspeed
Climb gradient charts only apply to turbine aircraft, so piston aircraft use a different standard entirely
Feet-per-minute requirements are always identical regardless of groundspeed since gradient is itself a rate of climb
questions.explanation: A gradient expressed in feet per nautical mile is independent of speed; a faster aircraft covers that mile sooner and must climb more feet per minute to achieve the same feet-per-mile gradient.

questions.front: What does a black triangle enclosing a white 'T' printed in the lower corner of an instrument approach procedure chart indicate?
questions.back: Nonstandard IFR takeoff minimums and/or a departure procedure apply — see the Takeoff Minimums and ODP page.
options: Nonstandard IFR takeoff minimums and/or a departure procedure apply — see the Takeoff Minimums and ODP page
The airport has nonstandard IFR alternate minimums that must be checked before filing it as an alternate
The runway is temporarily closed to IFR takeoffs pending NOTAM cancellation
questions.explanation: Triangle T flags nonstandard takeoff minimums/ODPs and is easily confused with triangle A, which flags nonstandard alternate minimums instead — different letter, different purpose.

source.section: Terminal Procedures Publication - Takeoff Minimums symbology

questions.front: What does a black triangle enclosing a white 'A' on an instrument approach chart tell a pilot?
questions.back: The airport has nonstandard IFR alternate minimums; the pilot must look up the specific alternate minimums in the front of the Terminal Procedures Publication before filing that airport as an alternate.
questions.explanation: Triangle A (alternate minimums) is often confused with triangle T (takeoff minimums) — a useful memory hook is 'A is for Alternate.'

source.section: Terminal Procedures Publication - Alternate Minimums symbology

questions.front: An IFR departure has no textual obstacle notes and no charted ODP, so standard diverse-departure obstacle clearance criteria apply. Which combination of assumptions describes what TERPS assumes about the initial climb?
questions.back: Cross the DER at least 35 ft AGL, climb to 400 ft above DER elevation before turning, then climb at least 200 ft/NM to the MEA/MOCA.
options: Cross the DER at least 35 ft AGL, climb to 400 ft above DER elevation before turning, then climb at least 200 ft/NM to the MEA/MOCA
Cross the DER at pattern altitude, turn immediately on course, and climb at the aircraft's best rate of climb to any published altitude
Remain below 1,000 feet AGL until reaching the airport boundary, then climb at 500 ft/NM to the en route structure
questions.explanation: These three linked assumptions (35 ft crossing height, 400 ft AGL before any turn, 200 ft/NM climb gradient) are the baseline TERPS design criteria for diverse departures; missing any one means standard obstacle clearance is not guaranteed.

source.section: Chapter 1, Departure Procedures - Obstacle Clearance Criteria

questions.front: Unless a departure procedure specifies otherwise, to what height above the departure end of runway (DER) elevation is a pilot assumed to climb before making any turn, for obstacle clearance purposes?
questions.back: 400 feet above the DER elevation.
options: 200 feet
400 feet
1,000 feet
questions.explanation: This 400-foot-before-turning assumption is built into the standard obstacle evaluation; turning earlier than that without a charted procedure authorizing it can put the aircraft outside the surveyed obstacle-clearance area.

source.section: Chapter 1, Departure Procedures - Obstacle Clearance Criteria

questions.front: ATC clears an aircraft 'via the (STAR name) arrival' and later assigns 'descend and maintain 10,000' without using the phrase 'descend via.' How should the pilot treat the STAR's published altitude restrictions below 10,000?
questions.back: Level off and maintain 10,000 until ATC issues further descent clearance; the STAR's lower altitudes do not apply automatically.
options: Level off and maintain 10,000 until ATC issues further descent clearance; the STAR's lower altitudes do not apply automatically
Continue descending through 10,000 to meet each published crossing restriction on the STAR since the STAR was already accepted
Descend at the pilot's discretion to the lowest altitude depicted anywhere on the STAR chart
questions.explanation: Without 'descend via,' the STAR only defines lateral routing; the pilot flies whatever altitude ATC last assigned and must not descend further based on the chart alone — a common trap for pilots used to 'descend via' phraseology.

questions.front: What does an ATC clearance to 'descend via' a STAR authorize a pilot to do?
questions.back: Descend at the pilot's discretion from the previously assigned altitude, navigate the STAR's lateral path, and meet all published altitude and/or speed restrictions along the arrival, unless ATC amends or cancels them.
questions.explanation: 'Descend via' bundles lateral navigation, vertical navigation, and speed compliance into one clearance so ATC does not have to issue a separate instruction at every waypoint.

questions.front: While descending on a STAR under a 'descend via' clearance, a pilot realizes that flying an efficient continuous descent would cross an upcoming fix below its published 'at or above 8,000' restriction. What is the pilot required to do?
questions.back: Adjust the descent to cross the fix at or above 8,000 as published; every restriction on a 'descend via' clearance is binding.
options: Adjust the descent to cross the fix at or above 8,000 as published; every restriction on a 'descend via' clearance is binding
Disregard the restriction as long as the final STAR altitude is met, since only the last restriction on a 'descend via' clearance is binding
Query ATC before continuing, since 'descend via' clearances only apply to speed restrictions, not altitudes
questions.explanation: 'Descend via' is not just permission to eventually reach the bottom altitude — every charted crossing restriction along the way is a hard constraint unless ATC specifically cancels it.

questions.front: A pilot files a route including an RNAV STAR but determines, before departure, that the aircraft's navigation system cannot fly one of the published RNAV legs on that arrival. What is the appropriate action?
questions.back: Notify ATC before accepting the clearance — e.g., by advising ATC "unable RNAV" or noting the limitation in the flight plan — so a different arrival can be assigned.
options: Depart as filed and ask ATC for vectors once approaching the affected leg
Notify ATC before accepting the clearance — e.g., by advising ATC "unable RNAV" or noting the limitation in the flight plan — so a different arrival can be assigned
Fly the STAR using dead reckoning between the fixes since RNAV STARs are advisory for non-RNAV aircraft
questions.explanation: Just as with SIDs, the pilot must self-assess aircraft/equipment suitability for an RNAV STAR and tell ATC in advance if unable, rather than accepting a clearance that cannot be flown as published.

questions.front: Where in the Chart Supplement (formerly the Airport/Facility Directory) would a pilot find information such as airport operating hours, fuel availability, and prior-permission-required (PPR) notices?
questions.back: The Airport Remarks section of that airport's entry in the Chart Supplement.
questions.explanation: The Chart Supplement carries the textual airport data that doesn't fit on a chart — hours, services, fuel, and operational cautions — under each airport's Remarks entry.

questions.front: A pilot needs to perform the periodic VOR receiver accuracy check and wants to find a nearby ground or airborne checkpoint. Where should this information be found?
questions.back: The 'VOR Receiver Checkpoints' listing in the Chart Supplement.
options: The 'VOR Receiver Checkpoints' listing in the Chart Supplement
The notes section of the en route low altitude chart
The obstacle departure procedures page of the Terminal Procedures Publication
questions.explanation: The Chart Supplement lists both ground and airborne VOR checkpoints, including the frequency, radial, and (for airborne checkpoints) the altitude, so pilots can satisfy the periodic equipment check.

questions.front: An instrument approach procedure was amended after the current 56-day chart cycle was printed. Where would a pilot find this change before flying the approach?
questions.back: An FDC NOTAM for that procedure.
options: An FDC NOTAM for that procedure
The Aeronautical Chart Bulletin in the Chart Supplement
The Airport Remarks section of the Chart Supplement
questions.explanation: Changes to instrument approach and departure procedures between chart cycles are issued as FDC NOTAMs, not through the Chart Supplement, which mainly carries airport data and, for VFR charts, the Aeronautical Chart Bulletin.

questions.front: What is the Aeronautical Chart Bulletin, found in the Notices section of the Chart Supplement, used for?
questions.back: It lists major changes to VFR charting products (sectional, terminal area, and helicopter route charts) that have occurred since each chart's last print date; it does not cover IFR approach or departure procedure amendments.
questions.explanation: It's a VFR-chart-currency tool, easily confused with the NOTAM system, which is what actually covers IFR procedure amendments between chart cycles.

source.section: Chart Supplements - Notices / Aeronautical Chart Bulletin

questions.front: On the 'Takeoff Minimums and (Obstacle) Departure Procedures' page, a runway entry lists a specific obstacle with its height and location relative to the departure end of runway. What is the purpose of this obstacle note?
questions.back: To alert the pilot to a significant obstacle that drives the nonstandard takeoff minimums or climb gradient for that runway.
options: To alert the pilot to a significant obstacle that drives the nonstandard takeoff minimums or climb gradient for that runway
To list every obstacle within the surrounding 25 nautical miles regardless of its effect on departure obstacle clearance
To satisfy an FAA requirement to depict all man-made structures on airport diagrams
questions.explanation: Obstacle notes exist because that specific obstacle penetrated the obstacle identification surface during procedure design — it's the reason the runway needs nonstandard minimums or a steeper gradient in the first place.

questions.front: A pilot planning an IFR departure sees a triangle-T note on the approach chart but departs without checking the referenced takeoff minimums page, reasoning that 10 miles visibility and a high ceiling make it unnecessary. What risk does skipping that check create?
questions.back: Triangle T can indicate nonstandard weather minimums, a required minimum climb gradient (needed for obstacle clearance regardless of weather), or both; skipping the check means the pilot may not know about a climb-gradient requirement the aircraft must still meet in good VMC.
questions.explanation: Good VMC satisfies a visibility/ceiling minimum but does nothing to satisfy a published climb-gradient requirement — the two are separate protections against separate hazards (weather versus obstacles).

source.section: Terminal Procedures Publication - Takeoff Minimums symbology

questions.front: ATC wants to radar-vector an IFR departure off runway heading before the aircraft has climbed to an altitude that guarantees standard obstacle clearance on its own. Under what condition may ATC do this below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude?
questions.back: Only within an established Diverse Vector Area (DVA), evaluated to ensure obstacle clearance below the MVA/MIA.
options: Only within an established Diverse Vector Area (DVA), evaluated to ensure obstacle clearance below the MVA/MIA
Anytime, since ATC's radar separation standards already guarantee terrain and obstacle clearance for all vectors
Only at night, when obstruction lighting requirements provide an equivalent level of protection
questions.explanation: Radar vectors below the MVA/MIA are only safe from an obstacle standpoint inside a DVA that was specifically surveyed for that purpose; outside a DVA, ATC must keep vectored aircraft at or above the MVA/MIA.

source.section: 5-2-9, Instrument Departure Procedures (DP) - Diverse Vector Area

questions.front: What is a Diverse Vector Area (DVA), as published for some IFR departures?
questions.back: An area around an airport, evaluated using the same obstacle-clearance criteria as a diverse departure, within which ATC may vector a departing aircraft off runway heading and below the MVA/MIA while still ensuring required obstacle clearance (which may require a nonstandard climb gradient).
questions.explanation: A DVA lets ATC vector departures for traffic flow without waiting for the aircraft to reach the minimum vectoring altitude, because the obstacle survey already accounts for vectors flown within that area.

source.section: 5-2-9, Instrument Departure Procedures (DP) - Diverse Vector Area

questions.front: What is the primary purpose of a Standard Instrument Departure (SID), in contrast to an Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP)?
questions.back: SIDs mainly streamline ATC communication and traffic flow while still providing obstacle clearance; ODPs exist solely for obstacle avoidance.
options: SIDs mainly streamline ATC communication and traffic flow while still providing obstacle clearance; ODPs exist solely for obstacle avoidance
SIDs exist only for obstacle avoidance in mountainous terrain, while ODPs exist only to reduce radio congestion
SIDs and ODPs serve the identical purpose and differ only in which government agency publishes them
questions.explanation: Both guarantee obstacle clearance, but a SID's routing and altitudes are also shaped by traffic-management needs — that's why SIDs are usually assigned by ATC while ODPs are largely pilot-initiated.

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.179, when operating IFR in level cruising flight in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL on a magnetic course of 180 through 359 degrees, what class of altitude must a pilot fly?
questions.back: Any even thousand-foot MSL altitude (for example, 6,000 or 8,000 feet), unless assigned a different altitude by ATC.
questions.explanation: The odd/even hemispheric rule (odd for magnetic course 0-179 degrees, even for 180-359 degrees) applies to IFR cruising altitudes in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL and keeps opposite-direction IFR traffic separated by at least 1,000 feet; unlike the VFR cruising altitude rule in 91.159, IFR altitudes under 91.179 are plain thousands with no 500-foot addition.

source.section: 91.179, IFR cruising altitude or flight level

questions.front: A pilot computes that the aircraft's maximum available climb gradient in current conditions is 250 ft/NM, but the only usable runway's published ODP requires a minimum climb gradient of 320 ft/NM to clear terrain. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Delay the IFR departure from that runway until the gradient can be met — e.g., a different runway, lighter weight, or better conditions.
options: Delay the IFR departure from that runway until the gradient can be met — e.g., a different runway, lighter weight, or better conditions
Depart as planned, since the 200 ft/NM standard climb gradient always overrides a runway-specific published requirement
Depart VFR-on-top instead, since obstacle clearance requirements only apply to aircraft operating on an IFR clearance
questions.explanation: A published climb-gradient requirement exists because the standard 200 ft/NM clearance is not sufficient at that runway; an aircraft that cannot meet it has no guaranteed obstacle clearance and must find another way to comply, not accept the risk.

questions.front: What does the Communications section of a Chart Supplement airport entry provide to an IFR pilot?
questions.back: The frequencies for services available at or near that airport, such as the FSS, approach/departure control, ATIS, and CTAF/tower, needed to contact ATC and other facilities during arrival and departure.
questions.explanation: Charts show routes and altitudes, but the Chart Supplement is where a pilot finds the actual frequencies to use at each facility along the way.

questions.front: In the absence of any specific charted floor, at what altitude does Class E airspace typically begin above the surface in the continental United States?
questions.back: 1,200 feet AGL. (Class E can also begin at 700 feet AGL around airports with instrument approaches, at the surface where designated, or as high as 14,500 feet MSL in some remote areas.)
questions.explanation: The 1,200-foot AGL default is the baseline every instrument pilot needs to know because it defines where controlled airspace — and ATC's ability to separate IFR traffic — actually begins; sectional charts show a 700-foot floor with a fading magenta vignette and a 1,200-foot floor with a fading blue vignette.

questions.front: Class B airspace is commonly nicknamed after its typical appearance in cross-section because of how its altitude layers are structured. What is that nickname?
questions.back: An upside-down wedding cake — Class B tiers into progressively wider rings as altitude increases, narrowest at the surface near the primary airport.
options: An upside-down wedding cake
A stacked doughnut
An inverted funnel
questions.explanation: The 'upside-down wedding cake' shape matters for IFR planning because each ring has its own floor and ceiling; a route that clips the airspace at one altitude might be clear of it at another, so pilots must check the specific segment, not just the overall Class B boundary.

questions.front: An IFR flight is 8 nautical miles from the primary airport of a Class C airspace area, at an altitude 3,000 feet above the airport's elevation. The area uses the standard Class C configuration: a 5 NM inner core from the surface to 4,000 feet above airport elevation, and a 10 NM outer shelf from 1,200 to 4,000 feet above airport elevation. Is the aircraft inside Class C airspace?
questions.back: Yes — the aircraft is within the 10 NM outer shelf laterally and within its 1,200–4,000 foot AGL vertical range.
options: Yes — 8 NM falls within the 10 NM outer shelf, and 3,000 feet is within its 1,200–4,000 foot vertical range.
No — the outer shelf only extends to 5 NM, so 8 NM is outside Class C laterally.
No — 3,000 feet is below the outer shelf's floor, which doesn't begin until 4,000 feet.
questions.explanation: The classic mix-up is swapping the 5 NM inner-core radius with the 10 NM outer-shelf radius, or forgetting the outer shelf's floor is 1,200 feet rather than the surface — both distractors here reflect those two common errors.

questions.front: How are the ceiling and floor altitudes of a Class B airspace segment typically printed on a sectional chart?
questions.back: As a fraction such as '80/30' — ceiling over floor, both in hundreds of feet MSL.
options: As a fraction such as '80/30,' meaning a ceiling of 8,000 feet MSL and a floor of 3,000 feet MSL for that segment.
As a single AGL number representing only the floor, with the ceiling assumed to be 10,000 feet MSL.
As a range of magnetic headings rather than altitudes, since Class B floors don't vary by segment.
questions.explanation: Reading these numbers correctly is essential for planning a route beneath Class B: the floor (bottom number) varies segment to segment, so a pilot must check the number for the specific ring their route crosses rather than assume one altitude clears the whole area.

questions.front: What are the vertical limits of Class A airspace over the contiguous United States?
questions.back: 18,000 feet MSL up to and including flight level 600 (60,000 feet MSL).
questions.explanation: 18,000 feet is the dividing line where altimeter settings switch to standard (29.92) and where operations transition from the odd/even MSL cruising rule to the flight-level system — a boundary every IFR pilot must know cold.

questions.front: What is required of every aircraft operating within Class A airspace?
questions.back: An IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance; VFR flight is never permitted in Class A airspace.
options: An IFR flight plan and ATC clearance — no VFR operations are permitted in Class A regardless of weather.
A VFR flight-following arrangement with ATC, since Class A is advisory-only above 18,000 feet.
Nothing beyond a Mode C transponder — clearance is optional if traffic permits.
questions.explanation: A frequent misconception is that VFR-on-top or good weather lets a pilot legally operate VFR above 18,000 feet — it doesn't; Class A is IFR-only airspace by rule, with no VFR exception.

questions.front: An instrument-rated pilot wants to cruise at 18,500 feet MSL in clear skies without filing IFR. Is this legal?
questions.back: No — Class A airspace requires an IFR flight plan and clearance at all times; there is no VFR option, even in clear weather.
options: No — all flight in Class A airspace must be conducted under IFR, regardless of visibility or cloud clearance.
Yes, as long as standard VFR cloud clearance and visibility minimums for that altitude are maintained.
Yes, but only above flight level 240.
questions.explanation: Unlike every other airspace class, Class A has no VFR weather-minimums escape clause — the requirement is procedural (must be IFR), not visibility-based, which trips up pilots used to thinking in terms of cloud clearance and visibility.

questions.front: What distinguishes a Prohibited Area from other types of special use airspace?
questions.back: Flight is completely forbidden within its boundaries for all aircraft — it's the only special use airspace category where entry is flatly prohibited rather than merely restricted or hazardous (for example, P-56 over the White House and Capitol).
questions.explanation: Restricted and Warning Areas may sometimes be entered when inactive or with coordination; a Prohibited Area is a hard no at any time, which is the key distinction to remember.

questions.front: An IFR flight's filed route passes directly through an active Restricted Area. How does ATC typically handle this?
questions.back: ATC reroutes or vectors the flight around the active Restricted Area, coordinating with the using/controlling agency as needed.
options: ATC reroutes or vectors the aircraft around the area, since active Restricted Areas aren't available to IFR traffic without coordination with the controlling agency.
ATC clears the aircraft straight through, since an IFR clearance overrides restricted-area boundaries.
The pilot must personally contact the military or controlling agency for permission before ATC will act.
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes assume they must call the controlling agency themselves, but that coordination is ATC's job — the pilot's responsibility is simply to expect a reroute or altitude change if the area is hot.

questions.front: How does a Warning Area differ fundamentally from a Restricted Area?
questions.back: A Warning Area lies over international or coastal waters, so the U.S. government lacks the authority to restrict flight there — it only warns pilots of potential hazards, rather than prohibiting entry.
options: A Warning Area extends outward from the coast over international/domestic waters, so the FAA cannot legally prohibit flight through it the way it can within a Restricted Area's domestic boundaries.
A Warning Area is always inactive during IFR operations, unlike a Restricted Area.
A Warning Area requires the same prior military clearance as a Prohibited Area.
questions.explanation: The distinction hinges on sovereignty: Restricted Areas sit over U.S. sovereign land and can legally exclude traffic, while Warning Areas extend over waters where that authority doesn't apply, so they can only advise, not restrict.

questions.front: How does an active Military Operations Area (MOA) affect an IFR flight routed through it, compared to an active Restricted Area?
questions.back: A MOA does not exclude IFR traffic the way an active Restricted Area does. ATC will either provide separation from the military activity or vector/reroute the IFR flight around it, but the pilot doesn't need prior permission to be routed through — unlike a Restricted or Prohibited Area, entry isn't legally barred.
questions.explanation: Memory hook: Restricted and Prohibited Areas can lock IFR traffic out entirely, while a MOA is a 'traffic advisory and possible reroute' situation — the airspace stays technically available, just riskier due to military training traffic.

questions.front: What is the radius of the Mode C veil around a Class B primary airport, and what does it require?
questions.back: 30 nautical miles from the Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL. Aircraft operating anywhere within that 30 NM ring must have an operating Mode C (altitude-reporting) transponder, even if they never enter the actual Class B airspace boundaries.
questions.explanation: The veil is a transponder requirement, not an airspace boundary — pilots often confuse it with Class B itself, but it's a separate 30 NM circle that exists purely to ensure ATC has altitude data on everyone near a busy hub, charted as a thin solid blue/magenta circle.

questions.front: A pilot plans an IFR flight at 4,000 feet MSL, 25 nautical miles from a Class B primary airport but well outside the charted Class B lateral boundaries. Is an operating Mode C transponder required?
questions.back: Yes — the aircraft is within the 30 NM Mode C veil, and that requirement applies up to 10,000 feet MSL regardless of whether the flight is inside the Class B boundaries themselves.
options: Yes — the aircraft is inside the 30 NM Mode C veil, which applies regardless of the Class B lateral boundaries.
No — the requirement only applies to aircraft actually inside the charted Class B airspace.
Yes, but only because the flight is above 10,000 feet MSL.
questions.explanation: This is the exact scenario that trips people up: the veil extends well beyond the actual Class B shape in many places, so 'outside Class B' does not mean 'transponder not required.'

questions.front: Which of the following correctly describes the Mode C veil's relationship to the underlying Class B airspace?
questions.back: The Mode C veil applies to the entire 30 NM circle up to 10,000 feet MSL independent of the Class B shape — an aircraft can be well clear of Class B laterally or vertically and still be inside the veil.
options: It applies up to 10,000 feet MSL within 30 NM of the primary airport even beneath Class B shelves that don't reach the surface, so aircraft can be inside the veil while remaining clear of Class B itself.
It only applies to aircraft actually operating within the charted lateral limits of the Class B airspace.
It disappears above the highest charted Class B ceiling, since the veil is meant only to protect the Class B core.
questions.explanation: The veil and the Class B boundary are two separate, overlapping constructs; treating them as the same thing is the most common error, since much of the 30 NM circle lies outside the actual 'wedding cake' tiers.

questions.front: What does the acronym TRSA stand for, and how is its boundary distinguished on a sectional chart?
questions.back: Terminal Radar Service Area. It's charted with a solid black (gray) line, distinct from the magenta lines used for Class B and the blue lines used for Class C.
questions.explanation: TRSA outlines are easy to mistake for a Class B or C boundary at a glance; the line style and color are the quick visual tell that it's a voluntary radar service program, not a controlled-airspace class.

questions.front: For an IFR arrival into an airport with an underlying TRSA, how does the availability of radar services change compared to the same airport without a TRSA?
questions.back: Nothing changes for the IFR pilot — a TRSA adds optional sequencing/separation service for participating VFR traffic, but IFR aircraft already receive standard radar separation whether or not a TRSA exists.
options: It doesn't change — TRSA participation is a program for VFR aircraft; IFR traffic already receives full radar separation service regardless of the TRSA.
The IFR pilot must specifically request 'TRSA services' before ATC will provide separation.
The IFR aircraft must remain outside the TRSA boundary until cleared for the approach, similar to a Restricted Area.
questions.explanation: TRSAs exist to close a safety gap for VFR traffic near busy non-Class-B/C airports; IFR pilots sometimes assume there's a special procedure to request, but IFR service there is unchanged from any other radar environment.

questions.front: A sectional chart shows a TRSA around an airport whose underlying controlled airspace is Class D. For regulatory purposes, what airspace classification must a pilot comply with?
questions.back: Class D — the pilot follows the entry, equipment, and weather requirements of whatever airspace class actually underlies the TRSA; the TRSA designation itself is only a service program, not a Part 71 airspace class.
options: Class D — a TRSA is a radar service program overlaid on existing airspace, not a distinct class of airspace under 14 CFR Part 71.
Class C, because a TRSA automatically upgrades the underlying airspace to Class C entry requirements.
TRSA itself is a separate class of airspace with its own unique entry and equipment requirements.
questions.explanation: This is a favorite exam trap: TRSAs were a legacy attempt at Class-C-like service before Class C existed, but they were never folded into the modern A–G classification, so the regulatory requirements always come from the underlying class.

questions.front: Under the IFR cruising altitude rule for uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL, what altitude is appropriate for a magnetic course of 090°?
questions.back: Any odd-thousand-foot MSL altitude, such as 3,000, 5,000, or 7,000 feet — magnetic courses 000° through 179° use odd thousands, while 180° through 359° use even thousands.
questions.explanation: This 'odd course, odd altitude' pairing (and even/even) is the foundational IFR cruising rule; it only applies in uncontrolled airspace, since in controlled airspace ATC simply assigns the altitude.

source.section: 91.179(b)(1) — IFR cruising altitude, uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 MSL

questions.front: At or above flight level 290 in non-RVSM airspace, what flight levels are appropriate for a magnetic course of 180° through 359°, and how does the starting point differ from the pattern used below FL290?
questions.back: FL310, FL350, FL390, and so on — 4,000-foot intervals starting at FL310, not FL300. Below FL290 (from 18,000 feet MSL up to FL290), the eastbound and westbound starting levels are only 1,000 feet apart (FL190 eastbound vs. FL180 westbound). At FL290 and above, that gap widens to 2,000 feet (FL290 eastbound vs. FL310 westbound), reflecting the greater vertical separation required between opposite-direction flights in non-RVSM airspace at these higher altitudes.
questions.explanation: The FL290/FL310 offset (not FL290/FL300) is a classic 'gotcha' — pilots who assume the simple odd/even-thousands logic continues unchanged above 18,000 feet get this one wrong.

source.section: 91.179(b)(3) — IFR cruising flight levels at or above FL290, non-RVSM airspace

questions.front: Which range of magnetic courses requires an odd-thousand-foot MSL cruising altitude when flying IFR below 18,000 feet MSL in uncontrolled airspace?
questions.back: 000° through 179° requires an odd-thousand-foot MSL altitude; 180° through 359° requires an even-thousand-foot MSL altitude.
options: 000° through 179°
090° through 270°
Any course — the pilot may choose either odd or even at their discretion
questions.explanation: A simple way to remember it: courses roughly eastbound (000°-179°) fly odd, roughly westbound (180°-359°) fly even — this keeps opposite-direction IFR traffic vertically separated by at least 1,000 feet.

source.section: 91.179(b)(1) — IFR cruising altitude, uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 MSL

questions.front: A pilot receives an IFR clearance that includes 'maintain VFR-on-top.' Which cruising altitude rule now applies?
questions.back: The VFR cruising altitude appropriate to the course flown (the odd-thousand-plus-500 / even-thousand-plus-500 rule), not the IFR odd/even-thousand rule.
options: The VFR cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown, per the standard VFR hemispheric altitude rule.
The same IFR odd/even-thousand rule used for standard IFR cruising, since the flight plan is still IFR.
Any altitude at or above the MEA, chosen at the pilot's discretion, since VFR-on-top removes altitude restrictions.
questions.explanation: VFR-on-top is a hybrid: the clearance is still IFR, but 91.179 specifically directs the pilot to altitudes prescribed by the VFR cruising altitude rule instead of the IFR one — mixing these two up is one of the most common VFR-on-top errors.

source.section: 91.179(a) — IFR cruising altitude in controlled airspace, including VFR-on-top

questions.front: Besides selecting a VFR cruising altitude, what other requirements still apply to a pilot operating 'VFR-on-top' under an IFR clearance?
questions.back: The pilot must still operate under IFR procedures — complying with ATC clearances for any altitude change, minimum IFR altitudes, and applicable position reporting — while also meeting VFR cloud clearance and visibility minimums for the altitude flown. It's a blend of IFR clearance discipline and VFR weather/altitude rules, not a release from IFR entirely.
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes treat VFR-on-top as 'basically VFR now,' but the clearance and its IFR obligations remain in force; only the cruising-altitude selection and weather-minimum rules shift to the VFR standard.

source.section: 91.179(a) — IFR cruising altitude in controlled airspace, including VFR-on-top

questions.front: When operating IFR in controlled airspace, who determines the cruising altitude or flight level to be flown?
questions.back: ATC assigns the altitude or flight level in controlled airspace; the odd/even magnetic-course rule only governs altitude selection in uncontrolled airspace, where no ATC assignment exists.
options: ATC assigns it, and the pilot maintains whatever altitude or flight level is assigned.
The pilot selects any altitude at or above the MEA that satisfies the odd/even cruising rule.
The pilot selects the altitude before departure, and it cannot be changed en route without filing a new flight plan.
questions.explanation: This is the key contrast to keep straight: the odd/even cruising rule most pilots memorize actually only applies when there's no ATC assignment — i.e., in uncontrolled airspace — not as a general IFR cruising rule everywhere.

source.section: 91.179(a) — IFR cruising altitude in controlled airspace

questions.front: What is the practical consequence of Class G airspace being 'uncontrolled' for a pilot flying IFR within it?
questions.back: ATC does not provide separation service to IFR traffic in Class G airspace. The pilot is responsible for terrain and obstacle clearance and for selecting the appropriate cruising altitude under 91.179 without ATC assigning it, since ATC has no jurisdiction over uncontrolled airspace.
questions.explanation: IFR flight in Class G is legal, but 'legal' doesn't mean 'separated' — this is the distinction that catches pilots who assume an IFR flight plan automatically means ATC is providing traffic and terrain separation everywhere.

source.section: 91.179(b) — IFR cruising altitude in uncontrolled airspace

questions.front: In which parts of the United States is Class G airspace most likely to extend from the surface all the way up to 14,500 feet MSL, rather than the typical 700- or 1,200-foot AGL ceiling?
questions.back: Remote, sparsely served regions such as parts of the western U.S. and Alaska — where there isn't enough radar/NAVAID infrastructure to support controlled (Class E) airspace lower down, Class G extends all the way up to 14,500 feet MSL.
options: Remote and mountainous regions, such as parts of the western U.S. and much of Alaska, where radar and navigation coverage is sparse.
Directly beneath every Class B shelf nationwide.
Within 30 nautical miles of any Class C primary airport.
questions.explanation: The controlling factor is ATC's ability to provide service, not terrain height alone — where infrastructure is thin, the floor of controlled airspace simply moves up, leaving a much taller column of uncontrolled Class G beneath it.

questions.front: A pilot files an IFR flight plan for a short trip that begins and ends entirely within Class G airspace at a remote, non-towered airport with no radar coverage below 3,000 feet AGL. What should the pilot expect regarding an ATC clearance?
questions.back: ATC can only provide a clearance for the portion of the route within controlled airspace; within Class G the pilot self-navigates and self-separates while following the standard IFR cruising altitude rule, since there is no ATC clearance authority in uncontrolled airspace.
options: ATC can only issue a clearance for the portion of the flight that occurs in controlled airspace; while in Class G, the pilot proceeds under the 91.179 cruising altitude rule and provides their own separation, since ATC has no authority there.
ATC will deny the IFR flight plan outright, since IFR flight is not permitted anywhere within Class G airspace.
The flight is automatically treated as VFR until it reaches controlled airspace, and the pilot must refile IFR once airborne.
questions.explanation: Two common misconceptions collide here: that IFR is banned in Class G (it isn't) and that an IFR flight plan guarantees an ATC clearance everywhere along the route (it doesn't) — uncontrolled airspace is exactly that, uncontrolled, regardless of the pilot's IFR intentions.

source.section: 91.179(b) — IFR cruising altitude in uncontrolled airspace

questions.front: What are the maximum permissible bearing errors for a VOR check using (a) a VOT, (b) a ground checkpoint, and (c) an airborne checkpoint?
questions.back: (a) VOT: ±4°, (b) ground checkpoint: ±4°, (c) airborne checkpoint: ±6°. Dual-VOR cross-check: 4° between indicated bearings.
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.171 requires a VOR check within the preceding 30 days for IFR flight using VOR navigation, with these tolerances.

source.section: VOR equipment check for IFR operations

questions.front: To use VOR navigation under IFR, the VOR equipment check must have been performed within the preceding:
questions.back: 30 days.
options: 30 days
10 days
24 calendar months
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.171: the VOR check must be within the preceding 30 days (and logged). 24 calendar months applies to the altimeter/pitot-static and transponder checks, not the VOR.

source.section: VOR equipment check for IFR operations

questions.front: Describe the basic principle a VOR receiver uses to determine an aircraft's radial from a VOR ground station.
questions.back: The VOR station transmits two 30 Hz signals: an omnidirectional 'reference phase' signal with constant phase in every direction, and a rotating 'variable phase' signal whose phase shifts with azimuth. The airborne receiver measures the phase difference between the two signals; that difference in degrees equals the aircraft's magnetic radial from the station.
questions.explanation: This phase-comparison technique is what makes VOR fundamentally different from ADF/NDB, which uses signal-strength direction finding rather than phase comparison; it's also why VOR bearing accuracy doesn't degrade with distance the way NDB bearing accuracy does.

questions.front: A VOR ground facility is classified with a Terminal (T) standard service volume. Out to what maximum distance from the station is signal reception designed to be reliable?
questions.back: 25 nautical miles
options: 25 nautical miles
40 nautical miles
100 nautical miles
questions.explanation: Terminal (T) service volumes cover only 25 NM (up to 12,000 feet AGL) because they support instrument procedures near an airport; the Low (40 NM) and High (up to 130 NM) classes extend much farther for en route use.

questions.front: What is the standard service volume (distance and altitude ceiling) for a VOR classified in the Low altitude (L) category?
questions.back: 40 nautical miles, from 1,000 feet AGL up to (but not including) 18,000 feet AGL.
questions.explanation: The Low SVV is the one most relevant to typical piston IFR cruise altitudes; it's double the Terminal SVV's range and caps out right where the High-altitude structure begins at 18,000 feet.

questions.front: An aircraft is cruising at FL350 (35,000 feet), 110 NM from a VOR facility classified with a High-altitude (H) standard service volume. Is the aircraft within that facility's charted service volume?
questions.back: Yes, because the High SVV extends to 130 NM between 18,000 and 45,000 feet MSL
options: Yes, because the High SVV extends to 130 NM between 18,000 and 45,000 feet MSL
No, because High-altitude SVV is capped at 40 NM above 18,000 feet
No, because standard service volumes don't apply above 18,000 feet
questions.explanation: The High (H) SVV steps up with altitude, reaching 130 NM between 18,000 feet and 45,000 feet MSL; pilots sometimes wrongly assume the 40 NM Low-altitude figure applies everywhere, which would make them doubt a perfectly valid signal.

questions.front: Why did the FAA create the VOR Minimum Operational Network (MON)?
questions.back: To retain a reduced, strategically spaced subset of VOR stations (while decommissioning many others as GPS became primary) so pilots can still navigate conventionally and fly an approach into a MON airport if GPS becomes unavailable, whether from an outage, interference, or jamming.
