questions.explanation: MON is a deliberate downsizing, not an upgrade — the memory hook is 'fewer VORs, but always enough left to get you to an airport without GPS.'

questions.front: Which statement correctly describes what the VOR Minimum Operational Network (MON) program is doing to the VOR system nationwide?
questions.back: Decommissioning a large number of VOR stations while retaining a reduced, spaced-out network as a GPS backup
options: Decommissioning a large number of VOR stations while retaining a reduced, spaced-out network as a GPS backup
Installing new VOR stations everywhere GPS coverage is weak, in addition to all existing VORs
Replacing all ground-based VORs with a satellite-only backup system
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that MON adds equipment; in reality it removes many legacy VORs but keeps enough of them, appropriately spaced, to preserve basic conventional navigation nationwide.

questions.front: An aircraft flies directly over a VOR/DME station at 6,000 feet AGL. What distance will the DME receiver display at that instant?
questions.back: Approximately 1.0 NM
options: Approximately 1.0 NM
0.0 NM
Approximately 6.0 NM
questions.explanation: DME measures slant range, the straight-line distance to the station, not horizontal distance; since 1 NM is about 6,076 feet, an aircraft 6,000 feet directly above the station is roughly 1 NM away in a straight line, not 0.

questions.front: What rule of thumb tells a pilot when DME slant-range error has become operationally insignificant?
questions.back: Once the aircraft's distance from the station (in NM) is greater than its altitude above the station (in thousands of feet), slant-range error is negligible — for example, at 10,000 feet AGL the error becomes insignificant beyond roughly 10 NM from the station.
questions.explanation: The error is largest close to and above the station, where the slant angle is steep; it shrinks toward zero as distance grows and the geometry flattens out.

questions.front: How does DME actually measure the distance between an aircraft and a ground station?
questions.back: The airborne unit transmits paired interrogation pulses; the ground transponder replies after a fixed delay, and the airborne unit converts the round-trip time to distance
options: The airborne unit transmits paired interrogation pulses; the ground transponder replies after a fixed delay, and the airborne unit converts the round-trip time to distance
The airborne unit measures the phase difference between two amplitude-modulated signals broadcast by the ground station
The airborne unit measures the Doppler frequency shift of a continuous signal reflected off the ground station
questions.explanation: DME is a pulse round-trip-time system, fundamentally different from VOR's phase-comparison bearing technique; mixing the two up is a common exam trap.

questions.front: A VOR is providing a strong, steady signal and normal-looking CDI indications, but you can't hear its Morse code identifier. What should you do?
questions.back: Discontinue using that facility for navigation. A usable-looking signal without an audible identifier does not guarantee the station is reliable — it may be undergoing maintenance or otherwise officially unreliable even while still radiating a signal.
questions.explanation: Needle indications alone can't tell you a station is trustworthy; the identifier is the only positive confirmation you're receiving a correctly identified, in-service facility.

questions.front: Which of the following would indicate a VOR facility may be unreliable for navigation, even though the CDI appears to be functioning?
questions.back: The station's Morse code identifier cannot be heard despite receiving a usable signal
options: The station's Morse code identifier cannot be heard despite receiving a usable signal
The TO/FROM indicator flips as the aircraft passes through the station's cone of confusion
The CDI needle oscillates briefly while directly overflying the station
questions.explanation: Flag flips and brief needle wander directly over the station are normal station-passage behavior; a missing identifier is the real red flag that the facility shouldn't be trusted.

questions.front: What does a VOR receiver's TO/FROM indicator actually tell the pilot?
questions.back: Whether flying the course currently selected on the OBS would take the aircraft toward or away from the station. It does not show the aircraft's current heading, direction of flight, or position relative to the selected course — that's the CDI needle's job.
questions.explanation: Pilots often mistake TO/FROM for a heading indicator; it only evaluates the selected OBS course against the station's location, independent of which way the aircraft is actually pointed or moving.

questions.front: What causes 'reverse sensing' on a VOR CDI, and what's the practical effect on the pilot?
questions.back: Reverse sensing occurs when the OBS course selected is roughly 180 degrees off from the course actually needed to correctly track the desired radial (for example, an inbound course left selected while tracking outbound). The CDI then deflects opposite to the aircraft's true position relative to the course, so 'flying toward the needle' moves the aircraft farther off course instead of correcting it.
questions.explanation: Memory hook: reverse sensing is an OBS-setting problem, not a receiver malfunction — always confirm the selected course matches the direction you intend to fly relative to the station.

questions.front: A pilot intends to track outbound on the 090 radial of a VOR but mistakenly leaves the OBS set to 270 (an inbound course, with a TO indication displayed). If the aircraft drifts off course, how will the CDI needle behave?
questions.back: It will deflect in a direction that, if the pilot flies 'toward the needle' as normal, actually increases the deviation from the desired course
options: It will deflect in a direction that, if the pilot flies 'toward the needle' as normal, actually increases the deviation from the desired course
It will deflect exactly as it would with the correct 090/FROM setting, since CDI deflection depends only on the aircraft's position relative to the radial, not the OBS setting
It will remain centered, since only the TO/FROM flag, not the needle, is affected by having the OBS set to the wrong course
questions.explanation: This is reverse sensing in action: because the OBS is set 180 degrees off from the intended track, the needle's deflection is backwards relative to normal 'fly toward the needle' logic, so uncorrected habit makes the deviation worse, not better.

questions.front: The VOR CDI is centered with a FROM indication displayed. What does the course value shown under the OBS index represent?
questions.back: The radial the aircraft is currently positioned on, extending outward from the station through the aircraft
options: The radial the aircraft is currently positioned on, extending outward from the station through the aircraft
The magnetic heading the pilot must fly to reach the station by the most direct route
The reciprocal radial, meaning the course that would take the aircraft to the station
questions.explanation: With a centered needle and FROM flag, the OBS reading is the radial you're on; if the flag instead read TO at that same centered setting, the aircraft would be on the reciprocal radial.

questions.front: Compared to a conventional VOR/CDI head with a fixed compass card, why does flying with an HSI reduce the risk of orientation errors?
questions.back: The HSI's compass card rotates with the aircraft's actual heading, so the course pointer and deviation bar are displayed in the context of the current heading, making corrections more intuitive to visualize
options: The HSI's compass card rotates with the aircraft's actual heading, so the course pointer and deviation bar are displayed in the context of the current heading, making corrections more intuitive to visualize
The HSI electronically detects and automatically corrects for reverse sensing, so the pilot never needs to verify the OBS or course setting
The HSI displays the station's identifier as text, eliminating the need to listen for the Morse code identification
questions.explanation: A fixed-card CDI forces the pilot to mentally rotate the picture to match reality, which is where classic orientation mistakes creep in; the HSI's rotating card removes that mental step, though it can still be reverse-sensed if the course arrow is set backward.

questions.front: Flying in a mountain valley well below the surrounding ridgelines, a pilot notices the VOR signal from a station beyond the ridge becomes erratic and then unusable, despite being well within the facility's charted service volume distance. What's the most likely explanation?
questions.back: VOR signals travel by line of sight and can be blocked or degraded by intervening terrain regardless of horizontal distance from the station
options: VOR signals travel by line of sight and can be blocked or degraded by intervening terrain regardless of horizontal distance from the station
The VOR ground station's identification feature has failed
The aircraft has entered the station's cone of confusion
questions.explanation: Charted service volumes assume clear line of sight; terrain, not distance, is very often the real limiting factor for VOR reception at low altitude in mountainous terrain.

questions.front: What is the 'cone of confusion' in VOR navigation, and what should a pilot expect while flying through it?
questions.back: It's the cone-shaped zone of ambiguous or erratic signal directly above a VOR station, caused by the geometry of the transmitted signal near the antenna. Expect brief CDI needle wandering and a TO/FROM flag flip as you pass through it — normal behavior confirming station passage, not a malfunction.
questions.explanation: Recognizing this as expected behavior, rather than a failure, keeps a pilot from chasing a needle that's simply doing what it's supposed to do directly over the station.

questions.front: En route, a pilot notices the VOR CDI needle making small, rapid, erratic deflections that don't correspond to any real course change, a phenomenon often called 'scalloping.' What commonly causes this?
questions.back: Reflection of the VOR signal off nearby terrain, buildings, or other obstructions, producing multipath interference at the receiver
options: Reflection of the VOR signal off nearby terrain, buildings, or other obstructions, producing multipath interference at the receiver
Normal signal loss from flying just beyond the facility's rated service volume
The aircraft passing directly over the station within its cone of confusion
questions.explanation: Scalloping is a multipath problem, reflected signals arriving slightly out of phase with the direct signal, distinct from simple range-related signal loss or the expected cone-of-confusion wander overhead.

questions.front: When a VOR and a DME (or TACAN) are co-located as a single VOR/DME facility, how does a pilot tune the DME?
questions.back: By tuning the paired VOR frequency — the associated DME channel is automatically selected along with it, so there's no separate DME frequency to dial in for a co-located facility.
questions.explanation: This automatic channel pairing is why selecting a VOR/DME identifier on a nav radio brings up distance information with no extra tuning step.

questions.front: Using a single VOR/DME facility, what information lets a pilot establish a specific position fix along a route without reference to any second navigation facility?
questions.back: The radial the aircraft is currently on, combined with the DME distance from that same station
options: The radial the aircraft is currently on, combined with the DME distance from that same station
The radial alone, since DME distance only confirms groundspeed, not position
Two different radials from the same station, since DME distance cannot be combined with a VOR radial to define a fix
questions.explanation: A radial plus a DME distance from one co-located facility defines a unique point, a real advantage over VOR-only cross-fixes, which require two separate stations.

questions.front: An aircraft is tracking outbound from a VOR on the 180 radial, correctly flying a heading of about 180 with the OBS set to 180 and a FROM indication displayed. A crosswind pushes the aircraft west of the intended course. Which way will the CDI needle deflect, and what's the correct correction?
questions.back: The needle deflects left, and turning left (toward the east) will re-intercept the course
options: The needle deflects left, and turning left (toward the east) will re-intercept the course
The needle deflects right, and turning right (toward the west) will re-intercept the course
The needle stays centered because the OBS already matches the outbound course
questions.explanation: With the OBS correctly matched to the direction of flight, sensing is normal: since west of course is to the right side of the aircraft when heading south, the needle points left toward the course, and 'flying toward the needle' by turning left correctly re-intercepts it.

questions.front: What's the simplest way for a pilot to avoid accidentally creating reverse sensing on a VOR CDI?
questions.back: Always set the OBS to the course you actually intend to fly relative to the station, not its reciprocal, and confirm the TO/FROM flag matches your direction of travel before trusting the needle for corrections.
questions.explanation: Reverse sensing is a setup error, not a receiver defect — a quick TO/FROM-versus-intended-track sanity check before trusting the needle prevents it entirely.

questions.front: VOR ground stations operate within which frequency band?
options: 190-535 kHz LF/MF
questions.explanation: VOR's VHF band is why it's immune to the precipitation-static problems that plague NDBs on the LF/MF band, but limited to line-of-sight range; the UHF band listed as a distractor is actually used by glideslope and DME, not VOR.

questions.front: What is the minimum number of satellites a GPS receiver must receive to compute a three-dimensional position (latitude, longitude, and altitude)?
questions.back: 4 satellites
options: 3 satellites
5 satellites
4 satellites
questions.explanation: Three satellites can resolve only a two-dimensional fix (latitude/longitude); a fourth satellite is needed to also resolve altitude and correct for receiver clock error, giving a true 3D position. Mixing up the 2D and 3D satellite counts is the most common error on this topic.

questions.front: How many satellites must a GPS receiver track, with suitable geometry, for RAIM to detect a faulty satellite signal — and how many for the receiver to both detect AND automatically exclude the bad satellite (FDE)?
questions.back: 5 satellites for fault detection; 6 satellites for fault detection and exclusion (FDE).
questions.explanation: RAIM needs redundant satellites beyond the 4 required for a position fix so it can cross-check for a bad signal; one additional satellite beyond that lets the receiver identify and exclude the faulty one automatically.

questions.front: What does the acronym RAIM stand for in the context of IFR GPS navigation?
questions.back: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring
options: Redundant Aircraft Instrument Monitoring
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring
Radio Altitude Interference Management
questions.explanation: RAIM is the GPS receiver's own internal cross-check of redundant satellite signals to detect a faulty satellite, without needing any ground-based input — the key word test writers hinge distractors on is 'Autonomous.'

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – Global Positioning System (GPS)

questions.front: A pilot plans an IFR flight using a non-WAAS IFR-approved GPS receiver as the primary means of navigation for an RNAV (GPS) approach at the destination. What does the AIM recommend the pilot do during preflight planning regarding GPS integrity?
questions.back: Obtain a RAIM prediction for the estimated arrival time at the destination.
options: Confirm the receiver shows a valid position fix before engine start
Plan to fly a VOR approach instead, since GPS reliability can't be assured
Obtain a RAIM prediction for the estimated arrival time at the destination
questions.explanation: A non-WAAS receiver relies solely on satellite geometry for integrity, so the AIM recommends checking RAIM availability — via the receiver's own prediction function or another approved tool — for the ETA at the destination before depending on GPS for the approach.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – GPS RAIM Prediction

questions.front: A preflight RAIM prediction shows RAIM will be unavailable at the pilot's ETA for a planned RNAV (GPS) approach. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Plan an alternate means of navigation for the approach — such as a procedure based on a different navaid — or adjust the arrival time until RAIM is predicted to be available; GPS should not be relied on as the sole means of navigation for that approach.
questions.explanation: This is a very common scenario: a predicted RAIM outage simply means GPS cannot be trusted for that approach at that time, so the pilot must have another approved plan, not just hope the prediction is wrong.

questions.front: While flying a non-precision RNAV (GPS) approach in an aircraft without WAAS, the receiver annunciates a loss of RAIM (integrity) just after passing the final approach fix. What is the correct pilot response?
questions.back: Execute the missed approach procedure, since GPS position integrity can no longer be assured.
options: Switch the receiver to a 2D fix mode and continue using a barometric altitude input in place of GPS altitude
Execute the missed approach procedure, since GPS position integrity can no longer be assured
Continue the approach normally, since RAIM loss only affects en route navigation, not final approach
questions.explanation: Once integrity can't be verified past the FAF, the displayed GPS position can no longer be trusted for the approach — the correct response is a missed approach, not pressing on and hoping the position is still accurate.

source.section: Chapter 9, GPS Approach Operations and Loss of RAIM

questions.front: Name two acceptable ways a pilot can obtain a GPS RAIM availability prediction before an IFR flight.
questions.back: Using the GPS receiver's own self-contained RAIM prediction function, or an approved prediction source such as flight-planning software, a Flight Service Station briefing, or an FAA/vendor RAIM prediction tool.
questions.explanation: RAIM availability is a predictable quantity based on satellite ephemeris and geometry, not something to just assume — multiple approved sources exist, and knowing you have options (not just one required method) is the test point.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – GPS RAIM Prediction

questions.front: What primary navigational capability does WAAS add to a GPS receiver that a basic, non-WAAS IFR GPS receiver does not provide?
questions.back: Vertical (glidepath) guidance for instrument approaches.
options: The ability to receive signals from more satellites
Automatic frequency selection for VOR stations
Vertical (glidepath) guidance for instrument approaches
questions.explanation: WAAS augments GPS with differential corrections and integrity data broadcast from geostationary satellites, accurate enough to support approach procedures with vertical guidance such as LPV — a capability basic (LNAV-only) GPS cannot provide.

questions.front: What does an 'LPV' line of minima represent on an RNAV (GPS) approach chart?
questions.back: Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance — a WAAS-based approach providing both lateral and vertical guidance to a decision altitude (DA), structurally similar to an ILS, but classified as an approach with vertical guidance (APV) rather than a precision approach.
questions.explanation: A very common point of confusion: LPV looks and flies like an ILS, but it is legally an APV procedure, not a precision approach, because its signal-in-space doesn't meet the same integrity standard as ILS.

questions.front: An RNAV (GPS) approach chart publishes 'LP' minima at an airport where terrain prevents publishing a vertically guided line of minima. What does this indicate to a WAAS-equipped pilot?
questions.back: Lateral guidance only, similar to a localizer, with no vertical guidance provided despite WAAS.
options: Lateral guidance only, similar to a localizer, with no vertical guidance provided despite WAAS
The approach requires the aircraft to have a functioning ILS localizer receiver installed
LP minima are usable only by non-WAAS GPS receivers as a backup lateral mode
questions.explanation: LP (Localizer Performance) is a WAAS product published where obstacles or missing data prevent a vertically guided line of minima; despite the receiver's WAAS capability, only angular lateral guidance is provided and minima are flown to an MDA, not a DA — pilots often confuse it with LPV because the names look similar.

questions.front: Why is a separate preflight RAIM prediction generally not required for a WAAS-equipped GPS receiver operating within WAAS coverage?
questions.back: Because the WAAS ground reference network continuously monitors satellite signal integrity and broadcasts corrections and integrity data through geostationary satellites in real time, performing the same integrity function that RAIM performs for a non-WAAS receiver.
questions.explanation: This is a favorite distinction on exams: WAAS doesn't eliminate the need for integrity monitoring, it simply provides that function a different way, so a receiver-based RAIM prediction check becomes unnecessary.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)

questions.front: What Required Navigation Performance (RNP) value applies to the final approach segment of a standard, non-AR RNAV (GPS) approach procedure?
questions.back: RNP 0.3
options: RNP 1.0
RNP 0.3
RNP 2.0
questions.explanation: Standard RNP APCH procedures tighten containment as the aircraft nears the runway: RNP 1.0 for the initial and intermediate segments, RNP 0.3 for the final segment, and RNP 1.0 again for the missed approach; only RNP AR procedures are authorized below 0.3.

source.section: Chapter 9, RNP Values by Phase of Flight

questions.front: What navigation specification and accuracy value is used for standard domestic (CONUS) en route RNAV operations in the U.S. National Airspace System?
questions.back: RNAV 2 — 2 NM lateral accuracy for domestic en route operations.
questions.explanation: Domestic en route uses the RNAV 2 specification; despite commonly being called 'RNP 2' in casual conversation, it's officially an RNAV specification (no onboard performance monitoring/alerting requirement), unlike true RNP specifications such as RNP APCH.

source.section: Chapter 9, RNP Values by Phase of Flight

questions.front: Compared to conventional RNAV, what additional requirement legally defines an RNP navigation system?
questions.back: The system continuously monitors its own accuracy and alerts the crew if required performance is not met.
options: The system continuously monitors its own accuracy and alerts the crew if required performance is not met
The system requires a redundant standby GPS receiver to be installed as a backup
The system requires continuous radar contact with ATC throughout the flight
questions.explanation: RNP is RNAV plus onboard performance monitoring and alerting — that built-in self-check, not the specific accuracy number, is what legally distinguishes an RNP procedure from a plain RNAV procedure.

questions.front: How does an RNP AR (Authorization Required) approach differ from a standard RNP APCH procedure in terms of allowable RNP values and who may fly it?
questions.back: RNP AR approaches may be authorized with RNP values smaller than the standard 0.3 NM — down to as low as 0.1 NM — and can include curved (radius-to-fix) segments, but they require specific aircraft equipment approval and specially trained, authorized crews and operators; they are not available to every IFR-equipped aircraft or pilot.
questions.explanation: The word 'AR' is the key: extra navigational capability comes with extra authorization requirements, unlike a standard RNP APCH procedure that any properly IFR-GPS-equipped aircraft can fly.

source.section: Chapter 9, RNP Authorization Required (RNP AR) Approaches

questions.front: How often is the aeronautical navigation database used by IFR-approved GPS/RNAV systems typically updated?
questions.back: Every 28 days (AIRAC cycle).
options: Every 28 days (AIRAC cycle)
Every 56 days
Once per calendar year
questions.explanation: Navigation databases follow the international AIRAC (Aeronautical Information Regulation and Control) 28-day cycle, keeping waypoints, procedures, and airspace data synchronized with current charts.

questions.front: If a pilot's GPS navigation database has expired, what must be done before that pilot uses it to fly a published instrument procedure by its charted waypoint identifiers?
questions.back: The pilot must independently verify the currency and accuracy of the procedure's waypoints and course data against a current source, such as the current published approach chart, before relying on the expired database for that procedure.
questions.explanation: An expired database isn't automatically illegal to keep flying with, but blindly trusting stale waypoint data for a published procedure is the trap — always cross-check against a current chart once currency has lapsed.

questions.front: A pilot's GPS navigation database expired yesterday. Which use of the GPS remains acceptable without further verification, and which does not?
questions.back: Point-to-point navigation with pilot-verified waypoints is fine; flying a named published procedure is not, without independent verification.
options: Neither use is acceptable in any form until the pilot updates the expired database
Both uses remain fully acceptable without restriction as long as the lapse is recent
Point-to-point navigation with pilot-verified waypoints is fine; flying a named published procedure is not, without independent verification
questions.explanation: The distinction hinges on whether the pilot is trusting the database's built-in procedure/waypoint linkage (SIDs, STARs, approaches) or simply using GPS as a point-to-point tool with self-verified coordinates — the former demands current data, the latter doesn't.

questions.front: An instrument approach procedure requires DME to identify a stepdown fix, but the aircraft has no DME equipment installed. What may be used instead, per AIM guidance?
questions.back: An IFR-approved GPS navigation receiver.
options: A handheld VOR receiver carried as a backup
An IFR-approved GPS navigation receiver
ATC providing radar identification of the fix
questions.explanation: The AIM specifically authorizes a properly certified IFR GPS receiver to substitute for DME (and ADF) equipment on procedures that call for it, letting GPS-equipped aircraft fly procedures that would otherwise require dedicated DME hardware.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – GPS as a Substitute for ADF and DME

questions.front: List at least three specific ADF/NDB functions that an IFR-approved GPS receiver may substitute for, according to the AIM.
questions.back: Any of: navigating to or from an NDB; determining aircraft position over an NDB; determining position over a fix defined by an NDB bearing crossing a VOR or localizer course; and holding over an NDB fix.
questions.explanation: The AIM lists specific approved substitutions rather than a blanket 'GPS replaces ADF' statement — knowing the actual listed uses, not just the general idea, is what gets tested.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – GPS as a Substitute for ADF and DME

questions.front: For a procedure that includes a DME arc, what is an IFR-approved GPS unit authorized to do, per the AIM's GPS substitution guidance?
questions.back: Flying the DME arc itself, not just identifying a point on it.
options: Flying the DME arc itself, not just identifying a point on it
Only identifying the start of the arc, not flying it
GPS cannot be used for DME arcs under any circumstance
questions.explanation: GPS substitution for DME explicitly includes flying the arc, not merely fixing a single point along it — a detail some pilots incorrectly assume is excluded.

source.section: Chapter 1, Navigation Aids – GPS as a Substitute for ADF and DME

questions.front: In GPS/RNAV terminology, what is the functional difference between 'loading' an approach procedure and 'activating' it?
questions.back: Loading adds the procedure to the flight plan for reference; activating makes it the receiver's current navigation guidance.
options: Loading and activating both mean the same thing to a GPS/FMS receiver
Loading engages the autopilot to fly the procedure; activating only displays it on the moving map
Loading adds the procedure to the flight plan for reference; activating makes it the receiver's current navigation guidance
questions.explanation: A loaded-but-not-activated approach sits in the flight plan without providing CDI or autopilot guidance to it; only activation makes the GPS sequence and steer to those waypoints — a frequent source of 'why isn't it guiding me' confusion.

source.section: Chapter 9, GPS Approach Operations – Loading and Activating Procedures

questions.front: ATC vectors an aircraft to intercept the final approach course of an RNAV (GPS) approach, bypassing the initial and intermediate fixes. What should the pilot select on the GPS/FMS to receive correct guidance for this scenario?
questions.back: Activate the 'vectors-to-final' (VTF) option for the approach rather than activating the full procedure from the initial fix; this arms the final approach course and sequences the receiver to intercept it directly, without trying to navigate back to the bypassed fixes.
questions.explanation: Activating the full procedure while being vectored can cause the GPS to try to sequence to an already-passed initial fix; selecting vectors-to-final avoids that trap and is a classic scenario-based test question.

questions.front: In most IFR-approved GPS navigators, must a procedure be loaded into the flight plan before it can be activated?
questions.back: Yes — the procedure must first be loaded before it can be activated.
options: Yes — the procedure must first be loaded before it can be activated
No — activation automatically loads any procedure into a blank flight plan
It depends on whether the aircraft has an autopilot installed
questions.explanation: Loading always precedes activating in the normal workflow: the pilot selects and loads the procedure, then activates it (or a specific leg of it) to command guidance to it — this ordering is fundamental to correctly setting up a GPS approach.

source.section: Chapter 9, GPS Approach Operations – Loading and Activating Procedures

questions.front: The angular width of an ILS localizer course is adjusted so that full-scale needle deflection corresponds to a linear distance of approximately how many feet at the runway threshold?
questions.back: 700 feet
options: 700 feet
1,000 feet
250 feet
questions.explanation: Localizer course width (edge to edge) is set between roughly 3° and 6° specifically so it always spans about 700 feet at the threshold — a shorter localizer-to-threshold distance needs a wider angle, and a longer one needs a narrower angle, to hit that same 700-foot target.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Localizer)

questions.front: What is the standard glidepath angle used for an ILS glideslope?
questions.back: 3 degrees. A typical usable range is about 2.5° to 3.5°, but 3° is the design standard used at most ILS installations.
questions.explanation: A steeper-than-standard published glidepath (occasionally used where obstacles require it) increases both descent rate and approach speed sensitivity, which is why 3° is the default design target.

questions.front: On a standard ILS, the glideslope beam is about 1.4° thick vertically. Full-scale fly-up or fly-down deflection on the glideslope indicator therefore corresponds to roughly how far off the 3° glidepath the aircraft is?
questions.back: About 0.7° above or below the glidepath
options: About 0.7° above or below the glidepath
About 2.5° above or below the glidepath
About 5° above or below the glidepath
questions.explanation: Since the glideslope beam is roughly 1.4° thick top to bottom, full-scale deflection on each side represents about half of that, 0.7° — a much tighter tolerance than most pilots expect, which is why small glidepath deviations move the needle quickly near minimums.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Glide Slope)

questions.front: At what vertical angles can false ILS glideslope courses occur relative to the normal 3° glidepath, and how should pilots avoid capturing one?
questions.back: False glideslope courses can occur at angles between roughly 6° and 12° above the true 3° path (signal reversals near 9°, false nulls near 12°, either type possible around 6°). Pilots avoid them by intercepting the glideslope from below at the altitude published on the approach chart and continuously cross-checking altitude versus distance from the runway; flown this way, false glideslopes are essentially never encountered.
questions.explanation: Intercepting from above — diving to catch a centered needle — is what exposes an aircraft to these higher false lobes; flying the charted altitudes and capturing the glidepath from below avoids the problem entirely.

source.section: Chapter 9, ILS Errors — False Courses (per Addendum B, Nov. 2019)

questions.front: Crossing the outer marker on an ILS approach is annunciated in the cockpit by which light-and-tone combination?
questions.back: A blue light with continuous dashes
options: A blue light with continuous dashes
An amber light with alternating dots and dashes
A white light with continuous dots
questions.explanation: The three markers get 'faster and whiter' as you approach the runway: blue with continuous dashes (outer), amber with alternating dot-dash (middle), white with continuous dots (inner).

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Marker Beacon)

questions.front: Where is the middle marker (MM) normally located relative to the runway, and what does crossing it approximate on a Category I ILS?
questions.back: The MM is located about 3,500 feet from the runway threshold, at the point where the normal 3° glidepath is at approximately 200 feet above the runway — roughly the Category I decision height.
questions.explanation: Before precise radio-altimeter DH callouts were common, the amber-light, dot-dash-tone MM served as a positional backup telling the pilot 'you're at about DH now.'

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Marker Beacon)

questions.front: The inner marker (IM), where installed, is used primarily to identify what?
questions.back: The Category II decision height point on the approach
options: The Category II decision height point on the approach
The missed approach point for a Category I approach
The outer edge of the localizer's usable course
questions.explanation: The IM (white light, continuous dots) is only found on runways equipped for Category II approaches, where the lower DH — as low as 100 feet — needs its own marker closer to the runway than the MM.

questions.front: If the glideslope portion of an ILS is inoperative or not used and the approach is flown using only localizer guidance, the approach is flown to what kind of minimum?
questions.back: A minimum descent altitude (MDA), as with a non-precision approach
options: A minimum descent altitude (MDA), as with a non-precision approach
A decision altitude (DA), identical to the full ILS
A decision height 100 feet lower than the full ILS DH
questions.explanation: Without vertical guidance there is no glidepath to fly a continuous descent to a DA, so a localizer-only approach reverts to the level-off-and-look non-precision profile, even though it uses the ILS localizer signal.

questions.front: Flying an ILS back course with a conventional (non-HSI) VOR/LOC head set to the front course value, what unusual needle behavior occurs if the aircraft drifts off course, and how must the pilot correct?
questions.back: The CDI shows reverse sensing: the needle deflects toward the same side the aircraft is already displaced to (for example, right deflection when the aircraft is right of course) instead of pointing back toward centerline. The pilot must fly opposite the needle's deflection — the reverse of the normal 'correct toward the needle' technique — to get back on course.
questions.explanation: Reverse sensing occurs because the receiver interprets any localizer signal as though the aircraft were flying the front course toward the antenna; flying the back course flips that geometry, so the normal correction technique produces exactly the wrong control input unless the pilot deliberately reverses it.

source.section: Chapter 9, ILS Approach — Localizer Back Course

questions.front: Flying a back-course approach using an HSI, how should the pilot set the course pointer to get normal, non-reversed needle sensing?
questions.back: Set the course pointer to the localizer's front course value, not the back-course inbound heading
options: Set the course pointer to the localizer's front course value, not the back-course inbound heading
Set the course pointer to the back-course inbound heading, matching the direction of flight
Set the course pointer to the current heading and adjust it continuously during the approach
questions.explanation: An HSI's course pointer orientation, not just which frequency is tuned, determines needle sensing; setting it to the front course makes the deviation bar behave normally ('needle left, fly left') even while flying the back course — a trick a simple VOR/LOC head can't replicate.

source.section: Chapter 9, HSI Presentation — Localizer Back Course

questions.front: What does the needle on an ADF (or RBI) indicator display, and how does that differ from a magnetic bearing to the station?
questions.back: It displays relative bearing: the angle measured clockwise from the nose of the aircraft (the aircraft's heading) to the direction of the NDB station. Relative bearing equals magnetic bearing to the station only when the aircraft is on a magnetic heading of 000°; otherwise the heading must be added to get the magnetic bearing.
questions.explanation: Confusing relative bearing with magnetic bearing is one of the most common ADF errors — the needle shows the station's direction relative to where the nose is pointed, not relative to magnetic north, unless heading happens to be 360°/000°.

questions.front: An aircraft flying a magnetic heading of 270° has an ADF relative bearing to the station of 090°. What is the magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station?
questions.back: 000° (magnetic heading + relative bearing = magnetic bearing to the station: 270° + 090° = 360°, which is 000°)
options: 000° (magnetic heading + relative bearing = magnetic bearing to the station: 270° + 090° = 360°, which is 000°)
180°, the reciprocal of the relative bearing reading
090°, since the relative bearing already equals the magnetic bearing
questions.explanation: The formula MH + RB = MB (subtracting 360° if the sum exceeds it) converts the ADF's relative reading into a true magnetic bearing — a step pilots often skip, mistakenly treating the relative bearing itself as the magnetic bearing.

questions.front: A pilot continuously adjusts heading so the ADF needle stays pinned on the nose (0° relative bearing) all the way to an NDB in a steady crosswind. What is this technique called, and what ground track results?
questions.back: Homing; the aircraft drifts into a curved ground track downwind of the direct course to the station
options: Homing; the aircraft drifts into a curved ground track downwind of the direct course to the station
Tracking; the aircraft holds a straight ground track directly to the station throughout
Bracketing; the aircraft holds a straight ground track using a constant wind correction angle
questions.explanation: Homing never establishes a wind correction angle — the aircraft is always pointed straight at the station relative to its own heading, so a crosswind keeps blowing it off the direct path, tracing a curved course. True tracking requires holding a constant WCA so the ground track, not just the heading, points at the station.

questions.front: How does the course width of a Simplified Directional Facility (SDF) compare to a standard ILS localizer?
questions.back: The SDF transmits a fixed course width of either 6° or 12°, whichever gives better flyability at that site, while an ILS localizer's angular width is adjustable, typically between about 3° and 6°, calculated to give 700 feet of width at the runway threshold.
questions.explanation: SDF signal quality is comparable to a localizer, but because the width is fixed rather than site-tuned to the runway, an SDF course is generally less precise than an ILS localizer.

questions.front: What distinguishes a Localizer-type Directional Aid (LDA) course from a standard ILS localizer course?
questions.back: The LDA course may be offset more than 3° from the extended runway centerline, unlike a standard localizer
options: The LDA course may be offset more than 3° from the extended runway centerline, unlike a standard localizer
The LDA course is always aligned exactly with the runway centerline, more precisely than a standard localizer
The LDA transmits from a mobile ground unit repositioned before each approach to match wind direction
questions.explanation: A localizer-type signal aligned within 3° of the runway is simply called a localizer; once the offset exceeds 3° it is classified as an LDA. Straight-in minimums can still be published if the offset does not exceed 30°, otherwise only circling minimums are given.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Localizer Type Directional Aid)

questions.front: Can a Localizer-type Directional Aid (LDA) approach include vertical glidepath guidance?
questions.back: Yes, in limited cases. Most LDA facilities provide course guidance only (non-precision, flown to an MDA), but a small number are paired with a glideslope and charted as 'LDA/Glideslope,' providing vertical guidance similar to an ILS.
questions.explanation: This is a key contrast with the SDF, which is never paired with a glideslope; an LDA sometimes is, so it's important to check the approach chart's minimums section rather than assume.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Localizer Type Directional Aid)

questions.front: Compared with a VOR CDI, where full-scale deflection typically represents about 10°-12° of angular displacement, a localizer CDI's full-scale deflection represents only about 2.5°. This makes the localizer indication approximately how much more sensitive than a VOR indication?
questions.back: About four times more sensitive than the VOR indication
options: About four times more sensitive than the VOR indication
About four times less sensitive than the VOR indication
Equally sensitive, since both use the same angular scale
questions.explanation: Because the localizer's full-scale width (roughly 2.5° each side) is about a quarter of the VOR's (roughly 10° each side), the same needle deflection represents a much smaller heading error on the localizer — which is why chasing a localizer needle with big VOR-style corrections leads to overcontrolling on final.

questions.front: What is a compass locator, and where is it typically installed relative to an ILS?
questions.back: A compass locator is a low-power NDB (25 watts or less, roughly a 15-mile range) collocated with an ILS marker — most commonly the outer marker (called the LOM) and sometimes the middle marker (LMM) — providing a bearing/homing signal on the ADF in addition to marking the beacon's location.
questions.explanation: Compass locators are handy backups: they let a pilot fly to and identify the outer marker fix using ADF alone if the marker beacon receiver or DME is unavailable.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-2 and 1-1-9 (NDB / Instrument Landing System — Compass Locator)

questions.front: On a 3° ILS glidepath, a pilot notices the glideslope needle centering while the aircraft is well above the altitude charted for that distance from the runway, consistent with intercepting the glidepath from above rather than from below. What should the pilot suspect, and what is the correct response?
questions.back: A false glideslope; hold the assigned altitude and confirm the true glidepath by cross-checking altitude against distance
options: A false glideslope; hold the assigned altitude and confirm the true glidepath by cross-checking altitude against distance
A false glideslope; follow the needle down immediately, since any centered needle confirms the true glidepath
A localizer signal reversal; switch the receiver over to the back-course frequency
questions.explanation: False glideslope courses (roughly 6°-12° above the true 3° path) are essentially never encountered if the glidepath is captured from below at charted altitudes — intercepting from above, as in this scenario, is exactly what exposes an aircraft to them, so altitude-versus-distance is the only reliable cross-check.

source.section: Chapter 9, ILS Errors — False Courses (per Addendum B, Nov. 2019)

questions.front: For the sharpest, most precise indication of marker beacon passage during an ILS approach, a marker beacon receiver's sensitivity switch should normally be set to:
questions.back: LOW
options: LOW
HIGH
It makes no difference; sensitivity doesn't affect marker beacon indications
questions.explanation: LOW sensitivity narrows the reception cone so the light and tone activate only when nearly overhead the marker, giving a precise passage indication for the ILS; HIGH sensitivity widens the cone and suits an earlier alert when using a marker, such as a compass locator, as an en route fix.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Marker Beacon)

questions.front: How does the ADF needle behave as an aircraft flies directly over the NDB station it is tracking?
questions.back: The needle swings rapidly and reverses, typically rotating through about 180°, as the station passes beneath and then behind the aircraft. This rapid reversal is called 'station passage' and confirms the aircraft has flown over the NDB.
questions.explanation: Station passage is the cue pilots use to start timing on an NDB approach's final segment, similar to how a TO/FROM flip is used on a VOR.

questions.front: Within the 108.10-111.95 MHz band that VOR and ILS localizer facilities share, how can a pilot tell from the frequency alone which type of facility it is?
questions.back: An odd digit in the first decimal place indicates a localizer; an even digit indicates a VOR
options: An odd digit in the first decimal place indicates a localizer; an even digit indicates a VOR
An even digit in the first decimal place indicates a localizer; an odd digit indicates a VOR
Frequency alone never distinguishes a localizer from a VOR in this shared band
questions.explanation: This odd/even split lets the two systems share the same VHF band without interference; above 111.95 MHz, up to 117.95 MHz, all frequencies belong to VOR/VORTAC facilities, with no localizers assigned there.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1 — Navigation Aids (VOR and ILS Frequency Assignment)

questions.front: An aircraft is on a magnetic heading of 050°, and the ADF relative bearing to an NDB reads 320°. What is the magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station?
questions.back: 010° (magnetic heading + relative bearing = magnetic bearing to the station; 050° + 320° = 370°, minus 360° = 010°)
options: 010° (magnetic heading + relative bearing = magnetic bearing to the station; 050° + 320° = 370°, minus 360° = 010°)
320°, since the relative bearing reading already is the magnetic bearing
190°, the reciprocal bearing from the station back to the aircraft
questions.explanation: A common error is reading the relative bearing itself as though it were already the magnetic bearing, ignoring aircraft heading entirely; another is confusing the bearing TO the station with the reciprocal bearing FROM the station. Always apply MH + RB = MB, subtracting 360° if the sum exceeds it.

questions.front: A compass locator installed at the outer marker of an ILS normally transmits which identifier?
questions.back: The first two letters of the associated localizer's three-letter identifier, in Morse code
options: The first two letters of the associated localizer's three-letter identifier, in Morse code
The complete three-letter localizer identifier, in Morse code, on the localizer frequency
A continuous unmodulated tone with no Morse identification
questions.explanation: For example, if the localizer identifier is I-ABC, its outer compass locator (the LOM) transmits just 'AB' on its own NDB frequency; a compass locator at the middle marker, when installed, instead transmits the last two letters.

source.section: Chapter 1, Section 1, Para 1-1-9 (Instrument Landing System — Compass Locator)

questions.front: In a standard holding pattern, which direction are all turns made?
questions.back: Right turns
options: Right turns
Left turns
Toward the nearest terrain-free side
questions.explanation: A 'standard' hold is defined specifically by right turns; when left turns are required the pattern is 'nonstandard,' and ATC or the procedure must explicitly say so, since right turns are otherwise assumed.

source.section: Chapter 9, Holding Procedures — Standard vs. Nonstandard Patterns

questions.front: ATC issues holding instructions that explicitly state 'left turns' for the pattern. How must the pilot fly the pattern differently from a standard hold?
questions.back: Make all turns to the left instead of the right
options: Make all turns to the left instead of the right
Use 1.5-minute legs instead of 1-minute legs
Enter the pattern only by the direct method, never parallel or teardrop
questions.explanation: Specifying 'left turns' simply converts the pattern to nonstandard; every other rule for timing, speed, and entry stays the same — only the turn direction reverses from the default right-turn standard pattern.

source.section: Chapter 9, Holding Procedures — Standard vs. Nonstandard Patterns

questions.front: If ATC gives holding instructions without stating a turn direction, what should the pilot assume?
questions.back: Standard turns — turn right at the fix and at the end of each leg. Left (nonstandard) turns must always be explicitly stated by ATC or depicted on the procedure.
questions.explanation: Right turns are the default; a controller or chart note only needs to appear when the pattern deviates from that default, which is why silence on turn direction always means standard.

source.section: Chapter 9, Holding Procedures — Standard vs. Nonstandard Patterns

questions.front: At or below 14,000 feet MSL, how long is the inbound leg of a standard holding pattern timed to be?
questions.back: 1 minute.
questions.explanation: The 1-minute inbound leg is the baseline everything else in holding timing is built around — outbound time is adjusted circuit to circuit to make the inbound leg come out as close to 1 minute as possible.

questions.front: Above 14,000 feet MSL, what is the standard inbound leg time in a holding pattern?
questions.back: 1.5 minutes
options: 1.5 minutes
1 minute
2 minutes
questions.explanation: Leg time increases from 1 minute to 1.5 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL to account for the higher true airspeeds typically flown at that altitude — a common trap is assuming 1 minute applies everywhere.

questions.front: On the very first outbound leg after entering a hold, before the pilot has observed any wind drift, how long should that leg be timed?
questions.back: The same as the inbound leg time (1 or 1.5 minutes)
options: The same as the inbound leg time (1 or 1.5 minutes)
Half the inbound leg time, to leave room for a later correction
Whatever distance equals one DME mile, regardless of the clock
questions.explanation: Wind effect can't be known until you've flown one circuit, so the first outbound leg uses the standard time; on later circuits you lengthen or shorten the outbound leg based on how far the wind pushed you off the target inbound time.

questions.front: While holding, a pilot applies a 6° left wind-correction angle to track the inbound course accurately. What correction should be applied on the outbound leg?
questions.back: 18° right (triple the inbound angle, opposite direction)
options: 18° right (triple the inbound angle, opposite direction)
6° left (match the inbound angle exactly)
12° right (double the inbound angle, opposite direction)
questions.explanation: The classic rule of thumb is to triple the inbound drift correction and apply it in the opposite sense outbound, because the outbound leg is flown away from the fix and needs a bigger correction to arrive positioned for a clean intercept back onto the inbound course.

source.section: Chapter 9, Wind Correction in Holding Patterns

questions.front: Unless a lower speed is charted for the pattern, what is the maximum holding airspeed at or below 6,000 feet MSL?
questions.back: 200 KIAS
options: 200 KIAS
230 KIAS
175 KIAS
questions.explanation: 200 KIAS is the base tier of the three-tier standard holding speed table, which steps up as altitude increases to keep protected holding airspace a manageable size relative to typical true airspeeds.

questions.front: What is the maximum standard holding airspeed for altitudes above 6,000 feet through 14,000 feet MSL?
questions.back: 230 KIAS.
questions.explanation: This is the middle tier of the standard holding speed table (200 / 230 / 265 KIAS) — memorize it as speed increasing in steps as the altitude band goes up.

questions.front: What is the maximum standard holding airspeed for altitudes above 14,000 feet MSL?
questions.back: 265 KIAS
options: 265 KIAS
230 KIAS
250 KIAS
questions.explanation: 265 KIAS is the top tier of the standard holding speed table; pilots sometimes mistakenly carry the 230 KIAS mid-altitude limit all the way up, forgetting the final step above 14,000 feet.

questions.front: An enroute chart notes 'Max holding airspeed 175 KT' at a fix where the aircraft's altitude would otherwise allow 230 KIAS under the standard table. Which speed governs?
questions.back: 175 KIAS — a charted maximum always overrides the standard table
options: 175 KIAS — a charted maximum always overrides the standard table
230 KIAS — the standard table always overrides a charted note
Either speed may be flown, since the note is advisory only
questions.explanation: A charted holding speed is published because the protected holding airspace at that specific fix was sized for a slower speed, often due to terrain or nearby airspace constraints; exceeding it risks flying outside protected airspace.

questions.front: What are the three standard holding pattern entry procedures, and what determines which one a pilot uses?
questions.back: Direct, teardrop, and parallel entry — the choice is determined by the direction the aircraft is approaching the holding fix from, relative to the holding course.
questions.explanation: All three entries accomplish the same goal — getting established on the inbound holding course — but the mechanics differ because the airspace around the fix is divided into three sectors, one keyed to each entry type.

questions.front: During a teardrop entry to a holding pattern, roughly what angle does the outbound track make with the outbound holding course?
questions.back: Approximately 30°
options: Approximately 30°
Approximately 70°
Approximately 110°
questions.explanation: After crossing the fix, the pilot flies outbound on a heading about 30° off the outbound course, on the holding side, for the standard leg time, then turns to intercept the inbound course — tracing the pattern's namesake teardrop shape.

questions.front: Describe the parallel entry procedure for a standard holding pattern.
questions.back: Cross the fix, turn to parallel the outbound holding course on the non-holding side for the standard leg time, then turn in the direction of the holding pattern through more than 180° to intercept the inbound holding course.
questions.explanation: The 'more than 180°' turn is the giveaway detail examiners test — it distinguishes parallel entry from a normal turn-to-outbound and is easy to forget since it's a bigger turn than the other two entries require.

questions.front: Of the three holding-pattern entry sectors arranged around the holding course, which one is narrowest, spanning only 70° and lying along the outbound course on the holding side?
questions.back: Teardrop
options: Teardrop
Parallel
Direct
questions.explanation: The airspace around a holding fix is conventionally divided into a 70° teardrop sector, a 110° parallel sector, and the remaining 180° direct sector — remember it as '70-110-180,' which sums to a full 360°.

questions.front: In a holding pattern defined by DME or GPS distance rather than time, how is the length of each leg specified?
questions.back: In nautical miles from the holding fix
options: In nautical miles from the holding fix
In minutes and seconds, same as a standard hold
In degrees of track change per leg
questions.explanation: DME/GPS holds substitute distance for time — e.g., '4 NM legs' — so the pilot or the RNAV system ends the outbound leg and begins the turn inbound at the specified distance rather than after a fixed number of minutes.

questions.front: In a DME-based holding pattern, how does wind affect the length of the outbound leg compared to a time-based hold?
questions.back: It doesn't affect the outbound leg length at all — the outbound leg always ends at the specified DME distance regardless of wind. Only the heading (wind-correction angle) is adjusted to keep the aircraft tracking the correct course; unlike a timed hold, there is no need to lengthen or shorten the outbound leg for wind.
questions.explanation: This is a commonly confused distinction: pilots trained on timed holds instinctively want to 'adjust the outbound time for wind,' but a DME/GPS leg is defined by distance, so that adjustment simply doesn't apply.

questions.front: When intercepting a VOR radial well away from the station, which intercept angle is generally most practical?
questions.back: A moderate angle, roughly 30-45°
options: A moderate angle, roughly 30-45°
The smallest possible angle, under 10°
The largest possible angle, 90° or more
questions.explanation: A shallow angle takes too long to close on the course, while a very steep angle causes the CDI to swing through center quickly and is easy to overshoot; a 30-45° intercept balances a timely intercept against enough time to roll out precisely on course.

questions.front: Why should a pilot use a smaller intercept angle when closing on a VOR course near the station versus far from it?
questions.back: Radials converge as they approach the station, so the same angular CDI deflection represents much less physical distance close in. A wide intercept angle near the station makes the needle swing through center very quickly, making it easy to overshoot the course.
questions.explanation: This is why the CDI feels 'twitchy' near the airport compared to out on the airway — the physical distance per dot of deflection shrinks as radial spacing narrows toward the station.

questions.front: What is a DME arc, in the context of an instrument approach or en route transition?
questions.back: A curved track flown at a constant distance from a DME-equipped navaid
options: A curved track flown at a constant distance from a DME-equipped navaid
A holding pattern flown using DME mileage instead of a timed leg
A straight course flown to intercept a VOR radial at a 90° angle
questions.explanation: DME arcs let ATC sequence an aircraft from the en route structure onto a final approach course, or between procedure segments, without radar vectors, by having the pilot hold a fixed radius from the DME station while turning.

questions.front: Using a standard (non-RNAV) VOR receiver, what is the common 'bracket' technique for hand-flying a DME arc?
questions.back: Rotate the OBS about 10° ahead of the current radial in the direction of travel; when the CDI centers, turn to intercept that new radial and repeat the process, 'walking' the course selector around the arc in small increments.
questions.explanation: The 10° bracket keeps the aircraft weaving gently in and out of the arc within a tight tolerance, since flying a true continuous curve isn't possible using discrete radial cuts from a fixed-station VOR receiver.

questions.front: When using an RMI bearing pointer to fly a DME arc, where should the pilot try to keep the pointer positioned?
questions.back: On the wingtip, at roughly the 90° relative bearing position
options: On the wingtip, at roughly the 90° relative bearing position
Directly on the nose, at the 0° relative bearing position
Directly on the tail, at the 180° relative bearing position
questions.explanation: Keeping the bearing pointer on the wingtip means the aircraft is abeam the station at the correct radius; if the needle falls aft of the wingtip the aircraft is drifting outside the arc (turn slightly toward the station to bring it back up), and if it creeps forward the aircraft is drifting inside the arc, cueing small heading corrections.

questions.front: Why should a pilot lead the turn onto (or off of) a DME arc rather than waiting until reaching the exact arc distance?
questions.back: Because the aircraft's turn radius means it continues moving toward or across the arc distance while the turn is in progress; leading the turn — starting it slightly before the exact DME distance — rolls the aircraft out already established on the arc or course instead of overshooting it.
questions.explanation: The same 'lead the turn' logic applies whenever intercepting any curved or angular path — waiting for the exact number on the DME readout before turning guarantees an overshoot.

questions.front: In a typical light training aircraft, which flight instruments are driven by the vacuum system?
questions.back: The attitude indicator and the heading indicator.
options: Attitude indicator and heading indicator
Attitude indicator and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: The vacuum system typically spins the gyros in the attitude and heading indicators. The turn coordinator is usually electric; airspeed/altimeter/VSI are pitot-static.

questions.front: The pitot tube's ram inlet and drain hole both become blocked by ice, but the static ports stay clear. How does the airspeed indicator behave?
questions.back: It acts like an altimeter — indicated airspeed increases in a climb and decreases in a descent, regardless of actual airspeed.
questions.explanation: Trapped pressure in the pitot line stays constant while static pressure changes with altitude, so the ASI responds to altitude changes instead of airspeed.

source.section: Ch. 5 — Flight Instruments: pitot-static system failures

questions.front: During cruise flight, insects build a nest that completely blocks the ram air inlet of the pitot tube, but the drain hole underneath stays open. What happens to the airspeed indicator?
questions.back: It drops to and indicates zero, regardless of the airplane's actual speed.
options: It slowly climbs to full-scale deflection and stays there.
It drops to and indicates zero, regardless of the airplane's actual speed.
It freezes at the last airspeed reading and stops responding to speed changes.
questions.explanation: With the ram-air inlet sealed but the drain hole open, any pressure trapped in the pitot line leaks out through the drain and equalizes with static pressure, leaving no differential to drive the diaphragm. This differs from a full blockage of both inlet and drain, which traps pressure and makes the ASI mimic an altimeter instead.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: A pitot tube's drain hole becomes clogged with dried mud, but the ram air inlet stays completely clear. What is the immediate effect on the airspeed indicator?
questions.back: None initially — ram air pressure still reaches the diaphragm and the ASI keeps indicating normally.
options: The ASI immediately begins reading zero, just as if the ram inlet itself were blocked.
The ASI immediately begins acting like an altimeter, rising and falling with altitude.
None initially — ram air pressure still reaches the diaphragm and the ASI keeps indicating normally.
questions.explanation: The drain hole's job is only to let condensation escape; as long as the ram-air path is open, pressure still builds normally against static pressure. The real hazard is delayed: trapped moisture can freeze in flight and eventually plug the tube, so a normal reading now doesn't guarantee one later.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: Climbing through a cloud layer with pitot heat inadvertently switched off, ice seals only the ram air inlet of the pitot tube; the two separate static ports on the fuselage remain completely clear. Which instrument(s) will be affected, and how?
questions.back: Only the airspeed indicator is affected; it drops to and remains at zero.
options: The airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator are all affected, since they share the same pitot-static plumbing.
Only the airspeed indicator is affected; it drops to and remains at zero.
Only the vertical speed indicator is affected, since it is the most sensitive pitot-static instrument.
questions.explanation: The altimeter and VSI are driven solely by the static ports, not the pitot tube, so a pitot-only blockage cannot touch them; only the ASI, which needs ram-air (impact) pressure, is affected. Mixing up which instruments depend on pitot pressure versus static pressure is a common exam trap.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Impact Pressure Lines

questions.front: The static port becomes completely iced over while the airplane is level at 8,000 feet, and the pilot does not select the alternate static source. What will the altimeter subsequently do as the airplane climbs or descends?
questions.back: It will freeze and continue displaying 8,000 feet no matter what altitude the airplane actually reaches.
options: It will freeze and continue displaying 8,000 feet no matter what altitude the airplane actually reaches.
It will slowly drift toward zero as residual air leaks out of the static line.
It will continue tracking altitude changes accurately using pitot pressure as a substitute.
questions.explanation: A blocked static line traps the pressure that existed at the moment of blockage, so the altimeter is stuck showing the altitude at which the port became obstructed — it can neither rise nor fall with the airplane's real altitude changes.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: With that same iced-over static port, how will the vertical speed indicator behave during a subsequent climb or descent?
questions.back: It will settle at and remain on zero, giving no indication of the actual climb or descent.
options: It will show an increasingly exaggerated rate, since the calibrated leak can no longer bleed off pressure.
It will reverse sense, showing a descent during an actual climb.
It will settle at and remain on zero, giving no indication of the actual climb or descent.
questions.explanation: The VSI compares current static pressure to static pressure delayed through a calibrated leak; with no new static pressure reaching either side, the differential collapses to zero and the needle parks there — arguably the most dangerous static-blockage error because it falsely suggests level flight.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: The static port ices over at 8,000 feet while the pitot tube stays clear and heated. If the pilot then climbs to 10,000 feet without selecting alternate static air, how will the indicated airspeed compare to the airplane's actual airspeed?
questions.back: Indicated airspeed will read lower than the airplane's actual airspeed.
options: Indicated airspeed will read lower than the airplane's actual airspeed.
Indicated airspeed will read higher than the airplane's actual airspeed.
Indicated airspeed will remain completely accurate because the pitot source is unaffected.
questions.explanation: The ASI is fed ram pressure minus static pressure; because the trapped static pressure is stuck at the higher 8,000-foot value while true static pressure at 10,000 feet is lower, the instrument subtracts too much and under-reads. Descending back below the blockage altitude reverses the error into an over-read.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: If a static port blockage traps pressure at a given altitude and the airplane then descends below that altitude, how does the resulting airspeed indicator error differ from the climb-above case, and why?
questions.back: It over-reads (shows higher than actual airspeed): the trapped static pressure is now lower than the true, higher static pressure at the lower altitude, so the sensed pitot-minus-static differential is larger than the real one — the opposite of the under-read seen when climbing above the blockage altitude.
questions.explanation: The blocked static line acts like a pressure 'snapshot' taken at the moment it clogged; below that altitude, real static pressure is higher than the trapped value, which mirrors and reverses the error seen above the blockage altitude.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Blockage of the Pitot-Static System

questions.front: In a typical unpressurized single-engine airplane, selecting the alternate static source (which vents into the cockpit) after the primary static port fails usually causes the altimeter to indicate...?
questions.back: A slightly higher altitude than the airplane's actual altitude.
options: A slightly lower altitude than the airplane's actual altitude.
A slightly higher altitude than the airplane's actual altitude.
Exactly the same altitude, since alternate static air is pressure-compensated.
questions.explanation: Airflow over the fuselage typically makes cabin static pressure slightly lower than outside ambient pressure; the altimeter interprets lower pressure as a higher altitude, so indicated altitude, indicated airspeed, and VSI reading commonly all increase a bit when the alternate source is selected.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Alternate Static Source

questions.front: When the alternate static source is selected in an unpressurized airplane (with windows and vents closed), what typically happens to indicated airspeed compared to using the normal static port?
questions.back: It typically increases slightly, because cabin static pressure is usually a bit lower than outside ambient static pressure, which widens the sensed pitot-minus-static pressure differential.
questions.explanation: This is why many POHs publish a small alternate-static airspeed correction table — pilots should expect indicated numbers to run a few knots fast, not slow, when flying on alternate static air.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Alternate Static Source

questions.front: Immediately after a pilot switches to the alternate static source while holding stabilized, level flight, what should be expected on the vertical speed indicator?
questions.back: A brief, momentary indication of a climb before the needle settles back near zero.
options: A permanent full-scale climb indication that never returns to zero.
A brief, momentary indication of a climb before the needle settles back near zero.
No change whatsoever, since the VSI is isolated from the static system.
questions.explanation: The instant drop in sensed static pressure when switching to the typically lower-pressure alternate source produces a quick, transient VSI 'jump' showing a climb, which settles out once pressure stabilizes; pilots should expect this and not mistake it for a malfunction.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Alternate Static Source

questions.front: What is pressure altitude, and what Kollsman window setting produces it?
questions.back: Pressure altitude is the altitude read when the altimeter's Kollsman window is set to 29.92" Hg (standard sea-level pressure); it represents height above the standard datum plane and is the starting point for computing density altitude.
questions.explanation: Setting 29.92" Hg removes the effect of the day's actual sea-level pressure, standardizing every altimeter to the same reference plane — this is also why pressure altitude (29.92) is used above 18,000 feet MSL when flying flight levels.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Altimeter (Types of Altitude)

questions.front: Define density altitude and identify the two inputs needed to compute it.
questions.back: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard (non-ISA) outside air temperature; it is computed from pressure altitude and the current temperature, and it directly correlates with aircraft and engine performance.
questions.explanation: Density altitude has no direct instrument readout; pilots calculate it from pressure altitude and temperature because it — not indicated or true altitude — determines actual takeoff, climb, and landing performance.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Altimeter (Types of Altitude)

questions.front: If a pilot sets the current local altimeter setting in the Kollsman window and reads the altimeter directly, what type of altitude is being displayed?
questions.back: Indicated altitude — the altitude shown on a properly set altimeter, which only equals true altitude when temperature and pressure exactly match the standard atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Because the altimeter mechanism corrects for nonstandard pressure via the Kollsman setting but not for nonstandard temperature, indicated altitude and true altitude diverge whenever outside air temperature departs from the standard lapse rate.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Altimeter (Types of Altitude)

questions.front: How is absolute altitude defined, and how is it typically measured in flight?
questions.back: Absolute altitude is the airplane's height above the terrain directly below it (AGL); it's commonly measured with a radar altimeter rather than the pressure altimeter, which instead reads height above mean sea level (MSL).
questions.explanation: Absolute altitude changes constantly with terrain even in level flight, which is why it matters for terrain-clearance systems like a radar altimeter but is not what a standard pressure altimeter displays.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Altimeter (Types of Altitude)

questions.front: What memory aid describes the altimeter error produced when flying from higher pressure into lower pressure without updating the altimeter setting, and what is the actual effect on true altitude?
questions.back: "From high to low, look out below" — true altitude ends up lower than indicated altitude, meaning the airplane is actually flying lower than the altimeter shows.
questions.explanation: The mnemonic captures why failing to update the altimeter setting is dangerous specifically when moving toward lower pressure — obstacle clearance erodes silently, with no cockpit indication that anything is wrong.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Altimeter Errors

questions.front: An airplane flies from a warm air mass into a significantly colder air mass, and the pilot never touches the altimeter setting (which remains current for the local pressure). How does the airplane's true altitude compare to its indicated altitude?
questions.back: True altitude ends up lower than indicated altitude.
options: True altitude ends up lower than indicated altitude.
True altitude ends up higher than indicated altitude.
True and indicated altitude stay equal, since the altimeter setting already compensates for temperature.
questions.explanation: Cold air is denser than standard, compressing pressure levels closer to the ground; because the altimeter is calibrated for a standard atmosphere, it over-reads in cold temperatures — the airplane is actually lower than shown, the same hazardous direction as flying from high to low pressure.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Altimeter Errors

questions.front: An airplane departs with the altimeter set to 30.42" Hg. Without resetting the Kollsman window, it flies into an area where the actual local altimeter setting has dropped to 29.92" Hg. Using the standard rule of thumb, roughly how much error is now present, and in which direction?
questions.back: About 500 feet — indicated altitude reads higher than the airplane's true altitude.
options: No meaningful error, since altimeters only need resetting for temperature changes, not pressure changes.
About 500 feet — indicated altitude reads lower than the airplane's true altitude.
About 500 feet — indicated altitude reads higher than the airplane's true altitude.
questions.explanation: Using roughly 1 inch Hg per 1,000 feet, the 0.50" Hg drop from 30.42 to 29.92 corresponds to about 500 feet: since the airplane flew into lower pressure than the altimeter is set for, true altitude is about 500 feet lower than indicated — a concrete case of 'high to low, look out below.'

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Altimeter Errors

questions.front: Which two common atmospheric conditions cause an altimeter to display a higher reading than the airplane's true altitude if the pilot never updates the altimeter setting?
questions.back: Flying from an area of higher pressure into an area of lower pressure, and flying from warmer air into colder-than-standard air — both leave true altitude lower than indicated altitude, meaning the airplane is actually lower than the instrument shows.
questions.explanation: Both errors share the same root cause: the altimeter is calibrated to the standard atmosphere, so any nonstandard condition that compresses pressure levels closer to the ground makes indicated altitude read higher than true altitude.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Altimeter Errors

questions.front: Roughly how long does a conventional (non-instantaneous) vertical speed indicator take to settle on an accurate reading after a change in vertical speed?
