questions.back: About 6 to 9 seconds, due to the calibrated leak (restricted orifice) inside the case that intentionally delays the pressure equalization used to derive rate of climb or descent.
questions.explanation: That multi-second delay is why pilots are taught not to chase the VSI needle with abrupt pitch corrections during instrument flying — by the time it catches up, an overcorrection is often already underway.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Vertical Speed Indicator

questions.front: What design feature is responsible for the several-second lag inherent in a standard (non-instantaneous) vertical speed indicator?
questions.back: A calibrated leak that restricts how quickly air can equalize between the instrument case and the static line.
options: A calibrated leak that restricts how quickly air can equalize between the instrument case and the static line.
A small vacuum-driven gyroscope that must spin up before sensing pitch changes.
A heated element in the static line that delays moisture evacuation.
questions.explanation: The VSI's diaphragm compares immediate static pressure against static pressure that reaches the case only through a small calibrated restriction; that deliberate metering produces the characteristic lag. It's a pressure instrument, not a gyroscopic one, which is a common point of confusion.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Vertical Speed Indicator

questions.front: How does an instantaneous vertical speed indicator (IVSI) reduce the lag that affects a standard VSI?
questions.back: It adds accelerometer-actuated pumps that generate an initial vertical-speed indication from vertical acceleration before the usual pressure differential builds up.
options: It removes the calibrated leak entirely and equalizes case pressure to the static line instantly.
It adds accelerometer-actuated pumps that generate an initial vertical-speed indication from vertical acceleration before the usual pressure differential builds up.
It replaces the diaphragm with a GPS-driven digital rate computer.
questions.explanation: An IVSI still relies on the same calibrated-leak pressure mechanism as a standard VSI for sustained readings, but adds small accelerometer-driven pumps that momentarily change case pressure the instant a climb or descent begins, offsetting the normal lag rather than eliminating the underlying mechanism.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Vertical Speed Indicator

questions.front: What airspeed range does the yellow arc on an airspeed indicator represent, and how should it be flown?
questions.back: The yellow (caution) arc spans from VNO (maximum structural cruising speed) to VNE (never-exceed speed); it should be flown only in smooth air, since turbulence encountered at these speeds risks exceeding the airplane's structural limits.
questions.explanation: The yellow arc exists because structural margins shrink as speed increases; gusts or turbulence there can combine with maneuvering loads to exceed design limits, which is why it's placarded for smooth air only.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Airspeed Indicator Markings

questions.front: The top of the green arc on an airspeed indicator marks which airspeed?
questions.back: VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed.
options: VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed.
VNE, the never-exceed speed.
VFE, the maximum flap-extended speed.
questions.explanation: The green arc covers the normal operating range from VS1 up to VNO; VFE marks the top of the separate white (flap) arc, and VNE is shown as a single red radial line just beyond the top of the yellow caution arc, not the green arc.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Airspeed Indicator Markings

questions.front: On a Mach meter, the movable red-and-white striped marker that shows the current never-exceed Mach/airspeed limit, which shifts with altitude, is commonly known as the...?
questions.back: Barber pole.
options: Coffin corner marker.
Standard datum needle.
Barber pole.
questions.explanation: The 'barber pole' is a movable marker, driven by an altitude/airspeed capsule, that automatically repositions to display VMO/MMO — the never-exceed limit, which typically decreases with altitude due to compressibility effects. 'Coffin corner' is a related but separate concept: the high-altitude convergence of low-speed stall buffet and high-speed Mach buffet.

source.section: Chapter 5, Pitot/Static Flight Instruments – Airspeed Indicator Markings

questions.front: What two fundamental properties of a spinning gyroscope allow gyroscopic flight instruments to work?
questions.back: Rigidity in space (a spinning gyro resists any force that tries to tilt its spin axis, so the axis stays fixed relative to space) and precession (a force applied to the spinning rotor produces its effect roughly 90° later, in the direction of rotation).
questions.explanation: Rigidity in space is what lets the attitude and heading indicators hold a stable reference; precession is what causes their small errors, since any applied force shows up displaced 90° from where it was applied rather than where intuition suggests.

source.document: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C
source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Gyroscopic Flight Instruments

questions.front: A pilot pushes down on one edge of a spinning gyro rotor to tilt it. Because of gyroscopic precession, where does the rotor actually respond to that push?
questions.back: It dips at a point roughly 90° farther around, in the direction of rotor rotation
options: It dips right at the point where the push was applied, with no delay
It dips at a point roughly 90° farther around, in the direction of rotor rotation
It doesn't dip at all — the rigidity of the spin keeps it locked in place
questions.explanation: This 90°-offset response is the definition of precession, and it's the same principle that causes heading indicator drift and small attitude indicator errors during turns — the error shows up somewhere other than where the disturbing force was applied.

source.document: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C
source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Gyroscopic Flight Instruments

questions.front: In a mechanical attitude indicator, how is the gyro oriented, and what does that let the instrument show?
questions.back: The gyro's spin axis is oriented vertically; because it stays rigid in space, the horizon bar attached to the gimbal directly shows the aircraft's actual pitch and bank relative to that fixed reference.
questions.explanation: A vertical spin axis lets the instrument reference true 'up' independent of how the airplane pitches or rolls around it — that's why the attitude indicator alone shows both pitch and bank directly.

questions.front: In a mechanical heading indicator (directional gyro), how is the gyro oriented, and what does that let the instrument show?
questions.back: The gyro's spin axis is oriented horizontally; rigidity in space keeps that axis pointed in a fixed direction, so the card attached to the gimbal shows the aircraft's heading as the airplane yaws around the gyro.
questions.explanation: Because the spin axis is horizontal instead of vertical, the heading indicator senses rotation about the vertical (yaw) axis rather than pitch or bank — that's the key difference from the attitude indicator's gyro orientation.

questions.front: A mechanical attitude indicator is most likely to display a brief, self-correcting pitch or bank error under which condition?
questions.back: During and immediately after a steep turn or other abrupt maneuver
options: During and immediately after a steep turn or other abrupt maneuver
During steady, unaccelerated straight-and-level cruise flight
Only during the first five minutes after engine start, before the gyro spins up
questions.explanation: The gravity-referenced erecting mechanism that keeps the gyro's spin axis vertical can be momentarily displaced by the accelerations of an abrupt maneuver; the display normally re-erects and reads accurately again within about a minute of returning to stabilized, unaccelerated flight.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Attitude Indicator errors

questions.front: About how often should a pilot check and, if necessary, reset the heading indicator against the magnetic compass during straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight?
questions.back: Every 15 minutes
options: Every 15 minutes
Once at the start of every flight only
Every 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Mechanical heading indicators precess over time from both bearing friction and the earth's rotation, so pilots are taught to cross-check and reset the heading indicator to the compass roughly every 15 minutes to keep heading information accurate.

source.document: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C

questions.front: What are the two causes of heading indicator drift that make periodic resetting against the magnetic compass necessary?
questions.back: Real drift, caused by mechanical friction within the gyro and its gimbals, and apparent drift, caused by the earth's rotation underneath the gyro's fixed orientation in space (its rate varies with latitude).
questions.explanation: Apparent drift is the more confusing of the two for students because the gyro itself isn't malfunctioning — the earth is simply rotating out from under it, which is why the correction needed grows with latitude.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Heading Indicator, precession errors

questions.front: What does the needle on a turn-and-slip indicator actually sense?
questions.back: Only the rate of turn (yaw) about the vertical axis
options: Only the rate of turn (yaw) about the vertical axis
Both the rate of roll and the rate of yaw
Bank angle directly, the same as an attitude indicator
questions.explanation: The turn-and-slip's rate gyro is restrained so it only responds to rotation about the vertical (yaw) axis — that's why the needle alone can't tell a pilot anything about roll rate, unlike a turn coordinator, whose canted gyro senses both roll and yaw.

questions.front: A turn coordinator's gyro is canted upward about 30° from the horizontal rather than mounted flat. What advantage does this give the instrument over a turn-and-slip indicator?
questions.back: It lets the gyro sense both roll rate and yaw rate, so the display reacts as soon as banking begins
options: It lets the gyro sense both roll rate and yaw rate, so the display reacts as soon as banking begins
It removes any need for the instrument to draw electrical or vacuum power to operate
It allows the instrument to display exact bank angle directly instead of a turn rate
questions.explanation: Canting the gimbal makes the gyro sensitive to both roll and yaw, which is why a turn coordinator's miniature aircraft responds to the onset of a roll before a steady rate of turn even develops — a turn-and-slip needle can't do that.

questions.front: The inclinometer (the ball) mounted with a turn coordinator or turn-and-slip indicator is best described as...
questions.back: A non-gyroscopic instrument that shows coordination — slip or skid — using gravity and centrifugal force on a free ball
options: A non-gyroscopic instrument that shows coordination — slip or skid — using gravity and centrifugal force on a free ball
A second gyroscopic sensor, driven by the same rotor as the turn needle, used to sense rate of turn
A pendulum-based instrument that senses bank angle directly, independent of whether the turn rate is correct
questions.explanation: It's a common misconception that the ball is gyro-driven because it's housed with the turn coordinator; in fact it's just a sealed, curved glass tube with a free ball, and it reports coordination, not turn rate.

questions.front: What defines a standard rate turn, and how long does it take to complete a 360° turn at that rate?
questions.back: A standard rate turn ('rate one') is a turn at 3° per second, which completes a 360° turn in 2 minutes (180° in 1 minute).
questions.explanation: Every standard-rate turn is 3°/second regardless of aircraft type or airspeed — what changes with airspeed is the bank angle needed to hold that rate, not the rate itself.

questions.front: Which rule of thumb estimates the bank angle needed to hold a standard rate turn at a given true airspeed?
questions.back: True airspeed (in knots) divided by 10, plus 7
options: True airspeed (in knots) divided by 10, plus 7
True airspeed (in knots) divided by 2
A constant 30° of bank regardless of airspeed
questions.explanation: For example, at 120 knots TAS the rule gives about 19° of bank for a standard rate turn — a handy cross-check for the turn coordinator when flying partial panel or verifying the instrument.

questions.front: Why do some aircraft use a half-standard-rate turn (1.5° per second) instead of a standard rate turn at high true airspeeds?
questions.back: At high true airspeeds a standard-rate turn (3°/second) would require an excessively steep bank angle, so many aircraft flight manuals and operators specify a half-standard-rate turn to keep the bank angle reasonable.
questions.explanation: Since the bank angle needed for a given turn rate grows with true airspeed, cutting the required rate in half keeps bank angles manageable for faster airplanes — this is why some POHs call for a half-standard-rate turn above a stated speed.

questions.front: What is the rule of thumb for leading the rollout when returning to a desired heading from a standard-rate turn?
questions.back: Lead the rollout by approximately one-half the bank angle in degrees before reaching the desired heading.
questions.explanation: Because it takes a few seconds for the bank to come off and the turn rate to decay, starting the rollout early — by about half the bank angle — keeps the aircraft from overshooting the target heading.

questions.front: How do older air-driven mechanical attitude indicators differ from a modern solid-state AHRS-based attitude display in terms of pitch and bank limits?
questions.back: The mechanical gyro can tumble past its pitch/bank limits and lose its reference; the AHRS-based display has no such tumble limits
options: The mechanical gyro can tumble past its pitch/bank limits and lose its reference; the AHRS-based display has no such tumble limits
Both instruments share identical tumble limits, since they're built around the same physical spinning-gimbal design
The AHRS-based display actually tumbles and loses its reference more easily than the older mechanical gyro
questions.explanation: A mechanical gyro's gimbals physically run out of travel in extreme unusual attitudes, causing it to tumble and give unreliable indications until it re-erects; solid-state AHRS computes attitude mathematically from sensor data, so there's no mechanical limit to tumble past.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Attitude Indicator and Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: What does AHRS stand for, and what does it replace in a glass-cockpit airplane?
questions.back: Attitude and Heading Reference System — it replaces the traditional spinning vacuum or electric gyros with solid-state sensors (accelerometers, rate sensors, and a magnetometer) that compute attitude and heading electronically.
questions.explanation: AHRS performs the same job the mechanical attitude indicator and heading indicator used to do, but with no spinning mass and no vacuum system — this is why solid-state glass cockpits eliminate most of the traditional gyro failure modes.

source.document: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C
source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: What is the primary function of the Air Data Computer (ADC) in a glass cockpit?
questions.back: It computes pressure altitude, airspeed, and vertical speed from pitot-static data for the PFD
options: It computes pressure altitude, airspeed, and vertical speed from pitot-static data for the PFD
It computes aircraft attitude, heading, and turn rate from solid-state gyroscopic sensors
It manages engine fuel flow and other powerplant parameters shown on the multi-function display
questions.explanation: The ADC is the pitot-static side of the glass panel — it's the digital equivalent of the altimeter, airspeed indicator, and VSI — while the AHRS is the gyroscopic side; keeping the two systems straight matters because they fail independently.

source.document: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C
source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: On most primary flight displays (PFDs), how is an invalid or failed instrument parameter typically indicated to the pilot?
questions.back: A red X is displayed over the affected instrument or data field
options: A red X is displayed over the affected instrument or data field
The entire PFD screen goes completely black with no other indication
The affected parameter simply freezes at its last valid value with no other warning
questions.explanation: The red-X convention is deliberately hard to miss and applies whether it's the attitude sphere, airspeed tape, or heading tape that lost its data source — recognizing it quickly is essential to avoid trusting invalid information.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: What is a reversionary (backup) display mode in a glass cockpit airplane, and when is it used?
questions.back: Reversionary mode reconfigures the multi-function display (MFD) to present primary flight instrument data (attitude, airspeed, altitude, heading) if the PFD fails, so the pilot retains flight instrument information on the remaining screen.
questions.explanation: Reversionary mode is a system-level redundancy feature, separate from having a standalone standby instrument — losing the PFD doesn't necessarily mean losing glass-panel flight data if the MFD can pick up the role.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: In actual IMC, the AHRS in a glass cockpit airplane fails, and the PFD's attitude sphere and heading tape both display red Xs. What is the pilot's most appropriate immediate action?
questions.back: Transfer attention to the standby attitude indicator and fly partial panel using the remaining reliable instruments
options: Transfer attention to the standby attitude indicator and fly partial panel using the remaining reliable instruments
Continue referencing the PFD attitude sphere since it will briefly show the last valid data
Immediately declare an emergency and descend regardless of terrain or traffic
questions.explanation: An AHRS failure removes the pilot's attitude and heading source on the PFD; the trained response is the same as a vacuum-era partial panel emergency — shift the scan to the independent standby instruments rather than trusting a flagged display.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays, system failures

questions.front: A red X appears over the airspeed tape on the PFD while the attitude sphere and heading tape remain valid. This pattern is most consistent with a failure of which system?
questions.back: The Air Data Computer (ADC) or its pitot-static input, not the AHRS
options: The Air Data Computer (ADC) or its pitot-static input, not the AHRS
The AHRS, since airspeed data comes from the same gyroscopic sensors as attitude
The autopilot's servo motor that drives the airspeed tape needle
questions.explanation: Because attitude/heading (AHRS) and air data (ADC) are independent systems feeding the PFD, a failure isolated to airspeed while attitude and heading stay valid points to the ADC or its pitot-static source — recognizing which system failed tells the pilot which backup instrument to trust.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays, ADC and AHRS

questions.front: What is the key advantage of the standby (backup) attitude/airspeed/altitude instrument cluster found in many glass-cockpit airplanes?
questions.back: It operates independently of the aircraft's primary electrical system and the AHRS/ADC, often on its own battery
options: It operates independently of the aircraft's primary electrical system and the AHRS/ADC, often on its own battery
It receives its data from the same AHRS as the PFD, ensuring consistent readings
It only becomes active automatically once the autopilot has been engaged for several minutes
questions.explanation: The whole point of a standby instrument is independence — if it shared a power source or sensor with the primary system, a single failure could take out both the PFD and the backup at once.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays, standby instruments

questions.front: Which two independent systems feed data to a modern PFD, and what does each one supply?
questions.back: The AHRS supplies attitude, heading, and rate data; the ADC supplies airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed data
options: The AHRS supplies attitude, heading, and rate data; the ADC supplies airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed data
The AHRS supplies airspeed and altitude; the ADC supplies attitude and heading
A single integrated air data/attitude computer supplies all PFD data from one sensor set
questions.explanation: Keeping these two systems distinct matters operationally: an AHRS failure flags the attitude sphere and heading tape, while an ADC failure flags the airspeed, altitude, and VSI displays — they don't fail together.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments – Electronic Flight Displays

questions.front: On a turn coordinator, what does it mean when the miniature aircraft's wingtip aligns with one of the two index (reference) marks?
questions.back: The aircraft is turning at a standard rate — 3° per second, or a 2-minute turn for 360°.
questions.explanation: Those index marks (sometimes called the 'doghouse' marks) are calibrated specifically for a standard-rate turn, which is why the turn coordinator alone is enough to fly a standard-rate turn without doing airspeed-based bank-angle math.

questions.front: What is magnetic variation, and what causes it?
questions.back: Magnetic variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north at a given location, caused by the magnetic North Pole being located away from the geographic (true) North Pole. It is the same for every aircraft at that location and is depicted on aeronautical charts as isogonic lines.
questions.explanation: Variation is purely a function of geography — every compass at the same spot has the same variation, unlike deviation, which is unique to each airplane. Memory hook: variation = the VARying angle between true and magnetic caused by Earth's geography, not the airplane.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Variation

questions.front: Deviation of an airplane's magnetic compass is caused by which of the following?
questions.back: Magnetic fields produced by the airplane's own electrical equipment and metal structure
options: The angular difference between true north and magnetic north at the airplane's location
Magnetic fields produced by the airplane's own electrical equipment and metal structure
The dip of the earth's magnetic field toward the nearest magnetic pole
questions.explanation: Deviation is aircraft-specific interference from onboard wiring, radios, and metal, which is why every airplane carries its own compass correction card. Option A describes variation and option C describes dip, which drives turning and acceleration errors, not deviation.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Deviation

questions.front: Where is the deviation correction for a specific airplane's magnetic compass recorded, and what does it tell the pilot?
questions.back: It is recorded on the compass correction card mounted on or near the compass, determined by a 'compass swing.' The card lists the compass heading to fly for each of several magnetic headings (typically every 30°) so the pilot can convert a desired magnetic heading into the actual heading to steer on that compass.
questions.explanation: Because deviation changes with heading as the airplane's metal and electrical fields realign relative to magnetic north, a single offset can't correct it — hence a card with values for multiple headings rather than one static number like variation.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Induced Errors: Deviation (Compass Correction Card)

questions.front: A pilot notices the compass reads differently on the same runway heading in two different airplanes parked side by side. This difference is best explained by which error?
questions.back: Deviation, because each airplane's own equipment and metal distort its local magnetic field
options: Variation, because each airplane happens to be parked at a slightly different magnetic latitude
Deviation, because each airplane's own equipment and metal distort its local magnetic field
Dip error, because each airplane's compass float is mounted at a slightly different angle
questions.explanation: Variation is identical for both airplanes since it depends only on geographic location, not on the airplane. The airplane-to-airplane difference must be deviation, which is unique to each airframe's wiring, avionics, and metal.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Variation vs. Deviation

questions.front: What does the memory aid 'UNOS' stand for regarding magnetic compass turning errors?
questions.back: Undershoot North, Overshoot South — in the Northern Hemisphere, when rolling out of a turn onto a heading of North the pilot should stop turning before the compass reaches North, and when rolling out onto South the pilot should continue turning past South before leveling the wings.
questions.explanation: This dip-induced lag/lead only matters when turning through headings near North or South; it comes from the compass card tilting as the airplane banks. UNOS applies in the Northern Hemisphere and reverses south of the equator.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Northerly Turning Error

questions.front: Flying in the Northern Hemisphere, a pilot is rolling out of a standard-rate turn onto a heading of North using the magnetic compass. To roll out precisely on North, the pilot should:
questions.back: Stop the turn several degrees before the compass reaches North
options: Stop the turn when the compass indicates North
Stop the turn several degrees before the compass reaches North
Continue the turn several degrees past North before leveling the wings
questions.explanation: Because of northerly turning error, magnetic dip makes the compass sluggish and lag behind the airplane as it approaches North — it swings toward the new heading more slowly than the airplane is actually turning, so the airplane reaches North before the compass gets there. If the pilot waited until the compass read North the airplane would overshoot, so the Instrument Flying Handbook's rule is to stop the turn a few degrees before the compass reaches North (undershoot); once the wings are level the lag dissipates and the compass settles on North.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Errors: Northerly Turning Errors

questions.front: In the Northern Hemisphere, when rolling out of a turn onto a heading of South by reference to the magnetic compass, a pilot should:
questions.back: Continue turning past the compass's South indication before rolling out
options: Roll out immediately once the compass indicates South
Roll out several degrees before the compass reaches South
Continue turning past the compass's South indication before rolling out
questions.explanation: Because of southerly turning error, magnetic dip makes the compass lead the airplane as it approaches South — it swings toward the new heading faster than the airplane is actually turning, so the compass can indicate South before the airplane has truly arrived. If the pilot rolled out when the compass first showed South the airplane would be short of South, so the Instrument Flying Handbook's rule is to let the turn carry a few degrees past the compass's South indication (overshoot); once the wings are level the lead dissipates and the compass settles on South.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Errors: Southerly Turning Errors

questions.front: How does the UNOS compass turning error change for an airplane operating in the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.back: It reverses: the pilot should overshoot North (continue the turn past North before rolling out) and undershoot South (roll out before reaching South), the opposite of the Northern Hemisphere rule.
questions.explanation: The lead/lag is caused by magnetic dip, which points the opposite way below the equator, so every Northern Hemisphere compass turning rule flips when operating south of the equator. This reversal is a common trap for pilots who memorize 'UNOS' without understanding the underlying dip cause.

questions.front: An airplane is being flown near 30° south latitude and is turning from a heading of 270° to a heading of 180° (South) using the magnetic compass. How should the pilot roll out?
questions.back: Roll out a few degrees before the compass indicates South
options: Continue the turn a few degrees past where the compass indicates South
Roll out a few degrees before the compass indicates South
Roll out exactly when the compass first indicates South, no adjustment needed
questions.explanation: South of the equator the turning error reverses from the Northern Hemisphere rule, so approaching South the compass now lags (rather than leads as it does in the Northern Hemisphere) — it swings more slowly than the airplane, so the airplane reaches South before the compass does. The pilot must anticipate by rolling out early, the mirror image of the Northern Hemisphere South rollout.

questions.front: As a rule of thumb, the number of degrees of lead or lag to use when rolling out of a turn onto a heading of North or South using the magnetic compass is approximately equal to:
questions.back: 15° plus half the airplane's latitude
options: The airplane's true airspeed in knots
15° plus half the airplane's latitude
A fixed 15°, with no adjustment for latitude
questions.explanation: The FAA's rule of thumb is to lead or lag the rollout by 15° plus half the latitude — for example, near 40° latitude, the turn should be stopped about 15+20=35° before reaching the desired heading. The error grows with latitude because magnetic dip is steeper closer to the poles, and is negligible near the magnetic equator.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Errors: Northerly and Southerly Turning Errors

questions.front: The mnemonic 'ANDS' describes which magnetic compass error?
questions.back: The error that occurs when accelerating or decelerating on headings of East or West
options: The error that occurs when turning through a heading of North or South
The error that occurs when accelerating or decelerating on headings of East or West
The error caused by turbulence bouncing the compass card
questions.explanation: ANDS stands for Accelerate North, Decelerate South (Northern Hemisphere) and describes the acceleration error, which is greatest on easterly and westerly headings — the complement of UNOS, which affects turns through North and South.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Acceleration Error

questions.front: Spell out what 'ANDS' stands for, and in which hemisphere does this version of the rule apply?
questions.back: Accelerate North, Decelerate South — in the Northern Hemisphere, accelerating on an east or west heading causes the compass to swing toward an indication of North, while decelerating causes it to swing toward South.
questions.explanation: This is caused by the pendulous mounting of the compass card reacting to inertial forces combined with magnetic dip; it is a momentary, false indication that disappears once the airplane returns to a constant airspeed.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Acceleration Error

questions.front: Acceleration/deceleration error of the magnetic compass (ANDS) is essentially zero on which headings?
questions.back: North and South
options: North and South
East and West
Northeast and Southwest
questions.explanation: ANDS error is maximum on East/West headings and fades to zero on North/South headings — the opposite pattern from UNOS turning error, which is maximum on North/South and zero on East/West. Confusing these two patterns is a common exam trap.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments — Dip Errors: Acceleration Error

questions.front: An airplane flying straight and level on a heading of 090° in the Northern Hemisphere advances the throttle and accelerates. With no actual heading change, the magnetic compass will temporarily indicate:
questions.back: A turn toward North
options: A turn toward North
A turn toward South
No change, since acceleration error only affects North and South headings
questions.explanation: On an easterly heading in the Northern Hemisphere, acceleration produces an apparent turn toward North per the ANDS rule (Accelerate North). The pilot should disregard this false indication and confirm the heading is unchanged once the airplane returns to a steady airspeed.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Acceleration Error

questions.front: In the Northern Hemisphere, an airplane flying a steady heading of 270° reduces power and decelerates. What does the magnetic compass momentarily show, and is it accurate?
questions.back: It momentarily shows an apparent turn toward South, per the ANDS rule (Decelerate South) — this indication is false; the airplane's actual heading has not changed, and the compass will settle back to 270° once airspeed stabilizes.
questions.explanation: On a westerly heading, deceleration triggers the same dip-driven card tilt that always shows an apparent turn toward South, regardless of whether the airplane is actually turning.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Acceleration Error

questions.front: Oscillation of the magnetic compass card in flight is most often caused by:
questions.back: Turbulence or abrupt control inputs disturbing the pendulously mounted compass card
options: Turbulence or abrupt control inputs disturbing the pendulously mounted compass card
A malfunctioning vacuum pump
Flying near the magnetic North Pole where variation is undefined
questions.explanation: The compass card is mounted on a pivot in damping fluid, so rough air or jerky flying makes it swing back and forth; the vacuum system has no connection to the magnetic compass, which is a self-contained, non-gyroscopic instrument.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Oscillation Error

questions.front: In turbulence the magnetic compass card is swinging back and forth instead of settling. How should the pilot determine the actual heading?
questions.back: Average the highest and lowest readings observed during the swings to estimate the actual heading, rather than trying to read a single instantaneous value.
questions.explanation: Because oscillation is roughly symmetric around the true heading, averaging the extremes cancels out the swing and gives a usable heading estimate until the air smooths out.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Oscillation Error

questions.front: A magnetic compass gives its most accurate, error-free heading indication under which flight condition?
questions.back: During straight-and-level flight at a constant airspeed
options: During any standard-rate turn
During straight-and-level flight at a constant airspeed
During acceleration on a northerly heading
questions.explanation: UNOS and ANDS errors are both created by turning or by changing airspeed; only unaccelerated, wings-level, constant-speed flight removes the dip-induced tilt of the compass card, making that the only condition where the compass reliably reads true magnetic heading.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass: Compass Reliability

questions.front: Contrast where the magnetic compass's turning error (UNOS) is greatest versus where its acceleration/deceleration error (ANDS) is greatest.
questions.back: Turning error (UNOS) is greatest when rolling out through headings of North or South and is essentially absent on East/West headings. Acceleration error (ANDS) is exactly the opposite: it is greatest on East/West headings and essentially absent on North/South headings.
questions.explanation: Both errors come from the same cause — the compass card tilting due to magnetic dip — but one is triggered by banking (turning error) and the other by longitudinal acceleration (ANDS), so their headings of maximum effect are perpendicular to each other. This is one of the most commonly mixed-up compass facts on the exam.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments — Dip Errors: Turning vs. Acceleration Errors

questions.front: The heading indicator has failed and the pilot must turn from a heading of 360° to a heading of 090° using only the turn coordinator, clock, and magnetic compass. What is the best technique?
questions.back: Roll into a standard-rate turn, time 30 seconds using the clock, then roll out and verify the heading once wings are level
options: Roll into a standard-rate turn and watch the compass continuously, rolling out the instant it reads 090°
Roll into a standard-rate turn, time 30 seconds using the clock, then roll out and verify the heading once wings are level
Roll into a steep turn to complete the heading change quickly before compass errors can develop
questions.explanation: A standard-rate turn covers 3° per second, so a 90° heading change takes 30 seconds; because the compass is unreliable while banked, the pilot should time the turn rather than chase the compass card, then confirm the new heading only after returning to straight-and-level flight.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Gyroscopic Instruments: Turn Coordinator (Standard-Rate Turn); Magnetic Compass Errors

questions.front: At a standard-rate turn of 3° per second, how long should it take to turn 90°, and how is this used with the magnetic compass?
questions.back: 30 seconds. Because the compass is unreliable in a bank, pilots executing a timed turn roll in at standard rate, time the turn with a clock or stopwatch instead of watching the compass, and check the resulting heading only after rolling out to wings-level.
questions.explanation: Timed turns are the standard workaround for compass turning/acceleration errors and for a failed heading indicator: 3°/second means every 30° of heading change takes 10 seconds, a ratio worth memorizing cold.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Gyroscopic Instruments: Turn Coordinator (Standard-Rate Turn)

questions.front: Why do pilots use a timed, standard-rate turn rather than simply watching the magnetic compass to roll out on a precise heading?
questions.back: Because UNOS and ANDS errors make the compass indication unreliable while banked or accelerating
options: Because the compass is damaged by centrifugal force during any turn
Because UNOS and ANDS errors make the compass indication unreliable while banked or accelerating
Because regulations prohibit reference to the magnetic compass during turns
questions.explanation: The compass card tilts with bank and lags or leads near North/South, and swings with acceleration near East/West, so it cannot be trusted to show a true heading until the airplane is again straight, level, and at constant airspeed — hence timing the turn instead.

source.section: Chapter 5, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Errors: Northerly/Southerly Turning Errors and Acceleration Error

questions.front: Does the ANDS acceleration/deceleration compass error reverse when operating in the Southern Hemisphere, and why?
questions.back: Yes — south of the equator it becomes 'Accelerate South, Decelerate North,' the reverse of the Northern Hemisphere rule, because the underlying cause, magnetic dip, points in the opposite direction below the equator.
questions.explanation: Both UNOS and ANDS trace back to the same dip-induced tilting of the compass card, so both errors flip together when crossing into the Southern Hemisphere — a pilot who only memorizes the Northern Hemisphere version will misread the compass south of the equator.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments — Dip Errors: Acceleration Error

questions.front: If the heading indicator fails in flight, which instrument remains available as the primary backup source of heading information?
questions.back: The magnetic compass
options: The turn coordinator
The magnetic compass
The attitude indicator
questions.explanation: The magnetic compass is a self-contained, non-gyroscopic instrument independent of the vacuum or electrical systems that drive the heading indicator, so it remains the pilot's ultimate heading reference even though it must be read carefully due to UNOS and ANDS errors.

source.section: Chapter 8, Flight Instruments — Magnetic Compass Overview

questions.front: In the control and performance concept of attitude instrument flying, which two flight instruments are classified as 'control instruments'?
questions.back: The attitude indicator and the power indicators (manifold pressure gauge and/or tachometer) — together they show the immediate result of any pitch, bank, or power change the pilot commands.
questions.explanation: Control instruments display cause, not effect — the attitude indicator shows pitch and bank instantly, and the power gauges show power output instantly, without the lag seen in performance instruments as the aircraft actually responds.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Control and Performance Method (Control Instruments)

questions.front: Under the control and performance concept, the airspeed indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, and heading indicator are grouped together as which type of instrument?
questions.back: Performance instruments
options: Performance instruments
Control instruments
Navigation instruments
questions.explanation: Performance instruments show the actual results (airspeed, altitude, rate, heading) produced by a control input, but they lag slightly behind the control instruments because the aircraft has to actually respond first.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Control and Performance Method (Performance Instruments)

questions.front: During straight-and-level flight at a constant altitude, which instrument is primary for pitch?
questions.back: Altimeter
options: Altimeter
Attitude indicator
Vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: Because the goal of the maneuver is holding a specific altitude, the altimeter directly measures success at that goal and is primary for pitch, while the attitude indicator and VSI only support the cross-check.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Primary and Supporting Method (Example of Primary and Support Instruments)

questions.front: In straight-and-level flight on a constant heading, which instrument is primary for bank?
questions.back: The heading indicator (directional gyro) — it directly shows whether the aircraft is holding the assigned heading, which is the goal of the maneuver.
questions.explanation: The attitude indicator and turn coordinator support the bank cross-check, but only the heading indicator confirms the actual performance goal: staying on the assigned heading.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Primary and Supporting Method (Example of Primary and Support Instruments)

questions.front: In level, unaccelerated flight at a constant airspeed, which instrument is primary for power?
questions.back: Airspeed indicator
options: Airspeed indicator
Manifold pressure gauge/tachometer
Vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: Since the goal is a specific airspeed while holding altitude constant, the ASI directly reflects whether the chosen power setting is correct; the engine gauges only confirm the setting itself and are supporting.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Primary and Supporting Method (Example of Primary and Support Instruments)

questions.front: Once established in a constant-airspeed climb, which instrument is primary for pitch?
questions.back: Airspeed indicator
options: Airspeed indicator
Altimeter
Attitude indicator
questions.explanation: In a constant-airspeed climb the pilot adjusts pitch to hold a target airspeed while power stays fixed at climb power, so the ASI — not the still-climbing altimeter — becomes primary for pitch.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Straight Climbs and Descents (Constant Airspeed Climb)

questions.front: In a constant-airspeed climb, once climb power is set, which instrument is primary for power?
questions.back: The manifold pressure gauge and/or tachometer — power is fixed at a specified climb setting, so the engine gauge itself is the primary reference that the setting is correct.
questions.explanation: Pitch, not power, is used to control airspeed in this maneuver, so power just needs to be held at the briefed value, making the engine instrument primary instead of merely supporting.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Straight Climbs and Descents (Constant Airspeed Climb)

questions.front: While rolling into and holding a standard-rate, level turn to a new heading, which instrument remains primary for pitch?
questions.back: Altimeter
options: Altimeter
Attitude indicator
Vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: Altitude is still being held constant during a level turn, so the altimeter continues as primary for pitch exactly as in straight-and-level flight — only the bank reference changes, shifting from the attitude indicator during roll-in to the turn coordinator once the turn is established.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Turns (Standard Rate Turns)

questions.front: In instrument cross-check technique, what is 'fixation' and why is it dangerous?
questions.back: Fixation is staring at a single instrument for an extended period while neglecting the rest of the scan; it lets the aircraft drift from the desired attitude, altitude, or heading undetected because no other instrument is being checked.
questions.explanation: Fixation often happens when a pilot becomes absorbed correcting one deviation (like a CDI needle) and forgets the instrument cross-check must keep moving to catch other developing errors.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Fundamental Skills, Instrument Cross-Check (Common Errors: Fixation)

questions.front: A pilot who develops a habit of never glancing at the vertical speed indicator during climbs, even though it is part of the prescribed scan, is demonstrating which cross-check error?
questions.back: Omission
options: Omission
Fixation
Emphasis
questions.explanation: Omission is leaving an instrument out of the scan altogether; unlike fixation (staring too long at one) or emphasis (over-trusting one), omission means a needed instrument is never checked, so deviations it would reveal go unnoticed.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Fundamental Skills, Instrument Cross-Check (Common Errors: Omission)

questions.front: A pilot who trusts the attitude indicator so heavily that heading and altitude deviations shown elsewhere are cross-checked far less often is committing which type of scan error?
questions.back: Emphasis
options: Emphasis
Fixation
Omission
questions.explanation: Emphasis is placing too much reliance on a single instrument, often the attitude indicator because it seems to show 'everything,' at the expense of properly integrating all the other instruments in the cross-check.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Fundamental Skills, Instrument Cross-Check (Common Errors: Emphasis)

questions.front: While tracking a VOR radial in cruise, a pilot becomes absorbed in centering the CDI needle and does not notice the altimeter has unwound 300 feet below the assigned altitude. This is best described as which cross-check error?
questions.back: Fixation
options: Fixation
Omission
Emphasis
questions.explanation: Becoming absorbed staring at one indicator to the exclusion of the rest of the scan is fixation; the altitude loss went unnoticed only because the pilot's eyes never returned to the altimeter during that time.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Fundamental Skills, Instrument Cross-Check (Common Errors: Fixation)

questions.front: What instrument indications alert a pilot to an unusual nose-high attitude before recovery is initiated?
questions.back: A rapid decrease in airspeed, the attitude indicator showing the miniature aircraft well above the horizon bar, and the altimeter/VSI showing a climb — the decaying airspeed toward a stall is the most urgent cue.
questions.explanation: Recognizing the attitude quickly from these combined indications, rather than any single instrument, is what allows the pilot to begin the correct recovery before a stall develops.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recognizing Unusual Attitudes)

questions.front: Which combination of instrument indications signals an unusual nose-low attitude?
questions.back: Airspeed increasing rapidly while the altimeter and VSI both show a descent
options: Airspeed increasing rapidly while the altimeter and VSI both show a descent
Airspeed decreasing rapidly while the altimeter shows a climb
Airspeed constant while the heading indicator spins rapidly
questions.explanation: A nose-low attitude drives airspeed up quickly while the altimeter unwinds and the VSI shows a strong descent; these cues are recognizable even before the attitude indicator is cross-checked.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recognizing Unusual Attitudes)

questions.front: What is the correct control sequence for recovering from a nose-high unusual attitude?
questions.back: Add power (as necessary in proportion to the observed airspeed decay) to prevent an approaching stall, apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, then return smoothly to straight-and-level flight.
questions.explanation: Power is added first because the nose-high attitude is bleeding off airspeed toward a stall; pitching down and leveling the wings follow almost simultaneously but in that sequence, referencing the attitude indicator throughout the recovery.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recovery from Unusual Attitudes: Nose-High Attitudes)

questions.front: A pilot notices the attitude indicator shows a steep nose-down, wings-banked attitude with airspeed increasing rapidly toward the yellow arc. What is the correct first action?
questions.back: Reduce power toward idle
options: Reduce power toward idle
Add full power
Roll the wings level before touching the throttle
questions.explanation: In a nose-low unusual attitude, power is reduced first to stop the rapid airspeed buildup and avoid exceeding structural limits; only after power is reduced are the wings leveled and the nose smoothly raised.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recovery from Unusual Attitudes: Nose-Low Attitudes)

questions.front: Why does the standard nose-high unusual attitude recovery call for adding power before applying forward-elevator pressure?
questions.back: It builds an airspeed margin before the decaying airspeed reaches a stall
options: It builds an airspeed margin before the decaying airspeed reaches a stall
Power changes alone return the aircraft to level flight with no other inputs
Reducing power first, not adding it, would overstress the airframe at that pitch
questions.explanation: A nose-high attitude is bleeding off airspeed toward a stall, so power is added immediately for a safety margin; the forward-elevator and wings-level inputs that follow then lower the nose without risking a stall.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recovery from Unusual Attitudes: Nose-High Attitudes)

questions.front: Why is power reduced as one of the first actions when recovering from a nose-low unusual attitude?
questions.back: The steep nose-down pitch is causing airspeed to build rapidly; reducing power keeps airspeed from exceeding the aircraft's structural or maneuvering speed limits and prevents further loss of altitude while the wings are leveled and the nose is raised.
questions.explanation: If power were left at cruise or climb settings while the nose stayed low, the aircraft could accelerate past Va or Vne before the pilot finishes rolling the wings level and raising the nose.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recovery from Unusual Attitudes: Nose-Low Attitudes)

questions.front: What is the correct role of trim when transitioning from one attitude to another in instrument flight?
questions.back: Trim only relieves pressure after the flight controls establish the new attitude
options: Trim only relieves pressure after the flight controls establish the new attitude
Trim is used to initiate and hold the new pitch attitude instead of the elevator
Trim should be adjusted continuously throughout the maneuver to move the nose
questions.explanation: The elevator establishes a new attitude; once the desired attitude and airspeed are confirmed on the instruments, trim is applied only to relieve residual control pressure so the aircraft holds that attitude hands-off. Using trim alone to establish an attitude change results in erratic aircraft control.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Trim Control / Four-Step Process (Establish, Trim, Cross-Check, Adjust)

questions.front: When changing from cruise to a climb attitude, should the pilot set attitude and power first and then trim, or trim first and let it establish the new attitude?
questions.back: Set the pitch attitude and power with the primary flight controls first, confirm the desired performance on the instruments, and only then trim to relieve the control pressure — trim never leads the attitude change.
questions.explanation: Trimming before establishing the attitude would let the trim, rather than a deliberate control input, determine the new attitude, degrading precision and delaying instrument cross-check confirmation.

source.section: Chapter 6: Attitude Instrument Flying – Trim Control / Four-Step Process (Establish, Trim, Cross-Check, Adjust)

questions.front: During an unusual attitude recovery, the attitude indicator is found tumbled and unusable. Which instrument now provides the primary reference for bank while the wings are leveled?
questions.back: Turn coordinator
options: Turn coordinator
Heading indicator
Vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: When the attitude indicator's upset limits have been exceeded or it has failed, recovery is made by reference to the ASI, altimeter, VSI, and turn coordinator; the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft is the only one of these that directly shows bank/roll information.

source.section: Chapter 7: Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers – Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries (Recovery from Unusual Attitudes)

questions.front: What conditions must be met before you may descend below the DA or MDA on an instrument approach?
questions.back: The aircraft is in a position to make a normal descent to landing, flight visibility is at or above the published minimum, and a required runway environment reference is distinctly visible.
options: Normal descent-to-landing position, required flight visibility, and a listed runway environment reference in sight
The runway environment in sight and ATC clearance to land
Required flight visibility and the ceiling reported at or above published minimums
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.175(c) lists all three conditions; reported ceiling is not one of them — flight visibility controls.

questions.front: What is the difference between a DA and an MDA?
questions.back: DA (decision altitude) applies to approaches with vertical guidance: you decide to continue or go missed while still descending through it. MDA (minimum descent altitude) applies to nonprecision approaches: it is a floor you may not descend below without the visual references required by 91.175.
questions.explanation: At DA the momentary dip below during the missed is expected; the MDA must not be penetrated at all without visual references.

questions.front: What indicated airspeed range defines Category A for instrument approach category purposes?
questions.back: Less than 91 knots. Approach category speed is based on VREF at maximum certificated landing weight if specified, or if VREF is not specified, 1.3 times the aircraft's stall speed (Vso) in the landing configuration at that weight.
questions.explanation: Approach category is a speed-based classification, not an aircraft type — it drives which minima line and circling radius apply. Category A covers the slowest aircraft, typically light singles.

source.section: 5-4-7, Instrument Approach Procedures — Aircraft Approach Category

questions.front: What is the minimum indicated airspeed that places an aircraft in approach Category E?
questions.back: 166 knots or more, based on VREF at maximum certificated landing weight if specified, or if VREF is not specified, 1.3 Vso at that weight — the fastest of the five approach categories.
questions.explanation: Category E is reserved for very high-speed aircraft; most civil transport-category jets fall in Category C or D instead.

source.section: 5-4-7, Instrument Approach Procedures — Aircraft Approach Category

questions.front: A pilot flies the final segment of an instrument approach at 130 knots indicated airspeed. Which approach category minima line applies?
questions.back: Category C
options: Category B
Category C
Category D
questions.explanation: Category C covers 121-140 knots. Using a lower category's minima would apply a protected area and visibility minimum sized for a slower, tighter-turning aircraft than the one actually being flown.

source.section: 5-4-7, Instrument Approach Procedures — Aircraft Approach Category

questions.front: An aircraft is normally Category B, but the pilot must maneuver the circling approach at a speed above the upper limit of the Category B speed range. What minima should the pilot use?
questions.back: The next higher category's minima, sized for the faster maneuvering speed.
options: The Category B minima, since that's the pilot's normal category
The next higher category's minima, sized for the faster maneuvering speed
The Category A minima, since a slower category is always more conservative
questions.explanation: The AIM requires using the higher category's minima whenever maneuvering speed exceeds the upper limit of the aircraft's normal category, because the protected circling area is sized for that faster speed.

source.section: 5-4-7, Instrument Approach Procedures — Aircraft Approach Category

questions.front: Why do higher approach categories (e.g., Category D) generally have higher circling minimums than lower categories (e.g., Category A) at the same airport?
questions.back: Faster aircraft need a larger protected circling area to clear obstacles farther out.
options: Faster aircraft need a larger protected circling area to clear obstacles farther out
Faster aircraft are assumed to have less accurate altimeters and instruments
Category assignment is based on engine type, not maneuvering speed or radius
questions.explanation: Circling protected areas are radii keyed to each category's speed and turning radius; a faster, wider-turning aircraft needs clearance over more ground, which often forces a higher MDA and/or visibility for that category.

questions.front: The 'briefing strip' across the top of a standard FAA instrument approach chart is designed to provide what?
questions.back: A quick-reference summary of the data needed to brief the approach: NAVAID, course, elevations, missed approach.
options: A quick-reference summary of the data needed to brief the approach: NAVAID, course, elevations, missed approach
A full listing of every radar and approach control frequency used in the surrounding ARTCC
The complete text of the current NOTAMs published for that airport and its approaches
questions.explanation: The briefing strip groups the must-brief items in one place at the top of the chart so a crew can review them quickly, rather than hunting through the plan and profile views.

questions.front: Which portion of an instrument approach chart shows the vertical picture of the procedure — altitudes at each fix, the descent angle, and the missed approach point?
questions.back: The profile view
options: The plan view
The profile view
The minima section
questions.explanation: The plan view is the overhead (lateral) picture; the profile view is the side (vertical) picture showing altitudes, descent gradient, and the MAP.

questions.front: Which part of an approach chart gives an overhead view of the procedure, including feeder routes from the en route structure to the initial approach fix?
questions.back: The plan view
options: The plan view
The profile view
The airport diagram inset
questions.explanation: The plan view is drawn from directly above and depicts the lateral course, fixes, feeder routes, and terrain/obstacle area; vertical information is reserved for the profile view below it.

questions.front: How does the airport diagram inset at the bottom of an approach chart differ in purpose from the plan view above it?
questions.back: It is a to-scale, true-north depiction of the runway pattern meant chiefly to help a pilot recognize the airport from the air, not a detailed taxiway diagram — taxiways are shown only when the airport has no separate published Airport Diagram chart
options: It is a to-scale, true-north depiction of the runway pattern meant chiefly to help a pilot recognize the airport from the air, not a detailed taxiway diagram — taxiways are shown only when the airport has no separate published Airport Diagram chart
It replaces the profile view whenever the approach is a non-precision procedure
It shows the missed approach holding pattern in more detail than the plan view does
questions.explanation: The airport sketch's primary purpose is airport/runway recognition from the air and basic ground-navigation cues, not a substitute for the full Airport Diagram chart, which is the actual detailed taxiway reference at busier airports.

questions.front: A non-precision approach's final approach course is offset 42 degrees from the extended runway centerline. What is the effect on the published minima?
questions.back: Only circling minimums are published, since the offset exceeds the maximum allowed for straight-in minima.
options: Only circling minimums are published, since the offset exceeds the maximum allowed for straight-in minima
Straight-in minimums are still published because 42 degrees is within tolerance for non-precision approaches
The approach becomes not authorized (NA) because any offset from runway centerline is disqualifying
questions.explanation: Straight-in minima require the final approach course to be within 30 degrees of the runway's extended centerline; beyond that, only circling minima are published because the pilot cannot align with the runway from the final course without maneuvering.

source.section: Chapter 4, Approaches — Straight-In versus Circling Minimums

questions.front: On a minima box, the row labeled 'S-ILS 22' provides minimums that apply to what type of operation?
questions.back: A straight-in landing on Runway 22 using the ILS.
options: A straight-in landing on Runway 22 using the ILS
A circling approach to any runway using the ILS
A side-step maneuver to a parallel runway
questions.explanation: The 'S-' prefix followed by a runway number marks straight-in minima for that specific runway; rows simply labeled 'CIRCLING' apply when landing on a runway other than the one the approach serves.

questions.front: Why are circling minimums typically higher (in MDA and/or visibility) than the straight-in minimums for the same approach?
questions.back: Circling requires the pilot to maneuver visually at low altitude to align with a different runway, so the protected obstacle-clearance area is wider and more time/visibility is needed to see and maneuver around obstacles and other traffic; straight-in only requires clearing obstacles along one fixed final approach path.
questions.explanation: The extra maneuvering margin needed for circling — sizing the protected area to each approach category's turning radius — is why circling minimums are almost always equal to or higher than the matching straight-in minima.

questions.front: During an ILS approach, the glideslope fails after the final approach fix. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Continue using the S-LOC (localizer-only) minimums on the same chart.
options: Continue using the S-LOC (localizer-only) minimums on the same chart
Immediately execute the missed approach; no other minimums apply
Continue to DA using the ILS minimums, since the localizer is still valid
questions.explanation: An ILS is really two guidance sources bundled together; lose the glideslope and the approach reverts to a non-precision localizer approach, with its own higher MDA and visibility shown on the same chart.

questions.front: What does the approach lighting system abbreviation 'MALSR' stand for?
questions.back: Medium-intensity Approach Lighting System with Runway alignment indicator lights (RAIL) — sequenced flashers extending out toward the approach path.
questions.explanation: MALSR is one of the most common Category I ILS lighting configurations at U.S. airports; recognizing the abbreviation on the chart tells a pilot what visual system to expect at minimums.

questions.front: An approach chart shows 'ODALS' for the runway in use. What does this lighting system provide?
questions.back: A row of omnidirectional flashing lights leading visually to the runway threshold.
options: A row of omnidirectional flashing lights leading visually to the runway threshold
Vertically-aimed lights that show glide path deviation on final approach
High-intensity centerline lights built to Category II/III lighting standards
questions.explanation: ODALS (Omnidirectional Approach Lighting System) is a basic sequenced-flasher system typically installed at non-precision runways, giving directional guidance to the threshold without the higher-intensity hardware used for precision Category II/III systems.

questions.front: Compared to an otherwise identical procedure with no qualifying approach lights, what operational credit does a high-intensity approach lighting system generally allow?
questions.back: A lower published visibility minimum for that approach and category.
options: A lower published visibility minimum for that approach and category
A lower published MDA/DA for that approach and category
Waiver of the requirement to have the runway environment in sight at minimums
questions.explanation: TERPS criteria let procedure designers publish lower visibility minimums where a qualifying lighting system is present, because it gives pilots earlier and more reliable visual cues in reduced visibility; it does not by itself lower the altitude minimum.

questions.front: What operational standard does the ALSF-2 approach lighting system primarily support that a basic MALS (Medium-intensity Approach Lighting System, no RAIL) does not?
questions.back: ALSF-2 is a high-intensity Approach Lighting System with Sequenced Flashers built to Category II/III standards; a basic MALS is a lower-intensity system intended for Category I operations only.
questions.explanation: Lighting system intensity and hardware scale with how low the visibility minimums go — Category II/III approaches require the more elaborate ALSF-2 (or equivalent) system.

questions.front: What does the abbreviation 'NA' mean when printed next to a line of minima or as a chart note on an instrument approach procedure?
questions.back: 'Not Authorized' — the specific minima line, circling category, or (if noted for the whole procedure) the approach itself may not be used under the stated condition.
questions.explanation: NA is a blanket prohibition tied to whatever condition follows it, such as a time of day, a circling direction, or missing equipment; pilots must read the full note to know exactly what's restricted.

questions.front: A chart note reads 'Circling NA east of Rwy 18.' What does this restrict?
questions.back: Circling to the east side of the runway, usually due to obstacles or terrain there.
options: Circling to the east side of the runway, usually due to obstacles or terrain there
The entire procedure any time the surface wind favors an easterly landing
Use of DME only when the pilot elects to circle toward the east
questions.explanation: 'NA' notes that specify a direction or sector restrict the circling maneuvering area in that direction, not the straight-in portion of the approach or the approach as a whole.

source.section: 5-4-20, Approach and Landing Minimums — Circling Minimums

questions.front: An approach chart note states 'Approach NA at night.' What is the most likely reason for this restriction?
questions.back: Unlit obstacles/terrain make the approach unsafe without daylight visual cues.
options: Unlit obstacles/terrain make the approach unsafe without daylight visual cues
ATC does not staff or provide radar service to the airport at night
The published visibility minimums apply only during daylight hours
questions.explanation: Night NA restrictions are almost always driven by obstacle lighting/visibility limitations along the procedure, not by ATC service availability or the published minima themselves changing.

questions.front: A chart note states 'DME REQUIRED.' What is the consequence for a pilot flying an aircraft without functioning DME or an approved substitute (such as IFR-approved GPS)?
questions.back: The pilot may not fly that approach procedure, because required fixes on the procedure depend on distance information that can't otherwise be identified; without DME or an authorized substitute, the approach is not available to that aircraft.
questions.explanation: 'Required' equipment notes are not optional recommendations — if the listed equipment (or an approved substitute) isn't functioning, the whole procedure is unavailable for that flight.

questions.front: What obstacle clearance does the Minimum Safe Altitude (MSA) circle on an approach chart guarantee, and out to what typical radius?
questions.back: At least 1,000 feet of obstacle clearance within a typical 25 NM radius of the MSA's reference facility or fix (the radius can be published differently in unusual cases).
questions.explanation: MSA is a single conservative altitude meant to be quick to remember in an emergency, not a precisely tailored operational altitude.

source.section: 5-4-5, Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts — Minimum Safe Altitudes

questions.front: After losing situational awareness in IMC, a pilot climbs to the MSA depicted on the approach chart in use. What is true about relying on this altitude?
questions.back: It's an emergency-only altitude — no guarantee of navigation signal coverage or clearance beyond the charted radius.
options: It's an emergency-only altitude — no guarantee of navigation signal coverage or clearance beyond the charted radius
It guarantees safe obstacle clearance if used for normal descent planning during the approach
It guarantees reliable NAVAID signal reception everywhere within the charted sector, day or night
questions.explanation: A common mix-up is treating MSA like a normal operational altitude; the AIM is explicit that MSA is for emergencies only and offers no assurance of signal coverage, unlike altitudes actually built into the procedure's route.

source.section: 5-4-5, Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts — Minimum Safe Altitudes

questions.front: Why can an MSA circle on an approach chart show more than one minimum altitude number around its circumference?
questions.back: The MSA circle is divided into sectors (typically drawn as pie slices) around the primary NAVAID or fix, and each sector's altitude is set independently to give at least 1,000 feet of clearance over the highest obstacle in that specific direction — so different sectors can require different altitudes.
questions.explanation: Pilots sometimes assume MSA is one number for the whole chart; recognizing the sector breakdown avoids picking an altitude that only applies to a different quadrant.

source.section: 5-4-5, Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts — Minimum Safe Altitudes

questions.front: What is the maximum decision height (DH) that still qualifies an ILS approach as Category I?
questions.back: 200 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (HAT) — CAT I DA/DH may not be published lower than 200 feet AGL.
questions.explanation: The 200-foot AGL ceiling is the classic dividing line between CAT I and the lower CAT II (100 feet) and CAT III (below 100 feet, or no DH at all) ILS approaches.

source.section: Chapter 4 – Approach (ILS Approach Categories I, II, III)

questions.front: A standard Category I ILS approach is typically published with a visibility minimum no lower than:
questions.back: 1/2 statute mile (RVR 2400, reducible to RVR 1800 with touchdown zone and centerline lighting)
options: 1/2 statute mile (RVR 2400, reducible to RVR 1800 with touchdown zone and centerline lighting)
1/4 statute mile (RVR 1200)
1/8 statute mile (RVR 600)
questions.explanation: The standard CAT I floor is DH 200 feet with visibility not less than 1/2 mile or RVR 2400; with operative touchdown zone and centerline lighting, RVR may be reduced to 1800. RVR 1200 and RVR 600 belong to CAT II and CAT III operations, which require special aircrew, aircraft, and airport certification.

source.section: Chapter 4 – Approach (ILS Approach Categories I, II, III)

questions.front: What is required for an operator to use Category II or III ILS minimums instead of standard Category I minimums at the same airport?
questions.back: Special aircrew, aircraft, and airport certification for lower minimums
options: Special aircrew, aircraft, and airport certification for lower minimums
Briefing the approach as 'CAT II' before the descent begins
Flying the approach with an autopilot instead of hand-flying
questions.explanation: CAT II/III minimums require FAA-approved airborne equipment, specific crew training, and enhanced ground infrastructure — they are not available simply by choosing to brief them or by using an autopilot.

source.section: Chapter 4 – Approach (ILS Approach Categories I, II, III)

questions.front: What does the 'LPV' minima line on an RNAV (GPS) approach chart stand for?
questions.back: Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance — a WAAS-based line of minima with angular lateral guidance (like a localizer) and electronic vertical guidance to a DA, flown much like an ILS.
questions.explanation: LPV is the only APV/GPS minima line using angular lateral sensitivity, which is why its minimums can approach ILS-like lows; the 'P' stands for Performance, not Precision, since LPV is technically an APV procedure.

questions.front: Compared to LPV minima on the same RNAV (GPS) approach, LNAV/VNAV minima are generally:
questions.back: Equal to or higher, since its vertical guidance is less precise than LPV's
options: Equal to or higher, since its vertical guidance is less precise than LPV's
Always lower, because it uses a ground-based ILS glideslope
Unusable unless the aircraft also has a working ILS receiver
questions.explanation: LNAV/VNAV can be flown with baro-VNAV or WAAS vertical guidance, both less precise than LPV's WAAS-based lateral/vertical solution, so its published DA and visibility are typically no better than the LPV line.

questions.front: An RNAV (GPS) approach chart lists a minimum temperature limitation on the LNAV/VNAV line that doesn't apply to the LPV line. Why?
questions.back: Baro-VNAV vertical guidance is skewed by non-standard temperatures
options: Baro-VNAV vertical guidance is skewed by non-standard temperatures
All autopilots require a temperature limit below 0°C to engage
The limit applies only to circling minimums, not straight-in LNAV/VNAV
questions.explanation: Baro-VNAV computes the glidepath from barometric altitude, which shifts with non-standard temperature, so charts publish a temperature limit for that line; LPV avoids this because WAAS vertical guidance isn't temperature-dependent, and baro-VNAV is not authorized on LPV procedures.

questions.front: An aircraft has a WAAS-certified GPS navigator but no baro-VNAV capability. On an RNAV (GPS) approach published with LPV, LNAV/VNAV, and LNAV lines of minima, which vertically-guided line can this aircraft use?
questions.back: LPV, because WAAS itself supplies the vertical guidance for that line
options: LPV, because WAAS itself supplies the vertical guidance for that line
LNAV/VNAV only, since WAAS receivers default to that line without baro-VNAV
Neither LPV nor LNAV/VNAV — only the LNAV line is available without baro-VNAV
questions.explanation: WAAS avionics generate their own precise vertical guidance, so LPV never requires baro-VNAV; baro-VNAV is only an alternate way for non-WAAS aircraft to fly the typically less favorable LNAV/VNAV line.

questions.front: What must a pilot do immediately upon reaching DA on a precision or APV approach without the runway environment in sight?
questions.back: Begin the missed approach immediately — DA is a go/no-go decision point, not an altitude to level off at while searching for the runway.
questions.explanation: Unlike MDA, which permits level flight while looking for the runway, DA is designed for a continuous descent that transitions directly into the missed approach with no level segment.

questions.front: Why is a DA-based approach considered better suited to a stabilized, continuous-descent profile than an MDA-based approach?
questions.back: It's flown as one continuous descent, with no required level-off at DA
options: It's flown as one continuous descent, with no required level-off at DA
DA is always numerically lower than MDA on the same runway
DA approaches don't require the runway environment in sight to land
questions.explanation: MDA approaches often involve leveling off at the MDA while searching for the runway, which breaks a stabilized descent; DA approaches are flown down the glidepath with the missed-approach decision made within the descent itself.

questions.front: A pilot flying an ILS to DA starts the missed approach exactly at DA, but due to momentum and reaction time, the aircraft dips a few feet below DA before climbing away. Is this a violation?
