questions.back: No — DA accounts for this momentary descent, unlike the hard floor of an MDA
options: No — DA accounts for this momentary descent, unlike the hard floor of an MDA
Yes — any altitude below the published DA is a violation regardless of cause
No, but only if the approach lighting system was in sight at DA
questions.explanation: The DA concept specifically builds in the expectation that momentum will carry the aircraft slightly below it as the missed approach climb begins, which is why DA and the hard floor of MDA are not interchangeable concepts.

questions.front: What is the technical distinction between 'glideslope' and 'glidepath' in FAA approach terminology?
questions.back: Glideslope refers specifically to the ground-based ILS radio signal providing vertical guidance; glidepath is the general term for the descent path itself, used for ILS, LPV, LNAV/VNAV, PAR, and other vertically-guided procedures.
questions.explanation: All ILS glideslopes produce a glidepath, but not all glidepaths come from a glideslope — RNAV approaches compute a glidepath electronically with no ground transmitter involved.

questions.front: The vertical guidance display on an RNAV (GPS) approach flown to LPV minima is properly described as the aircraft's position relative to the:
questions.back: Glidepath
options: Glidepath
Glideslope
Localizer course
questions.explanation: Because LPV vertical guidance is computed by WAAS avionics rather than received from a ground-based ILS transmitter, calling it a 'glideslope' is technically incorrect even though the cockpit display looks similar.

questions.front: If an ILS glideslope transmitter or receiver fails in flight, does any electronic glidepath remain available from that same ILS equipment?
questions.back: No — losing the glideslope removes vertical guidance entirely; there is no backup electronic glidepath built into a basic ILS, so the pilot must revert to localizer-only (LOC) minimums.
questions.explanation: Because the ILS glidepath depends entirely on the ground glideslope signal, once that signal or its receiver is lost, only lateral (localizer) guidance remains.

questions.front: What does TDZE represent on an instrument approach chart, and how is it defined?
questions.back: Touchdown Zone Elevation — the highest elevation within the first 3,000 feet of the landing runway, measured from the runway threshold.
questions.explanation: TDZE is the reference point subtracted from the DA/MDA (in MSL) to calculate the Height Above Touchdown (HAT) shown in parentheses next to the minimum altitude on the chart.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedure Charts – Landing Minima Data

questions.front: The Height Above Touchdown (HAT) published in parentheses next to a straight-in DA on an ILS chart is found by subtracting which value from the DA?
questions.back: TDZE (touchdown zone elevation)
options: TDZE (touchdown zone elevation)
Airport elevation
Threshold crossing height (TCH)
questions.explanation: Airport elevation is a single field-wide reference and can differ from the actual touchdown zone elevation on runways with sloped terrain, which is why charts use TDZE rather than airport elevation for HAT.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedure Charts – Landing Minima Data

questions.front: A pilot flying a coupled ILS cross-checks DA against a radar (radio) altimeter readout. Why might the radar altimeter reading differ slightly from the charted HAT at that same moment?
questions.back: The radar altimeter reads true terrain height, which may differ from TDZE on sloped terrain
options: The radar altimeter reads true terrain height, which may differ from TDZE on sloped terrain
Radar and barometric altimeters always read identically below 2,500 feet AGL
HAT is calculated directly from radar altimeter data, so the two are always identical
questions.explanation: HAT is a fixed, published value referencing TDZE, while a radar altimeter dynamically measures true clearance above whatever terrain lies directly below the aircraft — the two only agree exactly if that terrain matches the touchdown zone's elevation.

questions.front: What is the pilot's responsibility while flying a coupled (autopilot-flown) ILS or LPV approach?
questions.back: Continuously monitor the autopilot's tracking of lateral and vertical guidance and be ready to disconnect and hand-fly immediately if the automation deviates — the PIC remains responsible for the approach regardless of automation.
questions.explanation: Coupled approaches reduce workload but never transfer legal responsibility for a safe, stabilized approach away from the pilot in command.

questions.front: Before flying a coupled approach in actual instrument conditions, a pilot should confirm that:
questions.back: The approach mode is AFM/POH-approved for coupling and properly annunciated
options: The approach mode is AFM/POH-approved for coupling and properly annunciated
Any heading-and-altitude-hold mode is sufficient for a coupled approach
ATC's approach clearance alone authorizes coupling regardless of equipment
questions.explanation: Not every autopilot mode is designed to track an ILS or GPS glidepath with the required precision — pilots must verify the correct approach mode is armed/captured, per the aircraft's approved flight manual limitations.

questions.front: Who retains final responsibility for a safe outcome when an autopilot is coupled to fly an instrument approach?
questions.back: The pilot in command — coupled automation does not relieve the PIC of the duty to monitor, verify, and take manual control if needed.
questions.explanation: This is a foundational automation-management principle: automation assists but never replaces the requirement for active pilot monitoring and decision authority.

questions.front: What is a No Transgression Zone (NTZ), and why does it exist for simultaneous independent parallel ILS approaches?
questions.back: A radar-monitored buffer (about 2,000 feet wide on standard-spacing runways) centered between two parallel final approach courses. A deviating aircraft is directed back to its course; if it penetrates the NTZ and threatens the adjacent approach, the aircraft on that adjacent approach is issued an immediate breakout instruction.
questions.explanation: The NTZ is the radar-monitored safety buffer that makes simultaneous independent parallel approaches possible in the first place; final monitor controllers watch it continuously and can override the tower frequency to issue instructions.

questions.front: Independent simultaneous approaches to parallel runways generally require the runway centerlines to be separated by at least:
questions.back: 4,300 feet (less is possible with PRM/NTZ monitoring)
options: 4,300 feet (less is possible with PRM/NTZ monitoring)
1,000 feet, the same as visual approach spacing
10,000 feet, to avoid any need for radar monitoring
questions.explanation: 4,300 feet is the threshold for standard simultaneous independent approaches; below that, Simultaneous Close Parallel PRM approaches can be run with runway centerlines as close as 3,000 feet, and Simultaneous Offset Instrument Approaches (SOIA) can go down to 750 feet using an offset course with high-update-rate radar monitoring.

questions.front: During a simultaneous parallel ILS approach briefing, ATC assigns a discrete monitor frequency in addition to the tower frequency. What is this frequency for?
questions.back: So the controller can issue immediate breakout instructions if radar shows a deviation
options: So the controller can issue immediate breakout instructions if radar shows a deviation
So the pilot can request a runway change mid-approach
So the pilot can talk directly to the aircraft on the parallel approach
questions.explanation: The discrete monitor frequency exists purely for rapid safety-of-flight communication, letting the monitoring controller reach the pilot instantly without competing for tower frequency time.

source.section: 5-4-16 Simultaneous Close Parallel PRM Approaches and Simultaneous Offset Instrument Approaches (SOIA)

questions.front: During a simultaneous close parallel approach, ATC issues a breakout instruction while the pilot is stabilized on the localizer and cannot see the traffic on the adjacent approach. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Comply immediately with the breakout instruction without waiting to see the other traffic
options: Comply immediately with the breakout instruction without waiting to see the other traffic
Query ATC and continue the approach until the conflicting traffic is visually confirmed
Disregard the instruction if the aircraft's own instruments show no localizer deviation
questions.explanation: Breakout instructions are time-critical, radar-based safety commands — the entire simultaneous close parallel system depends on immediate compliance, since visually confirming the conflict would already be too late.

questions.front: If the glideslope portion of an ILS fails or flags invalid during the approach, what must the pilot do?
questions.back: Revert to the localizer-only (LOC) approach, using the higher published LOC MDA and associated visibility minimums instead of the ILS DA.
questions.explanation: Losing the glideslope removes all vertical guidance, converting the procedure from a precision DA-based approach to a nonprecision, MDA-based localizer approach with correspondingly higher minimums.

questions.front: A pilot flying an ILS sees the glideslope flag appear shortly after intercepting the localizer, well before the final approach fix. What minimums apply for the rest of the approach?
questions.back: Localizer (LOC) MDA and visibility, which are higher than the ILS DA minimums
options: Localizer (LOC) MDA and visibility, which are higher than the ILS DA minimums
The same ILS DA, since the glideslope may reappear before the missed approach point
Circling minimums, since precision guidance is no longer available
questions.explanation: Once glideslope guidance is lost, the pilot must fly the published LOC-only line of minima — continuing toward the lower ILS DA without vertical guidance would remove the approach's built-in obstacle clearance margin.

questions.front: An aircraft is descending on the ILS glidepath approaching DA, already below the published LOC MDA, when the glideslope abruptly fails. What is the correct action?
questions.back: Execute the missed approach — continuing below LOC MDA without vertical guidance isn't authorized
options: Execute the missed approach — continuing below LOC MDA without vertical guidance isn't authorized
Continue the descent to the ILS DA using pitch and airspeed to approximate the lost glidepath
Level off at the current altitude and wait for the glideslope signal to return
questions.explanation: Once the glideslope is lost, the only valid remaining minimum is the LOC MDA; if the aircraft is already below that altitude when the failure occurs, no valid minimum remains to descend to, so a missed approach must be flown.

questions.front: What does the LNAV line of minima on an RNAV (GPS) approach provide, and what altitude is it flown to?
questions.back: LNAV stands for Lateral Navigation — GPS-based course guidance only, with no vertical guidance. It is flown to a Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA), the same as a VOR or LOC approach.
questions.explanation: LNAV is the GPS-only lateral line of minima; it provides no vertical guidance, so it's flown to an MDA just like a VOR or LOC approach — remember 'LNAV = Lateral only, no glidepath.'

questions.front: To fly the LNAV/VNAV line of minima on an RNAV (GPS) approach, what must the aircraft be equipped with?
questions.back: A WAAS receiver or a certified baro-VNAV system capable of computing the vertical path
options: A basic IFR-approved GPS receiver, since LNAV/VNAV is available to any RNAV aircraft
A WAAS receiver or a certified baro-VNAV system capable of computing the vertical path
DME and ADF to cross-check the stepdown fix altitudes
questions.explanation: LNAV/VNAV adds computer-generated vertical guidance to a DA, but only if the aircraft's WAAS or baro-VNAV system can actually compute that path — a basic non-WAAS IFR GPS can fly LNAV but never LNAV/VNAV.

questions.front: A LOC-only approach typically has a higher minimum descent altitude than the full ILS to the same runway. Why?
questions.back: Because the LOC approach lacks glide slope/vertical guidance, so it is flown to an MDA rather than a lower DA
options: Because the LOC approach lacks glide slope/vertical guidance, so it is flown to an MDA rather than a lower DA
Because LOC approaches require a wider protected obstacle clearance area than ILS
Because LOC transmitters have shorter range than glide slope transmitters, requiring an earlier missed approach point
questions.explanation: Without a glide slope, a LOC-only approach is nonprecision and must be flown level at an MDA before the runway is in sight, which is why its minimums sit higher than the full ILS DA to the same runway.

questions.front: What is an intermediate stepdown fix on a nonprecision approach, and what does crossing it allow?
questions.back: A fix between the FAF and the MAP (identified by a NAVAID cross-radial, DME, or GPS waypoint) that, once positively identified, permits further descent to a lower MDA than would otherwise be authorized before that point.
questions.explanation: A stepdown fix lets you descend lower once you've verified you're past a controlling obstacle — think of it as the chart's way of saying 'you may go lower here, but only once you prove where you are.'

questions.front: If a pilot cannot positively identify a charted stepdown fix on a nonprecision final approach, which MDA must be used?
questions.back: The higher MDA that applies before/without crossing the stepdown fix
options: The lower MDA that applies after the stepdown fix, since it still provides safe obstacle clearance
The higher MDA that applies before/without crossing the stepdown fix
Either MDA may be used, since the difference reflects only a minor obstacle clearance margin
questions.explanation: If you can't positively identify the stepdown fix, you must treat the segment as if you never crossed it and stay at the higher, more conservative MDA — obstacle clearance for the lower MDA is only guaranteed once the fix is confirmed.

questions.front: On a VOR approach with a charted stepdown fix, a pilot crosses the FAF and levels at the higher MDA but cannot identify the stepdown fix because the DME used to identify it has failed. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Continue to the MAP at the higher (pre-stepdown) MDA, since the lower MDA may only be used once the stepdown fix is positively identified
options: Continue to the MAP at the higher (pre-stepdown) MDA, since the lower MDA may only be used once the stepdown fix is positively identified
Descend to the lower charted MDA once enough time has elapsed to estimate passing the fix
Descend to the lower MDA immediately, since the stepdown fix is only a suggested reference rather than a hard requirement
questions.explanation: Estimating a fix by elapsed time isn't the same as identifying it; without a working means to positively fix your position over it, the higher pre-stepdown MDA remains your legal floor all the way to the MAP.

questions.front: What is a Visual Descent Point (VDP), and how is it marked on an approach chart?
questions.back: A defined point on the final approach course, marked by a bold italic 'V' in the profile view, from which a normal descent from the MDA to the runway touchdown point may begin — provided the required visual references are in sight.
questions.explanation: The VDP marks where a normal, stabilized descent from the MDA meets the runway; descending before it means an unnecessarily steep dive to the touchdown zone.

questions.front: How is a Visual Descent Point typically computed when one isn't charted?
questions.back: Divide the height above touchdown (HAT) by 300 to get the distance in nautical miles from the runway threshold
options: Divide the height above touchdown (HAT) by 300 to get the distance in nautical miles from the runway threshold
Divide the MDA by the groundspeed to get a time in minutes back from the FAF
Multiply the runway length by the aircraft's approach category factor
questions.explanation: HAT divided by 300 is the classic rule-of-thumb VDP formula pilots use when it isn't charted, approximating the distance for a normal descent path from the MDA to the runway.

questions.front: A pilot reaches the charted VDP at MDA without the runway environment in sight. What is the correct action?
questions.back: Level off and continue at MDA to the MAP, executing the missed approach there if the runway still isn't in sight
options: Descend anyway, since the VDP guarantees obstacle clearance all the way to touchdown
Level off and continue at MDA to the MAP, executing the missed approach there if the runway still isn't in sight
Immediately execute the missed approach, since visual contact must be established exactly at the VDP
questions.explanation: The VDP isn't a decision point requiring an immediate go/no-go — it's just the last reasonable place to start descending; if the runway still isn't in sight, level flight continues at MDA until the actual MAP.

questions.front: What is the Continuous Descent Final Approach (CDFA) technique?
questions.back: A technique for flying the final segment of a nonprecision approach as one continuous, stabilized descent from the FAF (or glidepath intercept altitude) down to the MDA, without leveling off early — rather than descending immediately to the MDA and remaining level (dive-and-drive).
questions.explanation: CDFA replaces the old 'dive to MDA and level off' technique with one continuous stabilized descent, treating the nonprecision approach more like a precision approach profile.

questions.front: What is the main safety advantage of flying a CDFA instead of dive-and-drive on a nonprecision approach?
questions.back: It reduces the risk of controlled flight into terrain by avoiding prolonged level flight at low altitude near the MDA
options: It eliminates the requirement to identify the Final Approach Fix
It reduces the risk of controlled flight into terrain by avoiding prolonged level flight at low altitude near the MDA
It allows the pilot to legally descend below the MDA before the visual references required by regulation are in sight
questions.explanation: Most CFIT accidents on nonprecision approaches happen during extended level flight at MDA while searching for the runway; CDFA removes that exposure by keeping the aircraft descending on a stable path instead.

questions.front: A stabilized CDFA descent to minimums on a nonprecision approach typically approximates what vertical path angle?
questions.back: Approximately 3 degrees, similar to a precision approach glideslope
options: Approximately 3 degrees, similar to a precision approach glideslope
Approximately 7 degrees, matching the steepest published nonprecision approach angle
A varying angle that must be recalculated at each stepdown fix
questions.explanation: A roughly 3-degree path mirrors a normal ILS glideslope, which is why CDFA profiles are typically built using that vertical angle even on approaches without electronic vertical guidance.

questions.front: When must a pilot fly a timed nonprecision approach using the printed time/groundspeed table instead of distance?
questions.back: When the aircraft has no means of determining distance to the Missed Approach Point — no DME and no suitable RNAV/GPS distance readout — timing from the FAF (or another charted timing fix) is the only way to identify the MAP.
questions.explanation: Timing exists as a backup MAP-identification method for aircraft without DME or a suitable GPS distance readout — if you have reliable distance information, you don't need the timing table at all.

questions.front: Timing tables published on nonprecision approach charts key the time to the Missed Approach Point to which variable?
questions.back: Groundspeed
options: Groundspeed
True airspeed at cruise power settings
Density altitude at the destination airport
questions.explanation: The published table converts time to distance based on groundspeed, not indicated or true airspeed, because it's actual travel over the ground that determines when you reach the MAP.

questions.front: A pilot flying a timed nonprecision approach picks up a stronger-than-forecast headwind after the FAF, reducing groundspeed. What is the effect on the correct time to the MAP?
questions.back: The time to the MAP increases, since the aircraft covers the same distance more slowly
options: The time to the MAP increases, since the aircraft covers the same distance more slowly
The time to the MAP decreases, since the aircraft reaches the FAF sooner
Timing is unaffected by wind, since it is based on true airspeed rather than groundspeed
questions.explanation: Slower groundspeed means the same distance takes longer to cover, so a stronger headwind after the FAF requires more time — not less — to reach the MAP; using the un-adjusted time would trigger the missed approach too early.

questions.front: What determines a pilot's circling approach category, and what must the pilot do if planned maneuvering speed exceeds it?
questions.back: The category is based on 1.3 times the aircraft's stall speed (Vso) in the landing configuration at maximum certificated gross landing weight. If the pilot will circle faster than that category allows, they must use the minimums for the next higher (faster) approach category.
questions.explanation: Category is defined by 1.3 x Vso at max landing weight, not by aircraft type; if you'll maneuver faster than your normal category allows, you must fly the next faster category's larger minimums.

source.section: 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures, Aircraft Approach Category

questions.front: What are the standard (non-expanded) circling approach protected-area radii published for Categories A through E?
questions.back: Category A: 1.3 NM, Category B: 1.5 NM, Category C: 1.7 NM, Category D: 2.3 NM, Category E: 4.5 NM.
questions.explanation: These are the baseline TERPS circling radii still printed in chart legends; bigger, faster categories need more room to complete the visual maneuvering circuit, which is why the radius grows from A to E.

source.section: 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums, Circling Approach Area

questions.front: Under the FAA's expanded circling approach areas, why can the protected-area radius for the same category be larger at one airport than another?
questions.back: The radius now also scales with the MDA (airport/pattern altitude), since true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed increases with altitude, requiring more room to maneuver
options: The radius now also scales with the MDA (airport/pattern altitude), since true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed increases with altitude, requiring more room to maneuver
Each ATC facility can adjust the published radius locally based on local traffic patterns
The radius depends on which runway serves as the missed approach course, not on category or altitude
questions.explanation: True airspeed for a given indicated airspeed increases with altitude, so the same category flown from a high-elevation MDA needs a larger turning radius than the same category at a low-elevation airport — this scaling was built into the expanded protected areas.

source.section: 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums, Circling Approach Area

questions.front: What does a 'Circling NA' (not authorized) notation on an instrument approach chart mean, and why is it published?
questions.back: Circling maneuvers are prohibited for that approach (or for the specific category/direction annotated) — typically because obstacles penetrate the circling protected area and adequate obstacle clearance cannot be guaranteed if the pilot maneuvers visually around the airport.
questions.explanation: 'Circling NA' means the visual maneuvering protected area isn't obstacle-free, so procedure designers simply prohibit the maneuver rather than publish unsafe circling minimums.

questions.front: An approach chart shows the note 'Circling NA Category D.' What is the most likely reason for this restriction?
questions.back: The circling maneuvering airspace for Category D speeds would be obstructed by terrain or obstacles that a slower category could safely clear
options: The circling maneuvering airspace for Category D speeds would be obstructed by terrain or obstacles that a slower category could safely clear
Category D aircraft must instead fly the approach as straight-in only, regardless of runway alignment with the final approach course
The notation restricts circling for all categories, and 'Category D' simply identifies the fastest one affected
questions.explanation: A category-specific 'Circling NA' restricts only the categories whose larger, faster protected area would be obstructed — slower categories with smaller circling radii may still circle safely.

questions.front: An approach publishes straight-in minimums to a runway but notes 'Circling NA east of Rwy 18.' What may a pilot legally do?
questions.back: Fly the approach straight-in to the runway, or circle only to the area west of the runway if using circling minimums
options: Fly the approach straight-in to the runway, or circle only to the area west of the runway if using circling minimums
Not fly the approach at all, since any circling restriction invalidates the entire procedure
Circle to either side of the runway as needed, since the restriction is advisory only and not mandatory
questions.explanation: A directional circling restriction is a hard limit on the maneuvering area, not on the whole procedure — straight-in remains available, and circling is simply confined to the unrestricted side of the runway.

questions.front: During a circling approach, at what point may a pilot descend below the MDA?
questions.back: Only once the aircraft is in a position from which a descent to a normal landing on the intended runway can be made using normal maneuvers and a normal rate of descent
options: Only once the aircraft is in a position from which a descent to a normal landing on the intended runway can be made using normal maneuvers and a normal rate of descent
As soon as any part of the airport is in sight, even if the aircraft is not yet positioned for a normal approach to the runway
Once established on a base leg, regardless of the aircraft's altitude relative to obstacles in the circling area
questions.explanation: Being over the airport isn't enough; the aircraft must be positioned so a normal-rate, normal-maneuver descent to the runway is achievable before starting down from MDA — circling too tight or too high still keeps you at MDA.

source.section: 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums, Circling Approach

questions.front: What visual reference must a pilot maintain throughout a circle-to-land maneuver, from leaving the MDA until touchdown?
questions.back: The runway of intended landing, or the airport/runway environment, must remain in sight; if that visual reference is lost at any time while circling, the pilot must immediately execute the missed approach for that procedure.
questions.explanation: Continuous visual contact with the runway environment is the thread that lets a pilot legally stay below MDA while circling; the instant that thread breaks, the airplane must go missed.

source.section: 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums, Circling Approach

questions.front: While circling to land on the downwind leg at MDA, a pilot temporarily loses sight of the runway environment in a rain shower. What must the pilot do?
questions.back: Execute the missed approach for the approach being flown, since visual contact was lost
options: Execute the missed approach for the approach being flown, since visual contact was lost
Continue circling at MDA and reacquire visual contact before continuing the descent, since altitude was never compromised
Turn toward the airport and attempt to reacquire the runway visually before deciding whether to land
questions.explanation: Momentary loss of the runway environment during circling isn't a 'wait and see' situation — the required response is an immediate transition to the missed approach rather than continuing to circle blind at MDA.

source.section: 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums, Circling Approach

questions.front: What is the recommended initial maneuver when executing a missed approach after losing visual reference during a circle-to-land?
questions.back: A climbing turn in the direction of the landing runway, continuing until established on the missed approach course
options: A climbing turn in the direction of the landing runway, continuing until established on the missed approach course
A climbing turn away from the airport to avoid overflying the runway environment
Fly straight ahead on the circling heading until reaching the missed approach altitude, then turn
questions.explanation: Turning toward the landing runway keeps the airplane inside the charted circling protected area during the climb, rather than drifting toward unprotected obstacles on the far side of the pattern.

questions.front: If a pilot loses visual contact with the airport while circling to land, which missed approach procedure must be flown?
questions.back: The missed approach procedure published for the instrument approach that was flown to the circling minimums — not an improvised route — initiating a climbing turn toward the landing runway/airport to remain within the protected circling area before joining the published course.
questions.explanation: There's no improvised 'direct to the airport' missed approach from circling — pilots fly the same published missed approach for that instrument approach, just beginning with a climbing turn toward the runway to stay protected.

questions.front: An approach chart's profile view contains the note 'Procedure Turn NA' for a given transition. What does this note require of arriving pilots?
questions.back: Arrive via a straight-in transition, radar vectors, or other routing that avoids any course reversal.
options: Arrive via a straight-in transition, radar vectors, or other routing that avoids any course reversal
Fly the procedure turn anyway, but hold the maximum speed to 200 KIAS
Request a special ATC waiver before beginning any part of the approach
questions.explanation: 'Procedure Turn NA' means the course reversal is not authorized at all, usually due to terrain, traffic, or airspace constraints, so a pilot must be established on the approach some other way besides flying a PT.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedures - Procedure Turn / Course Reversal notes

questions.front: Name the three conditions under which 14 CFR 91.175(j) prohibits a pilot from making a procedure turn unless specifically cleared to do so by ATC.
questions.back: (1) When receiving radar vectors to the final approach course or fix, (2) when flying a timed approach from a holding fix, or (3) when the approach procedure specifies 'No PT.'
questions.explanation: This is a direct regulatory limitation, not just guidance - in these three cases the pilot needs an explicit ATC clearance to add a procedure turn back in, since ATC has already sequenced traffic assuming no course reversal.

questions.front: During a charted 45-degree procedure turn, which restriction applies to the pilot's flight path?
questions.back: Stay on the charted side of the course, remain within the charted distance, and don't descend below the PT altitude until established inbound.
options: Fly on either side of the course, provided total track distance stays under 10 NM
Stay on the charted side of the course, remain within the charted distance, and don't descend below the PT altitude until established inbound
Descend to the MDA immediately to save time before turning inbound
questions.explanation: TERPS obstacle protection for a PT is built around the charted side and distance; descending early or turning to the wrong side removes the obstacle clearance margin the procedure was designed with.

questions.front: What shape is flown for a hold-in-lieu-of-procedure-turn (HILPT), and how does that constrain the pilot compared to a standard 45-degree procedure turn?
questions.back: A HILPT is flown as the charted racetrack holding pattern; unlike a standard PT (where the pilot chooses the outbound heading/turn method within limits), the pilot must fly the specific depicted pattern to reverse course.
questions.explanation: Because a HILPT doubles as a holding pattern, its entry and shape are fixed by the chart, removing the pilot discretion that a classic 45/180 procedure turn allows.

source.section: 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn

questions.front: An approach profile view shows the procedure turn barb pointing to only one side of the course. What does that single barb indicate to the pilot?
questions.back: The procedure turn must be flown on that depicted side to stay within the protected obstacle clearance area.
options: The pilot may fly the turn on whichever side is more convenient given the wind
The barb shows the direction of the missed approach turn, not the procedure turn
The procedure turn must be flown on that depicted side to stay within the protected obstacle clearance area
questions.explanation: The barb direction is not a suggestion - obstacle clearance during the PT is only guaranteed on the charted side, so flying it on the opposite side can put the aircraft outside protected airspace.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedures - Procedure Turn depiction

questions.front: ATC clears a pilot direct to a fix that is the IAF for an ILS approach. The chart shows a standard procedure turn at that fix, with no 'NoPT' notation and no mention of vectors or a straight-in clearance. What must the pilot do at the fix?
questions.back: Fly the charted procedure turn, since none of the no-procedure-turn conditions in 91.175(j) apply.
options: Fly the charted procedure turn, since none of the no-procedure-turn conditions in 91.175(j) apply
Proceed straight to the final approach fix, since a 'direct to' clearance implies straight-in authorization
Hold indefinitely at the fix until ATC issues a further clearance
questions.explanation: Being cleared 'direct' to an IAF is not the same as being vectored to final, told 'NoPT,' or cleared straight-in - none of the 91.175(j) exceptions are met, so the procedure turn is still required.

questions.front: Reaching the missed approach point with the runway environment not in sight, what must a pilot do?
questions.back: Execute the missed approach procedure immediately, without delay.
options: Continue level at MDA for up to two minutes in case the weather improves
Execute the missed approach procedure immediately, without delay
Circle the airport visually while awaiting further clearance
questions.explanation: Lingering at or past the MAP without the required visual references erodes the obstacle clearance the approach was designed to guarantee only up to that point.

questions.front: If ATC issues instructions that differ from the published missed approach procedure, which one does the pilot follow?
questions.back: The ATC instructions take priority; absent any ATC instruction, the pilot flies the published missed approach procedure exactly as charted.
questions.explanation: Published procedures are the default obstacle-protected path, but ATC can substitute alternate instructions for traffic or airspace reasons - the pilot must comply with whichever is currently active.

questions.front: Just before a pilot reaches the MAP, ATC transmits an amended missed approach instruction that differs from the charted procedure the pilot already briefed. What should the pilot do if the missed approach becomes necessary?
questions.back: Comply with the ATC-issued instruction instead of the previously briefed published procedure.
options: Fly the originally briefed published procedure, since it was already loaded and reviewed
Ask the tower to cancel the amendment and revert to the published procedure automatically
Comply with the ATC-issued instruction instead of the previously briefed published procedure
questions.explanation: A pilot's pre-approach briefing is a plan, not a binding clearance - the most recent ATC instruction supersedes the charted missed approach, so situational awareness has to update in real time.

questions.front: For a nonprecision straight-in approach, how is the missed approach point (MAP) typically defined?
questions.back: As a fix, a specified distance from the FAF (often measured by DME or GPS), or a navigation facility - the point beyond which descent below MDA is no longer protected and the missed approach must begin if references aren't in sight.
questions.explanation: Because nonprecision approaches lack continuous vertical guidance, the MAP is a discrete point rather than an altitude, which is why it's frequently defined by timing or distance rather than glidepath intercept.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedures - Missed Approach Point

questions.front: A pilot loses required visual references well before reaching the charted MAP and needs to miss the approach early. What is the recommended technique?
questions.back: Continue along the approach's lateral path to the MAP before turning, then fly the published missed approach from there.
options: Continue along the approach's lateral path to the MAP before turning, then fly the published missed approach from there
Immediately fly the missed approach turn and climb heading from the current position, regardless of where that is along the approach
Descend to the MDA first, then begin the missed approach turn once level
questions.explanation: The obstacle clearance for the missed approach's turning segment is built around the aircraft's position at the MAP - turning early from an unpublished position can put the aircraft outside protected airspace.

questions.front: For a straight-in landing minimum to be published, what are the general maximum alignment angle and descent gradient limits between the final approach course and the runway?
questions.back: The final approach course must be within about 30 degrees of the runway centerline extended, and the descent gradient from the FAF to the threshold must not exceed roughly 400 feet per nautical mile.
questions.explanation: If either limit is exceeded, the geometry no longer supports a stabilized straight-in landing, so only circling minimums are published for that runway.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedures - Straight-In Landing Minimums

questions.front: An approach chart labels the landing minimums 'Circling Only' for a runway that has a well-aligned final approach course. What does this labeling most likely mean?
questions.back: The final approach course exceeds the alignment or descent gradient limits required for straight-in minimums.
options: The runway is closed to instrument traffic entirely
The final approach course exceeds the alignment or descent gradient limits required for straight-in minimums
Only Category A aircraft are prohibited from landing on that runway
questions.explanation: Circling-only minimums are published when the geometry between the final course and runway doesn't meet straight-in criteria, even if the misalignment isn't obvious from the runway heading alone.

source.section: Instrument Approach Procedures - Straight-In Landing Minimums

questions.front: A feeder route on an approach chart is annotated 'NoPT.' What does this tell a pilot flying that route?
questions.back: The route already aligns the aircraft to proceed to the final approach segment without flying a course reversal.
options: The transition itself is not authorized and must not be flown
A procedure turn is optional but recommended for spacing
The route already aligns the aircraft to proceed to the final approach segment without flying a course reversal
questions.explanation: 'NoPT' is charted specifically where the feeder route's geometry already puts the aircraft on a reasonable intercept, so a course reversal would be redundant and unexpected by ATC.

source.section: 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn

questions.front: When ATC vectors an aircraft toward the final approach course, what must the assigned altitude allow the pilot to do relative to the glideslope or glidepath?
questions.back: Intercept the glideslope or glidepath from below, permitting a normal, stabilized descent rather than a dive to capture it from above.
questions.explanation: Intercepting from above forces an abnormally steep correction and can put the aircraft below the protected descent path before the antenna/receiver captures it - vectoring altitudes are chosen specifically to avoid that.

source.section: 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn (vectors to final approach course)

questions.front: While being vectored for an ILS, a pilot is told 'turn left heading 340, join the localizer, cleared ILS runway 36 approach,' with no mention of a procedure turn. What should the pilot infer?
questions.back: No procedure turn is required, since ATC has provided vectors that establish the aircraft on the final approach course.
options: No procedure turn is required, since ATC has provided vectors that establish the aircraft on the final approach course
The procedure turn must still be flown once established on the localizer, since none was explicitly waived
The clearance is incomplete and the pilot should request the missing procedure turn instruction
questions.explanation: Radar vectors to the final approach course are one of the situations in which 91.175(j) removes the procedure turn requirement entirely - asking for a PT here would actually disrupt the sequence ATC has built.

questions.front: A pilot receiving vectors notices the assigned heading is about to carry the aircraft across the final approach course, but ATC has not yet said 'cleared to intercept' or issued an approach clearance. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Continue flying the assigned heading and query ATC rather than turning inbound independently.
options: Turn inbound automatically once the course deviation indicator centers
Continue flying the assigned heading and query ATC rather than turning inbound independently
Begin descending to the FAF crossing altitude immediately regardless of heading
questions.explanation: Turning inbound before being cleared can put the aircraft in conflict with other traffic ATC is sequencing - pilots fly assigned headings until specifically released to intercept or cleared for the approach.

source.section: 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn (vectors to final approach course)

questions.front: What minimum obstacle clearance does a Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) generally guarantee in non-mountainous terrain versus designated mountainous terrain?
questions.back: 1,000 feet of obstacle clearance in non-mountainous terrain, and 2,000 feet in designated mountainous terrain.
questions.explanation: These are the same baseline clearance values used elsewhere in IFR altitude construction, which is why controllers can vector aircraft below charted MEAs and still guarantee protection.

source.section: Chapter 4 - Radar Vectoring / Minimum Vectoring Altitude

questions.front: Which approach type may only be initiated by pilot request, and is never offered proactively by ATC?
questions.back: The contact approach.
options: The visual approach
A charted visual flight procedure (CVFP)
The contact approach
questions.explanation: A visual approach can be offered by ATC or requested by the pilot, but a contact approach - with its lower visibility standard - can only ever come from a pilot request, never an ATC offer.

questions.front: What flight visibility and cloud clearance must a pilot have to accept a contact approach?
questions.back: At least 1 statute mile flight visibility and remain clear of clouds.
options: At least 1 statute mile flight visibility and remain clear of clouds
At least 3 statute miles flight visibility and a 1,000-foot ceiling
Standard VFR cloud clearances for the class of airspace involved
questions.explanation: The contact approach exists precisely because its visibility requirement (1 SM, clear of clouds) is lower than a visual approach's - which is also why a reported ceiling isn't even required for it.

questions.front: What reported ceiling and visibility must exist at an airport before ATC may authorize a visual approach there?
questions.back: Ceiling at or above 1,000 feet and visibility of 3 statute miles or greater.
options: Ceiling at or above 500 feet and visibility of 1 statute mile or greater
Ceiling at or above 1,000 feet and visibility of 3 statute miles or greater
No reported ceiling or visibility is required as long as the pilot has the airport in sight
questions.explanation: This 1,000-and-3 threshold is the same basic VFR-like benchmark that makes a visual approach appropriate; it's noticeably higher than the 1 SM/clear-of-clouds standard for a contact approach.

questions.front: To accept a visual approach clearance, what must a pilot have in sight, and what flight condition must be maintained?
questions.back: Either the airport or the preceding aircraft to be followed, while remaining in VFR conditions and clear of clouds to the airport.
questions.explanation: Having only the preceding traffic in sight (not the airport itself) is sufficient, which is a detail pilots often forget when thinking a visual approach always requires the runway to be visible.

questions.front: A pilot accepts a visual approach clearance but loses sight of the airport in a rain shower before landing. What is the appropriate action?
questions.back: Advise ATC immediately and request an instrument approach or other instructions, since a visual approach has no charted missed approach protection.
options: Continue toward the estimated runway position, since the approach clearance is already in effect
Fly the published missed approach procedure for the airport's standard instrument approach
Advise ATC immediately and request an instrument approach or other instructions, since a visual approach has no charted missed approach protection
questions.explanation: A visual approach is not an instrument approach procedure and carries no published missed approach segment, so a pilot who can't complete it must ask ATC for new instructions rather than assume a charted miss applies.

questions.front: In RNAV/RNP path terminator terminology, what does a 'TF' leg represent?
questions.back: Track to Fix - a straight ground track flown directly between two defined waypoints.
questions.explanation: TF legs are the default straight-segment building block of most RNAV routes and approaches, distinguishing them from curved 'RF' legs.

questions.front: How does an 'RF' leg on an RNAV/RNP procedure differ from a 'TF' leg?
questions.back: An RF leg is a constant-radius curved path between fixes, while a TF leg is a straight track between fixes.
options: An RF leg is a constant-radius curved path between fixes, while a TF leg is a straight track between fixes
An RF leg can only appear in the missed approach segment, while a TF leg can only appear on the final approach segment
An RF leg requires ground-based DME updating, while a TF leg is satellite-only
questions.explanation: RF (radius-to-fix) legs are used where a precise curved track is needed, often for terrain or airspace reasons, and require aircraft/autopilot systems capable of flying a defined-radius turn - a capability not all RNAV installations have.

questions.front: Why can't every RNAV-equipped aircraft fly a published RF (radius-to-fix) leg on an RNP approach?
questions.back: Flying an RF leg requires specific FMS/autopilot capability to fly a constant-radius curved path, which must be demonstrated and authorized for that aircraft - not all RNAV systems have this capability even if they meet basic RNAV/RNP accuracy requirements.
questions.explanation: This is why RF-leg procedures are typically restricted to specifically authorized aircraft/operators, unlike ordinary TF-leg RNAV approaches that most RNAV-capable aircraft can fly.

questions.front: You lose two-way radio communication in IMC. What route are you expected to fly?
questions.back: In this order (AVEF): the route Assigned; if being radar Vectored, direct to the fix/route/airway in the vector clearance; in the absence of an assigned route, the route ATC said to Expect; otherwise the route Filed.
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(1) — remember AVEF. Altitude is the highest of Minimum en route, Expected, or Assigned (MEA) for each segment.

source.section: IFR operations: two-way radio communications failure

questions.front: What transponder code should you squawk after a two-way radio communications failure?
questions.explanation: 7500 = hijacking, 7600 = lost communications, 7700 = emergency. Remember: 75 taken alive, 76 radio fix, 77 going to heaven.

source.section: 6-4-2 — Transponder operation during two-way communications failure

questions.front: Under 14 CFR 91.185, when flying IFR after a two-way radio communications failure, what altitude must a pilot maintain for each route segment?
questions.back: The highest of: (1) the altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance, (2) the minimum altitude for IFR operations for that segment (e.g., the MEA), or (3) the altitude ATC has advised the pilot to expect in a further clearance.
questions.explanation: This is the 'highest of three' rule in 91.185(c)(2) — pilots often misremember it as simply 'fly the last assigned altitude,' but the regulation requires comparing three numbers segment by segment and flying whichever is highest.

source.section: Two-way radio communications failure — altitude to fly

questions.front: An aircraft loses two-way radio contact while flying an IFR route. ATC's last clearance assigned 6,000 feet, and the MEA for the current segment is 8,000 feet; no expect-further-clearance altitude was ever issued. What altitude should the pilot fly?
questions.back: 8,000 feet, the higher of the assigned altitude and the MEA
options: 8,000 feet, the higher of the assigned altitude and the MEA
6,000 feet, because the last assigned altitude always controls until a new clearance is received
7,000 feet, splitting the difference to balance terrain clearance and the last clearance
questions.explanation: 91.185(c)(2) requires flying the highest of assigned altitude, MEA, and expected altitude for each segment; with no expected altitude in play, the MEA (8,000) beats the lower assigned altitude (6,000).

source.section: Two-way radio communications failure — altitude to fly

questions.front: During a lost-comm IFR flight, the last transmission received before the failure was 'expect 10,000, ten minutes after departure.' The segment MEA is 9,000 feet and the last assigned altitude was 7,000 feet. What altitude should the pilot fly once past the ten-minute mark?
questions.back: 10,000 feet, the expected altitude, since it is now the highest of the three values
options: 10,000 feet, the expected altitude, since it is now the highest of the three values
9,000 feet, the MEA, because an expect-altitude clearance only applies once the clearance limit is reached
7,000 feet, the last assigned altitude, since ATC never issued a formal amended clearance
questions.explanation: Once the time or place named in an 'expect' instruction arrives, that altitude is compared against the assigned altitude and the MEA, and the pilot flies whichever is highest — here, the expected 10,000 feet.

source.section: Two-way radio communications failure — altitude to fly

questions.front: On a lost-comm flight, segment 1 has an MEA of 7,000 feet and the last assigned altitude was 9,000 feet. Segment 2, further along the route, has an MEA of 11,000 feet with no assigned or expected altitude change specified for it. What altitude should the pilot fly in each segment?
questions.back: Segment 1: 9,000 feet (the assigned altitude, since it exceeds the 7,000 MEA). Segment 2: 11,000 feet (the pilot must climb, because the segment's MEA now exceeds the previously flown 9,000).
questions.explanation: 91.185(c)(2) is applied fresh to each route segment, not once for the whole flight — the pilot may need to climb (or could descend) as the highest-of-three value changes along the route.

source.section: Two-way radio communications failure — altitude to fly

questions.front: A pilot loses two-way radio communications while cruising at an assigned altitude of 11,000 feet. Twenty miles ahead, at a new route segment, the MEA drops to 5,000 feet, and no expect-altitude instruction was ever issued. What should the pilot do at the segment boundary?
questions.back: Remain at 11,000 feet, since 91.185 never authorizes a lost-comm descent below the last assigned altitude without a new clearance
options: Remain at 11,000 feet, since 91.185 never authorizes a lost-comm descent below the last assigned altitude without a new clearance
Descend to 5,000 feet at the segment boundary, since the MEA is now the highest of the applicable values
Descend gradually to level off at 8,000 feet, splitting the difference between the two altitudes
questions.explanation: The three values are compared and the highest wins; a lower MEA in a later segment does not authorize descending from a higher previously assigned altitude — only a new ATC clearance or the fixed EFC/ETA descent point can do that.

source.section: Two-way radio communications failure — altitude to fly

questions.front: A pilot's lost-comm clearance limit is also the initial approach fix for the destination. En route, the pilot maintains 8,000 feet, the last assigned altitude; the MEA to that fix is 4,000 feet, and no expect-altitude instruction was issued. At what point may the pilot descend below 8,000 feet?
questions.back: Not until beginning the approach at the appropriate EFC or, absent one, ETA, per 91.185(c)(3)
options: Not until beginning the approach at the appropriate EFC or, absent one, ETA, per 91.185(c)(3)
Immediately upon entering the segment where the MEA drops to 4,000 feet
As soon as the fix comes into view, regardless of EFC or ETA
questions.explanation: En route, the pilot flies the highest of assigned, MEA, and expected altitude (here, 8,000 feet); a lower en route MEA at the final fix does not itself authorize an early descent — that only happens when starting the approach at the EFC time or, lacking one, the flight-plan ETA.

source.section: Altitude to fly and when descent is authorized

questions.front: If a lost-comm pilot's clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, and ATC issued an EFC (expect further clearance) time before the failure, when should the pilot commence the approach?
questions.back: As close as possible to the EFC time.
questions.explanation: The EFC time lets ATC plan separation around a predictable descent point; the pilot times the approach to that clock time rather than descending as soon as convenient.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — fix from which approach begins

questions.front: A lost-comm flight's clearance limit is a fix from which the destination approach begins, but no EFC time was ever issued. When should the pilot begin the approach?
questions.back: As close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed (or amended) flight plan
options: As close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed (or amended) flight plan
Immediately upon reaching the clearance limit, since no EFC was given
As soon as the destination's weather is confirmed to be VFR
questions.explanation: Without an EFC time, 91.185(c)(3)(i) falls back to the flight-plan ETA rather than an immediate descent, which could put the NORDO aircraft in conflict with traffic ATC is still separating around it.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — fix from which approach begins

questions.front: A lost-comm pilot's clearance limit is a fix that is not part of any approach procedure, and an EFC time was received before the failure. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Leave the clearance limit at the EFC time and proceed to a fix from which an approach begins
options: Leave the clearance limit at the EFC time and proceed to a fix from which an approach begins
Hold at the clearance limit indefinitely until two-way communication is restored
Proceed immediately toward the nearest suitable airport, bypassing the clearance limit
questions.explanation: 91.185(c)(3)(ii) covers this case: because the clearance limit has no approach of its own, the pilot departs it at the EFC time — not immediately — and transitions to an approach fix, beginning the approach near the flight-plan ETA.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — fix not associated with an approach

questions.front: Suppose a lost-comm pilot's clearance limit is not a fix from which an approach begins, and no EFC time was ever received. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Leave the clearance limit upon arriving over it, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins and start the approach as close as possible to the flight-plan ETA
options: Leave the clearance limit upon arriving over it, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins and start the approach as close as possible to the flight-plan ETA
Hold at the clearance limit until the destination's ETA passes, then descend immediately without proceeding further
Divert to the nearest suitable airport rather than proceeding toward an approach fix
questions.explanation: This is the least-protected lost-comm case: with no EFC and no approach at the clearance limit, the rule is 'don't linger there, but time the approach start to the filed ETA' rather than descending immediately.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — fix not associated with an approach

questions.front: A NORDO IFR flight arrives at its clearance limit — a fix from which the approach begins — twelve minutes before the EFC time it was given. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Hold at the fix and commence the approach as close as possible to the EFC time
options: Hold at the fix and commence the approach as close as possible to the EFC time
Begin the approach immediately, since arriving early poses no risk to other traffic
Divert to an alternate airport rather than wait for the EFC time
questions.explanation: The EFC time exists so ATC can plan separation around a predictable descent point; arriving early does not authorize an early descent, so the pilot holds and starts down at the EFC time.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — fix from which approach begins

questions.front: What must a pilot do, per 91.185(b), if VFR conditions are encountered after a two-way radio communications failure on an IFR flight plan?
questions.back: Continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
questions.explanation: 'As soon as practicable' is not the same as 'as soon as possible' — the pilot retains discretion to choose a suitable airport rather than being forced to land at the very first field encountered.

questions.front: A pilot experiences a two-way radio failure while in IMC on an IFR flight and shortly afterward flies into an area of VFR conditions. What does 91.185(b) require?
questions.back: Continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable
options: Continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable
Continue under IFR per the lost-comm route and altitude rules, since the original clearance still applies
Squawk 7700 and divert immediately to the nearest airport regardless of suitability
questions.explanation: Encountering VFR conditions after a comm failure triggers a distinct rule — the pilot switches to VFR operation and lands as soon as practicable, rather than continuing the IFR lost-comm route/altitude/EFC procedures.

questions.front: 14 CFR 91.185(b) requires continuing under VFR and landing as soon as practicable in which of the following circumstances?
questions.back: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered at any point after the failure
options: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered at any point after the failure
Only if the aircraft was in VFR conditions at the exact moment the radios failed
Only if the pilot cannot comply with the assigned lost-comm route within 30 minutes
questions.explanation: The rule has two triggers, not one: VFR at the moment of failure, and VFR conditions encountered later in the flight both call for the same VFR-and-land-as-soon-as-practicable response.

questions.front: A lost-comm pilot who is flying VFR under 91.185(b) subsequently re-enters IMC before landing. What governs the flight from that point?
questions.back: The IFR lost-communications procedures of 91.185(c) resume — the route and altitude to fly, and the rules for when to begin the approach, apply again once the aircraft is back in instrument conditions.
questions.explanation: 91.185(b) is not a one-way switch; a pilot can move back and forth between the VFR rule and the IFR lost-comm rule depending on the conditions actually encountered.

source.section: VFR conditions encountered — return to IFR procedures if IMC resumes

questions.front: During a lost-comm flight, a pilot reaches a fix where ATC's last transmission instructed 'hold as published, expect further clearance at 1830.' The pilot arrives at the fix at 1815. What should the pilot do?
questions.back: Enter the published holding pattern and remain until 1830, then proceed per the lost-comm route and altitude rules
options: Enter the published holding pattern and remain until 1830, then proceed per the lost-comm route and altitude rules
Skip the hold, since two-way communication has already failed, and proceed directly toward the destination
Circle overhead using any convenient pattern, since the published hold no longer applies without radio contact
questions.explanation: A hold-and-expect-further-clearance instruction remains valid after a comm failure; the pilot flies the published pattern and departs the fix at the EFC time, exactly as instructed before the failure.

source.section: Two-Way Radio Communications Failure — holding instructions

questions.front: A pilot loses two-way radio communications while holding at a fix that has a charted holding pattern, but the ATC clearance never specified holding instructions for that fix. Which holding pattern should the pilot fly?
questions.back: The charted/published holding pattern for that fix, flown with standard entry and leg-timing procedures.
questions.explanation: When no other instructions exist, the published holding pattern is the default; inventing a pattern or guessing at leg length risks conflicting with the protected holding airspace ATC has planned around.

source.section: Two-Way Radio Communications Failure — holding instructions

questions.front: While flying a lost-comm IFR route, before reaching the clearance limit, must a pilot hold at each fix crossed along the way?
questions.back: No — holding is required only at the clearance limit (or at a fix ATC specifically instructed the pilot to hold at); intermediate fixes along the route are simply flown through without holding.
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that lost comm requires holding at every fix; in fact, holding is triggered only by an explicit ATC hold instruction or by reaching the clearance limit before the EFC/ETA — other fixes are overflown normally.

source.section: Leaving clearance limit — holding not required at intermediate fixes

questions.front: Before losing two-way communications, a pilot received two clearances in sequence: first 'hold at ALPHA, expect further clearance at 1830,' then a later update, 'expect further clearance at 1845.' The pilot then loses radio contact while holding. At what time should the pilot leave ALPHA?
questions.back: 1845, the most recently issued EFC time
options: 1845, the most recently issued EFC time
1830, the first EFC time received, since later updates are advisory only
Whichever time comes first, to minimize time spent holding
questions.explanation: 91.185 uses the EFC time from the pilot's last ATC clearance; when a later transmission revises the EFC, that newer time supersedes the earlier one and governs departure from the hold.

source.section: EFC time governs departure from clearance limit or holding fix

questions.front: What does squawking transponder code 7500 specifically communicate to ATC?
questions.back: That the aircraft is experiencing unlawful interference — a hijacking. Code 7500 must never be used for any other purpose.
questions.explanation: 7500 is reserved exclusively for hijack/unlawful interference; even an accidental selection prompts ATC to treat it as a possible hijacking and verify with the pilot.

questions.front: A pilot facing a general in-flight emergency — not a hijacking, and not a loss of radio communications — wants to alert ATC using the transponder alone. Which code should be selected?
questions.explanation: 7700 is the general emergency code; 7500 is reserved strictly for hijacking, and 7600 signals lost communications rather than a general emergency.

questions.front: An aircraft experiences a two-way radio failure and, shortly after, an engine fire — a genuine emergency beyond the comm loss itself. Which transponder code best reflects the aircraft's overall situation to ATC?
questions.back: 7700, because it signals a general emergency, which takes priority when more than just the radios have failed
options: 7700, because it signals a general emergency, which takes priority when more than just the radios have failed
7600, because lost communications is always the controlling condition regardless of any other emergency
7500, because any serious in-flight emergency should default to the most urgent-sounding code
questions.explanation: When a comm failure is compounded by a separate emergency, squawking 7700 communicates the more serious overall situation; 7600 alone would understate what's happening, and 7500 is reserved solely for hijacking.

source.section: Transponder Operation during Two-way Communications Failure

questions.front: If a transponder is inadvertently switched to code 7500 when no unlawful interference is actually occurring, what should the pilot do?
questions.back: Reset the transponder to the correct code and be prepared to respond normally to ATC, which will contact the aircraft to verify the code selection; a normal, cooperative response confirms it was an accidental selection rather than a real hijacking.
questions.explanation: Because 7500 automatically triggers an alert with no built-in 'false alarm' signal, ATC always follows up — responding normally, rather than going silent or acting oddly, is what reassures controllers it was accidental.

questions.front: A NORDO aircraft inbound to a towered airport is also critically low on fuel — a genuine additional emergency. The pilot has already squawked 7600 for the comm failure. Should the transponder code be changed before landing?
questions.back: Yes — change to 7700, since the fuel emergency is more serious than the comm failure alone and warrants the general emergency code
options: Yes — change to 7700, since the fuel emergency is more serious than the comm failure alone and warrants the general emergency code
No — once selected, 7600 must remain set for the entire flight regardless of any other emergency
Yes — change to 7500, since any life-threatening emergency should use the highest-priority code
questions.explanation: 7700 is appropriate whenever an emergency more urgent than a simple comm failure exists; 7500 is reserved exclusively for hijacking no matter how severe another emergency becomes.

source.section: Transponder Operation during Two-way Communications Failure

questions.front: In a typical light IFR trainer with a vacuum-driven attitude indicator and heading indicator, which flight instruments remain reliable after a complete vacuum system failure?
questions.back: Airspeed indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, and turn coordinator
options: Attitude indicator and heading indicator only
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, and turn coordinator
Attitude indicator, turn coordinator, and altimeter
questions.explanation: In the standard six-pack panel, the vacuum pump drives only the AI and HI, while the turn coordinator runs on the electrical system and the pitot-static instruments are pneumatic — so a vacuum failure takes out attitude and heading only, leaving the rest of the classic 'partial panel' available.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Pneumatic System Failure

questions.front: The vacuum pump fails in cruise flight in IMC. What technique should the pilot use to maintain pitch and bank control?
questions.back: Cross-check the turn coordinator, airspeed indicator, altimeter, and VSI while disregarding the failed attitude indicator
options: Continue cross-checking the attitude indicator normally, since a vacuum failure causes it to flag itself immediately
Rely on the heading indicator for bank information since it stays vacuum powered and accurate
Cross-check the turn coordinator, airspeed indicator, altimeter, and VSI while disregarding the failed attitude indicator
questions.explanation: Vacuum-instrument failures are often gradual and insidious rather than an obvious flag, and the heading indicator is vacuum-driven too, so pilots must actively recognize and ignore both failed gyros and instead fly pitch and bank off the electric turn coordinator plus the pitot-static trio.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Analog Instrument Failure

questions.front: Which two gyroscopic flight instruments are typically driven by the vacuum system in a conventionally equipped light IFR aircraft?
questions.back: The attitude indicator and the heading indicator (directional gyro).
questions.explanation: These are the two gyros most commonly vacuum-powered in legacy panels, while the turn coordinator's gyro is electric — that split is exactly why a vacuum failure and an electrical failure take out different instruments.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Pneumatic System Failure

questions.front: Following a complete electrical failure in IMC, with the vacuum system still operating normally, which primary flight instrument is lost?
questions.back: The turn coordinator
options: The turn coordinator
The attitude indicator
The altimeter
questions.explanation: The turn coordinator's gyro is electrically powered, so it goes first in an electrical failure, while the vacuum-driven attitude indicator, heading indicator, and the pitot-static instruments keep working normally.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Alternator/Generator Failure

questions.front: Besides the turn coordinator, what other cockpit systems typically fail during a total electrical failure in IFR flight?
questions.back: Radios and nav equipment, the transponder, most lighting, and any electric-only flight or engine instruments — everything powered by the electrical bus rather than the vacuum system or engine-driven mechanical sources.
questions.explanation: Because avionics, transponder, and lighting all ride the electrical bus, a total electrical failure is as much a communications emergency as an instrument emergency, so pilots should expect lost radio contact right alongside the turn coordinator.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Alternator/Generator Failure

questions.front: An alternator fails and the pilot continues on battery power alone. As battery voltage decays, which instrument is most likely to give erroneous or sluggish indications first?
questions.back: The electric turn coordinator, as its gyro slows with declining voltage
options: The vacuum-driven attitude indicator, since it depends on electrical power for gyro spin
The electric turn coordinator, as its gyro slows with declining voltage
The altimeter, because static pressure sensing requires electrical power
questions.explanation: A weakening battery starves the electric turn coordinator's gyro before anything else fails outright, producing sluggish or erratic turn indications; the vacuum-driven attitude indicator and the purely aneroid altimeter don't depend on electrical power at all, which is a common source of confusion.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Alternator/Generator Failure

questions.front: Which three flight instruments become unreliable or unusable after a total pitot-static system failure?
questions.back: The airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator — all three depend on pitot and/or static pressure.
questions.explanation: All three instruments are pneumatic and share the pitot-static system, so a blockage takes out speed, altitude, and rate-of-climb information together, while the gyroscopic instruments are unaffected.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Pitot/Static System Failure

questions.front: A pilot notices the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and VSI are all frozen or reading incorrectly while flying in icing conditions. What is the most likely cause and the first corrective action?
questions.back: A blocked pitot-static system; select the alternate static source
options: A vacuum pump failure; switch to the standby vacuum system
A blocked pitot-static system; select the alternate static source
An electrical failure; reduce electrical load and monitor the ammeter
questions.explanation: When all three pitot-static instruments misbehave together, ice-blocked pitot tube or static ports is the classic cause, and selecting the alternate static source (or confirming pitot heat) is the immediate fix, since neither vacuum nor electrical failures affect these pneumatic instruments.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Pitot/Static System Failure

questions.front: With the pitot tube blocked but the static ports clear, how will the airspeed indicator behave during a climb?
questions.back: It will read progressively higher than actual airspeed, in effect behaving like an altimeter
options: It will freeze at the airspeed present when the blockage occurred
It will read progressively lower than actual airspeed, eventually reading zero
It will read progressively higher than actual airspeed, in effect behaving like an altimeter
questions.explanation: The ASI display is trapped pitot pressure minus current static pressure; climbing lowers static pressure, so the reading rises even though true airspeed hasn't changed. This reversed climb/descent behavior — high in a climb, low in a descent — is a classic trap on the written test.

source.section: Chapter 11 — Aircraft System Malfunctions, Pitot/Static System Failure

questions.front: Flying partial panel with no attitude indicator, you notice rapidly increasing airspeed, decreasing altitude, and the turn coordinator showing a turn. What is happening and what's the first recovery action?
questions.back: A nose-low spiral; reduce power to idle, level the wings using the turn coordinator, then gently raise the nose
options: A nose-low spiral; reduce power to idle, level the wings using the turn coordinator, then gently raise the nose
A nose-high stall entry; apply full power and lower the nose immediately
A nose-low spiral; apply full power first and raise the nose to stop the descent
questions.explanation: Increasing airspeed with decreasing altitude signals a nose-low unusual attitude, often a spiral; the partial-panel recovery is power to idle first to prevent overspeed or overstress, level the wings by referencing the turn coordinator, then smoothly raise the nose using airspeed and altimeter trends.

source.section: Chapter 7 — Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers (Analog Instrumentation), Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries, Nose-Low Attitudes

questions.front: In a partial-panel nose-high unusual attitude, what is the correct order of pilot actions?
questions.back: Increase power to prevent an impending stall, then lower the nose to a level pitch attitude while correcting the bank to wings-level using the turn coordinator — the pitch and bank corrections are applied almost simultaneously, with the power increase leading.
questions.explanation: Nose-high attitudes are decelerating toward a stall, so power comes first; without an attitude indicator, the pilot lowers the nose and rolls the wings level (referencing the turn coordinator) in close succession rather than as one rigid, separated step after another.

source.section: Chapter 7 — Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers (Analog Instrumentation), Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries, Nose-High Attitudes

questions.front: Recovering from an unusual attitude with only a turn-and-slip indicator (no turn coordinator) for bank information, what must the pilot do differently than with a turn coordinator?
questions.back: Use rudder input guided by the slip-skid ball together with the needle, since the turn-and-slip indicator shows rate of turn but not bank angle directly
options: Nothing different; the turn-and-slip indicator and turn coordinator display identical information
Rely on the magnetic compass for bank angle since the turn-and-slip needle cannot be trusted during recovery
Use rudder input guided by the slip-skid ball together with the needle, since the turn-and-slip indicator shows rate of turn but not bank angle directly
questions.explanation: A turn-and-slip indicator's needle shows only rate of turn, not the miniature-airplane bank depiction a turn coordinator provides, so pilots must correlate needle movement with coordinated rudder and ball centering more deliberately to control bank during recovery.

source.section: Chapter 6 — Attitude Instrument Flying (Analog Instrumentation), Bank Control, Turn Coordinator/Turn-and-Slip Indicator

questions.front: What does declaring 'minimum fuel' to ATC mean, and does it authorize priority handling?
questions.back: It advises ATC that the aircraft's fuel supply allows little or no additional delay before landing, but it is not an emergency and does not by itself give the aircraft priority handling.
questions.explanation: 'Minimum fuel' is only an advisory; a pilot who actually needs priority handling due to fuel state must declare a fuel emergency outright — a distinction frequently missed because 'minimum fuel' sounds urgent but carries no priority guarantee.

source.section: 5-5-15 — Minimum Fuel Advisory; Pilot/Controller Glossary — Minimum Fuel

questions.front: A pilot's fuel state has progressed from tight to genuinely critical and needs guaranteed priority handling from ATC. What should the pilot state?
questions.back: "Fuel emergency," declaring an actual emergency under the pilot's emergency authority
options: "Minimum fuel," which guarantees no further vectoring or delay
"Fuel emergency," declaring an actual emergency under the pilot's emergency authority
"Low fuel," a standard phrase that automatically triggers priority handling from ATC
questions.explanation: Only declaring an actual emergency obligates ATC to provide priority handling; 'minimum fuel' and informal phrases like 'low fuel' are advisories only and don't carry the same guarantee.

questions.front: What is the difference between a 'distress' condition and an 'urgency' condition in AIM emergency terminology?
